World.title: Kenya: Kenya Confirms Second Ebola Case
World.content:
Nairobi — Kenya has confirmed a second case of Ebola (Bundibugyo virus disease), involving a 39-year-old man who is a close family member of the first patient who died, the Ministry of Health has announced.

The man was already in quarantine under daily monitoring when he developed fever, fatigue and joint pains on October 13.

Health officials isolated him immediately and collected samples that tested positive at both the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the KEMRI-CDC laboratory.

He has since been transferred to a designated treatment centre, where he is receiving supportive care.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The Ministry said early detection and isolation had helped limit the risk of further transmission, adding that both confirmed cases were linked, with no evidence of wider community spread.

Contact tracing is ongoing, with 128 people identified as contacts of the first patient. By October 13, authorities had traced 113, including 108 who are in quarantine in Kenya and undergoing daily clinical and temperature checks for 21 days.

The remaining five contacts are outside the country, and relevant health authorities have been notified. Efforts to trace the other 15 contacts are continuing.

Health teams are also assessing people who may have come into contact with the second patient since his symptoms began, including quarantine personnel and health workers.

The Ministry said infection prevention and control measures had been strengthened at quarantine and treatment facilities, while health workers had been provided with protective equipment.

It urged anyone experiencing fever, unusual fatigue, muscle or joint pains, vomiting, diarrhoea or unexplained bleeding to seek medical attention promptly.

The Ministry clarified that Ebola is not airborne but spreads through direct contact with the blood or body fluids of an infected person who is sick or has died from the disease.

Kenya remains open, with no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings, as the government continues coordinating the response with relevant health authorities and the World Health Organization.

The public has been urged to rely on official Ministry of Health updates and respect the privacy of the affected family. Members of the public can call the toll-free number 719 for information.

Principal Secretary for Public Health Dr Patrick Amoth said the response was being coordinated under the Public Health (Declaration of Formidable Epidemic Disease) Order, 2026, and the Public Health (Ebola Disease) Rules, 2026.

World.title: Mozambique: Mondlane's Appeal Regarding Live Broadcast of His Trial Rejected
World.content:
Maputo — Mozambique's Supreme Court has rejected an appeal filed by defendant Venâncio Mondlane, a former presidential candidate, seeking to have his trial broadcast live on television and social media.

During the trial, scheduled for November 17, the Supreme Court had also refused recording of sound and images. However, media outlets would be authorized to cover the hearing and produce written records of the proceedings. The decision also grants the public access to the courtroom.

In a statement released on Tuesday, the Supreme Court claims that it had dismissed Mondlane's appeal in a ruling issued on 12 October, explaining that the type of decision he was challenging cannot be appealed under the country's Criminal Procedure Code.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The Supreme Court's ruling maintains the restrictions on live broadcasting and audiovisual recording without overturning the principle that the trial is open to the public.

Mondlane, leader of the National Alliance for a Free and Autonomous Mozambique (Anamola), is accused of five criminal charges related to post-election mass demonstrations. The mass demonstration he called to protest against the alleged fraudulent results of the general elections held in October 2024 started peacefully but then degenerated into rioting.

Mondlane is accused of having committed the following crimes: public apology for a crime, incitement to collective disobedience, public instigation to crime, instigation and incitement to terrorism. Recently, the Council of State, the advising body to the Mozambican President, decided to lift Mondlane's immunity in order to allow him to stand trial.

The Supreme Court had also argued that a live broadcast could lead the public to form premature conclusions regarding guilt or innocence before a final verdict is reached. This is the most highly anticipated moment in the country, given that Mondlane is effectively the leading opposition figure, as a result of his political prominence and the crowds that attend his rallies across the nation.

World.title: Libya: Libya's Arsenals Are a Blind Spot in the Tripoli Agreement
World.content:
analysis

Disbanding militias is key to Libya's reunification, but could lead to weapons stockpiles being trafficked into neighbouring countries.

An agreement signed in Tripoli on 30 August between rival eastern and western Libyan camps could pave the way for national elections within two years. It could also restore political stability and territorial unity, which have remained elusive since the 2020 ceasefire that ended large-scale fighting in the country.

The African Union (AU) and United Nations (UN) Security Council welcomed the electoral agreement, and Hanna Tetteh, the UN Secretary-General's Special Representative for Libya, considers it an important step towards breaking the political and institutional deadlock. The deal has revived Libyans' hopes of emerging from a long crisis, but scepticism about its prospects remains.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

While eastern Libya's House of Representatives approved the agreement, the western faction's advisory body, the High Council of State, rejected it. The council argued that electoral changes should go through Libya's established constitutional mechanisms, and that the agreement bypassed earlier understandings between the two chambers.

The latest rapprochement also raises other complications. For Niger and Chad, which share nearly 1 400 km of border with Libya, and indeed for the Sahel as a whole, a reunifying Libya could paradoxically increase regional insecurity in the short term if the weapons issue remains unaddressed.

For the past 15 years, several Chadian and Tuareg rebel movements and terrorist groups have used southern Libya as a rear base to resupply with weapons and ammunition. South-eastern Libya is also a transit zone for equipment destined for the Rapid Support Forces, the paramilitary group that has been fighting Sudan's army since 2023. This supply line, which runs through Kufra, is already operational and could simply change clients.

Reunifying the army means disbanding the militias, integrating their fighters and recovering their arsenals, which have continued to grow despite the 2020 ceasefire. Without strict controls, these stockpiles - along with the surplus weapons accumulated during the second civil war (2014-2020), which was largely fuelled by foreign powers - could be diverted to trafficking networks in neighbouring countries.

A community leader from Agadez in Niger told the Institute for Security Studies (ISS) that some factions linked to these networks could encourage the resale of weapons on the cross-border black market. The natural outlets for this trade would be in the Sahel, a transit zone where many Nigerien and Chadian intermediaries facilitate arms smuggling.

A flood of Libyan weapons like the one following the fall of Muammar Gaddafi's regime in 2011 is a major concern, even if the circumstances differ. At that time, the state's collapse left weapon depots open to looting; today, the negotiated dismantling of the militias could release their stockpiles.

After 2011, looted weapons flooded the Sahel and Lake Chad Basin via the Salvador Pass in Niger's far north and Chad's Tibesti region. These flows contributed to the outbreak of the Malian crisis in 2012, the strengthening of Boko Haram and the expansion of terrorist groups from 2015.

A resumption of such trafficking could channel Libya's surplus weapons into the Lake Chad Basin, the Sahel and coastal states, fuelling insecurity there. In the hands of non-state armed groups, large quantities of mortars, rocket launchers and drones could shift the balance of power on the ground with devastating consequences for national armies and civilians.

The actors in this cross-border trade - local transporters and intermediaries - also traffic in fuel, drugs, gold and migrants along the routes linking Niger and Chad to Libya. With their intimate knowledge of the desert areas straddling these countries, they can easily move large quantities of arms and ammunition to various buyers, including terrorist groups.

Unless precautions are taken, the groups destabilising the Sahel, Lake Chad Basin and Gulf of Guinea countries risk becoming over-armed, a Tuareg community leader from Mali told ISS. Countries south of Libya, and the UN and AU, which sponsored the 30 August agreement, must act quickly to minimise this risk, rather than wait until the political crisis is resolved before intervening.

The first step is for Libyan parties to attach a mechanism to the political agreement that governs the collection and control of arsenals. The mandate of the UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL), which is mainly political, should be expanded without delay to include a dedicated disarmament component.

Working with Libyan actors, UNSMIL could, within six months, design a process for collecting, inventorying, marking and registering weapons as a prerequisite for integrating militia members into the unified army. Implementation could start before the end of 2027.

Close 

Closer military cooperation between Algeria, Niger and Chad should be encouraged. This could involve intelligence sharing and joint border patrols.

The UN and AU should also help Alliance of Sahel States (AES) countries and the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) tackle weapons proliferation through national commissions on small arms and light weapons. Ideally, this should be regionally coordinated, but the AES' withdrawal from ECOWAS may prevent that.

The AU could draw on its Strategy on the Control of Illicit Proliferation, Circulation and Trafficking of Small Arms and Light Weapons, and its Silencing the Guns initiative, to encourage countries to join forces against a resurgence of arms trafficking.

If nothing is done before a unified executive is installed in Libya, the militias' weapons will have headed south long before the polls.

For permission to re-publish ISS Today articles, please email us. In South Africa, News24 has exclusive rights to republish ISS Today articles. In Nigeria, Premium Times has exclusive rights to republish ISS Today articles.

Hassane Koné, Senior Researcher, ISS Regional Office for West Africa, Sahel, Lake Chad Basin and Central Africa

World.title: Nigeria: Special Report - Insecurity Exposes Zamfara Communities to Recurring Cholera Outbreaks
World.content:
Zamfara has been one of the states hardest hit by the insecurity that has spread across north-western Nigeria over the past decade.

It started with a sharp pain in Musa Saidu's stomach.

The 20-year-old initially thought little of it. But the pain was soon followed by fever, vomiting and frequent watery stools. Within hours, his condition had deteriorated.

This was August 2025, during a cholera outbreak in Bukkuyum Local Government Area of Zamfara State, where Mr Saidu and his family were living after fleeing their home in Dan Bago village following attacks by bandits.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Like thousands of people displaced by years of insecurity in the state, the family had already lost the stability of home. Now, as Mr Saidu became increasingly ill, they faced another problem: getting medical care.

His parents first tried what they could afford. They gave him some medicines and mixed a local herbal remedy with water, hoping his condition would improve. But it did not.

With the health facility serving their community no longer functional, the family eventually took Musa to the Orphan and Less Privileged Clinic (OLPC) in Bukkuyum town, where he was diagnosed with cholera.

But reaching a health facility did not immediately end their difficulties.

The clinic was struggling with an influx of cholera patients. Only three health workers were on duty, while essential medicines were unavailable.

Many residents affected by the outbreak were brought to the same facility, while some had to seek treatment elsewhere because of shortages of staff, medicines and space.

For displaced families such as Mr Saidu's, the outbreak exposed a problem that went beyond cholera.

Years of insecurity have displaced many communities across Zamfara, forced health workers away from some rural areas and disrupted access to healthcare, safe water and disease surveillance. These are services that become particularly important during an outbreak of a disease that can kill within hours if severe dehydration is not treated.

When insecurity becomes a health crisis

Zamfara is one of the states hardest hit by the insecurity that has spread across north-western Nigeria over the past decade.

What began largely as cattle rustling has evolved into organised violence by armed groups commonly referred to as bandits. Communities have been attacked, residents killed or abducted and thousands forced from their homes.

The armed groups have also imposed levies on some farming communities, stolen livestock and harvests and carried out kidnappings for ransom.

Data obtained from the Mass Atrocities Tracker show that 28,974 people were killed across Nigeria between 2021 and 2025. Borno recorded the highest number, with 4,539 deaths, followed by Zamfara with 3,936 and Kaduna with 2,811.

Zamfara recorded the highest number of abductions during the same period, with 5,447 people kidnapped. Kaduna recorded 4,050 and Niger 3,331.

But deaths, abductions and displacement are only some of the consequences.

In Bukkuyum LGA, residents and health workers told The ICIR that insecurity has also weakened access to healthcare. Some communities have been deserted, while health workers have stopped providing services in areas they consider unsafe.

Reports in 2025 indicated that only about 200 of Zamfara's more than 700 Primary Healthcare Centres (PHCs) were functional, with persistent insecurity blamed for the closure or abandonment of many facilities.

For residents of affected rural communities, the closures mean illness can require travelling several kilometres, sometimes through unsafe areas, before reaching a health worker.

For people displaced by violence, the risks are compounded by overcrowding, poor sanitation, poverty and limited access to safe water.

During a cholera outbreak, those conditions can become deadly.

Displaced, then confronted by cholera

Buba Muhammad had already fled his home in Sadawa with his family because of repeated bandit attacks when his son began vomiting and passing frequent watery stools.

The 40-year-old farmer and his family were living as displaced persons in Bukkuyum, where several families shared limited space and sanitation facilities.

Mr Muhammad immediately tried to find medical help.

There was no functioning health facility close to where they were staying.

"My first attempt when my son was affected was to go to a hospital, but there was no facility nearby," he said. "I had to take him to a medicine shop."

The medicines he obtained there did little to improve the boy's condition.

As the vomiting and diarrhoea continued, Mr Muhammad decided to take him to General Hospital Bukkuyum, the nearest facility where he believed the child could receive appropriate treatment.

But another problem awaited them.

The hospital was struggling with patients arriving from communities affected by the outbreak.

"We didn't receive the proper care we expected immediately because there were not enough staff," he recalled.

"There was no bed space. We even kept our patient on the floor before a staff member later found us a bed."

The illness also placed a financial burden on a family already displaced by insecurity.

Mr Muhammad said they spent heavily on transportation and medicines, including drugs they had to buy outside the hospital after receiving prescriptions.

"The only solution to ease the hardship of such unwanted incidents or outbreaks is to provide facilities in our local communities," he said.

But he said restoring healthcare without addressing insecurity would leave another part of the problem unresolved.

"We need security in our locations because we are not safe; there are attacks every day and night in our locations. The government needs to double its efforts to end the problem."

A preventable disease finds fertile ground

Cholera is an acute diarrhoeal disease caused by consuming food or water contaminated with the bacterium Vibrio cholerae. Without prompt treatment, severe cases can lead to rapid dehydration and death.

It is also largely preventable through access to safe water, adequate sanitation and good hygiene, while prompt administration of oral rehydration solution and other appropriate treatment can substantially reduce deaths.

Yet cholera has repeatedly affected communities in Zamfara State.

In 2023, a World Health Organisation (WHO) report recorded 907 suspected cholera cases in the state, representing about 28 per cent of Nigeria's suspected cases during the period covered.

The state was affected again in 2024. WHO reported more than 700 cases and over 30 deaths across Zamfara and neighbouring Sokoto during the period covered by its report.

By 9 July 2025, Zamfara had recorded 1,619 suspected cases, six confirmed cases and 31 deaths across 12 of its 14 local government areas, according to a UNICEF situation report.

UNICEF said suspected cases increased by 30 per cent within one week, with children and young people accounting for 62 per cent of reported cases.

The crisis continued.

In August 2025, an outbreak in communities in Bukkuyum LGA killed at least eight people and affected more than 200 across 11 communities, according to residents and local officials cited by Reuters.

For residents already dealing with displacement, unsafe water and weakened healthcare services, the outbreak exposed how insecurity can magnify an otherwise preventable public health emergency.

The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) identifies unsafe water, inadequate sanitation and poor hygiene as major factors driving cholera transmission.

In parts of Bukkuyum LGA, insecurity has made addressing those risks more difficult. Residents have been displaced into congested settlements, some health facilities are non-functional, and health workers say reaching remote communities for surveillance and other services can be dangerous.

For some patients, simply reaching treatment presents another risk.

For rural residents, treatment can mean a dangerous journey

In Masu community, Salihu Bello returned home one afternoon to find his two sisters seriously ill.

"They had stomach pain, and became very weak," he recalled. "Later we realised it was cholera."

With no health facility in the community, the family initially relied on local remedies.

But the sisters' condition continued to worsen. Seeking treatment meant undertaking a difficult journey to Bukkuyum town. Before reaching the town, they had to cross a river, a challenge that has become even more dangerous since insecurity forced many healthcare workers to stop visiting remote communities.

"Sometimes health workers used to come to our community, but because of security problems they stopped," Mr Bello said.

As night fell, the family began the trip. Fear of bandits lingered throughout the journey, but Mr Bello said concern for his sisters outweighed every other worry.

"At that moment, we were not thinking about insecurity. We only wanted to save them. It took about three hours before we received attention because we arrived very late at night," he said.

When a health worker eventually prescribed medicines, he had to wake a medicine vendor before dawn to obtain them.

His sisters remained under observation for about 24 hours before their conditions improved.

For Mr Bello, the experience showed the cost of having no functioning healthcare facility nearby.

"If we have a health facility in our community, things will be easier, considering how quickly the disease can affect the human body," he said.

"Before a patient from our community gets to the hospital, they suffer a lot. Having our own health facility would make access to treatment much easier."

But the health facility is only part of what residents say they need.

In Masu and other communities around Bukkuyum, preventing cholera begins with something even more basic: clean water.

Unsafe water keeps the risk alive

In communities around Bukkuyum, residents said access to clean water remains a major challenge.

Some depend on streams for drinking, cooking and other household needs. In Dan Bago, residents said people and cattle sometimes rely on the same water sources.

For a community already vulnerable to cholera, such conditions increase the risk of transmission.

Nigeria's 2021 Water, Sanitation and Hygiene National Outcome Routine Mapping (WASHNORM) report highlighted the scale of the country's water and sanitation challenge.

The report, based on a survey of more than 24,600 households, estimated that approximately 179 million Nigerians, about 87 per cent of the population, lacked access to safely managed drinking-water services.

The situation was particularly difficult in northern Nigeria. The Northeast had the lowest access rate at just two per cent, compared with 29 per cent in the Southwest.

Although 67 per cent of the population had access to basic water supply services, about a quarter of Nigerians still relied on unimproved or surface water sources.

Muhammadu Sadawa, a community leader, said insecurity has made the situation worse by forcing residents from their homes and concentrating displaced families in already strained settlements.

"Another major challenge we have in our community now is insecurity," he said. "Most of our people left the community because of banditry. Where we are now living is too congested and very dirty. That congestion helped the disease spread among us."

Mr Sadawa said access to healthcare had also deteriorated.

Although there is a health facility in his community, he said it is no longer functional.

"We have a facility, but it is not in existence. There are no staff, no drugs. The building is dilapidated and almost collapsing," he said.

During the cholera outbreak, residents therefore had to look elsewhere for treatment.

He said some families struggled to obtain care before outside assistance arrived, while others faced delays because of distance and the cost of treatment.

"Many people died, and it took a long time before we received any intervention. Some people were treated, some were not. I have a relative who spent over N50,000 on treatment. Many families went through the same thing," he said.

For critically ill residents, reaching another health facility can itself be difficult.

Mr Sadawa said residents must cross a river to reach Bukkuyum town, where they can get more comprehensive medical care.

"When someone is sick, we have to cross a river before reaching the hospital. We need the facility renovated, and we also need a bridge or canoes to help us cross," he said.

He estimated that more than 50 people in and around his community were affected during the outbreak, with some becoming ill in displacement settlements before being taken to Bukkuyum town for treatment.

Health workers struggle to reach vulnerable communities

At General Hospital Bukkuyum, Abdullahi Salihu remembers the pressure as cholera patients arrived from communities across the local government area.

"At the time of the outbreak, it was very tense and hectic considering how patients were being brought to the hospital," he said.

"Some survived, some were quarantined, and unfortunately some died."

According to Mr Salihu, insecurity complicated the response.

Patients who could leave affected communities were brought to the hospital. But health workers had limited options for people trapped in settlements that were difficult or unsafe to reach.

"As health workers, we faced a lot of challenges because of insecurity," he said.

"Some people managed to bring patients from their communities because they had no other option. But for those who could not come out, there was little we could do for them."

Mr Salihu said government officials, politicians and humanitarian organisations provided intravenous fluids, antibiotics, rehydration supplies and other support during the outbreak.

But insecurity was not the only challenge.

Many of the patients were displaced people who had lost livelihoods and struggled to afford transportation, food and other necessities.

"Most of them were displaced from their communities with nothing to eat," he said. "Then the outbreak added another difficulty to their lives."

Zaharadeen Abdullahi, a health worker at the Women and Children Welfare Clinic in Bukkuyum, also described insecurity as a major obstacle to preventing and responding to outbreaks.

"Insecurity is a major contributing factor to outbreaks like this," he said.

"We have services, vaccinations and awareness programmes, but because of security challenges many health workers cannot reach vulnerable communities."

Some affected settlements are more than 10 kilometres from health facilities, Mr Abdullahi said. In some areas, insecurity has also limited the transportation options residents can use.

"Some communities cannot use motorcycles because of security threats," he said. "People have to walk long distances or use donkeys. Because cholera requires urgent treatment, these delays can lead to deaths."

He said displacement had created additional risks.

"Most of the affected people are internally displaced persons living in congested conditions," Mr Abdullahi said. "Many rely on unsafe water sources, and stagnant water is still being used for drinking and household activities."

He acknowledged support from the Zamfara State government, UNICEF and other organisations during the outbreak but said greater investment was needed in health facilities, medical supplies and outreach to vulnerable communities.

Insecurity weakens disease surveillance

Shakir Balogun, an epidemiologist, said recurring cholera outbreaks in conflict-affected parts of Zamfara should not be viewed simply as a disease problem.

He said they also expose weaknesses in healthcare access and disease surveillance created or worsened by years of insecurity.

Mr Balogun said insecurity had affected the health system's ability to reach some communities even before recent cholera outbreaks.

"When insecurity makes communities difficult to reach, children can be missed by immunisation programmes, cases of Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) can escape surveillance, and cases of acute watery diarrhoea can similarly go undetected or reach treatment late," he said.

"The pathogen changes; the health-system vulnerability does not."

Mr Balogun said these weaknesses became particularly evident during the 2025 cholera outbreak.

According to him, the African Field Epidemiology Network (AFENET), with technical and financial support from the US Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, deployed eight Field Epidemiology Training Programme residents and a graduate to support Zamfara's response between 11 September and 2 October 2025.

The team worked with state authorities in four high-burden local government areas.

Mr Balogun said the response identified cases in inaccessible and insecure settlements. It also identified under-reporting linked partly to weak active case searches and insecurity, as well as delayed reporting and incomplete records.

Other challenges included transporting stool samples to the state reference laboratory, shortages of essential supplies outside initially prioritised LGAs and inadequate personnel in some health facilities.

The findings suggest that insecurity can affect almost every stage of outbreak control, from identifying a sick person and reporting a suspected case to testing samples and getting treatment to patients.

Mr Balogun said strengthening community-based surveillance could help close some of those gaps.

Close 

Trusted residents and community structures, he said, can help identify and report suspected cases when conventional health teams cannot safely reach affected settlements.

Treatment also needs to be brought closer to vulnerable communities.

"If insecurity means a severely ill patient has to travel several hours or cross an unsafe area before receiving ORS or intravenous fluids, geographical access itself becomes a determinant of survival," he said.

He recommended establishing oral rehydration points and treatment units close to vulnerable communities, backed by reliable referral systems for patients who develop severe disease.

Authorities should also use surveillance and previous outbreak data to identify communities repeatedly affected by cholera and position essential supplies there before outbreaks escalate, he said.

"You do not want to begin moving ORS, IV fluids, chlorine and other essential supplies into a hard-to-reach community only after an outbreak has accelerated," Mr Balogun said.

"We should use surveillance and historical data to identify recurrent hotspots and position supplies before the rainy season."

Treatment alone will not stop recurring outbreaks

Bringing treatment closer to affected communities could save lives, but Mr Balogun said it would not eliminate the conditions that allow cholera to return.

He said safe water and sanitation remain fundamental.

Vaccination and effective case management can reduce infections and deaths during outbreaks, he said, but communities will remain vulnerable if they continue to depend on unsafe water and inadequate sanitation.

Mr Balogun recommended strategic use of oral cholera vaccines among high-risk populations and in communities with recurring outbreaks, particularly where insecurity makes immediate improvements to water and sanitation infrastructure difficult.

But he cautioned against treating vaccination as a replacement for those investments.

"Vaccination is an additional layer of protection, not a substitute for water, sanitation, surveillance and access to treatment," he said.

Government turns to community-based response

The Zamfara State government said it has adopted community-based measures to maintain disease surveillance and provide basic cholera support in areas where insecurity makes conventional healthcare difficult.

The state Ministry of Health, working with the World Health Organisation (WHO) and other partners, has also begun developing a Multi-Hazard Incident Action Plan to strengthen preparedness and response to public health emergencies, including cholera.

Ahmad Muhammad, the Zamfara State epidemiologist, acknowledged the difficulty of reaching communities affected by insecurity.

He said one strategy has been to identify community health workers from insecure areas, bring them to safer locations for training and then send them back to support residents.

"We train them, particularly the community health workers there. So we train them and then allow them to go back to their community and support them," he said.

Mr Muhammad said trained workers are provided with available medical supplies and asked to report suspected cases so health officials can track whether infections are increasing or declining.

He said the approach forms part of the state's risk communication and community engagement strategy, under which people with health-related roles in affected communities are trained to support local outbreak response.

Patients who can safely be evacuated are moved to accessible areas for further treatment, including general hospitals and the treatment centre at the Infectious Disease Hospital in Gusau, he said.

He attributed the state's reduced cholera burden this year, compared with the previous year, to interventions including community sensitisation, improved hygiene, and oral cholera vaccination.

"Community sensitisation and improvement of hygiene, oral cholera vaccination campaign last time. The burden of the disease has reduced this year compared to last year," he said.

He said the government had also intensified water, sanitation and hygiene interventions, including measures aimed at reducing open defecation.

"So I think those strategies have really gone a long way in mitigating the impact," he said.

But for residents of communities where health facilities remain closed or poorly equipped and safe water remains difficult to obtain, the conditions that make cholera dangerous have not disappeared.

This reporting was supported by the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID).

World.title: Kenya: Gachagua Accuses Ruto of Using Fuel Price Hikes to Fund 2027 Campaigns
World.content:
Nairobi — Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has accused President William Ruto of exploiting fuel price increases to raise money for political bribery ahead of the August 2027 General Election, escalating his attacks on the government's economic management.

Gachagua, who leads the Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP), alleged that the President was facing growing public rejection over abductions, alleged extrajudicial killings, corruption, poor policies and the rising cost of living.

In a statement, Gachagua alleged that the President had ordered an increase of Sh12 per litre of petrol and Sh9 per litre of diesel to generate funds for political mobilization.

"Desperate to raise more cash, last evening, he ruthlessly ordered an increase in the price of diesel by Kshs. 9 and petrol by Kshs. 12, to be processed through Gulf Energy for political bribery.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Gachagua claimed the proposed increases would be processed through Gulf Energy and alleged that Energy and Petroleum Cabinet Secretary Opiyo Wandayi had been instructed to defend the adjustment by citing global oil prices.

He dismissed the anticipated explanation as dishonest, insisting that the alleged price increases were politically motivated rather than driven by international market conditions.

However, the statement did not provide evidence to substantiate the allegations of political bribery or establish a link between Gulf Energy and the alleged scheme.

Gachagua further claimed the government was increasingly relying on cash handouts to win public support, alleging that demands for money had followed Ruto even in the Rift Valley, his political stronghold.

Gachagua also launched a personal attack on Ruto, portraying the President as frustrated by mounting political pressure and accusing his administration of mismanaging the economy and failing to address public concerns.

He said the approaching August 10, 2027, election was increasingly weighing on the President, whom he accused of attempting to regain public support through financial inducements.

The latest remarks add to the political confrontation between the former deputy president and his former boss as the country moves towards the next general election.

Gachagua has increasingly positioned himself as a critic of the Ruto administration, with economic management, the cost of living and allegations of state-sponsored abuses forming part of his attacks on the government.

World.title: Minneapolis progressives turn on George Floyd-era public safety overhaul, push to dismantle office
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Minneapolis City Council leaders advanced a proposal Tuesday to eliminate the city's Office of Community Safety as part of a sweeping public safety restructuring, citing poor management and financial oversight concerns.

Mayor Jacob Frey warned the move could jeopardize critical services.

According to The Star Tribune, the office was created by Mayor Frey in 2022 in response to calls for police reform after the death of George Floyd.

3 DEAD, INCLUDING SUSPECTED GUNMAN, AND 3 OFFICERS INJURED IN MINNEAPOLIS SHOOTING

City Council President Elliott Payne and Council Member Robin Wonsley, who are spearheading the measure to eliminate the office, cited performance and cost concerns in a statement to FOX 9.

"It is good governance to stop investing in things that are not producing meaningful outcomes and are wasting taxpayer dollars," Wonsley said. "The Office of Community Safety has also contributed to increased audit costs due to poor management. It’s our responsibility to cut unnecessary bureaucracy that does not contribute to public safety."

The proposal marks a significant reversal for a city that reorganized public safety operations after Floyd's death. Frey, who established the office in 2022, criticized council members for seeking to dismantle a structure some had previously championed. In a statement to Fox News Digital, the mayor warned that the proposed elimination could threaten existing public safety programs.

"This office — one that these council members advocated for — manages services like mental health response, violence prevention and police reform. If council members want these services in jeopardy, that’s on them. This wholesale elimination without a plan, combined with other proposed cuts to MPD, is not a serious proposal when it comes to public safety in our city," Frey said.

According to the City of Minneapolis, the Office of Community Safety oversees five departments: police, fire, 911, emergency management and neighborhood safety. The office was designed to coordinate public safety services, improve communication between departments and establish a unified chain of command and accountability.

GOP ACCUSES WALZ ALLIES OF BURYING $52M MEDICAID FRAUD REPORT BEFORE ELECTION

The proposal comes amid mounting scrutiny of the city's violence prevention spending. A recent Minneapolis audit identified serious deficiencies in the Neighborhood Safety Department's oversight of community-based violence prevention contracts, including inadequate documentation and financial controls that increased the risk of fraud and misuse of taxpayer money.

According to the investigation, the city failed to properly oversee millions of dollars awarded to violence prevention organizations. The audit examined a system that has directed more than $36 million to five major violence prevention programs since 2023.

WALZ ADMINISTRATION IGNORED FRAUD WARNINGS AS BILLIONS VANISHED, HOUSE OVERSIGHT REPORT ALLEGES

Payne defended the proposed restructuring as a way to preserve services while reducing administrative expenses.

"These proposed changes to the government structure ensure that progress on issues such as public safety and racial disparities is not impacted by unnecessary costs and bureaucratic bottlenecks," Payne told FOX 9.

"Now more than ever, our city government must be responsive to the needs of residents, and its structure should reflect that."

The city's published 2026 public safety budget allocated more than $16 million to the Office of Community Safety, nearly $10 million to Neighborhood Safety and more than $225 million to the Minneapolis Police Department. It remains unclear how much money eliminating the office would actually save.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Wonsley defended the proposal in comments to Fox News Digital, explaining that key non-police programs that continue to show success, such as the Behavioral Crisis Response team, predated the Office of Community Safety and would continue to operate without it.

"The Office of Community Safety became administrative bloat that was a barrier to creating and expanding alternative responses rather than leading the development of a comprehensive public safety system," Wonsley said. She argued the $2 million office had become a "bureaucratic barrier" plagued by mismanagement by Mayor Frey and said taxpayers have paid the price.

"The city can advance a comprehensive safety system and support police reform much more efficiently without unnecessary bureaucratic layers that have proven to be ineffective," Wonsley added.

"Residents should not anticipate negative impacts because OCS was never able to effectively manage or oversee programs and services. The proposal does not eliminate any violence prevention or public safety programs that produce results. It simply removes administrative bloat."

This came just a few short months after he was arrested on charges of OWI in Wisconsin back in July, and happened the same day he was booted from the Korn Ferry qualifier for signing an incorrect scorecard.

It's probably safe to say that 2026 has not been Romo's year, but if anyone knows how to handle rough times amid public scrutiny, it's the former Dallas Cowboys signal-caller.

JIM NANTZ SPEAKS OUT ON 'GREAT FRIEND' TONY ROMO'S OWI ARREST, SAYS HE WILL 'ALWAYS' BE THERE FOR HIM

And OutKick's very own Tomi Lahren has proof.

During an episode of "Tomi Lahren is Fearless," Lahren explained to her guest, Barstool's Kevin "KFC" Clancy, that Romo once offered up some sage advice about dealing with online hate.

"It was actually Tony Romo at the time who told me, 'you think the whole world is talking about it, but really, nobody is,'" Lahren recounts.

This came on the heels of Lahren receiving some hateful comments for her appearance on "The Daily Show with Trevor Noah" just after Donald Trump won in 2016.

"Basically the message was, 'don't be so full of yourself that you think that everybody is talking about you,'" Lahren relayed. "Because most people aren't even on the internet."

Clancy concurred and took things even one step further.

"I think humans are not meant to be this connected and interact this much," he opined. "We can't handle it."

The longtime Barstool employee goes on to explain that for 99.9% of human history, we as humans were only confined to interacting with our small community.

COWBOYS OWNER JERRY JONES HAS TONY ROMO'S BACK, BELIEVES HE WILL 'WORK THROUGH' OWI ARREST

"The fact that you have access to millions of people's opinions ... I don't think we are even wired to be able to handle that."

It's great advice from all parties involved, and Romo would be wise to heed the words he offered up to Lahren nearly a decade ago.

He's going through a rough patch, but he will come out on the other side.

A guy as resilient as Romo is — undrafted from a small school in Eastern Illinois, coming back from a number of injuries — will be able to rebound just fine.

No one knows what the future holds for the former CBS commentator, but as for the noise online in the present, 46-year-old Romo just needs to listen to the 36-year-old version of himself.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"You think the whole world is talking about it, but really, nobody is."

World.title: DOJ threatens emergency legal action against California over suspected noncitizen voters
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Justice Department is threatening emergency legal action against California election officials unless they take steps to prevent suspected noncitizens from voting in November's midterm elections, setting a Thursday deadline as state officials push back.

In letters sent Tuesday, Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter demanded that California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan review a list of potentially ineligible voters within 48 hours. The DOJ instructed officials to segregate ballots from individuals whose citizenship cannot be verified and warned it would seek emergency legal relief if its demands were not met by noon Eastern on Oct. 15.

A DOJ spokesperson told Fox News Digital that thousands of potential foreign nationals ineligible to vote have been identified on California's voter rolls statewide, not just in Los Angeles County.

MAP IT: DOJ ILLEGAL VOTING CRACKDOWN SWEEPS 17 STATES AS RAZOR-THIN ELECTIONS FACE SCRUTINY

"This should not be controversial, as the criminal statute is clear: only American citizens may vote in federal elections. It is a federal crime for noncitizens to vote in U.S. elections, and the DOJ is asking California to ensure that is not occurring," the spokesperson said.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, pushed back during a Wednesday news conference, accusing the Trump administration of attempting to intimidate voters and promoting false allegations of widespread voter fraud.

JUSTICE DEPARTMENT CHARGES 16 ACROSS MULTIPLE STATES WITH ALLEGED ILLEGAL VOTING, ELECTION CRIMES

"There is no widespread voter preference, voter fraud problem. It doesn't exist. It is a lie. It is a conspiracy theory," Bonta said.

Bonta said his office is working with the secretary of state and Los Angeles County officials to review their options.

STATE DEPARTMENT CONSIDERS SHARING PASSPORT RECORDS FOR VOTER CITIZENSHIP CHECKS

Meanwhile, Logan said his office received a password-protected USB drive purportedly containing voter records but has not accessed it because of cybersecurity concerns.

"We have not accessed the drive because doing so would conflict with established data privacy and information security protocols. We do not consider the device a secure medium. Additionally, the letter does not specify the number of individuals involved or describe the information contained in the records," he said.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The dispute comes as Californians are already casting ballots ahead of the Nov. 3 election. Federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections, though the DOJ has not established that the individuals identified have cast illegal ballots.

World.title: Fox News Poll: Cost-of-living concerns weigh on GOP in midterms
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

When voters rate the economy and the president negatively just weeks before Election Day, the incumbent party is vulnerable, and that’s certainly the case in the latest Fox News survey.

The economic landscape is stark. Six in 10 voters say the cost of living is their top economic worry, overshadowing government spending (15%), jobs and income inequality (7% each), tariffs (6%) and taxes (5%).

Majorities rate the economy negatively (74%) and expect it to worsen next year (53%), while two-thirds are dissatisfied with how things are going in the country (66%). Few, 18%, say their family is better off compared to two years ago. Independents say they’re worse off (52%) and think the economy will get worse (70%).

FOX NEWS POLL: IT’S A LONE STAR SENATE SHOWDOWN BETWEEN TALARICO AND PAXTON

A majority of voters, 55%, say inflation is "not at all" under control. That’s up from a low of 45% earlier this year, and includes 30% of Republicans.

President Donald Trump’s lowest job rating is on inflation: 22% approve, a new low. Last summer, 36% approved. Four years ago, before the 2022 midterms, 29% approved of former President Joe Biden’s performance on inflation.

Disapproval of the job Trump is doing has reached 77% on inflation, 70% on the economy, 69% on tariffs and 64% on foreign policy. A smaller share, but still a majority, disapprove of his handling of immigration (56% disapprove), while border security is the only issue that is close to positive (50% approve, 50% disapprove).

Trump’s overall job approval is 36%, his lowest ever in a Fox News survey for either term. It had been holding steady at 39% since May. The decline is mainly driven by decreases among voters under age 45, those with annual household income below $50,000, non-White voters, and those without a college degree.

FOX NEWS POLL: MICHIGAN VOTERS SPLIT BETWEEN EL-SAYED AND ROGERS

Approval stands at a low of 76% among Republicans. That’s down 3 points since last month, 12 points since September 2025, and 16 points since early in his second term (March 2025).

As in most midterms, voters are prone to punish the party in power: 7 in 10 say they will vote to send a message to Trump, with nearly twice as many expressing opposition (47%) as support (25%).

If the election were today, 54% of voters say they would back the Democratic candidate in their House district and 45% would support the Republican. That is outside the margin of error and is a wider lead than last month when Democrats were ahead by 51%-44%. The race narrows among those saying they are certain to vote, with the Democratic candidate ahead by 52%-46%.

The survey finds about the same number self-identify as Democrats (43%) and Republicans (41%), and both parties feel equally certain about voting (62% and 64% respectively), while more Democrats (61%) than Republicans (52%) say they are extremely interested in the election.

Party loyalty is solid: 98% of Democrats support their party’s candidate, and 94% of Republicans back theirs. Independents favor the Democrats by 26 points.

The Democratic candidate is the choice among Whites with a degree, those under age 45, women, union households and Hispanics. The Republican is ahead among Whites without a college degree (White men without a degree in particular), those 65 and over, voters who attend religious services regularly, military veterans and White evangelical Christians.

While 43% of Hispanic voters supported Trump in the 2024 election, just 31% prefer the Republican candidate this year.

"When the country is this closely divided in terms of partisanship, slight differences in defection and turnout rates can make all the difference," said Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who helps conduct the Fox News Poll with Democrat Chris Anderson. "Republicans have time to close these apparent gaps, but it’s getting late."

Meanwhile, Democrats lead on 10 out of 13 issue concerns.

The top five voter concerns are government corruption (60% extremely concerned), inflation (58%), gas prices (50%), government leadership (49%), and healthcare (48%). And double digits more trust the Democrats than the Republicans to handle each of those.

Republicans retain the advantage on crime (by 10 points) and border security (R+8), while views are closely divided on immigration (R+3). The Democrats are seen as better on healthcare (D+22), inflation (D+16), gas prices (D+12), voting rights (D+12), election integrity (D+12), government leadership (D+11), what’s taught in public schools (D+11), artificial intelligence (D+10), government corruption (D+10) and foreign policy (D+9).

Republicans have lost ground on key issues compared to four years ago, when more voters trusted them by 21 points on border security, 13 points on inflation and 9 points on foreign policy.

Other issues that voters are extremely concerned about are the Iran war (42%), immigration (35%), crime (34%), voter suppression (32%), AI technology (32%), what’s taught in public schools (29%), voter fraud (28%) and border security (25%).

While corruption in government and inflation are the top two worries about both parties, far more Democrats (72% and 70%) than Republicans (47% and 49%) are extremely concerned.

The issue that helps explain the Democrats’ advantage isn’t an issue at all. By a 14-point margin, more voters think the Democrats will do a better job "fighting for people like you." Majorities of White voters with a college degree (53%), men (52%), women (60%) and non-White voters (77%) think Democrats will fight for them. Whites without a college degree are split 49-49%.

Despite their issue advantage, just 35% say Democrats have a clear plan for dealing with the country’s problems, and 33% say the same about the Republicans. That reverses the Republican advantage from July 2025, when 43% said the Republicans had a clear plan compared with 33% for the Democrats.

There’s deep dissatisfaction with lawmakers: 15% approve of Congress, while 84% disapprove. Remarkably, that’s above the low of 9% approval in October 2013.

Both parties are viewed negatively. The Democratic Party is underwater by 16 points (42% favorable, 58% unfavorable), while ratings of the GOP are net negative by 23 points (38% favorable, 61% unfavorable).

Yet, favorable ratings fail to translate directly into vote choice. One third of those backing the Democratic candidate (31%) dislike the party, while 23% of those supporting the Republican dislike the GOP. Among the 26% who dislike both parties (double haters), Democrats lead 62%-36%.

Here’s how polarized the parties are: Just 16% of Republicans say that Democrats love America and want what’s best for the U.S., and even fewer Democrats, 6%, think Republicans do.

Compared to four years ago, the number of voters saying Democrats want what’s best for the country is up four points, while fewer say Republicans love the country now by 6 points.

Poll-pourri

Fifty-one percent of voters have a favorable view of capitalism compared with 32% for socialism. Compared to a year ago, positive ratings of capitalism are down 2 points while they are up 5 points for socialism. Eight in ten of those with a positive view of socialism support the Democratic candidate, while 6 in 10 of those viewing capitalism favorably back the Republican.

Voters who plan to cast their ballots early favor the Democratic candidate (by 19 points) as do mail voters (D+33), while the candidate choice splits among those voting in person (early or on Election Day).

Six in 10 oppose U.S. military action against Iran, and they back the Democrats by 56 points.

CLICK HERE FOR CROSSTABS AND TOPLINE

A new high of 46% think the U.S. is too supportive of Israel, and those voters favor the Democratic candidate by 42 points, while the 4 in 10 who think U.S. support of Israel is about right pick the Republican by 27 points.

Nearly 6 in 10 have a negative view of artificial intelligence technology, and they back the Democratic candidate by 27 points.

Conducted Oct. 9-12, 2026, under the direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), this Fox News survey includes interviews with a sample of 1,202 registered voters randomly selected from a national voter file. Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (114) and cellphones (786) or completed the survey online after receiving a text (302). Results based on the full sample have a margin of sampling error of ±2.5 percentage points. Sampling error for results among subgroups is higher. In addition to sampling errors, question wording and order can influence results. Weights are generally applied to age, race, education and area variables to ensure the demographics are representative of the registered voter population. Sources for developing weight targets include the most recent American Community Survey, Fox News Voter Analysis and voter file data.

Fox News’ Victoria Balara contributed to this report.

World.title: Expert calls California 'Wild West' for surrogacy after couple charged with abusing surrogate-born children
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The case of a California couple recently accused of abusing children born to surrogates exposes the pitfalls of an industry one expert described as the "wild west."

Guojun Xuan, 66, and his wife, Silvia Zhang, 39, were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit child abuse. Authorities said the couple operated their own surrogacy agency out of their home in Arcadia, California.

"I say it all the time. It's the wild, Wild West," Kallie Fell, executive director of the Center for Bioethics and Culture, told Fox News Digital.

SURROGATE WHO REFUSED ABORTION TAKES FIGHT TO SUPREME COURT AS BABY'S LIFE HANGS IN BALANCE

Xuan and Zhang allegedly abused more than a dozen surrogate-born children — some as young as 2 months old — inside their multimillion-dollar Arcadia residence.

Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman called the alleged abuse "appalling and revolting."

OHIO MOM OF 16 CRADLES STOMACH IN COURT, PLEADS NOT GUILTY IN SEVERE ABUSE CASE INVOLVING OWN CHILDREN

"This was not a home where these children were loved and nurtured," Hochman said when announcing the charges. "This was a home where these young children were systematically beaten and punished if they did not do what they were told."

In addition to the alleged abuse, the couple operated Future Spring Surrogacy from their home, recruiting surrogates and paying them tens of thousands of dollars. At least eight surrogates reported aggressive tactics and false statements regarding the family's living situation, officials said.

SURROGATE WHO REFUSED ABORTION ASKS SCOTUS TO INTERVENE AS BABY COULD BE MOVED OUT OF TEXAS

"The thing about the case is that I wish it was shocking for me," said Fell, who opposes commercial surrogacy. "Because of the space I work in, I get to hear shocking stories around the globe — things that people don't realize the surrogacy industry has grown into. It's not just a place where couples who have been struggling with infertility go as a last resort to have a child."

"I mean, this has really turned into, if you have enough money to pay for it, then you can, by any means necessary, really have a child in California," she added.

SURROGATE, CALIFORNIA COUPLE CLASH IN COURT AS NEWBORN FIGHTS FOR LIFE AFTER HEART SURGERY

Unlike in some states, a license is not required in California to open a surrogacy agency, and there is no comprehensive regulatory framework to oversee the industry across the state.

Surrogacy is a billion-dollar global market used to help couples who are unable to conceive or carry a child. The issue, Fell noted, is that while the process is accessible to anyone who can afford it, there are no meaningful regulatory safeguards for the children born to surrogates.

"I was a foster parent," she said. "My husband and I went through gobs of courses, gobs of home studies, background checks, everything — really under a microscope. The same is not true for surrogacy. It doesn't apply."

As the surrogacy boom has expanded, foreign nationals — many from China — have increasingly used American surrogates to have children, according to a 2024 report by the Heritage Foundation.

Because commercial surrogacy is completely illegal inside China, wealthy Chinese individuals and couples frequently look abroad, primarily to the U.S., to grow their families.

While banned or heavily restricted in several other countries, cross-border surrogacy is not regulated at the federal level in the U.S., opening the door for foreign clients to secure American birthright citizenship for the resulting children, according to the conservative think tank.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"We absolutely need to close our borders to international surrogacy," Fell said. "Why do we need folks from overseas coming, renting wombs here in the United States?"

World.title: Wildlife influencer comes close to losing a wrestling match to a 19-foot reticulated python
World.content:
A wildlife influencer who goes by the name The Real Tarzann on social media put his blue belt jiu-jitsu skills up against a 19-foot reticulated python. Smart.

He realizes he's getting dangerously close to being in trouble when the snake wraps up one of his arms and both of his legs at the same time.

The Real Tarzann, real name Mike Holston, tells his cameraman as he's wrestling the snake, "I'm okay. For now. But I won't be in a second."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

After having the python strike towards him a couple of times, he grabs its head and is in for his "toughest battle with a snake yet."

That's because this gigantic snake doesn't want to go down without a fight. It immediately starts trying to wrap its body around the influencer.

Once it has Holston's arm and both of his legs wrapped up it appears to start tightening its grip on him. He admits, "I'm losing this battle, guys. For the first time, I've met one that I can't beat."

MMA FIGHTER CONFIDENTLY BELIEVES HE CAN BEAT A CHIMPANZEE IN A FIGHT AND CLAIMS IT WILL BE LIVESTREAMED

Despite the admission, he's not ready to give up. When asked if he needs help, he responds, "In a sec, I'm gonna flip him over. I still got head control, but my legs are and arm... watch. Ready?"

Once he flips the snake over and is lying on his back, he's able to eventually wrestle himself free, but not without admitting that his blue belt was nothing compared to the python and its "black belt in the jungle."

The Real Tarzann, after escaping and avoiding being squeezed to death, also admitted while trying to catch his breath that it was as close as he's "been in a long time to being wrapped up."

That's not my idea of a good time. But it's one way to get off the couch and spend an afternoon if you're looking for adventure.

I'd love to know what the plan was here if he wasn’t able to flip the snake and if he started to lose the fight even more. Was the cameraman jumping in?

OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Were there others there, making the whole wrestling a huge snake in the jungle by himself completely unnecessary? Was anyone armed?

Cool social media video, I guess.

World.title: Bear breaks into Alaska hospital at 2 am, helps itself to an early Halloween candy buffet
World.content:
Most people wait until Halloween to stuff themselves with candy. But one black bear in Alaska decided Oct. 12 was close enough.

And instead of going door-to-door like a civilized trick-or-treater, this guy just helped himself to whatever he could find.

The unexpected visitor showed up around 2 a.m. Monday at a hospital on Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson near Anchorage, Alaska. According to Alaska's News Source, the bear made his way through the hospital's emergency department before discovering a bucket of donated Halloween candy and proceeding to chow down.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

Probably even ate the candy corn. Gross.

A woman named Sherri Warnke — who was leaving the hospital after visiting her mother — spotted the massive animal about 30 feet away in a dimly lit hallway. To make things spookier, Warnke didn't have a hospital badge, meaning all the doors along the corridor were locked to her.

So there she was, trapped in a hallway with a hungry black bear.

Warnke slowly backed away, hoping the bear hadn't noticed her. Fortunately, that's when our furry friend discovered the candy bucket and apparently decided chocolate was better than human.

Eventually, an announcement came over the hospital intercom warning everyone that there was a bear in the building. But that didn't stop some doctors from coming out to take pictures.

MAMA BEAR TEACHES CUB THE FINE ART OF RIPPING OPEN A TRUCK BED COVER IN A PARKING LOT

Warnke made it out safely, and the bear reportedly exited through the same entrance he'd used to get inside. Nobody was injured.

Hospital staff later showed Warnke a surveillance photo of the bear standing at the emergency department reception desk, where they joked that he appeared to be checking in.



Of course, with winter approaching, bears are busy packing on the pounds before hibernation. Most bears are out there catching salmon, digging through dumpsters and scavenging for berries. But this guy figured out where they keep the good stuff.

He could have at least put on a costume, though.

BACKUP QUARTERBACK TYLER HUNTLEY LEADS BALTIMORE RAVENS TO IMPROBABLE OT WIN OVER ATLANTA FALCONS

World.title: Justice Department threatens legal action against California over alleged noncitizen voters
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Justice Department is threatening legal action against California unless state and local officials review a list of potential noncitizen individuals on their voter rolls.

Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter on Tuesday sent letters to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan with a list of names of possible noncitizens identified by the federal government. The letters demand they review the list by noon on Thursday.

“Allowing noncitizens to vote cancels citizen votes,” McCotter wrote in the letter, which was obtained by NBC News.

McCotter wrote that the DOJ provided a password-protected thumb drive with a list of individuals the federal government “believes are likely noncitizens who were sent a vote-by-mail ballot” for the 2026 election. He asked that county election officials “segregate — not cancel — those individuals’ vote-by-mail ballots” until their citizenship status was determined.

“This should not be controversial, as the criminal statute is clear: only American citizens may vote in federal elections,” a Justice Department spokesperson said in a statement. “It is a federal crime for noncitizens to vote in U.S. elections, and the DOJ is asking California to ensure that is not occurring.”

Reuters first reported on the letters.

Justin Levitt, an NBC News contributor who was a Justice Department official during the Obama administration, said the federal government has no authority supporting its demands.

“They can send the letter,” he said. “California doesn’t have to do anything about it.”

Federal law prohibits systemic list maintenance within 90 days of a federal election. At this point, less than three weeks out from Election Day, the only changes to the voter rolls can come from individualized information, like notification from the Social Security Administration that someone has died.

A DOJ spokesperson said the department is asking California to sequester ballots, not change their voter list.

In a statement Wednesday, Logan said his office had not accessed the thumb drive the DOJ provided “because doing so would conflict with established data privacy and information security protocols.” He added, “We do not consider the device a secure medium.”

“Maintaining accurate voter registration records is a fundamental responsibility of our office,” Logan said in the statement. “Federal and state laws are clear on how voter eligibility is established — and any action to remove a voter from eligibility must be based on verifiable information, not assertions of unconfirmed data matching.”

Weber did not respond to requests for comment.

All registered voters in California receive mail-in ballots, which started going out on Oct. 5.

The legal threats came amid a broader campaign by the Trump administration to zero in on what voting experts say is a relatively rare phenomenon of voting by noncitizen individuals. Trump has long made unfounded claims that voting is marred by widespread fraud.

Election officials in several states — including Georgia, Connecticut, Nevada and Washington state — say they have received federal subpoenas in recent months for election records.

Some officials said they fear these actions were designed to set up possible legal challenges after the midterm elections.

“What we have seen is some groundwork laid out for postelection challenges,” said Stuart Holmes, the director of elections in Washington state. “Whether that’s the seizure of voting equipment, ballots themselves, tabulation equipment ... we’re preparing for any and all eventualities in that case.”

Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar, a Democrat, said officials in his state are also preparing for potential challenges to this November’s results. He added that he viewed the administration’s moves as “an effort to dissuade people from participating in the elections.”

“You have a president who’s trying to choose the voter base rather than the voters choosing the elected, and that’s not how our democracy works,” he said in an interview. “It’s the people control our elections, and when you try to take that control out, you do it through intimidation, you do it through threats, and you do it by trying to dissuade people from participating.”

Levitt agreed with the election officials’ conclusions.

“Are they laying the groundwork to say that voting was fraudulent? Of course they are, 100% they are,” he said, referring to the Trump administration. “Is the boy who cried wolf going to cry wolf? Yes, that’s what the boy who cried wolf does.”

Since Trump took office, his administration has brought over 100 cases involving allegations of voting by noncitizens. More than 154 million people voted in the 2024 election, according to the U.S. Census Bureau.

During the second Trump administration, the DOJ has sought voter registration data from every state in the country. It has filed lawsuits against 30 states and Washington, D.C., for refusing.

World.title: Feds seized Rep. Ilhan Omar’s phone, subpoenaed family members in immigration status probe
World.content:
Federal agents seized Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar’s phone when they searched her Washington, D.C., home this week as part of a federal investigation into potential immigration-related crimes, and they have sent roughly a dozen subpoenas out in the case, according to two people familiar with the investigation.

The possible charges cited by federal officials included conspiracy and making false statements in immigration paperwork, one of the people said.

The search came just three weeks before the midterms, within the window of time when the Justice Department has typically avoided overt actions in criminal cases that could affect an election. And the seizure of the phone of a sitting member of Congress would typically trigger a set of law enforcement protocols meant to ensure investigators aren’t infringing upon the “speech or debate” clause of the U.S. Constitution, which protects members of Congress from being questioned for their legislative acts.

On Friday, roughly a dozen subpoenas were sent out in the case, including to her family members, the second person familiar with the investigation told NBC News.

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., attends a news conference with members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus on funding and accountability for the Department of Homeland Security in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday, January 13, 2026. Tom Williams / CQ-Roll Call via Getty

The congresswoman herself was not subpoenaed, the person said, adding that the orders seeking information are tied to a federal grand jury in Minnesota, Omar’s home state. Federal agents also want to talk to Omar’s sister but haven’t reached her yet, the person said.

The New York Times first reported the subpoenas.

The investigation is being conducted by Homeland Security Investigations, the U.S. attorney in Minneapolis and the Justice Department.

A spokesperson for Omar didn’t respond to a request for comment. The Justice Department declined to comment.

Omar said in a statement posted online on Monday that she would not be silenced.

“Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she wrote.

One of the people familiar with the investigation said it involved whistleblowers, documents and witness testimony. The probe is examining matters surrounding Omar’s immigration status, including — but not limited to — her birthdate. Omar, who was born in Somalia and moved to the United States with her family in the 1990s, was naturalized when she was 17 years old, meaning she was a juvenile and could be conferred citizenship through a parent.

A criminal investigation could be complicated by the statute of limitations, which is typically five years, but investigators could look into Omar’s or her family members’ more recent actions that would fall within the statute of limitations.

Omar, who is part of a group of progressive women in Congress known as “the Squad,” has been a frequent target of Trump’s rhetoric against her and other members’ liberal positions, as well as Somali immigrants broadly.

Asked Monday if he had been aware of the search in advance, Trump said the federal government was looking at Omar “very carefully.” He also repeated his frequent attacks on her and Somalia.

“Then she comes over here and she complains about our Constitution,” Trump said. “I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ.”

That evening, Trump also attacked Omar in remarks at a rally he held for Republicans in Ohio.

“I don’t know what they’re doing with it, but I can tell you this: She’s a disaster,” Trump said. “She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military, where all they do is shoot each other, and she comes into our country and she says, ‘I have a constitutional right.’”

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin appeared to tease federal action against Omar last month when he said “something’s going to happen” with her, but they were still investigating.

“If we actually move a case forward, it’s not a political case,” Mullin said. “It’s an actual case because they did things wrong. If you decided to break the law or lie [about] the information you gave the United States to be able to come into the United States through either asylum or because you were just wanting to seek a better life, but you didn’t tell us who you actually were, you lied about certain things about your application — those things, there’s no expiration to that.”

World.title: Ukraine accuses SpaceX of restricting Starlink, disrupting military amid Trump pressure
World.content:
The Ukrainian government has yet to receive a response from SpaceX, a Ukrainian official told NBC News, and Ukrainian units are already reporting issues with performance even at lower UAV speeds.

Asked about the importance of the technology, Ukraine’s chargé d’affaires to the U.S., Denys Sienik, said Starshield is lifesaving. “The technology helps us save the lives of civilians and prevent more destructions in Ukraine caused by Russian side,” he said.

Drone disruptions

SpaceX had introduced speed limits on the operation of its Starlink satellite internet terminals overnight, according to Zelenskyy’s defense tech adviser, Serhii Beskrestnov.

“Our defence forces received no warning of such a restriction, and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” Beskrestnov said on Telegram. “It is obvious that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation,” he added.

An army unit fighting in the southeastern Zaporizhzhia region said Wednesday it had been forced to cancel some planned operations.

The 7th Rapid Reaction Corps of the Ukrainian air assault forces said it began “noticing Starlink connectivity problems caused by data transfer speed limits” overnight, adding that the changes directly affected drones that use the service for in-flight control.

“The drones kept flying, but the interruptions made them harder to control,” it said in a statement.

Beskrestnov said restrictions were specifically put on the operation of the military-grade version of Starlink at speeds above 100 mph.

Starlink was also key for Ukraine’s aerial defenses, as it was used to intercept the jet-powered drones that Moscow has unleashed on Ukrainian cities in recent months, he said. Asked about the importance of the technology, Sienik said, “The technology helps us save the lives of civilians and prevent more destruction in Ukraine caused by the Russian side.”

Ukraine has reached out to the U.S. government and SpaceX for clarification about the rationale for the new restrictions but has yet to receive a response, according to a Ukrainian official.

Ukraine’s armed forces learned about the limitations from customer support after they filed a complaint about operational issues, the official said, adding that SpaceX had not warned of the move.

Ukrainian military units were already reporting issues with drone performance at even lower speeds, the official added.

The White House, SpaceX and Starlink did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The disruption follows days of mounting tensions between Kyiv and Washington as Trump pushes to lower gas prices ahead of the midterm elections. Trump’s latest reversal in his bid to settle the war led him to stun Kyiv by striking a diesel deal with Russia that upended years of U.S. sanctions.

He then demanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries and called for Zelenskyy to be replaced. Trump also announced an “energy ceasefire” that neither warring side appears to have agreed to.

Kyiv said it had refrained from striking Russian energy targets to respect Trump’s wishes, but the Kremlin has continued to hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure in its annual effort to leave its neighbor in the freezing dark as winter sets in.

Intel uncertainty

Zelenskyy said Tuesday that Ukraine had not received any early warning from its partners about “a particularly vile ballistic missile strike on Kyiv” a day earlier. Explosions rang out before an alert was issued, according to an NBC News producer in the capital.

“Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues,” Zelenskyy said, without singling out the U.S.

Later Tuesday, he reported that another strike on Kyiv was “the second time Ukraine was not warned.”
