NPR confirmed with former Mazal Group employees that the company helps store owners secure retail space in malls and assists with the design and layout of individual locations. The company's marketing team designs product packaging and manages brand websites and social media accounts, they said.

toggle caption i Suzanne Kreiter/The Boston Globe via Getty Images

"The Mazal Group owners and officers are involved in every step of the process, from product design to distribution to store design and development to sales to post-sale concerns," concluded a research firm hired by the plaintiffs' attorneys.

Mazal Group's agreements with stores also reveal a direct link between company policy and customer complaints. The company requires branded stores — e.g., locations with Voupre or Lionesse in the store name — to exclusively sell products purchased from Mazal Group, adopt a refund policy determined by the group and direct all customer service inquiries to its headquarters, court records show. These agreements also establish guidelines for how salespeople should offer samples to passersby.

After four years of pretrial action, the Hawaii class action case was scheduled for a jury trial in July 2026 in Honolulu. In June, the parties announced they had reached a settlement.

Mazal Group, the Weingartens and Odeds, and two licensees in Hawaii agreed to pay $950,000 in restitution, according to a copy of the settlement agreement obtained by NPR. Mazal Group and the family are responsible for $650,000 of the total payout. After legal fees, funds will be distributed proportionately to 110 class members who filed a complaint with the state of Hawaii.

Mazal Group and the Weingartens and Odeds have denied wrongdoing, and the settlement releases them from future liability for the allegations in the case.

"Highly unusual" pricing and missing ingredients

toggle caption i Zayrha Rodriguez/NPR

To understand why salespeople can negotiate the price of a product on the fly, NPR looked into what these items actually cost to make and what's inside them.

NPR obtained internal order forms for Voupre and Avinichi — brands owned by the Weingartens and Odeds and distributed via Mazal Group. These documents show the brands set manufacturer-suggested retail prices at up to 130 times the wholesale price they charge to stores. Voupre's Cannabis Caviar Transforming Mask, for example, costs $23 wholesale, with a suggested retail price of $3,000.

"Pricing at that level typically raises red flags," said Joe Rowett, CEO of VELOX, an Idaho-based marketing agency for skincare and beauty brands.

Well-known luxury brands rarely stretch the suggested retail price to even 20 times the wholesale cost, and most skincare brands operate far below that, Rowett said, making Voupre's suggested markups "highly unusual."

Federal investigators and former employees suggested to NPR that this wide margin gives salespeople the flexibility to negotiate the best sales price to earn maximum commission.

toggle caption i Rosem Morton for NPR

NPR sent a single unopened box of a Voupre "best-seller" for chemical testing. The sample — one box of one product — is limited, but the results of the analysis raise questions about what the label promises and what the product contains.

toggle caption i Sophie Park for NPR

Many shoppers described being lured into a store with a sample of Voupre Anti-Aging Rescue Solution, which Mazal sells to stores for $19.50 per unit with a suggested retail price of $1,300. NPR obtained an unopened box of the solution from Suzann Roberts, a 90-year-old woman in Ann Arbor who bought the product from Beauty Essentials in 2024 and was unable to return it.

NPR sent the sample to Founders Science Group in Taunton, Massachusetts. CEO Robert Munroe has worked as a pharmaceutical scientist for three decades.

By looking at the product's ingredients list, Munroe identified three ingredients for analysis that could support Voupre's anti-aging claims: vitamin A to accelerate skin-cell turnover, vitamin E to fight collagen breakdown and acetyl hexapeptide-8, a powerful peptide that some call "Botox in a bottle."

The lab could not detect any trace of vitamin A or E, which Munroe said was "surprising and definitely suspicious." Vitamin A can degrade in strength over time without proper preservatives, he said, but it's not possible for vitamin E to disappear entirely. If the manufacturer did not include the actives at production and Voupre listed them on the packaging, he said, "that would be misbranding."

toggle caption i Sophie Park for NPR

Based on what the lab detected, which included a high concentration of the peptide, Munroe said the solution is comparable to The Ordinary's 10% Argireline Solution, which retails for under $10.

"As far as getting peptide on the skin, you don't need to spend $1,300 to do it," he said.

The formula for Voupre's Anti-Aging Rescue Solution is the basis for nearly identical wrinkle creams that the Weingartens and Odeds sell across other brands like Introstem, CbGäRDN, Venofye and Lavelier.

toggle caption i Collage by NPR

A new company, the same family

New stores selling the Weingartens and Odeds' brands crop up regularly across the U.S. and globally, especially in port cities and tourist destinations.

Complaints haven't slowed them down, one former Mazal Group employee told NPR.

"It wasn't like it was stopping the business. They were still expanding, opening, expanding, opening, expanding, opening."

The Weingartens and Odeds have also closed companies and shuttered numerous brands over the years. Just last month, Mazal Group itself — the hub of operations for the family business — terminated its business license in California.

NPR reporters visited the Chatsworth headquarters weeks before that, in August 2026. The building, which once sported a Mazal Group logo more than 10 feet high and wide, bore a similar sign saying INV Brands.

Innovation Brands Inc. was founded by Daphna and Eli Weingarten in 2024.

"Streamlining the journey from concept to consumer," the company's website reads. "We leverage global expertise to build, manage, and scale exceptional personal care brands."

If you have information to share, you can reach Caley Fox Shannon and Monika Evstatieva on Signal at caley_fox.17 and monikanpr.38.

Additional reporting from Israel was provided by Daniel Estrin and Itay Stern. The story was edited by Barrie Hardymon and Robert Little, with additional editorial support from Arielle Retting and editorial review by Kristian Monroe. Preeti Aroon was the copy editor. Matt Pollack conducted the legal review, with additional legal support from Mayeesha Galiba.

Design and development by Connie Hanzhang Jin and Alyson Hurt, with visual editing by Emily Bogle. Mito Habe-Evans and Bronson Arcuri produced and edited the video. Mia Venkat produced the audio.

World.title: VIDEO: The skincare sample is free. What happens next can cost thousands
World.content:
VIDEO: The skincare sample is free. What happens next can cost thousands

The products promise younger-looking skin. The salespeople promise special deals. But customers at skincare stores across the country say they've walked away with something else entirely: thousands of dollars in unexpected charges and purchases they can't return.

Over the past year, NPR investigated complaints from shopping malls in Michigan to hotel spas in Hawaii, where customers reported being pressured into spending thousands of dollars on skincare products they never wanted. The stores had different names and different owners, but shared a common connection.

Sponsor Message

NPR's Monika Evstatieva and Caley Fox Shannon interviewed more than 50 people, reviewed hundreds of consumer complaints and examined court records and internal documents. Their reporting led them to Mazal Group, a California-based company run by a family originally from Israel that controls dozens of skincare brands sold in independently operated stores around the world.

More than a decade ago, federal agents documented what they called a "credit card overcharge scheme" at stores selling some of the same brands. Their investigations also uncovered immigration and money-laundering crimes that led to more than a dozen guilty pleas.

Yet customers continue to report similar tactics at stores across the country. So NPR set out to trace the connections between the stores, the products and the family business behind them.

World.title: U.S. 'monitoring' Canada for signs of midterm election interference, ambassador says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra says American officials are "closely watching" Canadian politicians for signs of election interference ahead of the pivotal midterms next month.

During an interview on The Really Big Show podcast posted last week, Hoekstra said political ads run by the province of Ontario last year could be interpreted as political interference.

U.S. President Donald Trump ended trade talks with Canada in October 2025 after Ontario aired an ad during the World Series using clips of former U.S. president Ronald Reagan criticizing tariffs and supporting free trade.

Hoekstra also cited recent comments by Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and former prime minister Justin Trudeau and suggested they also could amount to interference.

Hoekstra warned Canadian politicians to keep their "nose out" of American politics in the weeks before the midterm elections.

Trudeau criticized the Trump administration during a discussion at Brown University on Sept. 22.

"There is a pattern here of doing things that are driving up prices for your consumers and not necessarily making anything better for America, by fighting with one of your oldest and best allies," Trudeau said during the conversation.

In the interview, Hoekstra said Joly made comments about targeting retaliatory tariffs at "politically sensitive states."

Joly pushed back on Wednesday, telling reporters that Canada would never engage in election interference and would "never accept that also being done to us in Canada."

Joly said she has been to the U.S. in recent months and has met with Democrats and Republicans.

WATCH | Canada 'absolutely not' interfering in U.S. midterms, Joly says: Canada 'absolutely not' interfering in U.S. midterms, Joly says | Duration closed caption 1:19 Asked about the United States Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra's comments about watching for Canadian interference in the U.S. midterm elections, Minister of Industry Mélanie Joly says 'we never do that and we never accept that also being done to us in Canada.' She says her recent visits to the U.S. were 'to attract investments' by American companies and she will continue to do so.

"Fundamentally, what I've done in the U.S. is to attract investments," she said. "I think I'll be able to have good news of investments by different American companies to Canada. And that's exactly what I'm doing and that will continue to be my strategy in the U.S. and also around the world."

Hoekstra said if any actions by Canadians end up amounting to election interference, the United States will respond.

"We're monitoring it, we're evaluating it and if some of it becomes election interference then America will respond to it," Hoekstra said.

The president has been actively campaigning in battleground states ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

The entire House of Representatives and one-third of U.S. Senate seats will be contested. Currently the Republicans hold a majority of seats in both, but polls suggest there is a chance that the Democrats wrest control of both chambers.

The Globe and Mail reported recently that Republican political operatives were on the ground in Alberta earlier this year to help the separatist campaign. CBC News previously reported that Alberta separatists also attended meetings in U.S. State Department offices in Washington, D.C., last year.

In August, Prime Minister Mark Carney ordered the Canadian negotiating team to call off renewed trade talks with the U.S. after accusing the Americans of making unreasonable demands.

WATCH | Trade war front and centre ahead of U.S. midterms: Canada-U.S. trade war emerges as key issue ahead of U.S. midterms | Duration closed caption 2:18 The Canada-U.S. trade war is solidifying itself as a major ballot-box issue in pivotal states ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre was in Detroit on Tuesday to make a case for tariff-free trade in the auto sector.

"We have a 200-year-old relationship. There's always going to be grievances on both sides of the border," he said on CNN.

"We have our grievances with the United States even predating this most recent trade dispute, but I would focus on what we can do together."

Hoekstra's comments come after one Trump's trade advisers threatened repercussions for Canada if it "interferes" in the upcoming midterms.

Peter Navarro dismissed Canada's approach to trade talks during an economic conference in Washington last month, saying that Canadian lobbyists need to "get the hell out of our country."

"The problem you have is you lobby this country and you've been successful in the past and you think you can keep doing that," Navarro said of Canada's approach.

WATCH | Trump adviser warns Canada not to 'interfere' in U.S. midterms: 'You will pay': Trump adviser warns Canada not to 'interfere' with U.S. midterms | Duration closed caption 2:54 White House trade adviser Peter Navarro warned Canada not to 'interfere' with U.S. midterm elections in border states such as Maine and Michigan by lobbying against the Trump administration's tariffs. Navarro said Canada would 'pay even more dearly' for doing so.

"Memo to Canada: You cannot do that. That game is up and if you interfere in our elections in Maine or Michigan you will pay even more dearly."

The trade war has become a pressure point on Republican candidates running for the Senate in the two border states Navarro mentioned.

Just last week, the Republican candidate for Michigan's open Senate seat released a new 30-second ad criticizing tariffs.

"Here in Michigan we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war now," Mike Rogers says in the ad.

Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who has represented Maine since 1997, has also tried to distance herself from Trump's tariffs.

World.title: What to know about the deadly U.K. tiger attack — and the 'offensive' video shared by Trump
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The family of a man mauled to death by a tiger at a U.K. wildlife park on Saturday is pleading with people to stop sharing footage of the attack online, calling it "deeply offensive" and painful.

The statement from the family of 23-year-old William Chapman came after U.S. President Donald Trump shared a clip of the fatal attack on his Truth Social platform Tuesday, writing "don't ⁠ever mess with nature!"

The 41-second video shared by Trump shows a large tiger repeatedly biting and clawing at Chapman. Trump's post was then shared by the White House's Rapid Response account on X, where commenters called it "sick" and "disgusting."

The U.S. president later posted ​an apparently AI-generated video depicting himself taming a tiger ​and then playing with it, accompanied by the song The Lion Sleeps Tonight.

His social media posts have sparked outrage, but they have also raised questions about how the tragedy happened.

Here's what we know about the tiger attack and the man who died.

Where did this happen?

The attack happened on Saturday in a tiger enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster in northern England.

The popular conservation and welfare park opened in 2009. The "Land of the Tigers" area opened in 2011, " where the majestic big cats can freely roaming their woodlands and grasslands or play in their very own waterfall pool," the park explains on its website.

It features a 300-metre-long raised walkway for spectators.

WATCH | Victim's family pleads for respect: Victim's family pleads for respect after Trump shares tiger attack video | Duration 1:24 The family of William Chapman, the 23-year-old killed after entering a tiger enclosure at a U.K. wildlife park on Oct. 10, is calling for people to stop sharing the video leading up to the fatal attack. Chapman’s family’s plea comes after U.S. President Donald Trump republished part of the video showing the tiger attack, along with two other clips, including an AI-generated video of Trump wrestling with the tiger.

How did the attack happen?

BBC News reports that emergency services were called to the park in the early afternoon Saturday for reports that a man had climbed into the tiger enclosure from a high walkway. Witnesses told multiple U.K. media outlets that the tiger had been lounging on a ledge until the man entered.

"The tiger got alerted. He went into stalk mode. The tiger came flying off the ledge and approached him," a witness told The Telegraph.

Witnesses reportedly tried to distract the tiger, shouting at it and banging on the fence, as the animal pawed and nipped at the man. Videos posted online appear to show the man pointing at the tiger, yelling "stop" and "no."

Staff reportedly erected screens to block the view as emergency services responded.

In a Facebook post, South Yorkshire Police confirmed that " despite the best efforts of medical personnel, the man was pronounced dead at the scene." The park was then evacuated, police said, adding there was no risk to the public.

Yorkshire Wildlife Park was closed and has yet to reopen to the public. The park is " working closely with the authorities," it notes on its website.

A coroner's inquest is scheduled to begin Thursday, reports the Doncaster Free Press.

William Chapman in an undated photo posted to Facebook by South Yorkshire Police on Wednesday. (South Yorkshire Police/Facebook)

Who was William Chapman?

Chapman, 23, was a former child actor, according to the BBC. The outlet notes he appeared in the 2009 ITV production May Contain Nuts and the 2012 BBC series True Stories.

The Jackie Palmer Stage School in High Wycombe shared a tribute to Chapman on Facebook Tuesday, noting he was a former student.

"We loved watching William grow, both as a person and as a performer, during his time with us," the school posted.

"It was a privilege to be part of his journey, and he will be remembered with great fondness by everyone who had the pleasure of knowing him."

Chapman's family described him as a "bright, warm and engaging young man w hom his family dearly loved" in a statement shared by South Yorkshire Police.

"Sadly, William suffered from significant mental illness over a number of years and was consequently prescribed strong medication," the family added.

The statement said it was for the coroner to determine whether his medical history played a role in his death.

"The family are hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their utmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did."

A Facebook tribute to William Chapman posted by the Jackie Palmer Stage School and Agency on Tuesday. (Jackie Palmer Stage School and Agency/Facebook)

How did he get in the enclosure?

Chapman reportedly entered it himself.

A witness told the Daily Mail that Chapman had been " dancing his way up and down the bridge with his AirPods in" before asking her to take a photo of him. Witnesses told the Telegraph that, shortly after, another woman tried to stop Chapman from jumping in but he overpowered her.

Witnesses described Chapman acting "in a trance" in the enclosure, sometimes dancing with his phone out.

Several U.K. media outlets reported that he uploaded a video of himself approaching the tiger in the enclosure to his Instagram account moments before he was attacked. His account has since been made private.

"He had arms wide open ready for the tiger to attack him. It was quite bad. We were just stood there, frozen… the last thing we saw was the tiger’s jaw on his neck," Scarlet Hogan, 21, told the Telegraph.

Observers online have pointed out that in the videos circulating online, Chapman appears to clench both fists with his little fingers pointing out. They suggest this may be the sign for "bad" in Makaton, an alternative form of sign language for people with limited speech.

These reports have not been confirmed.

A photo of William Chapman posted by South Yorkshire Mayor Oliver Coppard on Wednesday. (Oliver Coppard/Facebook)

What happens to the tiger?

The tiger involved in the attacked, named Altai, is "safe and well" and will not be euthanized, the park said in a statement posted on Instagram on Sunday.

The tigers at Yorkshire Wildlife Park are all e ndangered Amur tigers, also known as Siberian tigers. They're the largest big cats in the world.

An animal ranger at the park quoted by the Telegraph said it wasn't the tiger's fault, and that to the animal, Chapman was "just something else to play with."

"The keepers are all distraught," she added.

The park welcomed Altai in a 2025 Instagram post, saying he had just arrived from a zoo in Norway.

An Instagram post by Yorkshire Wildlife Park from 2025 shows Altai, the Amur tiger that mauled a man in an enclosure on Saturday. (Yorkshire Wildlife Park/Instagram)

Why did Trump post about it?

Trump has not offered an explanation for his posts about Chapman.

The U.S. president regularly uses social media to make commentary and share AI-generated images and videos. In April, for instance, Trump posted an image that appeared to depict himself as Jesus.

Chapman's family, in their statement, asked people to "please stop" sharing footage.

"The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened," the family said.

"The publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time."

South Yorkshire Mayor Oliver Coppard was among those to condemn Trump's posts.

"The President of the United States now using AI to mock that incident and the pain felt by the family … for little more than a cheap laugh on social media, should be greeted with the contempt it deserves," Coppard wrote on Facebook on Wednesday.

As of Wednesday, videos of the attack were still being shared across social media platforms including X, Threads and TikTok. The video shared on X by the White House had been viewed around 2.5 million times.

CBC News has contacted X to ask whether it will be removing videos that show the attack, but has yet to hear back.

World.title: 'Everything is on the table,' Joly says, as Ottawa weighs legal action over steelmaker layoffs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ottawa is considering a range of legal options against Stelco's American owner after the company rejected the government's demand to halt planned layoffs at the Hamilton steelmaker, Federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said Wednesday.

Speaking with reporters in Ottawa, Joly said the government is reviewing a letter from Cleveland-Cliffs and remains determined to enforce the employment commitments the company made when it purchased Stelco in 2024.

"We expect Stelco to follow the undertakings that they've committed to," Joly said.

"Right now, a business decision or even a change in market conditions cannot be used to not follow their commitment."

Joly said the government is examining its options under Section 40 of the Investment Canada Act, which could include financial penalties, a court order forcing the company to comply with its commitments or an order requiring it to sell its Canadian assets.

"Everything is on the table."

Speaking with reporters in Ottawa, Federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said the government remains determined to enforce the employment commitments Cleveland-Cliffs made when it purchased Stelco in 2024. (CBC)

The minister did not announce whether the government would launch court proceedings or provide a timeline for a decision. She said Ottawa remains in contact with the company and the union representing Stelco workers.

"I'm always open to sit down with the company and find a solution, but we're looking at everything that is possible to keep jobs in Canada," Joly said.

She also described the situation at the Hamilton steelmaker as "unacceptable."

The comments come after Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves said the company would proceed with layoffs despite Ottawa's warning that the cuts could violate the terms of its purchase of Stelco.

Cleveland-Cliffs agreed to maintain at least the same number of unionized employees, along with the vast majority of non-unionized employees, for five years following the announcement of its acquisition in 2024.

Goncalves has disputed the government's interpretation of those commitments, arguing the agreement does not require the company to maintain employment levels every day throughout the five-year period. He has described the layoffs as temporary, saying the jobs would return once Canada and the United States reach a trade agreement.

The company has also pointed to U.S. President Donald Trump's 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian steel as a factor behind its decision.

Layoffs already underway

Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, which represents Stelco workers, said layoffs are already affecting members.

Speaking on CBC Radio's Metro Morning on Wednesday, Wells said 90 workers were laid off last week, with another 85 expected to lose their jobs by the end of this week. Further layoffs are expected over the following weeks.

The union has estimated that 300 to 350 jobs could be cut in Hamilton, with additional layoffs possible at Stelco's Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke, Ont.

WATCH | Stelco owner open to selling company amid fight with Ottawa over layoffs: Stelco owner open to selling company amid fight with Ottawa over layoffs | Duration closed caption 10:00 Lourenco Goncalves, CEO of Stelco parent company Cleveland-Cliffs, speaks with CBC's Rosemary Barton following his company's official response to the federal government's threat of legal action amid layoffs at the company’s Hamilton, Ont.-based steel plant. In a letter obtained by CBC News, Stelco says it is not violating employment commitments.

Wells has argued that Cleveland-Cliffs is violating its employment commitments and urged the federal government to pursue legal action.

He also warned that the consequences could extend beyond the steelmaker, as other manufacturers depend on Stelco's products.

"Steel is essential to the supply chain," Wells said, warning that disruptions could affect businesses producing everything from appliances and garden sheds to automotive products.

Calls for public ownership of Stelco

The dispute has also prompted calls for public ownership of the steelmaker.

Federal NDP Leader Avi Lewis and Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles have urged the federal government to nationalize Stelco, arguing that court proceedings could take too long to protect workers and Canada's steelmaking capacity.

Stiles has also called on Ontario Premier Doug Ford to work with Ottawa to pursue public ownership and Canadian management, while pressing the province to provide tariff relief and adopt a "Buy Ontario First" procurement strategy.

Prime Minister Mark Carney previously said the government would take appropriate action after receiving and reviewing the company's response to Joly's demand.

World.title: Image of mournful elephant mom wins 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

(Federico Veronesi/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)

An Italian photographer's "heartbreakingly poignant" photo of a mother elephant carrying her dead calf has won this year's top Wildlife Photographer of the Year award.

Federico Veronesi captured "The Aftermath" while tracking elephants in the Huab River Valley in Namibia. He noticed unusual drag marks in the sand of the dry riverbed. When he caught up to a family of elephants, he saw an adult female with a calf's leg wedged between her tusk and trunk.

Kathy Moran, chair of the jury for the 2026 competition, described the photo as working on "so many levels."

"Emotionally it's a gut punch, heartbreakingly poignant. Intellectually, it's proof that animals have cognition," she wrote in a news release announcing the winners.

In addition to winning the grand prize, the photo also won the Behaviour: Mammals category.

Wildlife Photographer of the Year is developed and produced by the U.K.-based Natural History Museum in London, with a stated goal to share nature's stories and insights about environmental challenges that need our attention.

This year, the annual competition — the 62nd edition — attracted 65,403 entries from 121 countries and territories.

It awards top prizes to both an adult photographer and a young photographer under 18.

This year's Young Wildlife Photographer of the Year prize was won by Oscar Whitfield, a young British photographer who grew up in Zimbabwe and frequently returns there during school holidays.

His photo, captured while lying on the ground, shows a close-up of a dung beetle hard at work pushing a ball of dung. It was also the winner in the 11 to 14 years age bracket.

(Oscar Whitfield/Wildlife Photographer of the year)

Officially, there were no Canadian category winners this year. However, Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas, who lives in Germany and won this year's Rising Star Award, is a Canadian citizen who has previously told CBC News his parents were both born in Canada, and he has relatives in Ottawa and Nova Scotia.

His featured photo, "Afternoon snack," is a close-up of a robber fly preying on a flesh fly. "The bubbles forming in the victim's eyes indicate that the robber fly has injected digestive enzymes that liquefy its internal tissues before they are sucked out," the photo's description reads.

(Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)

Canadians can see the 100-photo exhibition at the Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto from Nov 7, 2026, to Feb 28, 2027, or at the Royal B.C. Museum in Victoria from Feb. 12, 2027, until April 18, 2027.

It opens at the Natural History Museum in London this Friday.

Here are some of the other category winners.

Amelie Davis, of the U.K., won the 10 years and under bracket with this photo of a common carder bee in southern England, captured with her father's smartphone.

(Amelie Davis/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)

A California newt lays eggs while clasping vegetation that already contains another newt's egg clutch in the winner of the Amphibians and Reptiles category, captured by U.S. photographer Anton Sorokin. The newt will stay like this until the egg mass swells to a size too large to be eaten by a predator.

(Anton Sorokin/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)

Greek photographer Agorastos Papatsanis used UV light to make these fluorescent bonnet mushrooms glow brightly on a decaying log on the lower slopes of Greece's Mount Olympus. The image won the Plants and Fungi category.

(Agorastos Papatsanis/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)

A young bull elephant sprays water on a group of zebras at a waterhole in the Chyulu Hills of Kenya in this photo, the winner of the Animals in their Environment category, captured by James Lewin using a camera converted to infrared to soften harsh lighting.

World.title: Katie Zacharia fails to impress in brief debut as White House press secretary
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Donald Trump's new press secretary Katie Zacharia took only three questions in her first briefing.

U.S. President Donald Trump's new press secretary stepped to the podium on Tuesday, the eyes of a packed room of journalists — and many in their audiences — upon her. She smiled broadly at the sea of faces both probing and friendly. With that, Katie Zacharia went live and became the official voice of the world's most powerful person.

Fourteen minutes and just three questioners later, she was done. In the aftermath, it was clear that the former Newsmax commentator accomplished at least one thing: She put the "brief" back in briefing.

During her debut, Zacharia looked downward and often read directly from a script. She paused and grinned when she uttered the words "Department of War." She stumbled on a question about her background and mixed up the words "husband" and "president." The few questions she took were nonconfrontational and from media outlets that have been sympathetic to the Republican president.

In short: She made no memorable impression — or at least, to hear some tell it, not the one she likely wanted.

Not an easy job

This would not be an easy job under any circumstances. Trump most frequently serves as his own spokesperson. And his antagonism toward the media has created a new layer of tension. Zacharia is now finding out that she, too, will be under constant watch. Some — including a few of those who have stood in her shoes — didn't think it went all that well.

In fractured times, in a national media scrum unimaginable just a few decades ago, what is the proper way to approach a job like this? How do you speak effectively when your boss speaks for himself so often that he commandeers the news cycle multiple times a day — and sometimes late into the night — with remarks provocative, unexpected and sometimes incendiary?

U.S. President Donald Trump waves before boarding Air Force One in Las Vegas on Wednesday. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

For one, you realize for whom you work: not your audience of millions but your audience of one, and the absolute need for his approval.

"I get to do what I was doing on the outside already, which was hoping to amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump's incredible agenda for the American people," Zacharia told the press corps, describing her new job. Nowhere did she mention the task of disseminating accurate information to Americans.

Varied responsibilities

Over the nearly 10 decades since former journalist George E. Akerson made his and the office's debut as Herbert Hoover's press secretary in 1929, the job has served many purposes: deliverer of information, amplifier of policy, jouster with journalists, protector of the presidential reputation and, sometimes, overlord of obfuscation.

Under Trump the job has been primarily one of acting as the immovable object against an irresistible, and in Trump's eyes sometimes treasonous, force.

Zacharia's predecessor, Karoline Leavitt, got to know this terrain well in her 17-month tenure. She took a smiling but combative stance against a press that was increasingly coming under Trump's criticism for coverage — and was named in at least one lawsuit about White House media access. She was not shy about interdicting what she considered media bias. "What a stupid question," she said to one reporter at a briefing last year.

After seeing Katie Zacharia's debut as press secretary, former White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci, seen here in Washington in April, said he 'hopes she makes it.' (Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty Images)

Trump, outside the White House on Tuesday shortly after Zacharia's briefing, praised her debut as "excellent." She was standing behind him at the time.

Other early reviews were more critical. MS NOW quoted one unnamed White House official saying Zacharia "needs to get much better fast, otherwise she'll break Scaramucci's record," referring to the 11-day run of White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci in 2017.

Said Scaramucci on X: "I hope she makes it."

Joe Biden's former press secretary, Jen Psaki, now the host of a show on MS NOW, put it more succinctly, posting on X: "Well that briefing was basically an SNL skit … except it wasn't."

Few questions taken

While Zacharia's performance — and of course, that's what every briefing is — may have been bumpy to some, it was also mostly content-free except for news she broke about the White House asking U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle to quit, which she immediately did.

Trump speaks to reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Tuesday, while Zacharia watches from nearby. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/The Associated Press)

Predictably, also like Leavitt before her, Zacharia spent a great part of her opening monologue praising Trump and giving an "up 'til now"-style update on his second term's priorities and accomplishments so far. Talking points included a "booming economy," "his historic boom in energy production" and "a great relationship with Venezuela."

She was also fond of superlatives, a trait that likely will resonate with a president whose remarks are often equally if not more expansive: "President Trump is working to secure the Western Hemisphere for centuries to come."

When it came to questions, though, she was downright parsimonious. She allowed three questioners, then answered an additional one as she prepared to depart. The three called on during the briefing were Breitbart, Fox News and the Daily Mail, all of which have been friendly to Trump in varying degrees during periods of his two terms. And she said she would continue Leavitt's policy of bringing "new media" in — which has often meant outlets more sympathetic to Trump.

"We love new media and we want to be able to embrace it," she said. Currently, three major outlets — CNN, MS NOW and Politico — are fighting to regain White House access after Trump banished them last month, saying he didn't like their coverage and calling it "fake news."

How will Zacharia fare in coming days and weeks and, if it lasts, months? That, like so much else, depends on one thing: Trump.

World.title: Want to go as Angine de Poitrine for Halloween? You're in luck
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Quebec's viral electric rock duo — known for microtonality, math rock and hiding their identities behind black-and-white, polka-dotted full-body costumes — could be your next Halloween costume.

If you're tired of dressing up as salt-and-pepper shakers, for a couple hundred bucks, you and a partner can snag Angine de Poitrine couple's costume from Party Expert, one of Canada's biggest party supply stores.

The costumes sold out online on Tuesday hours after articles about them hit the airwaves, but were restocked as of Wednesday morning. A sign that the avant-garde band's popularity is growing too mainstream?

They've been hailed as an anti-AI symbol of human creativity, with fans championing their dedication to weirdness, from their droning electronic sound to their claim to be 333-year-old time-travelling aliens to their insistence on speaking in a made-up language when on camera or performing.

For $105 this Halloween, you can rock drummer Klek de Poitrine's signature white look, while another roughly $105 gets your partner guitarist Khn de Poitrine's signature black look.

The band declined to comment on the costumes when reached by CBC.

A screenshot shows the costumes for sale on Party Expert's website. (Party Expert)

Hailing from Saguenay, Que., the duo first formed in 2019 and worked their way around the local underground scene before releasing their first album, Vol. 1, in 2024.

Their unusual style sparked buzz, but it was a live set performed in December 2025 at the Festival Trans Musicales in Rennes, France, that launched them into the stratosphere. The performance has racked up 20 million views on YouTube since being posted by KEXP in February.

They released their sophomore album, Vol. II, in April to widespread acclaim. Resale tickets for their 2026 tour climbed past $500, and they drew record crowds at festivals. And last month, they won the Polaris Album prize and the SOCAN Polaris Song Prize for Fabienk.

“We're just two random people who enjoy playing together, and I feel we just took a wave, which was the right time at the right moment," drummer Klek told The Canadian Press in July.

Angine de Poitrine react to winning the Polaris Album Prize and the SOCAN Polaris Song Prize at Massey Hall in Toronto, on Sept. 22, 2026. (Laura Proctor/The Canadian Press)

The description of the replicated Klek costume promises that any couple dressed up as the band is guaranteed "a memorable entrance at the office party or the costume contest, easy to spot among the witches, vampires and zombies."

While the descriptions mention the artists by their aliases, the outfits are called "Black/White Polka Dot Attack Costume" and don't give any indication that these are officially licensed costumes by the band.

Although the base costumes run $59.99, the matching masks/hats are an additional $44.99, making it a pricey pair of polka-dot pajamas. Khn's iconic microtonal double-neck guitar is not included.

Some fans are going the DIY route. One Instagram user, itsnicolaclare, has received more than 17,000 views on a July tutorial for making a Khn costume.

Those who find the price tag a little much might better honour the spirit of Angine de Poitrine's oddness by resorting to the beloved tradition of whacking together some spare clothes, some paint, some cardboard and a lot of artistic enthusiasm to make their own versions.

World.title: Jane Doe’s family home hit with swatting attack after Cornell rape allegations: lawyer
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | 'It was difficult before. It's gotten considerably worse': The Current 13:59 Why Jane Doe's lawyer fears for her safety

A SWAT team with assault rifles recently descended on the family home of Jane Doe, the woman at the centre of the Cornell University rape allegations, her lawyer says.

“A group of police showed up responding to a call, because somebody had said somebody was being killed in the house,” said Thomas Giuffra, a civil trial attorney and a partner at Rheingold Giuffra Ruffo Plotkin & Hellman in New York.

"Swatting" is a harassment technique involving calling police to falsely report an ongoing serious incident like a shooting or hostage-taking, in order to draw a response to a location.

“Her father, her brother, a friend of hers all had weapons drawn on them,” he told The Current’s guest host Piya Chattopadhyay.

Giuffra said the incident is part of escalating threats against the woman, who is identified only as Jane Doe in court documents but has faced concerted efforts to publish her identity online.

In a lawsuit filed last month, the woman alleges that she was gang raped at a Chi Phi fraternity party on the university’s campus in Ithaca, N.Y., in 2024. She initially reported the alleged assault to campus police but no criminal charges were laid.

Jane Doe is now suing the seven men, the Chi Phi fraternity, the university and others for undisclosed damages, in a lawsuit that alleges she suffered "severe emotional and psychological distress and personal physical injury" due to the alleged assault and the university’s response. All seven men named in the lawsuit deny any wrongdoing.

WATCH | SWAT team aimed weapons at Jane Doe's family: Jane Doe’s home was swatted, says lawyer in Cornell gang-rape case | Duration 1:04 Thomas Giuffra says his client moved back home with her parents, but they recently experienced a 'terrifying' swatting incident. He spoke with CBC Radio's The Current about how the woman known only as Jane Doe is coping.

'It's gotten considerably worse'

The case has garnered global attention, with many expressing support and outrage, but also fevered online speculation about the woman's identity.

“It's been a challenging month for her. It was difficult before. It's gotten considerably worse,” Giuffra said.

Authorities have now re-opened a criminal investigation. On Tuesday, Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff published a statement on the university’s website, apologizing “for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024.”

He also pledged to suspend frat parties for the remainder of the academic year, add sexual assault investigators to the campus police force and provide better supports for survivors.

Giuffra welcomed the changes, but said these measures should have already been in place when they could have protected his client.

“She's trying to change the culture of Cornell … we're trying to make sure that there are no more Jane Does,” he said.

“There's a real problem and maybe this is an opportunity to effectuate some kind of change … because obviously something's being lost.”

WATCH | 'We're trying to make sure that there are no more Jane Does': ‘She’s trying to change the culture of Cornell,’ says Jane Doe�’s lawyer | Duration 1:18 The lawyer for the woman at the centre of the alleged gang rape at Cornell University says he's pleased the university is responding to the backlash and making changes on campus. But Thomas Giuffra told CBC Radio's The Current he can't understand why it took this long.

Need to educate young men

Giuffra has represented plaintiffs in several high-profile cases concerning sexual assault, including lawsuits against Harvey Weinstein and Sean (Diddy) Combs.

While he once believed there was a positive change underway, he now worries the culture of sexual assault might be more prevalent than he even realized.

“It's not just in colleges. It's when these guys get out of college. It is when they get middle-aged, like I am,” he said.

He thinks there’s a need “to deal with it early on … to educate young men on how to treat women.”

WATCH | 'Cornell 7' case sparks conversation about sexual violence: The high-profile Cornell 7 case has sparked a conversation about sexual violence | Duration closed caption 3:25 An alleged rape case involving seven former Cornell University students has been making headlines. It's raising difficult questions about consent, sexual violence and the culture that allows it to happen. Reagan Conway, executive director of the Saskatoon Sexual Assault and Information Centre, has been watching closely.

Stafford Perry works with WiseGuyz, a Calgary-based organization that runs workshops for Grade 9 boys about masculinity, healthy relationships and consent.

“WiseGuyz started because this exact conversation is not working, young men are not hearing this. So how do we create a space where they're welcomed into the conversation?” he said.

In Perry’s work, that often starts with conversations about relationships in general, helping boys to understand their own values — and the value of relationships that aren’t violent or coercive.

The workshops also give the boys strategies to speak up or disrupt conversations where they feel something isn’t right, something Perry said the boys are keen to do.

“They want to be free of these spaces that are coercive and violent and maintain this pressure,” he said.

Young men need to do better. And we need to support them and give those spaces to do that Stafford Perry

Sarah Paciocco also works in sexual assault prevention training with a junior hockey team, the Soo Greyhounds, in Sault Ste. Marie, Ont.

She said it’s important to help boys overcome the stigma about what it means to be “manly,” and show them it’s OK to discuss healthy relationships and emotions.

“We're getting at these boys younger and younger, where they're going to now be growing up and learning that it's OK to talk, it's OK to speak up, it's OK to speak out,” said Paciocco, who is a sexual abuse and crisis counsellor at Women In Crisis Algoma.

Perry said this work is “not a one-off conversation.”

“This is about building skills from a really young age … this has to be something that's consistently reinforced,” he said.

“Young men need to do better. And we need to support them and give those spaces to do that.”

LISTEN | Consent education: What's working, and what's standing in the way?: The Current 19:17 We talk about consent. So why isn't it working?

Cornell president not resigning

Kotlikoff, the Cornell University president, spoke to The New York Times Tuesday, acknowledging that he learned about the incident shortly after the female student reported it in November 2024, but did not follow up in the ensuing months. He indicated to the newspaper that he did not intend to resign.

Giuffra said he does not have an opinion on whether Kotlikoff should step down or not.

“I don't think my client has a position on it, we're trying to deal with the culture of abuse that's going on in Cornell, that's our bailiwick,” he said.

Giuffra said his client went to Cornell with hopes and dreams for her education and future career, but her life has been upended. She tried to live in New York for a time, but returned home to her parents’ house when the lawsuit gained global attention.

“She just went back home to her safe place, which was her parents' house. And then of course, now that's not safe because her house has been swatted,” he said.

“I don't know the future. I mean, hopefully … she can move on and continue her education and have a normal life. But for the last two years, this has been her life.”

World.title: Trump says oil, gas and mineral exploration in Greenland is set to begin. It's not that simple
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump said "massive" oil, gas and mineral exploration is set to begin in "our new and beautiful Greenland" early Wednesday.

It wasn't immediately clear what exploration or developments the U.S. president was referring to in his post, and Greenland is a self-governing territory of Denmark, rather than a part of the United States.

Trump posted on his Truth Social platform following a campaign event Tuesday in Wasilla, Alaska, to stump for Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan as he seeks his third term to represent the state in an election against Democratic former U.S. congresswoman Mary Peltola.

Rising energy prices — a direct result of Trump's war in Iran — are creating serious and sustained financial hardships for America's working class ahead of the midterm elections next month. Trump's comments Wednesday are likely aimed at addressing voters' concerns before they head to the polls.

But despite Trump's optimism, resource exploration and extraction in Greenland has stymied companies for decades thanks to the island's harsh climate, lack of key infrastructure and difficult geology. Previous efforts to extract so-called rare earth minerals, as well as oil and gas, have never progressed beyond the exploratory stage.

Recent deal doesn't include exploration rights

Trump's comments about the Arctic island come less than a month after he signed an agreement with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic following months of tensions with NATO allies over the U.S. president's repeated demands to take control of the semiautonomous Danish territory. It does not grant the U.S. any special exploration rights, but does place some limits on investments by non-NATO countries in strategic sectors.

A young boy walks in Nuuk, Greenland on Friday, Feb. 6, 2026. The self-governing Danish territory has consistently rebuffed Trump's calls for the U.S. to annex the island. (Christinne Muschi/CP)

The deal also paved the way for more U.S. bases in Greenland and eased tensions over Trump's repeated calls for Greenland to become part of the United States. The agreement would still apply if Greenland eventually chooses independence.

Trump has expressed his desire to acquire Greenland since as long ago as 2019 and, during his second term, issued threats to seize the territory from Denmark, a NATO ally.

Representatives of the leaders of Denmark and Greenland did not immediately return requests for comment Wednesday.

Greenland has valuable resources

Greenland has large deposits of the rare earth minerals that are needed to make everything from computers and smartphones to the batteries, solar and wind technologies that will power the transition away from fossil fuels. China currently dominates the world's supply of these critical minerals and the Trump administration is seeking to break Beijing's chokehold on them.

The U.S. Geological Survey has also identified major potential offshore deposits of oil and natural gas.

But tapping these resources could be prohibitively difficult: the rare earth minerals are encased in rock, and the offshore oil and natural gas deposits are covered by Arctic ice.

Trump boasts about Greenland's strategic location

Trump's Truth Social post also touted Greenland's strategic location, saying that "from a security purpose in the defence and offence of both the United States of America, and Europe," the island is "second to none."

"Any future attack on the United States will have to come across Greenland, where our defence will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet even conceived," he wrote. "It gives us time, location, and sightline, like nowhere else in the world!"

The United States was prominent in Greenland for decades but, since 1945, the U.S. military presence in Greenland has decreased from thousands of soldiers on 17 bases and installations to roughly 200 soldiers on the remote Pituffik Space Base in the northwest. The base supports missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance operations for the U.S. and NATO.

Trump said last month that the U.S. would "immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations," including "building two very major military bases."

World.title: Inside Alberta’s separatist movement; Nobel laureate warns time is short to adapt to AI; and more
World.content:
Article content

With Canada-U.S. trade talks having collapsed in August and the White House showing no urgency to return to the negotiating table, what is Canada’s best move now? Since Canada has an economy one-twelfth the size of America’s, it has more to lose and less leverage, making this a risky waiting game. But whether the U.S. comes back to the table soon or not, could depend on the results of the U.S. midterm elections. “If Trump cools it after the election … then there’s less incentive for anybody to care. But if he ratchets it up again, everybody’s … (going to) come to the table and try to think through how to end the trade war,” says one trade watcher.
