World.title: Sheinbaum signs decree blocking violent and hostile content from minors’ social media feeds: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📱 Sheinbaum signs decree to curb harmful online content for minors: Social media sites and online forums will be barred from displaying or recommending content to minors that “generates or promotes” hate speech, violent extremism, self-harm, eating disorders, cyberbullying and illegal conduct. Platforms must also verify users’ ages, classify content by age group and offer parental supervision tools. The decree, drawn up after an Oct. 1 machete attack at a school in Torréon, Coahuila, takes effect one month after its publication in the government’s official gazette today.

🚓 Sheinbaum orders CNDH probe into alleged police torture in Guadalajara: The president said the National Human Rights Commission must conduct a “very thorough investigation” into allegations that Jalisco police tortured people detained at Sunday’s water contamination protest. “How is it possible that in 2026, there is still torture of young people by police?” she asked.

⚖️ Sheinbaum defers to judges on ex-INM chief Garduño’s exoneration: Asked about Francisco Garduño’s exoneration over the 2023 Ciudad Juárez detention center fire that killed 40 migrants, the president said, “It’s what the judges determined.” Lawyers for the victims will challenge the ruling.

Why today’s mañanera matters

At her Wednesday morning press conference, President Sheinbaum signed a decree that will bar social media sites and other online forums from displaying or recommending content to minors that “generates or promotes” hate speech, violent extremism, sexual exploitation or violence, suicide, self-harm, eating disorders, cyber-bullying and illegal conduct in general.

The government drew up the decree after a fatal Oct. 1 machete attack at a school in Torréon, Coahuila, that was allegedly perpetrated by twin 18-year-old brothers who authorities say were exposed to violent content and extremist ideology online.

Also of note at today’s mañanera was Sheinbaum’s response to allegations that Jalisco state police tortured people who were detained in Guadalajara on Sunday during a protest against contaminated water. One woman said that police beat her and stepped on her bare feet, causing fractures.

Jalisco Governor Pablo Lemus said Tuesday that all 39 people detained during Sunday’s protest had been released. He said that police used excessive force and made “unjust arrests.”

He also said that “serious mistakes that must be investigated and sanctioned” were made.

“… No one should have been exposed to violence,” Lemus said.

Sheinbaum signs ‘safe digital environments’ decree

Presidential legal adviser Luisa María Alcalde told reporters that she and other officials met with representatives of social media and other tech companies to discuss the “decree to guarantee safe digital environments for girls, boys and adolescents,” which was presented by the government last Friday.

“Far from demonstrating resistance, they perfectly understood the need for an instrument of this nature,” she said.

Alcalde said that the decree will be published in the government’s official gazette today and take effect one month later.

The decree will oblige social media sites to detect and “immediately” remove “accounts and content that promote or generate violent conduct,” she said.

📲 SHEINBAUM FIRMA DECRETO PARA QUE PLATAFORMAS DIGITALES EVITEN DIFUNDIR CONTENIDOS VIOLENTOS La presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum da un mes a las plataformas digitales para avanzar en la regulación de contenidos que inciten a la violencia, contra niñas, niños y adolescentes. ⚠️ Advirtió que, si las medidas no funcionan, se promoverá una reforma legal que establecería SANCIONES. Aclaró que no se trata de censura, sino de garantizar espacios digitales seguros. 📱🫡🫡 — Isabel Uribe (@Isa_Uribe) October 14, 2026

Alcalde said that social media sites will also have to “classify content” by its appropriateness for different age groups, verify the age of their users and “establish supervision tools” for mothers, fathers and legal guardians of minors.

Before signing the decree, Sheinbaum noted that social media and “digital platform” companies agreed with the government’s initiative.

“The only thing they asked for was a month to prepare their platforms so that this is a reality,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that the government’s Digital Transformation and Communications Agency will monitor social media sites to ensure that companies are complying with the decree.

“If we see they aren’t complying, we would move onto a law which would involve sanctions for the platforms,” she said.

Sheinbaum orders investigation into allegations of police torture in Guadalajara

Regarding allegations that police tortured people who were detained during a protest against water contamination in Guadalajara on Sunday, Sheinbaum said that the National Human Rights Commission (CNDH) has to conduct a “very thorough investigation.”

“Yesterday I was asked about the issue of torture in Jalisco. … What happened in Jalisco can’t be allowed,” she said.

“… In addition to the use of streams of water and tear gas [against protesters], the issue of torturing young people is something that has to disappear in our country,” Sheinbaum said.

“A police force cannot torture anyone,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that the CNDH investigation should examine “who gave the order” to torture detainees and interview “the victims.”

“… How is it possible that in 2026, there is still torture of young people by police?” she asked.

“… We, who came from the fight against [government] repression, cannot allow there to be police forces in Mexico that repress and torture,” Sheinbaum said.

Sheinbaum responds to exoneration of former INM chief

A reporter asked the president her opinion about the exoneration of former National Migration Institute (INM) chief Francisco Garduño, who faced a charge of improper exercise of public service in connection with a 2023 fire in an INM detention center in Ciudad Juárez that killed 40 migrants.

“It’s what the judges determined,” Sheinbaum responded.

Garduño, head of the INM between 2019 and 2025, was exonerated at a court hearing in Ciudad Juárez on Tuesday. Lawyers for the victims said they will challenge the decision.

Sheinbaum said that “a very thorough investigation” that examined “the responsibilities of each person” in connection with the fire was carried out. She then reiterated that the exoneration of Garduño was a decision made by “judges.”

According to authorities, the fire started when two detained migrants set a mattress alight to protest poor conditions in the INM detention center. Those two men survived the blaze and face homicide charges.

The Federal Attorney General’s Office began criminal proceedings against Garduño in April 2023, alleging that he failed to fulfill his duty to “supervise, protect and provide security to the people and facilities” under his control.

In September 2025, the former INM chief issued an apology to victims and relatives of the deceased.

There were “human rights violations that never should have happened” due to “omissions by personnel of the [INM],” he said at the time.

The Associated Press reported that Garduño “called for ‘those responsible’ to be punished and for reparations to be made without recognizing his own responsibility in the tragedy.”

To date, no one has been convicted of criminal wrongdoing in connection with the deadly fire.

World.title: MND Local Puerto Vallarta: Helping out after hurricanes, planning for Día de Muertos
World.content:
By the time you read this, Puerto Vallarta will be recovering from its third consecutive hurricane in the last few weeks. First came Polo, then Rachel, and now Simón — a Category 3 storm currently making its way up the Pacific coast. Luckily, the storms’ eyes stayed offshore, sparing the city the worst impacts. Still, our malecón and beachside resorts have taken a beating from intense tidal surges and waves; many neighborhoods have flooded, and we haven’t been able to safely enjoy the beach since Sept. 23, when the first red flags were raised.

Needless to say, many residents — myself included — are feeling a bit of a hurricane hangover these days and are thinking less about going out on the town and more about helping our communities recover.

So instead of entertainment listings, this week’s events roundup highlights a few volunteer opportunities and organizations that provide disaster relief and organize cleanup efforts after major storms and throughout the year. Whether you live in Puerto Vallarta permanently, seasonally, or just vacation here from time to time, there are ways you can help residents recover through these groups.

We’ve also thrown in what we know so far about Día de Muertos happenings. Even though we’ve been thrashed around by storms lately, this is still Mexico, so the celebrations will go on come hurricanes or high water.

Disaster relief, cleanup and community support organizations

Vallarta Cares

Vallarta Cares is a local charity that mobilizes food, water, hygiene and medical supply distribution to communities affected by natural disasters, including hurricanes, floods and other emergencies. The organization also operates a year-round soup kitchen that serves hundreds of meals daily, provides weekly medical services, including free dental services, and organizes medical brigades throughout the year.

Vallarta Cares was also recently awarded first place in the interior of Jalisco category for the 2026 Premio a la Generosidad Jalisco. You can inquire about volunteer opportunities and make a donation through its website.

Limpia Tu Mar

Limpia Tu Mar organizes trash cleanups along Vallarta’s beaches, rivers and at sea. Since its inception in 2017, the group’s cleanup brigades have removed more than 900 kilograms (1,984 pounds) of plastic, 125 kilograms (275 pounds) of styrofoam, 350 kilograms (771 pounds) of glass and 5,000 kilograms (11,023 pounds) of general garbage from the sea. Each week, volunteers set sail on boats from Puerto Vallarta to remove floating trash from the ocean.

Limpia Tu Mar also hosts one of Mexico’s largest environmental awareness events, the annual International Trash Fishing Tournament. This year’s tournament is coming up Oct. 18, and registration is still open if you want to participate or help sponsor the event. With all the recent storms washing tons of trash and debris into the bay, we could use all the help we can get to clean it up.

Local collection centers and cleanup brigades

If you are in Puerto Vallarta during hurricane season (June through November), local collection centers (centros de acopio) are often set up at community centers, fire stations and churches on short notice to organize relief efforts. Joining local community and business groups on social media is one of the fastest ways to find pop-up volunteering needs immediately following a storm.

One such brigade I join regularly is the Banderas Bay Project, started by local real estate agent Luis Salazar, which organizes monthly trash pickups around Boca de Tomatlán, one of the harder-hit areas from the recent storms.

Planning for Día de Muertos

Día de Muertos — Mexico’s annual celebration honoring departed souls — is around the corner, and that means Puerto Vallarta will again be pulling out all the stops.

This year, the city is participating in the statewide Festival de Las Almas (Festival of the Souls), featuring more than 350 free events across 11 municipalities in Jalisco from Oct. 24 through Nov. 2.

In Vallarta, the city is planning 28 free events and experiences Oct. 31 through Nov. 2 along the historic center, Los Arcos, Muelle de Los Muertos, Isla del Cuale, and, of course, the Malecón, which will again feature a monumental Catrina. The giant beauty has adorned the Malecón for the past several years, each time designed by a different Mexican artist. According to the Puerto Vallarta Tourism Board, this year she will be adorned with waves, whales, manta rays and bougainvillea.

If you do plan on heading downtown for the festivities, I recommend going early before the crowds get too big. Last year, we waited until after dark to go see the Catrina and were stuck in traffic for more than an hour trying to drive from the Marina to the Malecón.

Concierto de Día de Muertos

The Vallarta Symphony Orchestra will perform with the choirs of Puerto Vallarta and the University of Brasília for special Día de Muertos concerts on Oct. 30 at the Iglesia Reina de la Paz in Marina Vallarta at 9 p.m., and on Oct. 31 at the Haramara Auditorium at Universidad Tecnológica de Bahía de Banderas in Nayarit at 7 p.m. Tickets can be purchased from IAMPV.

Debbie Slobe is a writer and communications strategist based in Puerto Vallarta, Jalisco. She blogs at Mexpatmama.com and is a senior program director at Resource Media. Find her on Instagram and Facebook.

World.title: US congressional candidate says Mexico is where he gets healthcare as high costs dominate midterm debate
World.content:
Bobby Pulido, a singer and Democratic candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives in Texas’s 15th District, recently said that he does not have health insurance and has had to go to Mexico to receive medical care.

Pulido, who is running against Republican Mónica De La Cruz, made the unexpected remark to Council President and CEO Javier Palomerez during a virtual discussion on Monday with the U.S. Hispanic Business Council.

“I’m going to start off by telling you that I don’t have health insurance, Javier. And I’m embarrassed to tell you that I’ve had to go to Mexico for my health care,” Pulido said, as cited by news outlet Border Report, reportedly the only journalism outlet that accessed the meeting.

Pulido, 52, whose full name is José Roberto Pulido Jr., lives in Edinburg, a border city located in southern Texas. According to Border Report, he also owns a home in Mexico.

During the conversation, Pulido contrasted U.S. President Trump’s reported plans to boost military spending with the difficulties U.S. residents face in obtaining affordable medical care.

“I live in the richest country in the world. Now the president wants to give a million and a half trillion dollars for our military budget when we cannot provide affordable health care to our people,” he said.

Pulido’s statements did not describe what specific illness, procedure or medical emergency has brought him to seek care in Mexico. Nor does the information shared by Border Report specify which Mexican city he visits for treatment, how much he pays or the reasons why he lacks insurance in the United States.

However, this isn’t the first time Pulido has publicly shared that he has traveled to Mexico for healthcare. On Sept. 27, he told Univisión he sought medical services in Mexico due to high costs in the U.S., while questioning the power of insurance companies in that country.

Before turning to politics, Pulido had a renowned career as a Tejano singer, with a fan base spanning Mexico and the U.S. Over the course of a three-decade career, he won two Latin Grammy Awards for Best Tejano Music Album — one of which he won in November 2025.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: The MND Peso Index™ for October: Is the peso approaching its fair value?
World.content:
Listen to this article

THE MND PESO INDEX™

Tracking the exchange rate people actually experience

MND Intelligence · Sixth edition

Welcome to the sixth edition of the MND Peso Index™, part of the MND Intelligence™ suite of data products developed by Mexico News Daily.

The MND Peso Index™ is a monthly purchasing power parity measure that assesses whether the Mexican peso is overvalued, undervalued or fairly valued against the US dollar by comparing the prices of a standardized basket of 20 goods and services in Mexico and Dallas, Texas.

Since we published the September index, the peso has been on quite a ride.

Between Sept. 2, the date on which we collected prices for the September index, and Oct. 6, the date on which we collected prices for this index, the peso depreciated 5.5%, trading at 16.98 to the dollar on the former date and 17.97 to the greenback on the latter date.

The peso’s depreciation was the decisive factor behind our first undervaluation finding for the currency since we launched the MND Peso Index™ in May.

Our headline finding for October 2026 indicates that the peso was undervalued against the dollar by 0.7%, a swing of 6.5 percentage points compared to the 5.8% overvaluation we determined in September.

For a detailed explanation of the purpose of the MND Peso Index™, the makeup of the basket and more, please refer to the index article we published in June. You can read even more about the index in our introductory article published in early May.

What did the MND Peso Index™ tell us in October 2026?

In October 2026, the MND Peso Index™ suggests that the USD:MXN exchange rate on the date we collected prices in various Mexican cities and in Dallas, Texas, undervalued the Mexican peso by 0.7%.

The Mexican and Dallas prices were collected on Oct. 6, 2026. The MND Peso Rate — the simple average of the 20 item-level implied exchange rates, rather than the rate produced by dividing the total Mexican basket cost by the total Dallas basket cost — came in at 17.84 pesos per dollar, compared with a Banxico FIX rate of 17.97 pesos per dollar on Oct. 6.

The gap between those two figures indicates that the peso — at a rate of 17.97 to the US dollar — was undervalued by 0.7% in early October.

In the table above, you can see the Mexico and U.S. prices for all 20 goods and services in the basket, the total costs of the two baskets, the implied exchange rate for each item, the MND Peso Rate (i.e., the overall implied rate), the Banxico FIX rate on the date prices were collected and the undervalued assessment for the peso.

Why did the peso go from overvalued to undervalued in just one month?

In contrast to September, the MND Peso Rate for October (17.84) is lower than the Banxico FIX rate on the date prices were collected (17.97).

As a result, the peso has gone from being overvalued against the dollar in early September, per the MND Peso Index™ methodology, to being undervalued against the dollar in early October.

The shift was primarily driven by the significant weakening of the peso, as mentioned in the introduction to this article.

The peso depreciated 99 centavos from 16.98 to the US dollar on Sept. 2 to 17.97 to the dollar on Oct. 6, per the Banxico FIX rates for those dates. The U.S. Federal Reserve’s Sept. 16 interest rate hike and increased investor risk aversion are among the factors behind the peso’s recent depreciation. The Fed’s hike narrows the gap between U.S. and Mexican interest rates, making peso carry trades less attractive to investors.

The MND Peso Rate declined 12 centavos from 17.96 in September to 17.84 in October, reinforcing the shift toward undervaluation. Had the MND Peso Rate increased by 1 centavo, rather than declined by 12, it would have been exactly the same as the Banxico FIX rate, indicating that the peso was trading at fair value under the index’s methodology.

In any case, the difference between the Oct. 6 Banxico FIX rate and the MND Peso Rate in October was just 13 centavos. Hence, the undervaluation assessment for the peso is minimal, indicating that it was trading close to fair value on Oct. 6.

The slight variation in the MND Peso Rate is due to month-over-month changes in the implied rates for some individual goods and services. The implied rates that changed due to price fluctuations are highlighted in the table above.

6 months of the MND Peso Index™

Through the use of the MND Peso Index™, we have now determined that the peso was overvalued against the US dollar by 2.8% in late April, 4% in late May, 2.9% in late June, 2.4% in early August and 5.8% in early September. That’s right — there were five consecutive overvalued assessments for the peso before this month’s determination that the currency was slightly undervalued in early October.

The difference between this month’s undervalued assessment for the peso and the highest overvalued assessment — that in early September — is 6.5 percentage points.

So far in 2026, the peso has depreciated around 2% against the US dollar. It closed at 18.00 to the greenback on the final day of 2025, according to the Bank of Mexico, while the closing USD:MXN rate on Tuesday, Oct. 13 was 18.38. If the Banxico FIX rate was 18.38 when we collected the prices for the Mexican and Dallas baskets on Oct. 6, the undervaluation assessment for the peso would have been 2.9%.

* Price sources: Mexico prices were collected from the websites and apps of Walmart México, Costco México, AutoZone México, Telmex, Cinépolis, Petco México, McDonald’s, Starbucks, Netflix, Spotify and Microsoft. Dallas prices were collected from their U.S. equivalents. The Banxico FIX rate of 17.97 published on Oct. 6, 2026, was used as the official exchange rate reference.

World.title: Peru Probes Augusto Nava Over McDonald’s Row
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

Peruvian prosecutors opened a preliminary investigation on Wednesday 14 October 2026 into alleged homophobic harassment and a death threat at a McDonald’s restaurant in Miraflores, Lima. The incident was filmed on Monday 12 October, and the video spread on social media.

The case matters to US readers because McDonald’s is an American brand and Miraflores is a central district of the capital. It also shows how Peru handles complaints of discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity.

Key Facts —Who. Two men, Reinaldo Rivas and Cristhian Palomino, filed complaints against a man identified as Augusto Nava, who is a suspect only and has not been charged. —What. Peru’s Public Ministry opened a preliminary investigation into alleged discrimination, covering insults, harassment and threats linked to sexual orientation or gender identity. —Where. A McDonald’s restaurant in the Miraflores district of Lima, Peru. —When. The incident was filmed on Monday 12 October 2026, and the investigation opened on Wednesday 14 October 2026. —Status. Charges, detention and any response from McDonald’s have not been reported. —As of 14 October 2026, 22:45 GMT

What We Know

Two men, Reinaldo Rivas and Cristhian Palomino, reported homophobic expressions, harassment and an alleged death threat from a man identified as Augusto Nava. The confrontation took place at a McDonald’s in Miraflores and was recorded on video.

RPP, a Lima news outlet, quotes Nava in the video as saying “Los mato, lo peor es que no bromeo,” which means “I’ll kill you, I’m not joking.” RPP also reports that he said homosexuality is a sin and urged the two men to repent.

On Wednesday 14 October 2026, the Public Ministry opened a preliminary investigation for alleged discrimination. The case lies with prosecutor Luis Valdivia Calderón of the First Supraprovincial Corporate Specialised Prosecutor’s Office for Human Rights and Counter-Terrorism.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Peru ranks 5th of 14 with 54.7 points. Strongest pillar: military means (71); weakest: future resources (37). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Peruvian media report that prosecutors ordered urgent measures. These include reviewing security-camera and audiovisual evidence, taking statements from the victims and eyewitnesses, and ordering psychological assessments.

Investigators will also collect digital evidence of online posts and, according to Exitosa, coordinate with the National Police. A preliminary investigation is an early stage in which prosecutors gather evidence before deciding whether to bring charges.

RPP reports that Nava’s family attributed his behaviour to “Type I bipolar disorder.” The outlet adds that the family says he is currently hospitalised under psychiatric care.

We attribute that account to the family as reported by RPP. It is not a medical finding that we have confirmed, and it does not decide the legal case.

File photo: Plaza San Martín in central Lima.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What Is Not Known

The reports do not say whether prosecutors have filed charges against Nava. They also do not say whether he has been detained or questioned.

No statement from McDonald’s appeared in the reports we reviewed. We do not know whether the company has contacted the two men or reviewed its own footage.

Little is known about Nava beyond his name. A suspect is presumed innocent until a court rules, and the allegations remain unproven.

What It Means for Travelers and US Readers

The case is a local criminal matter, and the reports give no sign that it involves any other visitor or any change in travel advice. Peruvian prosecutors, not the restaurant chain, will decide what follows.

For US readers, it shows that Peru’s authorities treat alleged threats based on sexual orientation as grounds for an official investigation. The next public steps to watch are any charges, any word from McDonald’s and the outcome of the evidence review.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did prosecutors open in Peru on 14 October 2026?

The Public Ministry opened a preliminary investigation for alleged discrimination. It covers insults, harassment and threats motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity.

Who is Augusto Nava?

Augusto Nava is the name of the man accused by Reinaldo Rivas and Cristhian Palomino of homophobic harassment and a death threat. Nothing else about him has been confirmed, and he has not been convicted of anything.

What did RPP report about his health?

RPP reports that Nava’s family attributed his behaviour to Type I bipolar disorder and said he is hospitalised under psychiatric care. That is the family’s account as reported, not a confirmed medical finding.

Has McDonald’s commented on the incident?

No McDonald’s statement appeared in the reports from RPP, La República or Exitosa. The restaurant in Miraflores is where the incident was filmed on 12 October 2026.

Follow our wider Peru coverage for context on the country. We will update this report when prosecutors or McDonald’s say more.

World.title: Sencia El Campín Sanctions: 3 Steps Before Any Penalty
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

Estadio El Campín in Bogotá at night, seen from across the road (Photo: Gines-V, CC BY 2.0, via Flickr)

ANALYSIS · COLOMBIA

Key Facts — The country Colombia, where Bogotá owns El Campín, home of Millonarios and Independiente Santa Fe and the capital’s main concert stadium.

— Why it matters Sencia, a private concessionaire, runs the stadium under a 29.2-year partnership, so any penalty tests how Bogotá enforces such contracts.

— Why now The Dimayor cancelled Millonarios against Once Caldas on Tuesday 13 October because the newly laid turf was unfit for play.

— What happened On Wednesday 14 October the IDRD began assessing breaches, with quality discounts, fines and a penalty clause available under the contract.

— The numbers The contract tracks more than 500 indicators, and concerts set for 24 and 31 October are under review.

— What it means for you Ticket holders for late-October concerts or Bogotá league matches should check with promoters and clubs before booking travel.

— Still open The size of any sanction, the date of the supervisor’s report and the fate of the two concerts are all undecided.

— Power Index Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 51.9 points (October 2026 edition).

Sencia El Campín sanctions are not automatic, and Bogotá must follow a contractual process before any penalty applies. The city’s sports institute opened that review on Wednesday, a day after a top-flight match was cancelled over the pitch.

For foreign readers, the coming weeks will show whether a Latin American capital can enforce a large public-private partnership. They will also decide whether late-October concerts and Bogotá league matches go ahead at the city’s main stadium.

Where the Dispute Stands Now

The Dimayor, which runs Colombia’s professional football leagues, cancelled Millonarios against Once Caldas on Tuesday 13 October. It blamed the “lamentable” state of the field and said it acted to protect the players.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.9 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Mayor Carlos Fernando Galán then asked the IDRD, the Bogotá District Institute for Recreation and Sport, to open a breach process. On Wednesday the institute said it was assessing possible breaches by Sencia with its independent contract supervisor.

Sencia, the company that administers, operates and maintains El Campín, apologised to fans after the cancellation. It said it respects the decision of the sporting authorities and will work with the Dimayor, the IDRD and the clubs.

Our news report, Bogotá Eyes 3 Sanctions Over El Campín Pitch, sets out the cancellation and the city’s first response. The background on the concession is in El Campín Stadium Explained: Sencia’s US$754 Million Deal.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Colombia Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Sencia El Campín Sanctions: The Next Steps

The first step is technical rather than legal. The IDRD will ask Sencia for a contingency plan with recovery measures, timelines and the conditions for football to return.

The independent supervisor will then assess whether the operator breached its obligations on the grass. IDRD director Daniel García Cañón has stressed that any measure depends on that evaluation and the contractual procedure.

Only after that can the city choose among the tools in Chapter 12 of the contract. These are discounts tied to quality indicators, fines and the application of a penalty clause.

García Cañón told Caracol Radio that a cut in Sencia’s payment was also possible, and that the city was acting quickly. Speaking to Noticias RCN, he said the contract carries more than 500 indicators and all operating risks sit with Sencia.

A contract amendment signed on 27 February 2026 added a specific grass-monitoring procedure to the stadium’s operating manual. García Cañón says that change now gives the city the tools to track the turf and apply sanctions.

No timetable for the supervisor’s report or for a decision has been published. The process could therefore run on while the pitch problem keeps affecting matches.

What Happens to Matches and Concerts

The Dimayor postponed Santa Fe’s home game against Jaguares, set for Thursday 15 October, after a new pitch inspection on Wednesday. It then moved Millonarios against Once Caldas to Tuesday 20 October and Santa Fe against Jaguares to Wednesday 21 October.

Millonarios’ home match against Jaguares returns to its original date of Saturday 17 October, so El Campín faces three games in five days. The IDRD has offered the Estadio Metropolitano de Techo, another venue it manages, as an alternative for professional matches.

The IDRD will also ask Sencia to review the concerts set for 24 and 31 October so the grass can recover. That is a request rather than an order, because the operator controls the stadium’s programming under the contract.

“The priority of El Campín stadium is football, above shows,” García Cañón said in the institute’s statement. That line suggests the city will push to protect the league calendar if the two goals collide.

The Longer View for the Concession

The dispute comes as Sencia builds a new stadium on the same site, with work under way since Wednesday 30 September 2026. Galán expects the new ground, for more than 60,000 spectators, to open by late 2028.

Sencia committed COP 2.4 trillion (about US$754 million at Banco de la República’s 14 October rate of COP 3,181.74) in private investment. In return it earns income from the stadium and the surrounding complex across a 29.2-year concession.

The Sencia concession runs 29.2 years, most of it operation (Chart: The Rio Times; data: IDRD)

The IDRD has said the stands will be rebuilt one at a time, so football can continue during the works. That makes the state of the current pitch a recurring test rather than a one-off problem.

In January 2026 Corficolombiana, an investment holding company in the Grupo Aval financial group, agreed to buy 51% of Sencia. Any sanction would therefore also concern a major Colombian financial group, not only the operator.

What It Means for You

Travellers holding tickets for El Campín concerts on 24 or 31 October should check with promoters before booking flights or hotels. Football fans should follow club and Dimayor channels, since dates and venues may still change.

For US investors, the case shows how Colombian partnership contracts tie an operator’s income to quality indicators. A real penalty would show those indicators carry weight, while a quiet settlement would suggest they do not.

The city still holds clear contractual tools, and an alternative venue exists for league football. A credible recovery plan from Sencia could also limit the disruption for fans and visitors.

What Is Not Known

The IDRD has not said how large any fine, discount or penalty could be. Nor has it said when the supervisor’s technical report will be ready.

It is also unclear whether the pitch can cope with three games in five days from Saturday 17 October. The fate of the two late-October concerts remains undecided.

For wider context, see the Bogotá city page and What to Do in Bogotá in October 2026: BTS, Rock al Parque and SOFA. Country background is in Who Runs Colombia’s Economy, the Key Players in 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happens next for Sencia and El Campín?

The IDRD’s contract supervisor will assess whether Sencia breached its grass obligations, and Sencia must present a contingency plan. Any sanction comes only after that technical evaluation and the contractual procedure.

What sanctions could Sencia face?

The contract allows discounts tied to quality indicators, fines and the application of a penalty clause. The IDRD director has also said a cut in Sencia’s payment is possible.

Will the October concerts at El Campín go ahead?

The IDRD will ask Sencia to review the concerts set for 24 and 31 October so the grass can recover. The operator controls the programming, so ticket holders should follow promoters’ announcements.

Where will Millonarios and Santa Fe play?

The Dimayor has scheduled Millonarios against Jaguares for 17 October, Millonarios against Once Caldas for 20 October and Santa Fe against Jaguares for 21 October. The IDRD has also offered the Estadio Metropolitano de Techo as an alternative venue for professional matches.

When will the El Campín pitch be ready?

The Dimayor’s new schedule has El Campín hosting three league matches between 17 and 21 October. The contingency plan the IDRD will request is meant to set out recovery timelines and the conditions for play.

Sources: IDRD statement on possible Sencia sanctions; Dimayor cancellation statement; Caracol Radio interview with the IDRD director; Noticias RCN on the IDRD press conference; Canal 1 on Mayor Galán and Sencia’s response; Dimayor rescheduling statement; Caracol Radio on the new match dates; IDRD on the concession phases; IDRD on the start of construction (30 October 2024 to 14 October 2026).

World.title: Bahamas NIF Probe: What Comes Next After 13 October
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

Bay Street in downtown Nassau, the commercial heart of the capital. (Photo: Bluerasberry, CC BY 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

WHAT COMES NEXT · BAHAMAS

Key Facts — The country The Bahamas, an English-speaking island nation off Florida whose currency is fixed one-to-one to the US dollar.

— Why it matters Lawmakers are tracing B$700 million (about US$700 million) in borrowed public money that the government linked to a state fund.

— Why now On Tuesday, 13 October, the Public Accounts Committee chairman said the fund’s board never met and key records are still missing.

— What happened The committee expects to finish its main investigative work in October and publish a report by mid-November.

— What it means for you The probe tests how a dollar-pegged borrower accounts for money raised from international investors.

— Still open Whether the Ministry of Finance hands over transaction records and names the legal authority it used.

The NIF probe in The Bahamas now enters its decisive weeks, as a parliamentary committee pushes for records on B$700 million (about US$700 million). The Public Accounts Committee aims to finish its main investigative work in October and publish a report by mid-November.

For US readers, the stakes are fiscal credibility in a dollar-pegged country that borrows from international investors. Our explainer Bahamas National Investment Fund: What We Know sets out how the fund was meant to work.

Where the NIF Probe Stands Now

The National Investment Fund (NIF) is a state fund allowed under a 2022 law to invest in infrastructure and other national projects. The government publicly linked about B$700 million (about US$700 million) in excess borrowing to it.

Michael Pintard, leader of the opposition Free National Movement, chairs the Public Accounts Committee (PAC). The PAC is a House of Assembly committee that examines how public money is spent.

On 13 October, Pintard named five people appointed to the fund’s board, with appointment papers dating from August 2025. He said correspondence with Central Bank Governor John Rolle confirmed the board has never met.

Pintard stressed that the inquiry is ongoing and that the committee has made no final findings. He said the PAC will follow the evidence and will not prejudge the outcome.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on the Bahamas Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The Records the Committee Still Needs

The first next step in the NIF probe is documents. Pintard said the Ministry of Finance and the Treasury have not yet supplied the transaction records needed to trace the money.

He said the committee needs to know where the funds went, how they moved, which accounts were used and what transactions took place. Both agencies received formal requests at about the same time as the Central Bank and the Department of Legal Affairs.

Pintard credited Rolle and the Director of Legal Affairs with timely testimony and documents. Financial Secretary Simon Wilson and the Treasurer have both appeared, but he said gaps remain in the record.

.2 million at end-March 2026" data-lazy-src="https://www.riotimesonline.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/rt-chart-bahamas-nif-probe-next-steps-2026-1.png" /> .2 million at end-March 2026" /> The National Investment Fund's reported balance fell from B$265.3 million (about US$265.3 million) in December 2025 to B$0.2 million by end-March 2026, according to government budget reports cited by The Nassau Guardian.

The Legal Authority Question

The second open step in the NIF probe is legal. The committee wants the Ministry of Finance to point to the specific authority that let it act in the fund’s name without the board.

The PAC is examining an account at the Central Bank that has been publicly described as the fund’s account. Pintard said evidence so far suggests the Ministry of Finance and the Treasury created and controlled it.

The 2022 Act says the board opens the fund’s account with a bank recommended by the Central Bank. It also requires audited statements to be laid in Parliament within six months of the financial year’s end.

The government has defended its handling of the money, citing the Public Finance Management Act and legal advice. Finance Minister Michael Halkitis has said B$310 million (about US$310 million) meant for the fund went to public infrastructure.

Halkitis has not published a breakdown of that spending. The government has not responded in detail to the committee’s latest update.

The Timeline to Mid-November

The PAC expects to complete the main work of the NIF probe this month. It has set a target of publishing its report by the middle of November.

The committee is also preparing findings on B$1.56 million (about US$1.56 million) in vouchers handed out before the May general election. The vouchers were reportedly used for building materials, and the PAC has received payment records and testimony.

Pintard has renewed calls for PAC hearings to be broadcast on the Parliamentary Channel. He said the Speaker of the House has twice refused formal requests to carry the meetings live.

How the government answers the report will shape the next phase of the NIF probe. The Nassau Guardian reported that the government has yet to explain how money moved without the board convening.

What It Means for You

The Central Bank of The Bahamas keeps the Bahamian dollar at a fixed B$1 to US$1. That peg makes the country familiar to US tourists, investors and second-home buyers.

A clear accounting of borrowed money would support confidence among the bond investors the government relies on. A drawn-out dispute over missing records could keep the issue in front of lenders for longer.

Nothing in the NIF probe so far changes travel, banking or currency rules for visitors and residents. Our guides The Bahamas Explained: The Islands, the Economy, the Politics and What to Watch and Investing in the Bahamas as a Foreigner: Property, Funds and the Zero-Tax Frame give the wider picture.

Regional context sits in Bahamas and Its Neighbours in the Caribbean. The committee itself sits in Nassau, the capital, on New Providence island.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether the Ministry of Finance will supply the records before the committee’s October deadline. It is also unclear what legal authority it will cite for acting without the board.

It is not known whether the House of Assembly will debate the report or how the government will respond. No one has been charged, and the government says it acted lawfully on legal advice.

Frequently Asked Questions

When will the Public Accounts Committee report on the NIF?

The committee aims to finish its main investigative work in October. It has set a target of publishing its report by the middle of November.

What is the committee still waiting for?

It is waiting for transaction records from the Ministry of Finance and the Treasury. It also wants the ministry to name the legal authority it used to act in the fund’s name.

Has the NIF board ever met?

Pintard said correspondence with Central Bank Governor John Rolle confirmed that the board has never met. Appointment papers for its five members date from August 2025.

Has anyone been accused of a crime?

No one has been charged, and the committee says it has made no final findings. The government says it acted lawfully under the Public Finance Management Act and on legal advice.

Does the probe affect US visitors or investors?

Nothing announced so far changes travel, banking or currency rules for visitors. Investors are watching how the government accounts for money it borrowed from international markets.

World.title: Paraguay Central Bank Board: What Happens Next
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

The Palacio Legislativo in Asunción, where Paraguay's Senate would have to agree to any removal of central bank board members for poor performance. (Photo: Mx. Granger, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons)

WHAT HAPPENS NEXT · PARAGUAY

Key Facts — The country Paraguay is a landlocked South American farm and hydropower exporter, governed by President Santiago Peña of the conservative Colorado Party.

— Why it matters The Paraguay central bank board sets monetary policy and licenses every bank. Its credibility is part of the stability pitch Paraguay makes to foreign investors.

— Why now On Wednesday 14 October, ruling-party senator Gustavo Leite urged Peña to replace the whole board, and an opposition senator filed a removal motion.

— What happened Both moves rest on Article 17 of the bank’s charter law, which allows removal for poor performance only with the Senate’s prior agreement.

— The numbers The executive must send the Senate a replacement within 30 business days of any vacancy, and a successor only finishes the five-year term.

— What it means for you A drawn-out fight over the regulator could weigh on confidence in Paraguayan banks, bonds and businesses that US investors hold or deal with.

— Still open Whether Peña asks for resignations, whether the Senate votes on the motion, and what the bank’s review of ueno bank finds.

— Power Index Paraguay ranks 10th of 14 in Paraguay ranks 10th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 36.0 points (October 2026 edition).

The Paraguay central bank board faces removal demands from inside and outside the ruling party, but the law makes ousting it slow. On Wednesday 14 October, Senator Gustavo Leite urged President Santiago Peña to replace the entire board in Asunción.

Opposition senator Rafael Filizzola filed a motion the same day urging the executive to start formal removal. For US readers, the question is whether Paraguay can settle this without denting its reputation for financial stability.

How the Paraguay Central Bank Board Can Be Removed

The Banco Central del Paraguay (BCP) runs under Law 489 of 1995, its charter law, as rewritten by Law 6104 of 2018. Article 17 lists six ways a president or director leaves office early or on time.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Paraguay ranks 10th of 14 with 36.0 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (55); weakest: future resources (13). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

They are the end of the term, resignation, poor performance, intentional criminal offences, certified physical or mental incapacity, and death. Only poor performance, under paragraph (c), requires the Senate’s prior agreement.

That means neither the Senate nor the lower house can fire the board on its own. The executive must start the case, and the Senate must then agree before any member leaves.

Members are also suspended if a judge orders them detained for an intentional crime, under Article 18. No such case has been reported against any current board member.

Three Paths From Here

The fastest route is resignation, which the law says is presented to the executive and communicated to the Senate. Leite argued on Wednesday that Peña should order a complete change of leadership himself.

The second route is a removal case for poor performance, the path Filizzola’s motion invokes. It needs both a decision by Peña and a Senate vote, so it depends on how the ruling party splits.

The third route is that the board stays and the pressure fades. Lawmakers aligned with Peña voted down a lower-house motion against bank president Carlos Carvallo on Tuesday 13 October, by 31 votes to 26.

Leite, a Colorado Party senator, said he remains loyal to party leader and former president Horacio Cartes. That places the dispute inside a wider fight between Cartes’s faction and Peña’s allies ahead of 2028.

The Senate Vote and the Replacement Clock

Filizzola, of the opposition Progressive Democratic Party (PDP), filed a draft declaration that urges the executive to start removing every board member. ABC Color reported that it cites Article 17(c) and needs majority support to be debated immediately.

A declaration of this kind is not binding on the president. Its value is political, because it forces senators to show whether they side with Cartes or with Peña.

If a seat falls vacant through resignation or removal, the executive has 30 business days to send the Senate a candidate. Senate agreement is again required before the new member takes office.

A replacement director does not get a fresh mandate, because the law says they only complete the five-year period already under way. The bank president’s term runs alongside the president of the republic’s, which ends in 2028.

If the bank president’s post is empty, a director elected by a board majority runs the bank until a new president is named. That rule keeps monetary policy and supervision running during any changeover.

The superintendent of banks, whom Leite also wants replaced, follows a separate rule in Article 32. The executive picks that official from a shortlist of three drawn up by the board, for a five-year term.

Why the Pressure Is Building

Leite said the BCP left eight to ten of the Senate’s 31 questions unanswered, Radio Monumental reported. He called the official reply incomplete and said it raised more doubts than certainties.

The questions concern how the bank supervised lending to related parties and the case of ueno bank, a digital lender. These are political accusations, and no court or regulator has ruled against the board.

Hoy reported Leite as saying that business leaders had implored Peña to change the board at a meeting at the presidential residence on Friday 9 October. The presidency has not confirmed that account.

Former public works minister Arnoldo Wiens said a meeting between Cartes and former president Mario Abdo Benítez discussed the BCP situation. Hoy reported that another such meeting is planned for next week.

Background on the crisis itself is in Paraguay Central Bank Board Crisis: What Is at Stake. For the wider picture, see Paraguay Explained: The Country, Its Politics, Its Economy and What to Watch and our Asunción city page.

What It Means for You

For US investors and companies in Paraguay, the BCP is the regulator behind every bank account, loan and currency transfer they use. A credible, independent board is part of why the country is seen as predictable.

So far the fight is about how the regulator handled specific cases, not about the soundness of the whole banking system. The risk is a long standoff that erodes trust in supervision as the 2028 race heats up.

Watch for a resignation request from Peña, a Senate vote on the Filizzola motion, and the outcome of the ueno review. Our Paraguay economy guide for investors sets out the wider economic backdrop.

Paraguay's Chamber of Deputies rejected a motion urging the removal of central bank president Carlos Carvallo on Tuesday 13 October. (Chart: The Rio Times; data: Chamber of Deputies count via RDN, 13 October 2026)

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether Peña will ask the board to resign or open a removal case for poor performance. Revista Plus reported that Wednesday’s Senate session lost its quorum, pushing debate on Filizzola’s motion to next week.

The central bank’s full report to the Senate has not been published, so its answers cannot be checked independently. We found no public response from the bank to Leite’s latest demand by Wednesday evening.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can Paraguay’s Senate fire the central bank board?

No, because the charter law gives the Senate only a veto over removals for poor performance. The executive must start the case, and the Senate must then give its prior agreement.

What did Senator Rafael Filizzola propose?

He filed a draft declaration urging the executive to start removing every board member under Article 17(c). The text is not binding and needs majority support to be debated quickly.

How fast could new board members be appointed?

The executive has 30 business days after a vacancy to send the Senate a candidate. The Senate must then agree, so a full change could take weeks or months.

Who runs the bank if its president leaves?

A director elected by a majority of the board takes over until a new president is appointed. That keeps policy decisions and bank supervision running in the meantime.

Does this affect US investors?

It could, because the central bank licenses and supervises every bank in Paraguay. A prolonged fight over its leadership could weigh on confidence in the financial system.

Sources: Law 6104/2018 amending Law 489/1995, BCP charter (BACN) · Law 489/1995, BCP charter (BACN) · Hoy, 14 October 2026 · Radio Monumental, 14 October 2026 · RDN, 13 October 2026 · ABC Color, 14 October 2026 · Revista Plus, 14 October 2026

World.title: Santa Marta Travel After the Escape: 29 Still at Large
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

The Caribbean coast of Tayrona National Park, east of Santa Marta, Colombia. File photo. (Photo: Thomas Fuhrmann, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

GUIDE · COLOMBIA

Key Facts — The country Colombia, a major US security partner, is led by President Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office on 7 August and promises a hard line on armed groups.

— Why it matters Santa Marta is Colombia’s Caribbean gateway to Tayrona National Park, one of the country’s best-known nature destinations.

— Why now Forty-one detainees escaped a Santa Marta police holding centre on Monday 12 October, and a one-tonne cocaine seizure near Tayrona followed.

— What happened By Tuesday night 13 October, 12 escapees were back in custody and 29 remained at large, with 96 extra officers sent to the city.

— The numbers Colombia stays at Level 3, Reconsider Travel, in a US advisory last updated on 30 March 2026; Magdalena is not on its Do Not Travel list.

— What it means for you Santa Marta travel continues, with more police and no escape-related closure notice for Tayrona found on Wednesday 14 October.

— Still open Where the fugitives are, whether US officials issue a local alert, and the exact dates of Tayrona’s autumn cultural closure.

— Power Index Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 51.9 points (October 2026 edition).

Santa Marta travel remains open to US visitors after Monday’s escape of 41 detainees, but the city’s security picture has tightened. Colombia’s Caribbean gateway to Tayrona National Park now has reinforced police while 29 fugitives remain at large.

For Americans, the core guidance has not changed, since the US State Department rates Colombia at Level 3, Reconsider Travel. Magdalena, the department around Santa Marta, is not on its Do Not Travel list.

This guide sets out what changed, what the official advisories say and how the escape affects trips to Tayrona. It draws on the State Department, Parques Nacionales Naturales and Santa Marta’s mayor.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.9 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What Changed in Santa Marta This Week

Forty-one detainees broke out of the city’s Centro de Traslado por Protección, a police holding centre, early on Monday 12 October. Monday was a public holiday, and President Abelardo de la Espriella removed the city’s police commander after the breakout, Canal 1 reported.

De la Espriella, a conservative lawyer who took office on 7 August, has promised a hard line against armed groups. His decision on the police chief is covered in Santa Marta Police Chief Fired, 41 Escaped.

By Tuesday night, Mayor Carlos Pinedo Cuello, the city’s elected head, said 12 escapees were back in custody. Three had been arrested in Santa Marta and Ciénaga, and nine had returned voluntarily, Caracol Radio reported.

That left 29 people at large, with rewards offered for two priority targets known by the aliases Mongolo and El Guajiro. The mayor said 96 extra officers had arrived to support the search, coordinated from a unified command post.

The ACSN, or Autodefensas Conquistadoras de la Sierra Nevada, is the armed group that dominates the mountains above the city. Its background and its links to the escape are set out in Santa Marta Jailbreak: What We Know About the ACSN.

The president’s refusal to negotiate with the group is examined in Colombia’s President Rejects Talks With Santa Marta Group. For wider context on the country, see our Colombia explainer and our guide to Colombia’s key political players.

On Tuesday 13 October, police announced a one-tonne cocaine seizure in Calabazo, a rural area of Santa Marta near Tayrona. Preliminary findings tie the load to an ACSN unit, and investigators say it was bound for the United States.

The army and police ran the operation with the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), Caracol Radio reported. Brigadier General William Castaño Ramos, the police anti-narcotics director, praised the coordination between Colombian and US authorities.

What the US Travel Advisory Says

The State Department’s Colombia advisory was last updated on Monday 30 March 2026 and has not been reissued since the escape. It cites crime, terrorism, civil unrest, kidnapping and natural disasters as reasons to reconsider travel.

The advisory says violent crime, including murder, assault and robbery, is common in many areas of Colombia. It also warns of drugging, extortion and armed break-ins, including at hotels and other places tourists stay.

Its Do Not Travel list covers Arauca, Cauca outside Popayán, Valle del Cauca outside Cali and Norte de Santander. It also covers a strip within 10 kilometres (5 miles) of the border with Venezuela.

Magdalena department, which includes Santa Marta and Tayrona, is not on that list. Level 3 applies there, meaning US citizens should weigh the risks carefully before going.

The advisory tells crime victims not to resist if they are targeted. It adds that crimes against tourists in Colombia are not always prosecuted.

Santa Marta Travel and Tayrona Park Status

Parques Nacionales Naturales, the state agency running Tayrona National Park, had posted no closure notice tied to the escape on Wednesday. Its latest security closure came earlier this year, after threats against park staff.

On Tuesday 17 February, the government closed the park under Resolution 091 after blockades at the El Zaino and Neguanje entrances. Park staff had received threats on social media, and unauthorised fees were being charged at the gates.

On Wednesday 4 March, the government announced the park would reopen on 5 March under a new security plan. Parques Nacionales said 60 police officers were already inside the park and the number could rise to 80.

The plan included a permanent post for the Carabineros, the rural police unit, inside the protected area. The government presented it as a security guarantee for visitors, local communities and park staff.

Santa Marta travel plans should also allow for Respira Tayrona, a cultural rest period agreed with the Sierra Nevada’s Indigenous peoples. Parques Nacionales holds these closures of about 15 days three times a year, in February, June and between October and November.

The exact 2026 dates for the October to November closure were not confirmed on the agency’s website on Wednesday. Travellers should check the park’s official channels before booking entry, transport or campsites.

The cocaine was found in a makeshift warehouse in rural Bonda, near the park rather than inside it, police said. Officials have not linked the seizure to any threat against visitors.

What It Means for You

For US visitors, the practical effect of the escape so far is more police in the city, not new travel restrictions. We found no curfew, road closure or park closure tied to the escape in official notices on Wednesday.

Enrol in the State Department’s Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP) so the US Embassy in Bogotá can reach you with alerts. Follow the Santa Marta mayor’s office and Parques Nacionales for local changes during your stay.

Use registered taxis or ride services, avoid driving on rural roads at night and keep valuables out of sight. If confronted, do not resist, which is the State Department’s own advice.

Expats weighing Santa Marta travel or longer stays should keep plans flexible for the coming weeks. The ACSN’s armed strike in September showed how quickly shops and transport in the area can shut down.

The counterweight is a heavy state presence, with reinforcements in the city and police posted inside Tayrona since March. Recaptures are continuing, and the mayor said police had located two more fugitives.

What Is Not Known

It is not known where the 29 remaining fugitives are, or whether any have joined armed groups in the Sierra Nevada. Officials have not said how the guards lost control of the holding centre.

It is unclear whether the State Department or the US Embassy will issue a new security alert for Santa Marta. The exact dates of Tayrona’s autumn cultural closure also remain unconfirmed.

Investigators have not released full findings on the cocaine shipment or its planned route to the United States. Caracol Radio’s report on the seizure mentioned no arrests.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Santa Marta safe to visit after the prison escape?

The city remains open, with reinforced police and no escape-related travel restrictions in official notices on Wednesday 14 October. Visitors should stay alert, avoid night travel on rural roads and follow local authorities.

What is the US travel advisory for Colombia?

The State Department rates Colombia at Level 3, Reconsider Travel, in an advisory last updated on 30 March 2026. Magdalena, the department around Santa Marta, is not on its Do Not Travel list.

Is Tayrona National Park open?

Parques Nacionales Naturales had posted no closure notice linked to the escape on Wednesday 14 October. The park does close for about 15 days between October and November for the Respira Tayrona cultural rest period.

How many escapees are still at large?

Forty-one detainees escaped on Monday 12 October, and 12 were back in custody by Tuesday night. That left 29 at large, according to Santa Marta’s mayor.

Who are the ACSN?

The Autodefensas Conquistadoras de la Sierra Nevada are an armed group based in the mountains above Santa Marta. Police link one of its units to a one-tonne cocaine load seized near Tayrona and bound for the United States.

Sources: U.S. Department of State, Colombia Travel Advisory; State Department travel advisories data; Parques Nacionales (closure, Resolution 091); Parques Nacionales (reopening plan); Parques Nacionales (Respira Tayrona); Caracol Radio (recaptures); Caracol Radio (cocaine seizure); Canal 1; El Espectador; Caracol Radio (end of armed strike) (all accessed 14 October 2026).

World.title: Nasir El-Rufai: Power, Probes and Public Office Since 2015
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

Usman Dam at Bwari in the Federal Capital Territory around Abuja, Nigeria. (Photo: Uzoma Ozurumba, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

PROFILE · NIGERIA

Key Facts — The country Nigeria is Africa’s most populous country and a major oil exporter, with a presidential election set for 16 January 2027.

— Why it matters Nasir El-Rufai governed Kaduna State from 2015 to 2023 and now helps lead the main opposition presidential campaign.

— Why now On Wednesday 14 October he appeared at the Federal High Court in Kaduna, as anti-graft prosecutors opposed bail for his former aide.

— What happened He has been held by the ICPC since 18 February, and the Court of Appeal refused him bail on Friday 9 October.

— The numbers One case centres on a CCTV contract worth N8.68 billion (about US$6.5 million). He denies every charge.

— What it means for you His trials test whether Nigeria’s anti-graft agencies act independently before the 2027 vote, a question investors watch closely.

— Still open Whether he wins bail, how the courts weigh disputed audio evidence, and what role he can play in the campaign.

Nasir El-Rufai, the former governor of Kaduna State, has spent almost eight months in the custody of Nigeria’s anti-graft agency. On Wednesday 14 October he was back in a Kaduna courtroom, where prosecutors opposed bail for his former aide.

For foreign readers, his case is a test of how Africa’s most populous country treats a leading opposition figure before the 2027 election. El-Rufai has pleaded not guilty to every charge and says the prosecutions are politically motivated.

Who Is Nasir El-Rufai

El-Rufai governed Kaduna, a large state in northern Nigeria, from 2015 to 2023 as a member of the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC). The APC is the party of President Bola Tinubu, who leads the federal government.

He later broke with the ruling party and joined the opposition African Democratic Congress (ADC). In September 2026, former vice president Atiku Abubakar, the ADC presidential candidate, named him deputy chairman of his campaign council.

That makes El-Rufai one of the most senior opposition figures facing trial ahead of the vote on 16 January 2027. At recent hearings he arrived with Isa Ashiru Kudan, the ADC candidate for governor of Kaduna State.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The Probes Against Nasir El-Rufai

The cases are brought by the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC), the federal agency that prosecutes graft by public officials. Premium Times reports they stem largely from a 2024 Kaduna State House of Assembly probe of his administration.

At the Federal High Court in Kaduna, the ICPC has arraigned him with Jimi Lawal, his former senior special adviser, and five companies. The amended charge has 11 counts under the Money Laundering (Prevention and Prohibition) Act of 2022.

The ICPC alleges that in December 2015 he approved a CCTV contract worth N8.68 billion (about US$6.5 million) for Kaduna city. It says the contract went to Singularity Network Security Limited, a firm it alleges lacked the required experience.

The commission also alleges that more than N2 billion (about US$1.5 million) moved through several companies between 2017 and 2022. These are allegations in a charge sheet, and no court has ruled on them.

A separate ICPC case at the Kaduna State High Court covers alleged abuse of office and misuse of funds, on nine counts according to Daily Trust. Premium Times says the ICPC has also charged him with tapping the phone of National Security Adviser Nuhu Ribadu.

Custody, Bail and Disputed Evidence

El-Rufai has been held by the ICPC since 18 February under a court order, The ICIR reports. On Friday 9 October, a three-judge Court of Appeal panel in Kaduna unanimously upheld the refusal of his bail.

On Tuesday 13 October, a forensic expert from the State Security Service testified in the state case. He alleged that El-Rufai planned to spend US$600,000 to stall an investigation by another agency, the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission.

Premium Times stressed that this is prosecution evidence the court has not established. Defence counsel Paul Erokoro, a senior advocate, objected that the defence had no prior notice of the witness, but the judge allowed the testimony.

El-Rufai is also suing the ICPC at the Federal High Court in Abuja, seeking N1 billion (about US$751,000) in damages. He says the agency unlawfully blocked visits by his wife and son in July, while the ICPC says it restricted access lawfully on security grounds.

The state trial resumes on 30 November, and the federal trial is due to begin on 8 December. Our explainer Nigeria Opposes Bail for El-Rufai Aide Lawal covers the Friday 16 October bail hearing for Lawal.

What It Means for US Readers

The state-case witness described plans to keep investigators away from a company listed on the New York Stock Exchange, which Premium Times did not name. Daily Trust reported that the recordings mentioned the tower operator IHS, but no US-listed firm has been charged.

For investors, the trials are a gauge of judicial independence in Nigeria before a closely fought election. Dollar figures here use the Central Bank of Nigeria’s official rate of N1,332.09 per US$1 on 14 October.

The courts have so far followed normal appeal routes, and El-Rufai has been represented by senior advocates at his hearings. Travellers should note that the US State Department rates Nigeria at Level 3, “reconsider travel.”

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether El-Rufai will seek bail again or take his case to the Supreme Court. The audio evidence has not yet been tested in cross-examination, which resumes on 30 November.

It is also unclear how his detention will affect the ADC campaign he helps lead. The ICPC has not said when it expects either trial to conclude.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Nasir El-Rufai?

Nasir El-Rufai was governor of Kaduna State in northern Nigeria from 2015 to 2023. He is now deputy chairman of the opposition ADC presidential campaign council.

Why is Nasir El-Rufai in custody?

He has been held by the ICPC since 18 February under a court order linked to corruption charges. He denies the charges, and the courts have refused him bail.

What does the ICPC allege?

The ICPC alleges he unlawfully approved a CCTV contract worth N8.68 billion (about US$6.5 million) in 2015, among other counts. No court has ruled on the allegations.

Is a US company involved?

A witness described plans to keep investigators away from a company listed in New York. No US-listed company has been charged or accused of wrongdoing by a court.

When are the next hearings?

His former aide’s bail hearing is on Friday 16 October at the Federal High Court in Kaduna. The state trial resumes on 30 November, and the federal trial starts on 8 December.

Sources: ICPC, amended charge statement; Punch, 14 Oct 2026; Daily Trust, 14 Oct 2026; The ICIR, 13 Oct 2026; Premium Times, witness testimony; Premium Times, Court of Appeal ruling; Premium Times, rights suit; Central Bank of Nigeria exchange rates.

World.title: Solomon Asamoah: The Man Behind Ghana’s Sky Train Case
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

Independence Avenue in Accra, the capital where the Sky Train trial of former fund chief Solomon Asamoah is being heard, pictured in February 2023. (Photo: Matti Blume, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

PROFILE · GHANA

Key Facts — The country Ghana is a West African democracy and a leading gold and cocoa producer, with Accra as its capital.

— Why it matters Solomon Asamoah is a veteran African infrastructure financier who now stands trial over public money spent on a railway that was never built.

— Why now On Wednesday 14 October, a five-member Supreme Court panel dismissed his bid to quash a trial ruling and remove his trial judge.

— What happened The state says US$2 million left the Ghana Infrastructure Investment Fund in 2019 without board approval. He denies all six counts.

— What it means for you His career spans the African Development Bank, the Africa Finance Corporation and the IFC, lenders that US investors know well.

— Still open Whether the fund’s board approved the payment, what his defence evidence shows, and when the High Court will rule.

Solomon Asamoah, the former chief executive of Ghana’s state infrastructure fund, lost a Supreme Court challenge in Accra on Wednesday 14 October. He had asked the court to quash a trial ruling and to stop his trial judge from continuing.

Asamoah is the first accused in the Sky Train case, over a US$2 million payment for an Accra railway that was never built. For foreign investors, his trial tests how Ghana treats deals struck by state funds and their private partners.

He has pleaded not guilty to every count, and the charges remain allegations until the trial court rules. The Supreme Court decision means his defence will now be heard before the High Court.

Who Is Solomon Asamoah

Asamoah is a Ghanaian infrastructure financier whose career ran through some of the best-known development lenders in Africa. A World Bank speaker profile credits him with over 20 years of experience in investment banking and management.

He served as vice president for infrastructure, private sector and regional integration at the African Development Bank, the continent’s main public lender. Before that, he was deputy chief executive and chief investment officer of the Africa Finance Corporation in Lagos.

His earlier posts included a senior role at the Development Bank of Southern Africa. He also worked in investment advisory roles at the International Finance Corporation, the World Bank’s private sector arm, and at HSBC.

He holds a master’s degree in chemical engineering from Imperial College London, according to the same World Bank profile. That technical background is common among project financiers who assess roads, power plants and railways.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

How He Came to Run the Ghana Infrastructure Investment Fund

The Ghana Infrastructure Investment Fund (GIIF) is a state fund that invests public money in infrastructure projects alongside private partners. Asamoah led it as chief executive, with Prof. Christopher Ameyaw-Akumfi as board chairman.

When former President Nana Akufo-Addo inaugurated the fund’s board in April 2017, he called Asamoah one of the continent’s foremost specialists in infrastructure financing, Citi FM reported. Akufo-Addo also said Asamoah had been personally responsible for over US$4 billion in infrastructure investments across Africa.

Under his leadership the fund took a stake in the Accra Sky Train, a planned elevated rail network of five routes and 194 kilometres. The Auditor-General said the project was structured as a concession to design, build, finance and operate the line.

What the Solomon Asamoah Sky Train Case Alleges

In 2019 the fund paid US$2 million to South Africa’s Africa Investor Holdings Limited for 10 shares in a Mauritius project company. The Auditor-General later warned the money could not be recovered if the project failed to win approvals.

The railway was never built, and the railways minister said in November 2021 that Ghana would build no sky train. The Attorney-General charged Asamoah and Ameyaw-Akumfi in May 2025 with six counts, including wilfully causing financial loss.

The prosecution, led by Deputy Attorney-General Dr Justice Srem-Sai, says the GIIF board never approved the payment. Prosecutors say the deal was meant to give the fund a 10 percent local equity stake that was never secured.

On 2 July, Justice Audrey Kocuvie-Tay of the High Court ruled that the two men have a case to answer. That finding means the evidence must be answered, not that either man is guilty.

What the Supreme Court Decided

Asamoah’s lawyer, Prince Asafo-Agyei, argued that the trial judge exceeded her powers by calling his client “the direct cause of the loss.” He also objected that she had changed his bail conditions without hearing him.

The five-member panel, presided over by Justice Gabriel Pwamang, refused both his certiorari and prohibition applications, the Daily Graphic and JoyNews reported. A single Supreme Court judge had already refused to halt the trial on Monday 31 August.

Our full account of the ruling is in Ghana Sky Train Case: What the Supreme Court Ruling Means. The High Court is due to hold a case management conference on Monday 19 October.

What It Means for US Readers

Asamoah built his career inside development lenders, including the African Development Bank and the IFC, in which the United States is a shareholder. A trial of a former senior official from that world draws attention well beyond Ghana.

For US firms weighing Ghanaian infrastructure deals, the case shows that state fund decisions can be reopened years later. The stabiliser is that the courts, not politicians, are now deciding the question.

The US State Department rates Ghana at Level 2, “exercise increased caution,” in an advisory last updated in July 2026. The ruling does not change travel or business conditions on the ground.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether the GIIF board formally approved the payment, which is the central factual dispute. The exact dates of Asamoah’s appointment and departure as chief executive could not be confirmed from primary records before publication.

It is also unclear whether any of the US$2 million can be recovered from the Mauritius company. No verdict date has been set, and either side could appeal a final judgment.

Connected Coverage

For the wider political picture, read Ghana Politics Explained, Who Holds Power in 2026. The country’s basics are set out in Ghana Explained: The Country, the Mahama Government and What to Watch.

Visitors and new residents can start with our Accra City Guide for Expats and Visitors. It covers neighbourhoods, transport and costs in the capital where the trial is being heard.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Solomon Asamoah?

He is a Ghanaian infrastructure financier and the former chief executive of the Ghana Infrastructure Investment Fund. He previously served as a vice president of the African Development Bank.

What is he accused of?

The state says he helped cause a US$2 million loss through a 2019 payment for the planned Accra Sky Train. He has pleaded not guilty to all six counts.

What did the Supreme Court decide on 14 October?

A five-member panel refused his applications to quash a High Court ruling and to stop the trial judge from continuing. The trial therefore continues before Justice Audrey Kocuvie-Tay.

Was the Accra Sky Train ever built?

No, the elevated rail network planned for Accra was never constructed. The railways minister said in November 2021 that Ghana would not build a sky train.

What happens next?

The High Court holds a case management conference on Monday 19 October. The defence is then expected to present its evidence.
