World.title: IC WANTS SPENDING CHECK
World.content:
The scene in Black River after the town took a direct hit from Hurricane Melissa last October.

THE Integrity Commission (IC) has called for full documentation and independent review of 476 Government contracts valued at $5 billion that public bodies identified as related to Hurricane Melissa recovery, raising questions about how the spending will be reviewed as Jamaica rebuilds after the disaster.

The contracts were awarded in the final quarter of 2025, with most using emergency or single-source procurement methods.

In its special report to Parliament titled ‘Public Procurement in Jamaica: Key Trends and Issues — Contract Awards in 2025, with Trends from 2006 to 2025’, tabled in the House on Tuesday, the commission said 182 of the recovery-related contracts, valued at $3.9 billion, were awarded through emergency procurement.

Another 262 were awarded through single- source procurement, while 32 were awarded through restricted bidding. “These awards warrant full documentation and independent review by the relevant authorities, and will be examined further in the commission’s report on its special monitoring programme, which is ongoing,” Director of Investigation Kevon Stephenson wrote in the report.

The findings come against the background of a sharp rise in emergency contracting last year, as public bodies responded to urgent needs, including those arising from the hurricane. The commission reported that emergency contracts for the year totalled $16.3 billion across 588 contracts, a 63 per cent increase in value over 2024.

Of that amount, $10.5 billion, covering 331 contracts, was awarded in the final quarter of 2025. The report said $9.7 billion of that fourth-quarter spending, across 278 contracts, was awarded on or after October 28, 2025, when Hurricane Melissa struck Jamaica.

Stephenson acknowledged in the report the necessity for emergency procurement, but said the circumstances created heightened risks that required scrutiny. “The DI (director of investigations) recognises that emergency procurement was necessary to preserve life and to restore essential services.

However, the period following the hurricane was one of heightened procurement risk, by reason of the scale of emergency contracting, the size of certain individual awards, the use of emergency methods for contracts other than those identified as related to recovery, and the exemption of emergency procurement from the ordinary rules,” he wrote.

The report also raised concerns about how some hurricane-related contracts were recorded. It identified 360 single-source awards in 2025, valued at $840 million, whose descriptions referred to a hurricane but which were recorded as ordinary single-source contracts.

Of those, 337 were made in the final quarter of the year. The commission cautioned that some of these awards might already be included among the 262 single-source contracts identified as related to recovery. However, the report said the records indicated that emergency spending may have been understated and that the identification of disaster-related contracts was incomplete.

The findings do not establish that the recovery contracts were improperly awarded or that the spending involved wrongdoing. Rather, the commission is calling for the relevant authorities to examine the awards and the records supporting them. The report also recommends stronger checks after emergency spending.

These include requiring public bodies to report on their procurement activities following a declared disaster and improving oversight of emergency contracts, including checks on whether the Government received value for money.

The commission’s special monitoring programme remains under way, with further examination of procurement connected to the hurricane response and recovery expected to be addressed separately.

World.title: ‘A wish list’
World.content:
Opposition spokesman on health Dr Alfred Dawes responding to an announcement in Parliament on Tuesday by Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton that the Government will construct four new public hospitals. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

Opposition spokesman on health Dr Alfred Dawes has described as a “wish list” an announcement by Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton that the Government will construct four new public hospitals which will nearly double the bed capacity of the facilities they are replacing.

The facilities to be constructed are a new 250-bed Black River Hospital in St Elizabeth, a 250-bed Falmouth General Hospital in Trelawny, a 150-bed Noel Holmes Hospital in Hanover, and a 720-bed Kingston Public Hospital Campus at Orange Street, downtown Kingston.

“I must tell the honourable minister, that is indeed a very well put-together wish list,” Dawes said sarcastically as he rose to respond to Tufton’s 20-minute-long statement in the House of Representatives on Tuesday in which the minister told his fellow parliamentarians of the plans to construct the new facilities.

“We can rarely call it anything more than such because the weight of Cabinet approval is not a budget item,” Dawes added.

Tufton told the House that Cabinet had approved a partnership between his ministry and the National Reconstruction and Resilient Authority (NaRRA) for the works to be carried out.

It is being done in collaboration with the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB).

Dawes, the Member of Parliament (MP) for St Catherine South Eastern, told the Parliament that all Jamaicans want better, safer, and more resilient hospitals.

“The challenge we have consistently had is that whenever this Government is tasked with delivering, we don’t know the cost, we don’t know the completion time, and we don’t know who is going to staff it.

And we have seen that happen over and over again, Dawes said.

He reminded the legislature that in the early 1990s under an IDB-funded project to improve hospitals, there was a special implementation unit in the Ministry of Health.

“This project to rehabilitate and construct major hospitals is going to be lumped with the Montego Bay Hip Strip development, the Vernamfield development, and any other NaRRA project that they deem fit,” he said.

The first-term MP pointed to the continued rising costs associated with the Cornwall Regional Hospital redevelopment project and argued that patients in western Jamaica continue to suffer.

“In fact, patients all across Jamaica are suffering [and] the staff, they’re protesting almost weekly at this point.

And every time there is a protest or concern on social media we’re treated to tours of hospitals to come,” he said.

“This cannot be the status quo; we cannot continue to suffer while we hear about what is to come.

This Government has had 10 years to deliver and now they are delivering promises to come,” Dawes argued.

He said that the Opposition accepts that money must be spent on the hospitals that are being rebuilt, but said, “We would like to know how much money is going to be spent on the abandoned Black River Hospital, how much money are we sinking into these buildings that the minister has, quite honestly, said are unfit for inhabitation and occupation.” Dawes also argued that a hospital is not just a building and a bed, not [just] something to lie on.

“A hospital is service.

A bed without a nurse is a mattress,” he declared.

He lamented that there was nothing in Tufton’s presentation about a staffing plan and pointed out that by the health ministry’s own numbers Jamaica was experiencing an attrition rate of 500 nurses each year.

Dawes said the 47 nurses who arrived from Ghana recently are a welcome addition but that is a mere drop in the bucket.

In his statement, Tufton repeated that the climate-resilient facilities will be reconstructed and modernised by NaRRA.

He did not give a cost or timeline for construction.

“Together these projects will deliver some 1,370 beds inside modern, climate-resilient hospitals.

The three rural hospitals alone will raise beds from 260 today, to 650 beds, more than doubling the facility,” said the minister.

World.title: Jamaica Music Atlas active!
World.content:
Johnathon Kelly

Eager to share his enthusiasm for reggae music, Johnathon Kelly launched the Jamaica Music Atlas in August.

The website (jamaicamusicatlas.com) looks at the history of Jamaican music in 12 countries, among them the United Kingdom, United States, and Canada — home to some of the largest Jamaican Diaspora communities.

An information technology expert, Kelly used AI to gather data for the portal which he regularly updates.

It comprises almost 4,000 songs, 280 locations, and over 150 stories. “The response so far has been extremely encouraging.

What has been particularly rewarding is seeing interest come from well beyond Jamaica. Some of our strongest engagement and feedback has come from the United States and Europe, which really reinforces the fact that Jamaican music has a truly global audience,” Kelly told the Jamaica Observer.

“We have heard from music fans, members of the Jamaican Diaspora, researchers, and people who simply want to understand more about the history, culture, and stories behind the music.” Visitors to the website can discover reggae’s roots in each country featured.

For example, the first venues that played Jamaican music in the UK, the record labels, sound systems, artistes and producers who put reggae on the map there. There is similar comprehensive data for The Netherlands, Belgium, Germany, Spain, Panama, Japan, Brazil, Cote d’Ivoire, and Nigeria.

“A major part of the vision is to make Jamaican music history accessible to different kinds of audiences.

Some visitors may want to do deep research, while others may want to explore a story, follow a musical journey or play a game,” Kelly explained. “The site is gradually becoming a much broader digital experience around Jamaican music rather than simply a collection of information.” In the two months since jamaicamusicatlas.com was activated Kelly has consistently added stories and features.

“We never intended Jamaica Music Atlas to be a static archive, so we have been steadily adding new ways for people to explore and interact with the material,” he said.

World.title: KSAMC urges water party restraint
World.content:
Patrons at a recent water party (File Photo)

THE Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation (KSAMC) has urged water party organisers to carefully consider the timeliness and appropriateness of staging such events, as drought conditions persist and water restrictions threaten to become more stringent.

Speaking at the KSAMC’s monthly meeting on Tuesday, Deputy Mayor Lorraine Dobson, in the absence of Mayor Swaby, acknowledged the concerns of residents surrounding the issuance of licences for water parties.

She appealed to promoters to consider the plight of residents across the Corporate Area who are experiencing water shortages and have been urged to conserve, arguing that seeing water used for recreational purposes could cause frustration and distress.

“I therefore wish to make a direct appeal to the promoters of these events to act responsibly and with sensitivity to the circumstances confronting our residents.

I ask that they carefully consider the timing and manner in which these events are staged and ensure that their activities do not undermine the national call for water being experienced by members of our community,” said Dobson.

Water restrictions have been instituted by the National Water Commission (NWC) across Kingston and St Andrew, St Thomas, St Mary, Portland, St Ann, and St Catherine to protect depleted reservoirs amid an ongoing severe drought.

As of October 11, 2026, the Mona reservoir is at 36.3 per cent capacity, while Hermitage dam stands at 44.9 per cent capacity, leaving both critical facilities severely depleted despite recent rainfall.

Under the legal mandate, residents are strictly banned from using NWC-supplied water for any non-essential or unusual activities.

Prohibited actions include watering lawns, gardens, and farms; refilling swimming pools or ponds; washing vehicles with a hose; and washing down outdoor surfaces like roadways, pavements, or garages.

With no signs of the drought ceasing soon, Water Minister Matthew Samuda recently suggested that stricter regulations could be implemented.

Against that backdrop, Dobson explained that the KSAMC issues permits only to event planners who can provide evidence of a private water source.

However, she said the corporation recognises residents’ frustration and takes the responsible use of the increasingly scarce resource seriously.

“As an authority responsible for granting of permits for events within the municipality, we recognise the importance of exercising our regulatory responsibilities, responsibly in keeping with the national purpose to conserve water.

The KSAMC should not knowingly facilitate and even involve in the use of water supplied by the National Water Commission for recreational purposes in circumstances where such is prohibited,” she said.

“We have also taken note that the minister’s clarification that the current water prohibition order applies specifically to water supplied by the NWC and that promoters of water-based events are required to provide evidence of their water source where privately sourced water is being used,” added Dobson.

World.title: Central Kingston MP highlights big drop in murders
World.content:
Kingston Central Member of Parliament Donovan Williams making his contribution to the State of the Constituency Debate in Parliament on Tuesday. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

What was for a long time one of Jamaica’s most politically volatile constituencies, Kingston Central, which saw up to 50 murders per year, has recorded just four homicides since the start of 2026, Member of Parliament (MP) Donovan Williams has shared.

Williams, a second-term Jamaica Labour Party Government MP, spoke to the issue in the House of Representatives on Tuesday during his contribution to the 2026/27 State of the Constituency Debate.

“Major crimes are down, gang conflicts have plummeted, our murder rate is the lowest it has been when compared to previous years,” said Williams.

He pointed to the introduction of a zone of special operations (ZOSO) in the Parade Gardens community, noting that it has had an immediate impact.

“There was a time in Central Kingston when we were experiencing 50 murders per year across both police divisions that serve the constituency.

So far this year we recorded four murders across the entire constituency,” Williams said.

Highlighting that some communities were doing exceptionally well, he singled out Franklyn Town which, for the past two years, has had no murders.

He said that one murder has been recorded in the Allman Town community, one in Parade Gardens, and two in Rose Gardens.

The Rae Town community recorded a single murder in 2025 and none in 2026.

Williams’ report was specific to the constituency as Jamaica Constabulary Force data show that the Central Kingston Police Division, which expands beyond the riding, has reported eight murders so far this year, compared to 15 over the same period last year.

Williams told the Parliament that other major crimes have also plummeted.

“We still have some issues, we are working through them, but for the most part, we are doing exceptionally well,” he noted.

Our churches are open; our parties are in full swing.

Nightlife has returned to Central Kingston.

Our children are playing in the parks and in the streets and we intend to keep it that way,” he added.

“This is not the Central Kingston that we are accustomed to, this is not the Central Kingston I came and saw in September 2020,” Williams gushed.

He acknowledged the leadership of National Security Minister Dr Horace Chang, Commanding Officer Mishka Forbes of the Kingston Central Police Division, Commanding Officer Michelle Campbell of the East Kingston Police Division, and their predecessors who, he said, helped to lay the foundation of peace which now exists.

Williams also acknowledged the civic organisations that are playing their part in community engagement and peace initiatives such as Yard Empire, Social Development Commission, Project Star, Heavenly Culture, World Peace, Restoration of Light (HWPL), a UNESCOaffiliated non-governmental organisation, as well as the churches.

On the matter of the ZOSO, the two-term MP said the Jamaica Social Investment Fund has advised that an integrated infrastructural development plan has now been crafted for the zone and submitted to the Ministry of Finance for approval by the Public Investment Appraisal Branch (PIAB).

Williams said he was optimistic that the PIAB will approve the plan, especially given that the joint command has recommended the zone enters its build phase.

World.title: CHEQUES STILL COUNT
World.content:
THE Small Business Association of Jamaica (SBAJ) is calling for an extension of the timeline to phase out paper cheques as it warned that the pace of the transition could place additional pressure on micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) that still rely on the payment instrument for day-to-day business transactions.

Speaking in an interview with the Jamaica Observer this week, SBAJ President Garnett Reid said members across the association’s network of more than 700 businesses have raised concerns about the planned elimination of cheques — arguing that they need more time to adjust and access affordable alternatives before the payment method is completely withdrawn.

“Since the announcement of the phasing out, a number of our members have continued to ask us what will happen to those who use cheques. Right now, more than 20-30 per cent of them use cheques to settle transactions,” Reid told the Business Observer.

“We are not against the move to modernise Jamaica’s financial system, but the current schedule is too aggressive, particularly for a large number of small operators who lack the resources, digital infrastructure, and training needed to transition smoothly. What we are therefore calling for is an extension of the time frame by even a year,” he said, while noting that the extension would give businesses more time to adapt while the banking sector and other stakeholders strengthen the systems needed to support digital transactions.

Under the schedule established by the Bank of Jamaica (BOJ) and the Jamaica Bankers Association (JBA), the phased reduction in cheque clearing began on September 1, 2026, with cheques valued at $1 million or more no longer being accepted or processed. The threshold is scheduled to fall to $500,000 on March 1, 2027 and then $100,000 by September 1, 2027, before a complete elimination of cheques takes effect on March 1, 2028.

The BOJ, which has noted the phase-out as part of efforts to reduce systemic risks, said it will also encourage the settlement of high-value transactions through electronic channels, including the Real-Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system and Automated Clearing House (ACH) infrastructure.

Cheque usage locally, which has continued to decline steadily over the last two decades, saw volumes processed in 2025 falling 12.6 per cent to 2.4 million, as total value also declined 6.9 per cent to $444 billion. This compares with more than 8.4 million cheques valued at approximately $2.3 trillion processed in 2010.

Despite the decline, Reid said cheques remain important to some small businesses and as such, the transition must account for those that continue to depend on the instrument.

“Forcing micro-merchants into alternative routes like RTGS drives up ad valorem fees and transactional overheads that strip away the razor-thin profit margins of small businesses. We cannot strip a trusted financial instrument from the economy when the digital infrastructure remains broken,” he said.

SBAJ’s call comes amid recent legal challenges to the phaseout, which has seen at least two church groups stepping out recently to seek judicial review of the decision. The groups, in accusing the central bank of exceeding its legal authority, also said the planned phasing breaches the right of Jamaicans to equitable treatment. They have also similarly indicated that their members frequently use cheques to conduct business, pay bills, and settle debts.

The SBAJ said its concerns were further compounded by what has been a slow roll-out of the central bank digital currency JAM-DEX, which was introduced to support a more efficient and accessible payment system.

Reid said the pace of adoption, which has left some small businesses without practical alternatives to the payment methods they currently use, has also widened the digital divide between the push for financial modernisation and the readiness of merchants on the ground.

“We are in a digital era and SMEs are told every day to grow their digital footprint and increase digital acceptance… but I don’t think we’re all ready yet,” he said, pointing to the need for more training and support for business owners unfamiliar with digital payment platforms and online banking.

Highlighting gaps in the digital payment infrastructure, including limited access to compatible point-of-sale systems and digital wallets, the association further said these pose significant challenges for businesses seeking to make and receive digital payments across their supply chains. It stressed that merchants must be able to collect payments from customers, pay suppliers and purchase inventory using accessible and affordable options and in cases where digital currency is not widely accepted businesses will have to rely on alternative electronic transfers that usually attract higher transaction costs.

“We are modernising the top tier of the economy while leaving our grass roots businesses stranded. Right now, point-of-sale (POS) integration for JAM-DEX is incomplete and there are far too few active wallet providers in the market. Expecting a micro-merchant in rural Jamaica to instantly shift away from paper cheques to high-fee commercial options when they cannot even spend or accept JAM-DEX at local wholesalers is fundamentally unrealistic,” Reid said.

As part of the response, he urged the BOJ, commercial banks, and other stakeholders to work together to strengthen digital payment infrastructure, expand merchants’ access to digital wallets, and provide practical training to help business operators understand and use available payment options.

“Small businesses represent the backbone of the Jamaican economy. Modernisation should lift us up, not lock us out. We stand ready to collaborate with the central bank, but we will not sit quietly while our members are forced out of the financial system by an unforgiving timeline,” Reid said while stressing that the transition cannot be treated simply as a change in banking policy, but as a broader shift that must take account of the financial and technological realities facing small businesses.

World.title: BUTLER CRIES SHAME!
World.content:
Mona High Head Coach Craig Butler reacts during the rescheduled ISSA Walker Cup semifinal match against Jamaica College at Stadium East on October 10, 2026. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

WHILE expressing happiness that Mona High will be playing in the ISSA Walker Cup final, Head Coach Craig Butler has called for serious intervention in Jamaica College’s football programme which he believes is being undermined by a “must-win” mentality.

Butler’s team was granted a place in the urban area knockout final against Kingston College after the competition’s governing body, ISSA, removed Jamaica College (JC) from the tournament after using Reggae Boy Jamone Lyle who was found to be a professional player.

ISSA’s rules state professional athletes are barred from participating in ISSA-run competitions.

Lyle played in last Saturday’s semi-final in which JC beat Mona 4-3 on penalties after a 3-3 draw in regulation and extra time.

After Mona lodged an official complaint, ISSA investigated and it was confirmed that the 17-yearold signed a professional contract in August with Jamaica Premier League club Waterhouse.

ISSA’s disciplinary committee met and ruled JC’s semi-final win null and void which meant Mona will play in Friday’s final.

JC issued a statement early Tuesday afternoon, saying it “had no knowledge of Lyle having entered into a professional contract” while also seeking clarity on the application of ISSA’s rules.

The school, however, stressed that it “remains committed to working respectfully with ISSA and other stakeholders” to uphold the integrity of schoolboy football and support the development of Jamaica’s young sporting talent.

However, Butler who played Manning Cup for JC during his high school days, told the Jamaica Observer that he’s concerned about the direction that the school has been heading in and is urging past students to step in and provide guidance.

“I’m disappointed in the way that I see my school, JC, that I love and how they have allowed the boys to just basically do whatever they want and it has to change at some point and I hope that this is a wake-up call,” he said.

“I hope that the past students, Kit and Kirk Kennedy, Chris Williams — all of the past students that came from our era will go back into the school again and start to contribute in terms of mentorship and make sure the boys know what life is about.

Because guess what? This little football thing that we’re playing, it’s going to go and after that, what happens? Where are these boys being left? What are they being left with? Are they being left with some education? Are they being left with social education? Are they being left with integrity?” Butler, though, says he has nothing personal against Lyle but believes rules must be followed.

“I think that’s a disservice to the player because he’s young and malleable and he’s going to listen.

I don’t, in any shape or form, blame the kid.

I really like him as well.

After the game was over, I hugged him and told him, great game,” he said.

“But to know that the player is ineligible and still use him is something that for me questions Jamaica College’s ethos.

When I went to JC, there was a lot of ethics and a lot of honour in how they did things.

We didn’t need to win at all costs.

We wanted to give good contributors to society and to use football as a vehicle to teach boys how to be men and to lead.

I think this winning at all costs mentality has to stop and I think that JC needed this wake-up call.” Butler says more of his compatriots need to be vocal about JC’s situation before it gets worse.

“Unfortunately, I’m a brave man so I go and ask the questions.

I’m not going to be like my friends that sit down and say ‘yeah, Bullhead, you’re right’ but when the time comes, they keep quiet,” he said.

“I’m not going to keep quiet because guess what? That could have been me when I was a kid.

When Jimmy Sinclair and all of my mentors back then who coached at the school told me the right way to carry myself and behave.

Of course, there have been many times that I have not listened and many times that I have got myself in trouble but I at least knew what was the right thing to do.

I was able to come back to the nuclei of that.

So, I love Jamaica College and because I love Jamaica College, I want them to wake up and who don’t like it, I don’t give a damn.”

World.title: Macron and Merz hold keys to an EU budget deal — but may be too weak to use them
World.content:
Sealing agreement on the EU's long-term central budget, worth approximately €2 trillion, is the biggest challenge over the next few months facing leaders, all of whom must sign up to the final numbers. While it isn't just up to Macron and Merz, getting the chiefs of the bloc's two most powerful countries to overcome their differences would be a massive step in making all the pieces of the jigsaw slot into place.

But with Macron soon to leave office and Merz under severe pressure domestically, officials and diplomats in Brussels, Paris, and Berlin are playing down hopes of a Franco-German breakthrough this week.

"If the French and German leaders come hand in hand, I think that could change the game," an EU diplomat, granted anonymity to speak frankly, said. "You need [Italian Prime Minister Giorgia] Meloni and [Polish Prime Minister Donald] Tusk, but it starts with Merz and Macron."



While Merz and Macron may talk bilaterally during the summit, according to an Elysée official, there were no firm plans for a more formal sit-down, two EU diplomats said, adding they were expecting them to use the two-day meeting to hash out positions.

Domestic political weakness makes both leaders less likely to yield ground, three EU diplomats said.

Backfiring

For the French president, who leaves office next year, the fear is that making big concessions — like accepting cuts demanded by Berlin — could be weaponized by presidential candidates vying to replace him.

“Macron should not appear too conciliatory” in budget talks, said an ally of the French president. “It would backfire in the presidential campaign.”

World.title: Le Pen vows to downsize EU as she brings contribution cut fight to Brussels
World.content:
Le Pen also promised to “stop” the bloc’s Green Deal, which she claimed was harming economic growth, and eliminate institutions like the European Committee of the Regions and the European Economic and Social Committee.

“I’m not fooled by what the European Commission wants to do. The European Commission wants to turn itself into a state; we do not. And so we will stand in its way,” Le Pen said.

Though Le Pen has abandoned her calls for France to leave the European Union, she remains deeply skeptical of the bloc and its ambition.

She and her National Rally party last week said they would unilaterally slash France’s annual contribution to the EU budget by €11.1 billion as early as next year if Le Pen wins the presidency.

Le Pen frames the move as necessary to help fix France’s disastrous public finances — she is proposing €140 billion in savings by 2032 — but her critics say such a move would set up a dramatic showdown with Brussels that could end with France leaving the bloc.

Le Pen is in Brussels the day before EU leaders meet for key discussions over the bloc’s next seven-year budget, which Council President António Costa had hoped to get finalized before elections in France, Italy and Poland in 2027 that could derail the talks.

World.title: Albania’s capital burns as protests escalate
World.content:
Starting outside the Ministry of Education on Wednesday morning, masked individuals threw stones, paving slabs, bottles and improvised pyrotechnics at the institution. They ripped up metal railings from the side of the road and used them to batter the iron gates of the building. After several hours, police with batons, tear gas guns, water cannons, and riot gear moved in, forcibly removing protesters and citizens from the vicinity.

Over the following hours, the situation escalated further as protestors set fire to benches, trees, and several buildings. They breached the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Justice, and the Ministry of Finance, damaged several private businesses and billboards, then moved to the main boulevard and encircled the prime minister’s office. They later broke into shopping centers and banks.

Economy Minister Delina Ibrahimaj condemned the “burning and destruction of institutional premises,” calling them “unacceptable acts.”

As of Wednesday evening, at least 40 demonstrators had been arrested and dozens of injuries had been reported by protestors, civilians, and the police. Several journalists reported being prevented from conducting their work by police who physically blocked them or seized their equipment. On Tuesday evening, one young man had his legs broken and required emergency surgery following an altercation with police.

The situation remains tense as protestors, mostly in masks, and police continue to battle it out on the city’s main boulevard, home to several parliament buildings, the president’s office, and the prime minister’s office.

The U.S. Embassy in Tirana warned its citizens to be vigilant and avoid areas impacted by the protest, noting that it could spread. Explosions and sirens continue to be heard throughout the city center on Wednesday evening.

Meanwhile, the delegation of the European Union to Albania stated it has taken note of allegations of excessive violence by police against protestors and journalists and expects the police to prioritize full investigations. The EU delegation also called for de-escalation from both sides.

World.title: EU leaders gather to talk energy crisis, China and budget — live updates
World.content:
Thursday’s talks span demands for cheaper energy, stronger protection for European industry and a widening divide over the bloc’s spending priorities.

This European Council was meant to move the bloc closer to getting a deal on the bloc’s next seven-year budget. Instead, leaders face two days of talks ranging from energy prices and trade with China to Ukraine, maritime security and migration.

The budget debate remains a test for European Council President António Costa. Capitals have softened their commitment to a December deadline for a deal as the warring camps remain miles apart.

Thursday’s discussions will start with competitiveness, with soaring energy prices and the EU’s climate rules also in the spotlight. Leaders will then discuss China and calls for stronger trade defenses before turning to Ireland’s revised budget proposal in the afternoon.

Scroll down for all the updates, brought to you live from our team at the summit.

World.title: Ukrainian officers warn Starlink slowdown ‘comparable to a nuclear strike against us’
World.content:
“Since last night, all Starlink and Starshield terminals used by our forces have been subject to a speed limit of 100 kilometers per hour,” the officer said.

POLITICO talked to three frontline soldiers, who all spoke on condition of being granted anonymity, as well as a Ukrainian defense ministry spokesperson and the EU's top defense official.

The reported restrictions have revived a question Ukrainian commanders have worried about for years: how much of the country’s battlefield communications can rely on a service controlled by a U.S. company.

Ukrainian soldiers say the restrictions have halted some medium-range drone strikes over Ukraine, disrupting attacks on Russian logistics and leaving frontline Ukrainian troops with less support. The scale of the disruption — and whether it was deliberate — remains unclear.

In a comment on X, Musk said: "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," referring to the Starshield division of Starlink that is used for military purposes.

"Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX," he added. "Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."

World.title: Deadly drone strikes in NATO waters raise stakes for Black Sea trade
World.content:
Russia has been attacking Ukrainian ports and cities in the area since the start of its full-scale invasion. But the recent strikes have brought the spillover into NATO territory. If they continue, EU leaders will face pressure to protect Black Sea shipping and keep Ukrainian trade moving.

Those questions will be top of mind at Thursday’s European Council summit. According to draft conclusions obtained by POLITICO, leaders are expected to discuss the “immediate restoration of safe passage for grain cargo ships.”

A wider problem

Russia is not the only country using naval drones in the Black Sea. Ukraine has also used them against Russian-linked shipping. In June, a Ukrainian sea drone exploded in Romania’s Constanța port after Kyiv said it had veered off course because of Russian electronic interference.

“The Black Sea situation is quite dangerous because attacks are coming from both [sides],” said an EU shipping representative, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. “You have to worry about both.”

Attribution can also be difficult. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said Wednesday that investigators still have not proven that Russia is behind the strikes — although some have attributed his reticence to his broadly softer approach toward the Kremlin.

Drone operations by both Russia and Ukraine are likely to continue as long as each has the money and production capacity to sustain them, said Cristian Vlas, assistant research manager for Eastern Europe at the think tank ACLED.

World.title: NGO: Brussels confirms Czech PM’s agri business conflict of interest
World.content:
Babiš has been under renewed scrutiny over Agrofert — a large agro-chemical conglomerate and a major recipient of EU funds — as well as other companies since his return to power last year. Babiš placed the company in a trust fund in a bid to avoid a conflict of interest, but the arrangement has raised questions from both the Commission and the Czech opposition, partly because his children would benefit from it after his death.

Babiš has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing. “I don’t own Agrofert, I never will again and I don’t benefit from it in any way. I don’t know what else I’m supposed to do,” he told Czech media last month. “Apparently, even if I shot myself, it still wouldn’t be enough.”



Babiš’ office did not immediately reply to POLITICO’s request for comment about the contents of the letter.



Werner warned in the letter that Brussels would take all necessary steps to protect EU funds, “including the possible interruption of payment deadlines, suspension of payments or application of financial corrections,” according to TI Czechia.



TI Czechia Executive Director David Kotora told POLITICO that he received the letter in September. A follow-up letter from Werner dated Oct. 5 gives the NGO permission to share the contents of the letter without publishing it.

The conflict-of-interest dispute echoes Babiš’ first term as prime minister, when a Commission audit found he still controlled Agrofert. That left Czech taxpayers to foot the bill for EU subsidies deemed to be erroneously paid.



History could now repeat itself as Brussels last month froze €3.18 million in reimbursements to the Czech state for farm subsidies paid out to Agrofert. That followed its earlier May decision that it would not reimburse any paid-out subsidies until doubts about his involvement in the business could be put to rest.



Commission spokesperson Louise Bogey confirmed it had sent a letter to TI Czechia in September, but would not comment on its content. However, she pointed to her remarks at a Sept. 8 midday briefing, during which she said Babiš was in a “potential conflict of interest” and that “the Commission considers the trust fund set up by Mr. Babiš does not sufficiently mitigate this situation.”



Czechia’s agricultural paying agency, which earlier decided that the conglomerate is eligible for EU subsidies despite the Commission’s warning, said Tuesday it had sent clarifications to the Commission this week.



Agrofert spokesperson Pavel Heřmanský said neither Agrofert nor any of its subsidiaries were involved in the communication between the Commission and Czech authorities.



“The cited letter from DG AGRI expresses the opinion of one of the European Commission’s departments. It does not constitute an official position of the European Commission,” said Heřmanský in a statement, adding that “only the Court of Justice of the European Union can provide a binding interpretation of European Union law.”

He added: “We remain convinced that we have received and continue to receive subsidies in compliance with both Czech and European law.”

World.title: UK rolls out King Charles to welcome Zelenskyy after Trump rift
World.content:
Burnham told Zelenskyy the U.K. will continue to develop innovative military solutions for use on the battlefield in Ukraine — including retrofitting British capability onto equipment gifted from other partners, the spokesperson said. He also pledged to continue diplomatic efforts on international supplies of defensive equipment.

In an earlier interview with the broadcaster Piers Morgan, Zelenskyy said Trump’s deal with Russia meant he is “not the right side of history” and said Ukraine is “losing a strong partner.”

He said there had been a deliberate decision by Elon Musk’s SpaceX and the U.S. to block access to the satellite system Starlink, warning “this decision will bring a lot of human losses. Of course, people will die.”

Burnham has so far refused to condemn the U.S. president for making a deal with Russia, telling MPs Wednesday he wants to “try and repair bridges so that the support comes back.”

In an overnight statement issued by No. 10 ahead of the visit, Burnham said: “Our rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment they need to push back Russia.

“My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer, we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe. It is not just the right thing to do, but it’s the necessary thing to do. Russia’s aggression cannot be allowed to succeed on our continent.”

World.title: Indonesia: Bali fuel supply delays spark panic buying and hours-long queues
World.content:
Queues of motorcycles and cars spilled onto roads across the Indonesian resort island. One Denpasar resident said she had waited about seven hours in the heat to buy petrol.

 

Officials blamed distribution delays rather than depleted island-wide stocks. Indonesia’s state-owned energy company Pertamina said a tanker’s anchor problem had delayed unloading, while road congestion slowed deliveries to stations. Panic buying added to the pressure, particularly for cheaper, subsidised Pertalite petrol.

Bali Governor Wayan Koster urged residents not to panic, saying fuel remained available at storage depots. Pertamina said on Wednesday that an additional 57.9 million litres of petrol were scheduled to arrive in Bali between 14 and 17 October. Deliveries were stepped up around the clock, with 60 stations in Denpasar operating 24 hours a day. Queues persisted despite the additional supplies.

World.title: Macron warns student anger is being exploited as France braces for more protests
World.content:
Day after day, secondary school students continue to mobilise across France. Most of the actions take the form of peaceful blockades, yet they do not erase the memory of several violent incidents.

 

The security forces, for their part, are preparing for another day of protests on Saturday 17 October. The government, meanwhile, is issuing a warning.

"The President of the Republic stressed that young people are expressing legitimate anxieties, but that these anxieties are being exploited politically and turned into urban violence, with scenes that are unacceptable", government spokesperson Maud Bregeon said.

Since the start of the movement, more than 6,800 people, 86% of them minors, have been taken into police custody. In that time 36 investigations have been opened by the police regulator the IGPN.

In an attempt to calm the anger of lycée students, the government announced several measures a few days ago, including the deployment of 3,000 substitute teachers to certain schools.

Measures that the students consider insufficient.

World.title: Le Pen lands in Brussels lashing out at the European Commission
World.content:
French far-right leader Marine Le Pen is preparing to challenge the EU’s powers if she is elected president next May.

 

The National Rally leader said the European Commission should stop acting in policy areas she considers outside its remit, including health, security and international diplomacy.

"[The Commission] is like the frog in the fable that puffs itself up to be as big as the ox," she said, referring to La Fontaine’s fable, at a press conference in Brussels on Monday. It was following a meeting with leaders of Patriots for Europe, the far-right group her party belongs to.

Le Pen, who leads the polls ahead of the presidential election, also said France’s net contribution to the EU budget should be capped at €5 billion a year, a sharp cut from the current level of around €8 billion, according to figures published by the French Senate.

"Being pro-France does not mean being anti-Europe," she said, setting out several proposals for EU-wide action.

She called for a "real" carbon border tax on imports from countries with weaker environmental standards, with exemptions for products such as fertilisers and coffee that Europe does not produce. She also proposed harmonised taxes on tobacco and alcohol, as well as a common EU corporate tax for large companies, with a single rate of between 20% and 25%.

Le Pen said these measures would help ease the burden on French taxpayers. Last week, she unveiled a plan to save €140 billion over five years, aiming to bring France’s public deficit below 3% of GDP by 2030.

No more money for Ukraine, sanctions relief for Russia

If elected, Le Pen would halt French funding for Ukraine, arguing that France can no longer afford it given the state of its public finances, while pushing for an end to EU sanctions against Russia.

"This funding will stop, and it is a matter of honesty to tell [Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy] the truth," she said in response to a question from Euronews.

Her position would put France at odds with other EU leaders, who are expected to reaffirm their support for Ukraine at a summit in Brussels on Thursday and Friday.

In February, EU countries agreed a €90 billion loan to cover Ukraine’s budgetary and military needs, with a first tranche of €45 billion due next year. But Ukraine needs around €70 billion in additional funding, its Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko has warned.

Le Pen also broke with the broader EU consensus on the need to step up pressure on Russia to end the war.

As the European Commission prepares its 22nd package of sanctions, Le Pen claimed that the restrictions have hurt European economies more than Russia.

"We were right to say that sanctions would have had no impact on Russia and would have increased the price of the raw materials they sell," she said, arguing that EU countries have continued buying Russian oil and gas, thereby enriching Moscow.

World.title: Meloni warns Trump's Russian diesel deal is 'very risky' and legitimises Moscow
World.content:
The Trump-Putin deal on the purchase of Russian diesel “is a very risky choice” and “a legitimisation for Moscow while its bombs are still falling on Ukrainian cities”, Giorgia Meloni said in Rome on Wednesday, swiftly winning Kyiv’s approval and provoking a prickly response from Russia.

 

The Italian prime minister, speaking in Parliament before heading to Brussels for Thursday and Friday’s European Council, warned of an “implicit weakening of the sanctions lever”, which she said runs counter to what has so far been done, including by the United States, “to push Putin to sit down at the negotiating table”.

How Kyiv and Moscow reacted to Meloni’s remarks

On the Russian president, the Italian leader added that “he is provoking Europe because he needs to divert attention from how the conflict is going and is looking for a new enemy”, while on support for Ukraine she stressed that “Italy’s position does not change”.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy, visiting London on Wednesday, took to X to thank Meloni “for understanding who the aggressor is and what it means to build a dignified and lasting peace”.

In an interview in the United Kingdom, the Ukrainian president said it was “painful that President Trump chooses a different side”, implicitly referring to the alleged lack of cooperation by the US Starlink satellite network in providing data on incoming Russian missiles during the latest waves of attacks on Ukraine.

The tone in Moscow was very different. Commenting on Meloni’s words, Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told Italian media: “It is none of her business.”

Italy urges the E3 to negotiate on everyone’s behalf

The prime minister also touched on Europe’s presence at the negotiating table, where other European countries have already stepped in. “If France, Germany and Great Britain, in the well-known E3 format, believe they can do better on their own than we could all do together, and so far that is the choice they have made, then at the very least they should do so on behalf of everyone and with an official mandate from all,” Meloni told the Senate.

“What matters to me is that Europe does not move ahead in a haphazard way, does not expose itself to those who have an interest in fuelling divisions and speaks with a single voice,” she added, calling for “the Twenty-Seven to identify a respected figure, with a mandate from all, capable of bringing Europe’s voice to the table. And if we cannot agree on a name, we are ready to consider different solutions”.

But Italy’s governing majority itself is divided over Ukraine’s future.

“What we are doing on Ukraine is exactly what is written in our programme with which we presented ourselves to Italians and were elected,” Meloni later told the lower house, addressing MPs from Futuro Nazionale, the far-right party founded by MEP Roberto Vannacci.

Her deputy prime minister and League leader, Matteo Salvini, however, said that in Italy “we cannot go on indefinitely sending billions, not as loans but as gifts” to Ukraine. He later pointed out at a press briefing in the European Parliament that other EU states, including Belgium and Spain, “are buying energy and gas from Russia”.

World.title: Florence’s 'Maricarmen': 94-year-old faces losing her home of 60 years as rent nearly triples
World.content:
A 94-year-old woman in Florence faces losing the home she has lived in for more than 60 years after her landlord said her rent would rise from €450 to €1,200 a month.

 

Franca’s contract expires in February, and her family says she will not be able to afford to renew it on the new terms. Her case closely echoes that of María del Carmen Abascal, known as Maricarmen, the 87-year-old who became a symbol of the fight for housing in Spain after a steep rent rise led to her eviction in Madrid. She died in hospital a few days later.

"My mother gets a minimum pension and my father’s survivor’s pension. If she had to pay €1,200 in rent, she would be left with practically nothing to live on, not even enough to eat," her daughter told Corriere Fiorentino (source in Italian).

She has asked not to be named because she has not yet been able to bring herself to tell her mother.

The 70-square-metre flat has been Franca’s home since the early 1960s. She lived there with her husband, and her daughter was born there. According to her daughter, it is the only place her mother feels truly at home, filled with photos of her grandchildren, paintings of Florence’s narrow streets and mementoes from her daughter’s wedding.

The building contains several flats, all owned by the same landlord. It was once home mainly to Florentine families, many of whom had lived there for generations, but the tenants have changed over the years.

As far as her daughter knows, the flats are not being turned into holiday lets and remain ordinary residential tenancies. She believes, however, that the new management wants to squeeze far higher returns from the properties.

"They phoned me to tell me they would not renew the contract for my mother," she told the newspaper. "The contract was renewed every two years. They let me know that, for her to stay there, the rent would have to go up to €1,200 a month. But how can you ask for that kind of money from a 94-year-old pensioner?"

The family accepts that the rent cannot stay the same forever, and her daughter says she would help cover an increase so her mother could spend her final years at home.

"We could manage a small increase, I could help her out. But going from €450 to €1,200 is something else altogether. It is an impossible amount. And what pains me is that there was not even any chance to open a proper negotiation, to try to meet halfway."

She has since turned to the tenants’ union Sunia for help.

Franca’s case comes amid a wider squeeze on tenants in Tuscany, where 2,427 eviction orders were issued in 2025. Florence accounts for around 35% of all enforcement requests filed in the region.

World.title: Are Hungary and the EU friends again? The Ring in Budapest
World.content:
The Ring, the Euronews weekly debate show, travels to Budapest to find out how Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar is resetting relations with the EU after years of tension under the previous government.

 

Magyar, who won a landslide victory in April’s parliamentary election, has been warmly welcomed by Brussels. In May, he reached a deal with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on the release of €16.4 billion in funds blocked over longstanding rule-of-law and corruption concerns.

Hungary has also lifted its veto on opening of EU accession negotiation clusters for Ukraine.

However, some issues remain unresolved, including migration and the rights of sexual minorities.

So, has Magyar delivered on his promise to bring Hungary back to the heart of the EU?

In the Budapest edition of The Ring, Tibor Navracsics, a former minister in Viktor Orbán’s government and a former EU commissioner, and István Szent-Iványi, a foreign policy expert and former ambassador, debate the question.

World.title: How Azerbaijan is building its next chapter in tourism
World.content:
Florian Sengstschmid first set foot in Baku in 2001. After a career working in destinations around the world, the Austrian-born CEO of the Azerbaijan Tourism Board might be hard to surprise. Yet he says the country still has surprises in store.

 

A crossroads with European roots

Sengstschmid believes the South Caucasus is underrated. Its countries are often lumped together under a post-Soviet label, he says, without their individual histories and cultures being fully understood.

Azerbaijan sits where Europe meets Asia, and he points to a European thread that few visitors expect. Bridges built by the Siemens brothers can still be crossed. German heritage villages such as Helenendorf remain. Across the country, a mosque, a church and a synagogue sit side by side. With its distinctive red-tiled roofs, the country’s largest Jewish settlement is believed to have been the only entirely Jewish settlement outside Israel and the United States, as well as the world’s last surviving shtetl.That mix of cultures and faiths, he says, is part of everyday life in Azerbaijan.

He also sees the regional peace process, including the initial deal signed in Washington in August 2025, opening the door to multi-country journeys. That could make the South Caucasus easier to visit for long-haul travellers and raise the region’s profile.

A city that knows how to host

Just days before the summit, Baku hosted a Formula 1 weekend that drew more than 17,000 international visitors, alongside the Azerbaijan Investment Forum. Hospitality, Sengstschmid says, is deeply rooted in the country’s culture, with visitors treated as guests.

Baku’s profile has grown since Eurovision in 2011, and COP29 in 2024 tested its capacity further.

“Who can host a COP can host any other meeting and conference,” he said.

Beyond the capital

Still, Sengstschmid urges visitors not to stop in Baku.

Along the Silk Road lie side valleys, ancient heritage villages and the UNESCO-listed town of Shaki, set in the Greater Caucasus and known for its Khan palaces. There is also a wine route, while wellness cluster includes unique natural resources such as naftalan oil, which has been used for skin treatments for centuries.

The country spans a vast range of climate zones, from desert landscapes to peaks reaching 4,000 metres.

Winter tourism is another focus. A five-year partnership with the International Ski and Snowboard Federation (FIS) will bring races and World Cups to Azerbaijan, including FIS World Cup finals in freestyle moguls and dual moguls in the mountains of Shahdag in March.

Connectivity is improving too. Baku airport holds a five-star Skytrax rating, while Azerbaijan Airlines is taking delivery of new aircraft this year. From 8 May 2027, the carrier will fly four times a week between Brussels and Baku.

Entry is also straightforward. For major events such as F1, a passport and a valid ticket are enough, while other travellers can use the e-visa system, with standard processing within three days and urgent visas issued within three hours.

“Connectivity and accessibility are the key bottlenecks in tourism,” Sengstschmid said.

Building tourism with the people who live there

Behind the growth sits a new state program running to 2030. It aims to stimulate demand through incentives for charter airlines, new routes and tour operators. On the supply side, it encourages quality, green-built accommodation in the regions and supports micro and small entrepreneurs. It also asks transport, customs and other parts of the visitor journey to pull together.

Sengstschmid says protecting local life comes first. He cites Basgal, a mountain village on the Silk Road and a historic centre of silk printing that had been largely abandoned.

After investment in infrastructure, families returned. Today, the village has small tea houses and food stalls, while women practise traditional silk printing. Visitors can experience the village’s traditions alongside the people who live there.

In 2025, tourism contributed 7 billion manat, around €3.5 billion, or 5.4% of GDP. The target is 12 billion manat by 2030. Sengstschmid says the plan centres on longer stays and greater economic impact, with visitor numbers, currently just under three million, rising only modestly.

A village that feels like a secret

Asked to share a secret, he chose Sim, a village in the south of the country that he describes as a fairytale.

Moss covers the old wooden buildings and their balconies, water runs through the village, waterfalls tumble nearby and a UNESCO-listed forest begins at its edge. It feels like a jungle, he says, yet you are in Azerbaijan.

Asked to sum up the country in three words, he did not hesitate: real, warm and uplifting.

Warm, because of its people. Real, because he believes development has left much of the country genuine and intact. And uplifting, because Azerbaijan still has new things to show him.

For someone who first set foot in Baku in 2001, still being surprised 25 years later may be the strongest endorsement of all.

World.title: Ukraine says Musk's SpaceX limits Kyiv's Starlink access
World.content:
Ukraine accused SpaceX of restricting use of its Starlink system, impacting Kyiv's ability to control its drones as Russian attacks continue unabated. President Zelenskyy has asked Elon Musk to "switch" it back on.

Ukraine confirmed on Wednesday that its military has been cut off from full access to SpaceX's Starlink satellite system , which reportedly interrupted some missions overnight.

"Tonight SpaceX introduced a speed limit for the Starlink terminals in motion," said Presidential Adviser Sergiy Beskrestnov.

"Our defense forces were not warned about this restriction, which led to the disruption of a number of missions," he added.

"Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation," he added.

Ukraine presses allies on intelligence sharing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Starlink cut-off coincides with Trump's 'energy ceasefire'

That political situation refers to US President Donald Trump's recent decision to lift sanctions on buying Russian oil.

Trump has also criticized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy— saying he needs to stop attacking Russian oil infrastructure and that he should be replaced because "he won't make a deal" with Russia.

Oil and gas prices have skyrocketed this year due to the US and Israel's war on Iran.

Russia has meanwhile continued to target Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure as winter approaches.

Trump over the weekend insisted, without providing evidence, that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an "energy ceasefire." But Moscow and Kyiv have both denied this.

On Tuesday evening, Russian ballistic missiles hit a Kyiv power plant. Ukrainian officials said the Starlink outages had coincided with overnight Russian attacks.

Ukraine: Russian strikes continue as ceasefire questions remain To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Zelenskyy in UK asks Musk to turn Starlink back on

During a visit to the UK on Wednesday, Zelenskyy called on Starlink owner Elon Musk to fully restore the system.

"So they switched off. It's their decision," Zelenskyy said in an interview with UK journalist Piers Morgan.

"I hope that it's a mistake, maybe huge technical problem. I don't know, but we are asking to do it, to switch (it) on."

In a post on X, Musk later said that any "limits on speed or usage" are ultimately decided by the US military and the president.

Musk's post was in response to an earlier post from Ukraine's former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who said "Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h is being restored," while thanking Musk. This has not been immediately confirmed by standing Ukrainian military officials.

SpaceX move slowed down Ukrainian drones

Ukrainian troops use Starlink to conduct drone operations and internet terminals supplied by Elon Musk's company are key to operating long-distance strikes.

Presidential Advisor Beskrestnov said SpaceX had cut off access to its military-grade version of Starlink above 100 miles per hour (160 kilometers per hour), adding that Ukraine's 7th Rapid Reaction Corps, deployed in the southeast, had been forced to cancel some missions.

"According to our ‌observations, during flights, the connection could drop for 10–20 seconds at speeds of ‌just 110–120 ​km/h. The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control," a Reaction Corps representative told Reuters news agency.

Will Elon Musk give Ukraine Starlink's eyes over Russia? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry said such limitations significantly complicate logistics and ​drone operations.

Ukraine has used Starlink terminals as an alternative to radio control for its drones as well as for ground communications since shortly after Russia launched its invasion.

Starlink's resistance to electronic jamming has made it a crucial tool for flying long-range attack drones as well as large hexacopters that drop supplies for Ukraine's frontline troops.

Elon Musk, the world's richest man and a key Donald Trump supporter, has, however, repeatedly shifted his stance on Ukraine since the early days of Russia's invasion.

In August, Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said Kyiv was looking to create an alternative to Musk's Starlink, in concert "with a European country."

Zelenskyy recieves warm welcome in UK

Arriving in London on Wednesday for talks at 10 Downing Street, Zelenksyy received a strong show of support amid the tensions with Washington.

"You have seen the solidarity and the support you have got from everybody here in Britain ... we are behind you and that will not change," said UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

When asked by Piers Morgan about Trump's recent turn towards Russia, Zelenskyy said it was "pity" to lose a "⁠strong partner." "It's painful when President Trump chooses one ​side, not our side."

The Ukrainian president received a strong show of support from UK PM Andy Burnham Image: Alberto Pezzali/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Washington continues to share intelligence, for now

There has not yet been any follow-up from the US or Starlink regarding the speed restrictions in Ukraine, a senior Ukrainian official told DW.

"We view this as a signal regarding further restrictive measures," the official said under condition of anonymity.



The official confirmed Washington continues to share intelligence with Kyiv, for now, amid concerns that the US will use vital battlefield intelligence as a bargaining chip.

World.title: Nord Stream trial opens in Germany, defense seeks dismissal
World.content:
Serhii Kuznietsov is accused of attacking civilian infrastructure in the 2022 sabotage of the Russian gas pipeline to Germany. His lawyers called Nord Stream a military target, and said their client is sworn to secrecy.

The trial of a former Ukrainian special forces officer, Serhii Kuznietsov, opened in the northern German city of Hamburg on Wednesday amid considerable public and press interest.

Kuznietsov is accused of leading the September 2022 sabotage operation that put the undersea Nord Stream 1 and 2 gas pipelines linking Russian to Germany out of action. The pipelines remain inactive four years later, with no sign of plans to ever reactivate them as Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine heads into its fifth winter.

Prosecutors accuse the Ukrainian of participation in a war crime by targeting civilian infrastructure, but his defense lawyers on Wednesday argued that the case should be dismissed entirely on multiple grounds.

The defense lawyers argue that the case should be thrown out entirely, saying their client is forbidden from speaking with them or anybody else about the case Image: Markus Scholz/dpa/picture alliance

What did Kuznietsov's lawyers say on opening day?

A team of three lawyers representing Kuznietsov questioned the premise of the trial in court.

One of Kuznietsov's lawyers, Nicola Canestrini, argued that it was not valid to try the officer on war crimes charges for an attack on civilian infrastructure.

He argued that the pipeline, which provided half of Germany's natural gas imports prior to Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, was ultimately a "Russian weapon," given the importance of energy revenues for funding Moscow's military.

"Is it unlawful to destroy an aggressor's infrastructure without harming any human beings?" Canestrini asked the court.

After the charges were read out, the judge asked Kuznietsov if he wanted to comment, and he said that he did not.

His lawyers argue that this silence extends beyond not speaking in court and say this should be the main grounds for dismissal.

They say Kuznietsov is sworn to secrecy by his home government in Ukraine and so is unable to discuss his case or potential exonerating evidence with anyone, including his legal representatives.

"He is not permitted to speak. His two immediate superiors told him that he does not have authorization to make any statements — not even to his lawyers," defense attorney Jes Meyer-Lohkamp told the court. In German law, Meyer-Lohkamp argued: "Anyone who cannot speak out cannot be convicted."

A small group of demonstrators stood outside the court on Wednesday arguing that the wrong party to the war in Ukraine was on trial Image: Markus Scholz/dpa/picture alliance

What was the mood in court in Hamburg?

DW's Matthew Moore was on hand in the court in northern Germany on Wednesday.

There is huge interest in this court case, Moore reported. No sooner had the court doors opened at 07:30 local time in Hamburg than the first journalists, observers and protesters began arriving.

A small pro-Ukraine protest held up a banner saying, "Russia is a terrorist." One participant from Germany told Moore they wanted to remind the world of "the war crimes taking place against the Ukrainian people."

Inside, a Ukrainian student told DW that he and others had made the journey from Kyiv to show support for the defendant, Serhii Kuznietsov.

"Serhii Kuznietsov is a hero," the student said. In the eyes of the German prosecutors, it is another matter. They accuse him of carrying out a war crime. If found guilty of his part in the gas pipeline bombing, Kuznietsov faces a lengthy prison sentence.

Based on investigative reporting and a Bojan Pancevski book on the sabotage published this year, Kuznietsov coordinated a small and unlikely team made up not of professional spies or soldiers, but rather people with relevant specialist skills like deep-sea divers and explosives experts Image: Markus Scholz/dpa/picture alliance

Geramny's Wadephul: 'We will deal with any outcome'

The case has been highly politically awkward for Germany — a staunch supporter of Ukraine despite investigators pursuing a trail that led to Kuznietsov and other suspects.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly denied any Ukrainian involvement in the operation, and had also resisted Kuznietsov's extradition to Germany after his arrest in Italy last year, arguing that there was no case to answer.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul declined to comment on the trial on Wednesday, saying that the most important thing for now was for the case to proceed with no political interference or restrictions.

"We will deal with any outcome, and we will, of course, take it into account in our political calculations," he told a press conference in Berlin.

Nord Stream sabotage trial begins in Hamburg To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Court dates for the trial are currently scheduled through February of next year but this could be subject to change in either direction.

With additional reporting from DW's Matthew Moore in Hamburg.
