World.title: DSWD demos water filtration kits to push Marcos’ bucket wisdom
World.content:
FILTERED WATER. Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian and Presidential Communications Undersecretary Claire Castro drink filtered water in a briefing on October 14, 2026, to present government interventions for El Niño.

Government officials try out filtered water after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. tells Filipinos to buy pails that they can use with water filtration kits

Communities vulnerable to El Niño may soon receive water filtration kits from the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD).

Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian conducted on Wednesday, October 14, a live demonstration of how to use the kits, which may come in handy during water shortages.

For good measure, Gatchalian and Presidential Communications Undersecretary Claire Castro drank the filtered water in front of reporters.

The DSWD chief drank the filtered water thrice, even adding more soil to the water being filtered. Castro drank it twice.

Their live demo comes on the heels of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s advice to buy pails to collect rainwater.

Marcos said on Sunday, October 11: “Bumili na kayo ng balde para ‘pag umulan, makolekta na ninyo lahat (Buy pails so when it rains, you can collect rainwater).”

“We’ll give you the filter. We’ll teach you how to do everything so you won’t get sick and you can do the water filtration properly. And it will be healthy even for little children,” added the President in a mix of English and Filipino.

The “balde” advice drew criticism, with groups such as the August Twenty-One Movement saying it is not a real solution to the looming crisis.

On Tuesday, October 13, Castro fired back at what she called “obstructionists,” saying that the President’s remarks were serious and part of the government’s efforts to mitigate the effects of El Niño.

And, on Wednesday, Castro told Palace journalists during Gatchalian’s demo: “Alam ‘nyo, you should try [it] kasi ‘pag dumating talaga na kailangan ‘nyo ‘yan…‘di ba?” (You know, you should try drinking the filtered water because the time may come that you might need it, right?)

Reporters eventually tried the filtered water for themselves.

Play Video

Gatchalian said the DSWD will start to distribute the portable water filtration kits next week.

First in line will be local government units that have declared a state of calamity due to El Niño, as well as high-density areas in Metro Manila experiencing low water pressure.

“We’ll ask them to bring their pails and we’ll install the kits. It’s easy to install. Do they need a special pail? No,” the social welfare chief said in Filipino.

Actually, since 2024, the DSWD has been deploying buckets or jerry cans with built-in water filtration technology to disaster-hit areas without access to potable water.

Citing no actual figures, Gatchalian said many jerry cans are still in the DSWD’s stockpiles, and the agency could procure more through its quick response funds.

With the El Niño phenomenon, the DSWD is also looking into distributing the water filtration kits to families and teach them how to install the technology themselves.

All they need to do is drill a hole near the bottom of the bucket, screw on the connector, hose, and filter. All of the materials needed, including a cleaning plunger and instruction materials, are part of the DSWD kit. The filter can last for a minimum of five years with proper care and maintenance.

Each water filtration kit costs around $35 (about P2,200), according to the international non-government organization Waves for Water, which manufactured the filters for the DSWD.

For this year’s annual procurement plan, the DSWD allocated P26.9 million for 10,500 family water filtration kits sourced through its quick response funds in the 2026 national budget.

Gatchalian said the Department of Health has certified the water filtration kit as a “medical device” and vouched for the safety of the treated water. According to the DSWD, the water filtration system has 0.1 micron filters that can remove cholera, salmonella, E. Coli, and coliform bacteria.

Water sources could be deep wells, springs, rainwater, and water being rationed, according to Gatchalian.

He said the DSWD will also roll out community water depots, which are big rain catchers with a filter system and multiple faucets. The DSWD chief said these are more scalable, especially in communities with open areas and possibly, even schools.

Gatchalian said other DSWD initiatives for El Niño include the cash-for-work program for small water impounding projects and community gardens. They are also deploying air-to-water or atmospheric water machines to far-flung areas.

Castro said other government measures to boost water supply in Metro Manila are cloud seeding, better dam management, building water treatment plants, using water tankers, and activating 61 decommissioned deep wells.

All sound good, but for poor and large Filipino households that may need to store liters and liters of water, heeding the President’s advice will require them to buy multiple buckets, if not drums, to survive what is anticipated to be terribly warm and dry months ahead. – Rappler.com

World.title: Tatay Elmer honored with final caravan
World.content:
Family members and peers from PISTON pay their final respects to the late jeepney driver and activist Elmer Cordero

Late jeepney driver and activist “Tatay Elmer” Cordero is honored for the last time with a caravan from Claret Church in Quezon City to St. Peter Chapels La Loma, Caloocan City, where his remains were cremated on Wednesday, October 14.

Family members and his peers from Pagkakaisa ng mga Samahan ng Tsuper at Opereytor Nationwide (PISTON) all came to pay their final respects.

Cordero died on October 7 at 78 years old after suffering a heart attack during a protest.

He was part of the PISTON 6, a group of jeepney drivers arrested in 2020 for staging a protest to call for government aid at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic. – Rappler.com

World.title: New York Public Radio, Rappler co-present ‘Democracy Dialogues’ on October 15, US time
World.content:
New York Public Radio (NYPR) and Rappler, the Philippines’ leading digital media company, are proud to co-present the next edition of NYPR’s ongoing live event series “Democracy Dialogues” on Thursday, October 15 at The Greene Space (44 Charlton Street).

The program will feature WNYC’s Brian Lehrer, host of the Peabody Award-winning “The Brian Lehrer Show,” alongside Nobel Laureate Maria Ressa, one of the world’s most prominent advocates for journalism and co-founder and CEO of Rappler. The event will be live streamed on wnyc.org, Rappler.com, C-SPAN and YouTube at 7 pm ET (October 16, 7 am PH time). Portions of the conversation will air on WNYC as part of “The Brian Lehrer Show” on Friday, October 16 at 10 am ET. The full conversation will air as a special on WNYC at a later date.

“Democracy Dialogues” is New York Public Radio’s live event series that examines the state of democracy and the essential roles journalism, free expression and an informed public play in sustaining it. In this conversation, Lehrer and Ressa will focus on understanding, defending and rebuilding democracy in the age of AI.

The event will take place at The Jerome L. Greene Performance Space (“The Greene Space”), NYPR’s street-level event space and broadcast studio in Lower Manhattan, located at 44 Charlton Street. Tickets are available now by visiting https://wnyc.org/events/democracy-dialogues.

About Maria Ressa



Maria Ressa is the co-founder and CEO of Rappler, the Philippines’ independent news organization. Rappler has been a target of the country’s authoritarian government for its investigative reporting on corruption and malfeasance at the hands of the Duterte administration and endured multiple arrests in attempts to silence her, ultimately winning multiple accolades for her reporting and bravery. In addition to the Nobel Peace Prize, she won the UNESCO World Press Freedom Prize in 2021, was TIME’s Person of the Year in 2018, and was also named by TIME as one of the most inspiring and influential women of the century. Ressa is the author of a new book, “The Fight Back: A Citizen’s Guide to Standing Up to Dictators,” available on October 13, 2026.

About New York Public Radio

With an urban vibrancy and a global perspective, New York Public Radio (NYPR) produces innovative, critically acclaimed programming for local and national broadcast, on-demand and live-streaming audiences. NYPR’s brands include WNYC, WQXR, WNYC Studios, Gothamist, New Jersey Public Radio and The Jerome L. Greene Performance Space. The WNYC newsroom and Gothamist produce award-winning local journalism for New York City, New Jersey and the surrounding region. WQXR, the city’s only all-classical radio station, broadcasts new and archival classical recordings and makes live performances from New York City’s esteemed performance venues available to all. WNYC Studios is a premier producer of on-demand and national broadcast audio, and home to some of the industry’s most impactful award-winning podcasts and national radio shows, including “Radiolab,” “On the Media” and “The New Yorker Radio Hour,” among others. The Jerome L. Greene Performance Space is NYPR’s intimate street-level broadcast studio and live event space. Further information about programs, podcasts and stations may be found at www.nypublicradio.org.

About Rappler

Founded in 2012 by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa and a group of veteran Filipino journalists, Rappler has grown into one of the Philippines’ leading independent news organizations, recognized for its fearless investigative journalism and innovative use of technology. At a time when disinformation and attacks on press freedom threaten democratic institutions, Rappler has remained committed to journalism that holds power to account, exposes corruption and abuses, and delivers meaningful impact in the communities it serves.

Through independent journalism and technology-driven civic engagement, Rappler continues to champion a future where facts matter, communities have a voice, and technology serves democracy rather than undermines it. – Rappler.com

World.title: FAST FACTS: What changed in final version of the under-18 social media ban bill?
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines – The Senate has approved a bill seeking to ban children below 18 from accessing social media and other digital services considered high-risk, introducing stricter age verification requirements and new obligations for technology companies, with a copy of the bill made available online this week.

Senate Bill No. 2424, or the proposed Safe Media Access and Responsible Technology for Kids in Digital Spaces (SMART KIDS) Act, takes a stricter approach than the House of Representatives’ version, which proposes restrictions for children aged 13 and below and tiered access for older minors.

A comparison of the original proposal and the Senate-approved bill reveals six major changes.

An outright ban for children below 18

The original proposal sought to prohibit children below 16 from accessing age-restricted social media platforms.



The approved version raises the age threshold to 18. The new version also explicitly states that the prohibition cannot be overridden by parental consent, authorization, or supervision.



So this means even 16- and 17-year-olds would be barred from covered platforms, with no provision for graduated access for older teenagers.

Expanded coverage to ‘high-risk digital services’

The approved bill introduces the term “high-risk digital services,” covering social media platforms and online gaming services with social networking functions.



These include features allowing users to communicate, maintain social connections, join online communities, or share user-generated content, including livestreams. Roblox and Gorebox are explicitly cited as examples.



These two games were tagged as potential avenues for youth radicalization and violent behavior; Roblox for its communication functions, and Gorebox for its supposed violent content.



However, the bill exempts email, certain private messaging services, educational platforms, digital news services, and professional collaboration tools.



There is also no minimum audience size or revenue threshold for coverage. Smaller livestreaming platforms and online communities could therefore be subject to the same requirements as major technology companies.

Government IDs required for age verification

Unlike the original proposal, which allowed various age-assurance methods, the approved bill requires primary authentication through PhilSys or another government-issued ID. Age estimation and other verification technologies may supplement, but cannot replace, government ID authentication.



Simply entering a birthday would no longer suffice. As a measure of data minimization, platforms are prohibited from retaining copies of government IDs and should receive only information that users meet the age requirement.



Nevertheless, this requirement raises questions about online anonymity, surveillance risks, and access for adults without acceptable identification documents.

Restrictions on addictive social media features

The new version introduces requirements for platforms to mitigate potentially addictive design features, specifically mentioning autoplay, infinite scrolling, push notifications, engagement metrics, and algorithmic amplification, also requiring “safety-by-design” and “privacy-by-default” protections.



However, it does not specify how exactly such mitigation can be enforced nor does it delve into technical benchmarks for determining whether these features have been sufficiently mitigated. The Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) will be tasked with monitoring for compliance.



Violating platforms face fines ranging from P5 million to P20 million per violation, with additional daily penalties of up to P100,000 for continuing violations.

Emergency response to harmful content

The approved bill requires platforms to take immediate, proportionate action against harmful content following detection or credible reports.



Measures may include suspending livestreams, removing content, restricting its distribution, or stopping algorithmic amplification.

Foreign platforms must maintain an emergency escalation channel and designate a legal representative or authorized contact in the Philippines. Notably, the approved version drops the original proposal’s explicit requirement for foreign platforms to establish a physical local office.



The Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) must petition a Regional Trial Court, through the Office of the Solicitor General, to restrict an entire platform — a change from the unilateral banning actions that the DICT has performed, highlighted by the controversial Discord ban.



However, the DICT may still issue account-specific disabling orders if continuing harm can be proven. – Rappler.com

World.title: You can’t add senior discount on top of other deals – SC
World.content:
SENIORS. A number of senior citizens participate in a pre-screening and orientation on March 18, 2026, at the Department of Manpower Development and Placement (DMDP) office in Cebu City for employment opportunities available to those aged 60 to 65.

'When goods or services are offered at promotional prices, senior citizens may choose either the promotional discount or the 20% senior citizen discount, whichever gives them greater savings,' the High Court says

MANILA, Philippines – The Supreme Court ruled on Wednesday, October 14, that a senior citizen’s discount cannot be availed of by consumers simultaneously with other discounts.

“The SC explained that senior citizen discounts cannot be combined with other discounts. When goods or services are offered at promotional prices, senior citizens may choose either the promotional discount or the 20% senior citizen discount, whichever gives them greater savings,” the High Court said in its decision.

“Granting an additional discount beyond what the law allows would unfairly benefit the customer at the business’s expense,” it added.

In its decision, the High Court said that while Republic Act No. 7432 or the Senior Citizens Act protects and supports senior citizens, the law’s implementation must be fair and reasonable to businesses.

Under the law, Filipinos aged 60 and above are entitled to benefits and privileges, including 20% discount on services like hotel, restaurants, and recreation centers.

“[The] State’s pursuit of public welfare cannot be allowed to impose undue or confiscatory burdens on private establishments, whose continued viability is essential to the long-term effectiveness of the law,” the SC said.

The case stemmed from a case filed against a certain Orville Ong, general manager of a hotel in Bacolod City, for alleged violation of the Senior Citizens Act, as amended. The High Court acquitted Ong in the said case after he was charged for refusing to grant a senior discount to hotel guests Paul Alcazaren and Eric Gadiana.

In his case, Ong argued that the hotel already applied a 20% discount on the room rate for the Cebu Bikers Club. Alcazaren and Gadiana are members of this group.

Ong was later found guilty by the Municipal Trial Court in Cities, Regional Trial Court, and the Court of Appeals.

But the High Court reversed the rulings, explaining that the guests already received a 20% discount through the club’s negotiated rater. Therefore, the hotel was not obliged to give an additional 20% discount. – Rappler.com

World.title: JV Ejercito flags ‘major changes’ in House-approved 2027 budget bill
World.content:
'The cuts to preventive health programs are substantial, while medical assistance has increased,' says Senate finance committee chairperson JV Ejercito

MANILA, Philippines – Senate finance committee chairperson JV Ejercito on Wednesday, October 14, flagged billions of pesos in reductions to preventive health programs and infrastructure projects in the House-approved version of the P7.2-trillion 2027 general appropriations bill (GAB).

Ejercito said in a news briefing that the House version of the budget bill, which the Senate formally received on Tuesday, had major changes compared to the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP), including a P130-billion reduction in foreign-assisted projects, a P9.5-billion cut in calamity funds, and billions of pesos in reductions to health programs.

The “major changes” include a P4-billion reduction in the Department of Health’s (DOH) immunization program and a P4.5-billion cut in the DOH-Health Facilities Enhancement Program (HFEP), which funds the improvement and expansion of government health facilities. He also cited a P2.6-billion reduction in right-of-way funding and a P4.6-billion cut in funding for flood mitigation structures within major river basins.

The House version of the budget bill increased funding for the DOH’s Medical Assistance to Indigent and Financially Incapacitated Patients (MAIFIP) by P23.9 billion, allocated P10 billion for a new Presidential Assistance to Farmers and Fisherfolk program under the Department of Agriculture, and added P8.04 billion for flood mitigation structures under the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH).

“The cuts to preventive health programs are substantial, while medical assistance has increased. This is a puzzle for me because one of the key factors of Universal Health Care (UHC) is strengthening preventive care, yet that is what they reduced,” Ejercito said in Filipino.

“What are we supposed to do with this? Remove funding for immunization and health promotion, then provide medical assistance when people get sick?” he added.

Ejercito said the Senate received the House-approved GAB late Tuesday afternoon, and that copies have been distributed to the senators. An October 23 deadline was set for the Senate finance committee vice chairpersons to submit their committee reports.

The Senate temporarily paused from its impeachment court duties starting October 14 in view of the ongoing committee hearings for the proposed 2027 national budget.

Ejercito said the chamber is targeting to finish all budget-related committee hearings by October 23 before it goes on a brief recess. The senator also said he is eyeing to sponsor the 2027 budget bill in the Senate plenary by November 23, and have it approved by the second week of December.

“We are also planning to continue what Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian did when he was the finance chairperson — livestream the bicameral conference committee to ensure transparency. We are also keeping in touch with CSOs, the academe, and other watchdogs and will meet them to hear their observations on October 26,” said Ejercito.

The House of Representatives approved the proposed 2027 budget on Monday amid concerns from some lawmakers and civil society organizations (CSOs) that the spending plan is riddled with pork barrel allocations. – Rappler.com

World.title: Myanmar Regime Escalates Assault on Free Press Critical of Its Rule
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime has intensified its threats against independent media critical of its rule, vowing to eliminate outlets and journalists regardless of their location.

An editorial in the junta’s mouthpiece Kyemon on Monday urged the “elimination of any destructive element inside or outside the country,” echoing the Home Affairs Ministry’s threats last week.

On October 6, Deputy Home Affairs Minister Major‑General Min Thu told parliament the regime has opened cases against independent media outlets The Irrawaddy, Mizzima, DVB, Myanmar Now, and Khit Thit under the Counter‑Terrorism Law, Telecommunications Law, and Penal Code. He claimed the regime was coordinating with international law enforcement including Interpol and Aseanapol to detain staff working for these organizations.

Interpol bans any interventions on political grounds while Aseanapol’s focus is limited to transnational crimes.

The Kyemon editorial stated that anyone inside or outside the country who “disrupts peace, stability, and development, undermines national sovereignty, prestige, and unity, or obstructs the administrative mechanism must be eliminated.”

Junta leader Min Aung Hlaing branded outlets reporting his military’s mass-killing of civilians as “nation‑destroying media” during his October 13 trip to Dawei, claiming they were misleading the public. “Those outlets do not want to see national development,” said the president, whose February 2021 coup plunged the country into turmoil.

The putsch was followed by a brutal crackdown, targeting not only peaceful protesters but also media documenting the military’s abuses. The regime revoked licenses, raided offices, and arrested scores of journalists, forcing independent outlets into exile. After establishing itself as one of the world’s worst jailers of journalists, it is now seeking to target exiled media.

Independent media groups emphasize that journalism is not a crime and note that Interpol does not act on political requests. “Interpol does not intervene in political or religious cases. Only genuine criminal matters are considered,” said Toe Zaw Latt, secretary of the Independent Press Council of Myanmar. He added that while the regime may attempt to link reporting with criminal activities, such requests are weeded out by Interpol. “So, there is no need to worry, but we should still monitor the situation carefully.”

Lower House Speaker Khin Yi—who as former dictator Than Shwe’s police chief led deadly crackdowns on pro-democracy demonstrators—has advised the Home Affairs Ministry that criminal cases must be concocted to pursue arrests abroad.

The junta’s warning comes as its propaganda apparatus struggles to discredit the resistance movement while concealing its own war crimes. Circulation of regime newspapers has sharply declined since the coup, and junta news outlets have been barred from multiple social media platforms.

A Yangon street vendor said demand for state‑owned newspapers is practically non-existent, except for once a month when lottery results are printed.

The junta’s threats come as it faces ongoing international isolation. ASEAN has barred Min Aung Hlaing from summits since the coup for failing to implement its peace plan, while he is wanted on an international arrest warrant issued by Argentina over the Rohingya genocide. Rights groups have repeatedly called on Interpol to arrest the coup leader during his overseas trips.

On Wednesday, the International Federation of Journalists (IFJ) and its affiliate, the Exiled Myanmar Journalists Network (Exiled-MJN), condemned the regime’s threats as a blatant abuse of international policing mechanisms.

“Myanmar’s junta will stop at nothing to try to legitimize itself in the world’s eyes and to expand its repression against the brave and determined media and journalists who continue to expose its gross violations against its own people,” IFJ stated.

According to MJN records, at least seven journalists have been killed by the regime since the coup. The International Centre for Not-for-Profit Law has documented at least 227 journalists detained by the junta, with at least 20 still in jail.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Forces Burn Church in Bhamo, KIA Says
World.content:
Myanmar military forces burned a Christian church near Bhamo on Monday evening as the regime continues its campaign to recapture the Kachin State town, according to Colonel Naw Bu, a spokesperson for the Kachin Independence Army (KIA).

“They [the regime] burned a Christian church in Three Mile Village on the way to Momauk,” Naw Bu told The Irrawaddy. “There have been periodic clashes in that area.”

He added that there has been frequent fighting between regime troops and KIA-led forces around Light Infantry Battalion 47 and near Bhamo University.

The KIA and its allies launched an attack on Bhamo in late 2024 and captured the majority of the town in 2025. This year, however, it has lost some ground there to the regime, which has been reinforcing its troops in preparation for a counteroffensive.

Naw Bu claimed resistance groups still control a large part of the town. The Irrawaddy could not independently verify the claim.

Citing residents, local media reported that the arson attack on the Kachin Baptist Convention-run church followed heavy regime casualties in the face of fierce resistance defense.

Human rights activists condemned the torching of the church.

“This is a violation of freedom of religion; we condemn it,” Jacob from Kachin Human Rights Watch told The Irrawaddy. “The regime does not respect international laws and continues to violate them.”

He said the regime and allied militias have used religious sites for military purposes, carried out drone attacks on churches, and detained religious leaders. “Religious rights in Kachin State are being increasingly violated,” he said.

Mervyn Thomas, founder president of Church World Service, an international Christian human rights group, said the attack was a “grave crime” and a “clear violation” of international laws and freedom of belief, while calling on the international community to cut off the regime’s access to aviation fuel and military equipment.

In September, the regime-allied Shanni Nationalities Army used the compounds of a Baptist church and a Catholic church in Indaw as a military training ground and an office, sparking criticism from ethnic Kachin residents.

The regime and its allies conducted a suicide drone attack on another church in Mohnyin Township in October.

The regime’s attacks on places of worship do not discriminate by faith, however. Myanmar Witness in April said it documented over 300 airstrikes on religious sites, including churches, monasteries and mosques, between January 2024 and December 2025. Nearly 90 percent of them were conducted by the regime’s air force, with Sagaing Region and Shan State the worst-affected areas.

In August, 14 civilians were killed in Sagaing Region’s Myaung Township when the regime launched an airstrike on a Buddhist temple that was hosting around 100 people for a meditation retreat.

World.title: Myanmar’s Spies: A History of Surveillance, Power and Purges
World.content:
Myanmar: The Making of an Intelligence State

By Andrew Selth

ISEAS Publishing, Singapore, 2026

609 pp. US$48

This book is bound to become a classic. Never before has any international scholar described and analyzed the history of intelligence in Myanmar, from the days of the kings, through colonial rule, to democratic and military-dominated governments after independence. And no one would be more qualified to do this study than Andrew Selth, an Australian academic and former diplomat who has written extensively about Myanmar for several decades. The Burmese kings sent spies across the eastern as well as western borders before invading armies captured the old Siamese capital Ayutthaya and the old Arakan kingdom. And they developed what a British historian, quoted by Selth, has described as “a powerful and sophisticated internal espionage system” when the country was threatened by European colonial powers.

A new, entirely different intelligence apparatus emerged after the British conquest in the 19th century. In 1896, a Criminal Intelligence Bureau was formed within the headquarters of the Burma Police, and its duty was quite specific: to monitor domestic dissent and “deal with cases of a political nature.” A Special Branch of the police continued that work throughout the colonial era, and its work became especially important after the Saya San rebellion in the 1930s, which also prompted the British to send in military police officers from India.

In the years after Myanmar’s independence in 1948, Selth outlines how the new government created five main intelligence agencies, of which the Military Intelligence Service (MIS) became the most powerful, and even cooperated with foreign intelligence services. Some officers were trained by the British, and then chiefly to spy on Myanmar’s growing communist movement. The CIA also provided training on the US-held island of Saipan in the Pacific. Among those receiving instruction was “Spectacles Tin Oo,” who became a close associate of the dictator General Ne Win and, as such, one of the most feared men in the country. He collected intelligence not only on political dissidents but also, and perhaps primarily, on officers and the ranks of the military, on whose loyalty the Ne Win regime relied for its survival.

Tin Oo (not to be confused with General Tin Oo, one of the founders of the National League for Democracy) and his inner circle of followers eventually became too powerful, acting like a state within a state, which led to his downfall in July 1983 and a purge of the entire intelligence apparatus. The near vacuum that ensued has been seen as the reason why North Korean agents managed to infiltrate Yangon and, in October that year, detonate a bomb that killed 17 visiting South Korean officials and four Myanmar nationals.

With MI Tin Oo behind bars, Ne Win needed a new officer who could rebuild the country’s intelligence services, and that was his trusted protégé, Khin Nyunt. His Directorate of Defense Services Intelligence (DDSI) soon had agents all over the country, and surveillance—and repression—of the population at large became of utmost importance during and after the 1988 pro-democracy uprising. According to Selth: “The DDSI already was the largest and most powerful intelligence agency in Myanmar before 1988, but under the SLORC [the State Law and Order Restoration Council] it dramatically increased in size, sophistication and territorial presence. The refashioning of the SLORC into the State Peace and Development Council in 1997, possibly on the advice of an American public relations consultant, does not seem to have resulted in any significant changes to the intelligence structures and procedures that were set in train after the uprising.”

Selth provides detailed descriptions of how Khin Nyunt’s DDSI and its affiliated agencies were structured, and how they operated. Now, foreigners, among them diplomats and others who were suspected of having contacts with the pro-democracy movement, also became targets of its surveillance. But like MI Tin Oo before him, Khin Nyunt grew too powerful for comfort, and he was eventually ousted in October 2004 along with almost his entire intelligence apparatus. New intelligence outfits had to be created, and those were placed more directly under military command to avoid a repeat of what happened in 1983 and 2004.

During Burma’s decade of relative openness, from 2011 to 2021, the intelligence services remained wholly autonomous from the governments in Naypyitaw, and that separation became even more obvious during the years when the NLD—after an election in 2015—was allowed to appoint most ministers. I experienced this firsthand when I visited the country on many occasions between 2012 and 2019. I was under constant surveillance, and the intelligence agents often didn’t even bother to hide it.

Selth also describes how various opposition forces have treated suspected informants for the various intelligence services. In 1992, the All-Burma Students’ Democratic Front’s section in Kachin State killed 15 of their own comrades on suspicion of being spies. In 2021, 25 unarmed prisoners were executed by Karen rebels. In both cases, the opposition groups had depended on faulty intelligence, which their own agencies had provided.

Anyone who wants to understand how successive military-dominated governments have survived, and on what traditions Myanmar’s intelligence services were built, has to read this book. It contains a 43-page bibliography, which is the most extensive I have seen in any book about Myanmar. The book also lists, for the first time, military intelligence chiefs since 1959, regional military commands in 2024, and the various intelligence agencies that shaped today’s Myanmar. Its subtitle, “The Making of an Intelligence State,” could not be more appropriate.

World.title: China Sentences Myanmar Scam Clan Members to Death
World.content:
BEIJING—A Chinese court sentenced three members of a criminal gang to death on Tuesday for operating a network of brutal scam centers in Myanmar’s Kokang region on the border with China, while jailing dozens more.

China has stepped up cooperation with Southeast Asian nations to crack down on a vast industry that has flourished in the region in recent years to fleece people out of billions of dollars.

Those conducting the online scams are sometimes willing con artists. Others are trafficked foreign nationals—many Chinese—tricked into work and held in prison-like compounds.

Quanzhou Intermediate People’s Court said in a statement on Tuesday that it had sentenced Wei Huairen (aka Wei San), Chen Dawei and Liao Jingfang to death for their involvement in the “Wei family criminal gang”.

The gang was involved in crimes including drug trafficking, organizing prostitution, operating illegal casinos, telecommunications fraud and the murder of at least two Chinese citizens, the court said.

Wei Huairen was identified as one of the group’s leaders and found guilty of several crimes including murder, the court said.

The gang’s operations netted more than 12.2 billion yuan (US$1.8 billion).

Another three gang members were handed life sentences, while 55 more were given prison terms ranging from 24 years to three years and three months, the court said.

Analysts describe the Wei clan as one of the “four families” running crime syndicates in Kokang.

China’s state broadcaster CCTV on Tuesday called them the “most violent criminal force in northern Myanmar,” having created an “iron triangle of political, military and business criminal activities.”

It described the gang as operating 14 “large-scale” scam compounds and luring “large numbers” of Chinese to Myanmar through fake promises of high wages.

Police had also discovered remains of victims bound with iron chains and with bullet holes in their skulls, CCTV said.

Members of the Wei family were first indicted in October 2025.

In January, China executed 11 people, including members of the “Ming family criminal gang.”

The following month, four members of the notorious Bai clan were executed for crimes including “fraud, intentional homicide, intentional injury, kidnapping [and] extortion.”

World.title: Myanmar Regime Forces Beached in Battle for Sittwe
World.content:
Fierce battles have erupted around rebel-held Nga Pyi Island in Rakhine State’s Kaladan River delta, where regime forces keep trying to land troops despite heavy losses.

Local sources say scores of regime solders were killed or captured in the first three days of fighting as the Arakan Army (AA) defends the strategic outpost while laying siege to the state capital Sittwe across the water.

AA troops recently seized regime sentry bases at Amhyint Kyun Village at the entrance of Sittwe.

Since Oct. 7, the military has deployed six gunboats and a dozen speedboats backed by airstrikes and artillery fire from Sittwe in an effort to seize the island.

But AA fighters are entrenched there because it allows them to attack regime naval bases and ships stationed throughout the delta and along the coast.

Sources close to the AA said regime troops are reduced to trying to land troops with speedboats after three of their larger ships were hit by AA fire on Oct. 8, with two sustaining serious damage.

“Despite the casualties, they keep on coming,” one source told The Irrawaddy.

As many as 50 regime soldiers managed to reach the shore in the first two days of fighting but were either killed or captured, sources said.

As of Monday the regime had been unable to gain a foothold. Soldiers are reportedly being forced to advance under threat of being shot by their own commanders if they refuse.

“I’ve heard they are using conscripts as cannon fodder,” another source said.

Last month, the regime launched an offensive to retake lost territories in Rakhine, dispatching three columns to AA-held Ponnagyun north of Sittwe. Nearly one month later all three columns have been repelled, and the regime is retreating in Sittwe Township itself, according to the sources.

AA troops have captured four more outposts and are pushing at the gates of Shwe Mingan naval base and Sittwe Regional Operations Command, they added.

The attack on Nga Pyi Island was apparently launched because the regime sensed the danger of an imminent siege of its Sittwe stronghold, which sits on a peninsula surrounded by water on three sides.

“Regime navy vessels in Kaladan have repeatedly been attacked by AA drones and artillery from Nga Pyi, so the military wants to get control of the island,” said a Pauktaw resident.

Meanwhile, residents across Sittwe, Pauktaw, Ponnagyun and Rathedaung townships say the regime is bombarding the area daily and firing heavy artillery. “Every day, a dozen aircraft come and strike,” a Sittwe resident said. “Artillery units in Sittwe launches daily volleys toward Nga Pyi.”

Fighting is also intensifying in the state’s other major regime stronghold of Kyaukphyu, which is home to massive Chinese investment projects. There the AA has overrun two regime outposts near Taung Maw Oo naval base. The military is reinforcing positions as far afield as Chin State as well as the Rakhine borders of Magwe, Bago and Ayeyarwady.

Except for Sittwe and Kyaukphyu and the sparsely populated island of Manaung, the AA now controls all of Rakhine as well as Paletwa Township in neighboring Chin State.

World.title: Running for Cover: The Limits of Early Warning in Rakhine Air War
World.content:
In the week after the Sept. 28 massacre on Kyauktaw’s Indian market that killed 50 people and injured at least 58 others, Rakhine State endured another wave of aerial attacks. Local media reported at least nine bombing incidents across the townships of Ponnagyun, Rathedaung, Pauktaw, Kyauktaw, Thandwe and Kyaukphyu that killed at least another 12 civilians and injured more than 37 others. Some strikes hit locations where displaced people were sheltering.

The attacks were part of a wider pattern. The UN says aerial attacks killed more than 190 people in Rakhine in 2025. ACLED, an independent global conflict monitor, says Rakhine has suffered Myanmar’s highest reported casualties from airstrikes on local markets, recording at least 11 such attacks and 49 deaths even before the Sept. 28 massacre.

The immediate question for civilians under air attack is how they can know where a military aircraft is heading and reach safety in time.

Communities in Rakhine have improvised ingenious early-warning networks. To understand how they work, I spoke with six residents in Kyauktaw and Mrauk-U and reconstructed the warning timeline leading up to the Sept. 28 massacre.

A military jet is sometimes airborne one or two hours before an attack. What people often cannot know is where it will strike until the bombs have already begun to fall.

Watchers, channels and loudspeakers

The locals told me how warnings reach civilians in areas under Arakan Army (AA) control. What emerges is a kind of relay network: volunteer scouts track aircraft leaving airfields; their reports appear on public Telegram channels with takeoff times, directions and regions at risk; and in some communities those alerts are then announced through sirens and loudspeakers.

Warnings begin with a beeping alarm, followed by a spoken announcement. One Mrauk-U resident said at least three locations now broadcast such warnings, a system that began three or four months ago and can sometimes give people 10 to 15 minutes to find cover.

The timeline of Sep. 28

A reconstruction based on posts from a volunteer air-scout channel and the AA’s account of the strike times clearly shows the problem.

A Telegram channel with about 13,000 subscribers reported a fighter jet leaving Naypyitaw toward the southwest at 10:16 a.m., and another from the same airbase in the same direction at 11:08 a.m. Both alerts covered Rakhine, Ayeyarwady, Magwe, Bago, Karen and Chin. At 11:36, the channel reported another jet leaving Meiktila, with Mandalay, Rakhine, Magwe and Chin potentially at risk.

Yet the warning narrowed too late. An observation that a jet was circling over Kyauktaw at 12:10 was posted at about 12:13. A second observation, saying the aircraft was still circling at 12:15, appeared at about 12:16. But the AA says the first bomb struck at 12:10 and the second at 12:14.

The scouts were quick, but their information still had to pass from observer to channel operator before reaching the public. Even a few minutes matter. By the time the warnings narrowed down the target to Kyauktaw, the attack was already underway.

What’s more, phone and internet services have been severely restricted in much of Rakhine for years, and many residents cannot reliably access Telegram alerts. Repeated alarms can also cause warning fatigue.

“We can never assume where the jets are heading based only on the direction they take off in,” one resident told me. “Sometimes they appear to be flying toward another city, then turn back to drop the bombs.”

Ground observers may also lose track of sudden changes in course or altitude. The problem is not simply the speed of the volunteers, but the limits of the available information and ways to relay it.

What should change

International support should go beyond diplomatic statements. Donors, humanitarian organizations and local authorities should invest in warning systems that do not depend entirely on internet access, including radio networks, sirens and community warning posts. Air raid drills and clear protocols could reduce warning fatigue, while tiered alerts could distinguish a general aircraft warning from an imminent local threat.

Similar systems have been used elsewhere. In Syria, volunteer aircraft spotters fed flight information into warning networks that used social media, radio and street sirens to give civilians several minutes to seek cover.

The responsibility for the attacks lies with the Myanmar military. But local authorities can reduce civilian exposure by breaking up large commercial hubs into smaller neighborhood trading points, adjusting market hours to avoid peak crowds, taking any locally observed patterns of air patrols into account, and mandating the provision of proper shelters near hospitals, schools, markets and displacement sites.

Shelter is especially important for displaced families. Two people who fled Sittwe for Kyauktaw and Mrauk-U told me that many displaced people can afford only basic rented housing or makeshift accommodation, which offer no proper protection from airstrikes. Even a timely warning has limited value if there is nowhere safe to reach.

Historically, communities under heavy bombardment have adapted. During the Vietnam War, for instance, communities in North Vietnam built collective shelters, trenches and tunnels, while authorities adjusted school, work and market hours to reduce large daytime concentrations of people. Such measures cannot stop an air campaign, but they can reduce exposure.

International statements of concern will continue. But for civilians on the ground, the immediate challenge is to turn an early alert into a warning they can actually use. Closing the gap between knowing that a jet is airborne and knowing where it is heading may not prevent an attack. But it could give more people enough time to reach safety.

Khine is a researcher from Rakhine State with a decade of experience in peace processes, conflict issues, and human rights documentation. She is pursuing a master’s degree in Human Rights and Democratization at Mahidol University.

World.title: Philippine President Hails Diplomatic Engagement with Myanmar’s Regime
World.content:
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has hailed recent visits by Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing to fellow ASEAN countries as part of a “new approach” to resolving the country’s crisis.

In an interview with The Straits Times published Saturday, Marcos claimed credit for a recent engagement by various ASEAN governments with the putschist regime of Min Aung Hlaing.

Marcos conceded that ASEAN’s previous insistence on its Five-Point Consensus peace plan for Myanmar and refusal to engage with Myanmar’s regime at the political level were “absolutely correct.” But he added they were “not working.”

“Nothing’s happening, so we had to do something else,” he told the daily.

This prompted the Philippines during its 2026 chairmanship of the bloc to propose a “new approach” at the ASEAN Summit in Cebu in May, he said without going into detail.

He then pointed to coup leader Min Aung Hlaing’s recent visits to Malaysia and Cambodia as signs of progress, describing them as “shoots coming out of the ground” that had “not happened before” and would eventually lead to a “complete resolution.”

“Asked if ASEAN was moving towards recognizing the Myanmar government, Marcos said the grouping has to move towards that if it is going to play a part in resolving the conflict in the country,” the Straits Times wrote.

Since appointing himself president in April and rebranding his regime, Min Aung Hlaing has also visited ASEAN members Thailand, Laos and Vietnam, while reportedly being invited to Indonesia and Brunei.

However, the diplomatic engagement Marcos cited has yet to lead to any reduction in violence on the ground. In some cases, Min Aung Hlaing’s trips coincided with aerial massacres on civilians at home.

In the latest major atrocity, a military airstrike on a crowded market in Rakhine State on Sept. 28 killed at least 50 people, while further air raids in the state targeted locations where displaced people were sheltering. A week later the putschist leader was being welcomed in Kuala Lumpur.

ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus consist of ending violence, beginning dialogue among all parties, appointing an ASEAN special envoy, and ensuring that humanitarian assistance those in need. It was adopted in April 2021 in response of the military coup. However, the regime led by Min Aung Hlaing has since ignored the framework, and most recently the regime’s new rubber-stamp Parliament rejected it altogether.

The conflict since the 2021 coup has killed an estimated 100,000 people and internally displaced about 3.8 million as of June 2026.

“Shaking hands with war criminals is a threat to humanity,” Thinzar Shunlei Yi, a Myanmar democracy and human rights activist, told The Irrawaddy. “We are watching to see whether the ASEAN leaders will show accountability if their re-engagement with the regime does not work out.”

Some ASEAN members are standing firm. Timor-Leste, the bloc’s newest member, has supported Myanmar’s pro-democracy movement and initiated legal proceedings against the military regime in February over alleged war crimes. And Singapore, which stands to take over the rotating chairmanship at year-end, affirmed this summer that there can be “no political representation” for Myanmar at ASEAN meets.

World.title: JFM Slams US Lifting of Sanctions on Fifth Myanmar Regime Crony
World.content:
Rights advocacy group Justice For Myanmar has condemned the continued U.S. delisting of Myanmar cronies, following Washington’s removal of sanctions against an official of Myanmar military-linked Shwe Byain Phyu Group.

The U.S. Treasury Department removed from its sanctions list Theint Win Htet, a member of the founding family of the Shwe Byain Phyu Group, a Myanmar military-linked conglomerate with interests spanning mining, timber and petroleum trading.

Theint Win Htet, who was sanctioned by former President Joe Biden’s administration, has become the fifth Myanmar junta crony, including arms brokers, to be delisted by the Trump administration along with the companies they are connected to.

In August 2025, the Trump administration dropped sanctions against four Myanmar nationals: Jonathan Myo Kyaw Thaung (aka Jonathan Kyaw Thaung), Aung Hlaing Oo, Sit Taing Aung and Tin Latt Min.

Tin Latt Min is the mother of Theint Win Htet. Her father, Thein Win Zaw, remains on the U.S. sanctions list.

JFM said on Sunday: “The U.S. government must learn from the mistakes it made after the sham 2010 election and not appease a brutal military that commits genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity with impunity.

“The crisis in Myanmar continues to deepen and appeasement will only further embolden the junta to continue its campaign of terror against the people,” it said.

The rights group said the regime’s access to funds, arms and aviation fuel has allowed it to escalate attacks on civilian targets that amount to international crimes. It said sanctions should be widened to cover the full extent of the networks of companies and individuals enabling and profiting from the junta’s terror campaign.

Following the 2021 military coup that ousted the democratically elected civilian government led by democracy icon Aung San Suu Kyi, the Biden administration imposed sanctions on military officers, military-run companies and military-linked cronies and their companies for aiding or abetting the regime’s war crimes and violations of international law.

Its sanctions blocked Theint Win Htet’s U.S. credit cards, restricted her foreign bank accounts and forced her to abandon her master’s degree at Columbia University in New York. Recently she has been living in Thailand with her mother Tin Latt Min, according to Al Jazeera and Reuters.

According to those agencies, Washington-based law firm Ferrari & Associates, which specializes in sanctions cases, helped remove her from the U.S. list.

During an interview with The Insight Myanmar podcast, the law firm confirmed that of four Myanmar individuals and companies delisted by the U.S. in July last year, two individuals and one company were among its clients.

JFM said Shwe Byain Phyu Group took control of Telenor Myanmar, renamed ATOM Myanmar, in 2022. At that time, three business sources told The Irrawaddy that Khin Thiri Thet Mon, the daughter of coup leader Min Aung Hlaing, was an investor in Shwe Byain Phyu, which acquired an 80-percent stake in the telecom company.

ATOM Myanmar has since installed a commercialized version of China’s Great Firewall, giving what JFM described as the illegal junta unprecedented access to conduct surveillance on users.

Theint Win Htet has acted as a shareholder and director of One Telecom Company Limited, which was established during Shwe Byain Phyu’s acquisition of Telenor Myanmar.

In 2023, Theint Win Htet did an internship at ATOM Myanmar as a financial analyst while holding shares in Min Shwe Myine Enterprise Limited, a Myanmar petroleum company that formed a consortium in 2022 to find reliable suppliers from Russia “to tighten Myanmar Russian partnership,” JFM said.

In 2024, JFM reported Theint Win Htet to French authorities, requesting they freeze any of her assets in French territory and consider her removal from France, where she had been admitted to a school.

World.title: From Reading Culture to Reading Competence: What PISA 2025 Tells Kazakhstan
World.content:
Kazakhstan has set itself an ambitious goal: to become a reading nation. In May, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed a decree placing the development of reading culture among the country’s national priorities. The policy includes new libraries, a national digital library platform and a Reading Nation concept for 2027–2031. These are welcome developments. The latest international evidence also suggests that Kazakhstan needs to think carefully about what it means to be a strong reader.

The latest OECD PISA results for Kazakhstan provide an uncomfortable starting point. In PISA 2025, Kazakhstan’s average reading score was 385, compared with an OECD average of 461. Only 36% of Kazakh 15-year-olds reached at least Level 2 in reading, compared with 69% across the OECD. Almost no students in Kazakhstan reached the highest reading levels.

The more revealing number may be 36%. At Level 2, students should be able to identify the main idea of a moderately long text, locate information using several criteria and reflect on the purpose of a text when directed to do so. Higher levels demand increasingly complex skills, including comparing sources, recognising implicit meaning, separating fact from opinion and judging the reliability of information. PISA therefore gives us a picture of how confidently young people can use reading to make sense of unfamiliar information.

Kazakhstan’s reading difficulties are also longstanding. According to the OECD, reading performance has remained relatively stable since the country first participated in PISA in 2009. Kazakhstan scored 390 that year. Sixteen years later, it scored 385. The pattern stretches across several generations of students and predates the disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and the recent arrival of generative artificial intelligence.

Research conducted inside Kazakhstan offers some clues about what may be happening. Akhmetova, Imambayeva and Csapó examined more than 1,500 Grade 6 and Grade 8 students and found something that complicates the common claim that young people simply lack interest in reading. Around 85% of the Grade 6 students and 79% of the Grade 8 students reported that they enjoyed reading. Yet the relationship between positive attitudes towards reading and actual reading achievement was relatively weak.

Encouraging young people to pick up books clearly has value. Frequency alone tells us little about how readers respond when a text becomes difficult, unfamiliar or open to several interpretations. Students also need strategies for deciding what deserves attention, how different pieces of information fit together and when a claim should be questioned.

Their related work on reading strategies also identified weaknesses in how students approach texts, including deciding which sections deserve closer attention and using information from tables and figures to support understanding. Modern reading increasingly requires young people to move between an article, a graph, a website and several competing claims before deciding what information can be trusted.

Evidence from teachers presents a more encouraging picture. In 2025, Sarmurzin and colleagues surveyed 117 Kazakh literature teachers and interviewed experienced practitioners, finding a growing emphasis on reading comprehension, critical thinking, technology and more student-centred approaches. Teachers also identified continuing problems with curriculum coherence and the relationship between some reading materials and students’ everyday experiences.

Teacher preparation appears less settled. Research published in 2026 involving 254 final-year preservice teachers from five Kazakh universities found that 72% were uncertain about the distinction between functional literacy and traditional reading comprehension. The researchers also identified limited preparation in informational texts and critical digital reading, particularly among students preparing to teach Kazakh language and literature.

Greater professional support would help teachers respond to an increasingly complex reading environment. University programmes and professional development can give teachers more opportunities to work with inference, source comparison, evidence evaluation and critical digital literacy. Released PISA tasks can also show the kinds of reading processes students find difficult and provide useful material for lesson design and discussion.

There is an important limit to how far this should go. PISA measures particular forms of reading, and education should avoid turning those measures into a complete definition of what good reading looks like. Teaching students primarily to succeed on PISA-style tasks could narrow the curriculum and encourage another form of test preparation without necessarily creating more thoughtful or engaged readers. Reading also involves imagination, curiosity, emotional engagement, interpretation, enjoyment and the experience of spending time with ideas that do not lead towards a correct answer on an assessment.

PISA is most useful as a diagnostic tool. Its results can reveal weaknesses in areas such as inference, comprehension and source evaluation, while reading education itself should remain considerably broader. The aim should be to develop young people who can approach many kinds of texts with confidence, from novels and poetry to news reports, scientific arguments and digital information.

Kazakhstan could also make reading a clearer responsibility across the school curriculum. A history student comparing conflicting accounts of an event is practising reading. A science student deciding whether evidence supports a conclusion is doing the same, as is a geography student combining information from a map, graph and written report. Across these subjects, questions such as “How do I know this?”, “What evidence supports the claim?”, “What has been left out?” and “Which source should I trust?” can help students treat reading as a way of thinking rather than simply retrieving information.

Schools also need to protect space for sustained reading. Young people now encounter enormous quantities of written material through social media, messaging platforms, websites and increasingly AI systems. Much of this information arrives in short fragments. Regular opportunities to stay with longer and more demanding texts, discuss them, annotate them and return to difficult passages should remain part of school life. Sustained attention is itself becoming an important educational skill.

Generative AI adds another layer to this reading environment. AI can summarise a chapter, explain an argument and produce an answer within seconds. Students need strong skills for deciding whether that summary is accurate, what it has left out and whether the evidence supports the answer. One useful classroom activity might involve comparing an original article with an AI-generated summary. Students could identify missing qualifications, check claims against the original source and discuss how the meaning has changed. Used in this way, AI can support deeper reading.

Kazakhstan’s 2026 decree on developing reading culture already provides a framework for moving in this direction, particularly through its emphasis on reading in the era of artificial intelligence. Continued investment in books, libraries and positive reading cultures remains valuable. The next stage should connect that access more directly with how young people understand, question and use what they read.

A reading nation needs citizens who can stay with difficult ideas, recognise weak evidence, compare competing accounts and reach informed conclusions. It also needs readers who find pleasure in language, become absorbed in stories, encounter unfamiliar perspectives and sometimes read without being asked to extract a measurable skill from the experience. These abilities and experiences develop gradually through years of purposeful reading across classrooms, subjects and languages.

The PISA score of 385 should be treated as more than a position in an international ranking. It offers a useful warning about the depth of reading skills many young people currently possess and gives policymakers and educators a clearer sense of where attention is needed. Kazakhstan has already committed itself to becoming a reading nation. The next stage is to create the conditions in which young people can read widely, read carefully, enjoy what they read and learn to think for themselves through the process.

The author is Michael Jones, an writing and communications instructor, School of Social Science and Humanities, Nazarbayev University (Astana).

World.title: Kuwait’s Jazeera Airways Eyes Resumption of Direct Flights to Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – Kuwait’s airline Jazeera Airways is interested in resuming direct flights to Kazakhstan once regional conditions stabilize, potentially restoring a route suspended after its launch in 2021.

Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to Kuwait Yerzhan Yelekeyev discussed restoring direct air connectivity with Jazeera Airways CEO Barathan Pasupathi, the Kazakh Foreign Ministry reported on Oct. 13.

The officials explored opportunities to expand cooperation in civil aviation, tourism and trade. Yelekeyev emphasized that resuming flights would boost tourist flows, strengthen business ties and facilitate exports of Kazakh products to Kuwait.

Jazeera Airways reaffirmed its interest in the Kazakh market, saying it would consider resuming flights when the regional situation stabilizes and operating conditions become favorable.

The airline launched direct flights between Kuwait City and Almaty in 2021, but suspended the service later due to the regional situation.

World.title: Kazakhstan Claims Two Golds at U23 World Wrestling Championships in Las Vegas
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Greco-Roman wrestlers have secured two gold medals at the U23 World Wrestling Championships on Oct. 14 in Las Vegas, with Aibek Aitbekov and Yusuf Ashrapov winning their finals and Temirlan Turdakyn advancing to the title bout.

Aitbekov claimed the title in the 60-kilogram category, defeating Azerbaijan’s Elmir Aliyev, the reigning U23 world champion, in the final. En route to gold, the Kazakh wrestler also defeated Russia’s Alibek Amirov, Japan’s Seima Tokuharu, and Ukraine’s Yevhen Pokovba.

The victory adds to Aitbekov’s achievements this year, having previously won the U23 Asian Championship, according to the National Olympic Committee.

Ashrapov secured Kazakhstan’s second gold medal in the 72-kilogram category, defeating Armenia’s Gaspar Terteryan in the final.

The two victories have strengthened Kazakhstan’s Greco-Roman wrestling performance at the United States competition.

Turdakyn advances to gold medal bout

Turdakyn reached the final in the 87-kilogram category after defeating Russia’s Alexander Krikukha in the semifinals. He will face Iran’s Yasin Ali Yazdi for the gold medal.

With Turdakyn through to the final, Kazakhstan can add another title to its two gold medals at the U23 world championships.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Belgium Expand Academic Cooperation at Rectors’ Forum Attended by Tokayev and Royal Couple
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Belgium agreed to expand academic mobility, joint research and artificial intelligence cooperation as President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, King Philippe and Queen Mathilde attended a bilateral Rectors’ Forum on Oct. 13, bringing together leaders of 29 universities and research organizations.

Held at the Alem.ai International Center during the Belgian royal couple’s state visit, the forum focused on the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on higher education and scientific research. Kazakh and Belgian universities signed more than 20 agreements and memorandums of understanding, Akorda reported.

AI in education and research

Discussions focused on integrating AI into teaching, research and university management, adapting curricula to emerging technologies and strengthening digital competencies among students and faculty.

Participants also explored AI applications in language education, translation and multilingual academic communication, as well as the role of human expertise and trust in digital tools.

Kazakhstan highlighted its AI-Sana initiative, which aims to develop students’ AI skills, entrepreneurship and deep-tech startups. According to Deputy Minister of Science and Higher Education Gulzat Kobenova, the country plans to increase the share of universities incorporating AI courses into their curricula to 60% by 2029, according to the ministry’s press service.

The forum also discussed opportunities for Kazakh researchers to participate in European research programs, including Horizon Europe, and for universities to strengthen industry links.

Universities sign cooperation agreements

Al-Farabi Kazakh National University signed memorandums with Ghent University, KU Leuven and the University of Mons. The agreements provide for academic exchanges, joint educational initiatives and research cooperation. KazNU and Ghent University plan to develop exchanges in linguistics and a dual-degree program for doctoral students.

L.N. Gumilyov Eurasian National University signed three agreements with the same Belgian institutions, covering student and faculty mobility, joint educational programs, research projects and internships.

Serikbayev East Kazakhstan Technical University signed an agreement with KU Leuven and its SIM² research institute to establish a joint center focused on critical materials, including rare and rare-earth materials. The initiative is intended to combine research activities with specialist training.

Another initiative will advance the Mirror Lab, a joint Kazakhstan-Ghent University laboratory focused on mathematics, AI, modeling and engineering computations. It is expected to operate at the Institute of Mathematics and Mathematical Modeling and the Alem.ai International Center.

Building Kazakhstan’s AI ecosystem

The forum presented Alem.ai’s ecosystem development model, linking school education, universities, research laboratories and technology companies. Its annual targets include training 1,000 AI specialists, supporting 100 startups and developing 10 research projects.

Minister of Science and Higher Education Sayasat Nurbek said the high-level participation underscored the strategic importance of education and science in bilateral relations

The forum concluded with the signing of cooperation documents and the Belgian royal couple’s signing of the digital guestbook, marking another step toward expanding academic and research ties between Kazakhstan and Belgium.

World.title: Water After Glaciers: Preparing Kazakhstan for Different Water Future
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s water future may depend less on how much water reaches its rivers than on when it arrives. Climate change is shifting snowmelt, glacier runoff and river-flow peaks across Central Asia, forcing the country to rethink how it stores, forecasts and uses water.

For centuries, Central Asia’s mountains have acted as a natural water-storage system. Snow accumulates in winter, glaciers store water as ice, and meltwater feeds rivers during the warmer months. But that seasonal balance is changing.

Central Asian glaciers experienced their most severe year of ice loss on record in 2025, losing an estimated 30 cubic kilometers of ice, equivalent to nearly 2% of the region’s remaining glacier volume, according to a study published in Environmental Research Letters in May.

Kazakhstan has more than 2,400 glaciers covering approximately 930 square kilometers, according to data maintained by the Central Asian Regional Glaciological Center. Earlier estimates recorded 2,724 glaciers nationwide. In the Ile Alatau, the glacierized area declined by 47.4% between 1955 and 2021.

The changes have implications for regional water security: glacier melt accounted for approximately 25% of annual river discharge in the northern Tien Shan during 1991-2021, while 44.3% of Kazakhstan’s average annual surface-water resources originate beyond its borders.

When the water arrives matters

Tomas Saks, a senior researcher at the Department of Geosciences at the University of Fribourg, said snow cover remains the dominant source of river runoff in Central Asia, accounting for around 70-80% of total runoff.

Glaciers provide a smaller share annually, around 6-10% for the Syr Darya and Amu Darya. Their importance rises sharply during dry summer months, when most seasonal snow has already melted.

“In the dry summer seasons, when most of the snow has already melted, glaciers contribute up to 80%, making them a crucial water resource for the dry summer months,” Saks told The Astana Times.

This means glacier retreat is not simply a matter of declining annual water volumes. One of the first major changes is seasonality.

Saks expects the Syr Darya’s peak runoff to shift from roughly July-August towards May-June as snow melts earlier. Summer runoff is then expected to decline as glacier volumes decrease. The Amu Darya is also projected to reach its peak earlier, although its larger, higher-elevation glaciers are expected to continue supplying significant summer meltwater for longer.

Planning for a changing water calendar

Kazakhstan is adapting its water policy to this shift. The country’s Water Code, adopted in 2025, incorporates climate adaptation into water-sector management. The Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation told The Astana Times that it is now assessing long-term water availability at the basin level.

The ministry expects to complete eight basin plans by the end of this year. The Balkhash-Alakol, Aral-Syr Darya and Shu-Talas basins have been identified among the most climate-sensitive because of high water demand, snow- and glacier-fed rivers and dependence on transboundary flows.

For Saks, this basin-level approach is important because climate change will not affect every river in the same way.

Storage can buy time

Kazakhstan plans to build 42 new reservoirs, adding 2.6 billion cubic meters of storage, while modernizing existing reservoirs and irrigation infrastructure.

However, reservoirs cannot create water; they can only store it when it is available. That makes efficiency increasingly important. The ministry plans to reconstruct or modernize more than 4,600 kilometers of irrigation canals. This year alone, 962 kilometers are expected to be upgraded, improving water supply to around 200,000 hectares of irrigated land.

As Saks’s projections suggest, the challenge is not simply to store more water, but to capture it when it arrives and use it efficiently when it is needed.

Data is part of the solution

Saks also stressed the importance of turning scientific knowledge into timely decisions.

Central Asia has substantial research on glacier and snow-cover changes. But if snowmelt and river-flow peaks are moving earlier, governments need better forecasts of when water will arrive in each basin.

Kazakhstan is developing a National Information System of Water Resources to integrate information on water bodies, infrastructure, water users and water availability, strengthening monitoring and forecasting. Warning signs may appear long before glaciers disappear: earlier snowmelt, lower late-summer river flows, changes in smaller glacier-fed catchments, and growing pressure on irrigation systems.

A regional water system

Kazakhstan alone cannot manage the changes that Saks describes. Water resources are concentrated mainly in the Kyrgyz Republic and Tajikistan, while major demand is downstream in Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. Changes in snow and glacier melt therefore affect the entire regional system.

As water flows become less predictable, Saks said, cooperation between upstream and downstream countries will become increasingly important. For Kazakhstan, stronger data-sharing, forecasting and agreements over transboundary rivers will be essential.

Preparing for a different future

A “post-glacier” water system does not mean a future without glaciers or rivers. It means a future in which glaciers can no longer be assumed to provide the same seasonal buffer they have provided for generations.

Kazakhstan is responding with new reservoirs, modernized irrigation, basin-level planning and better forecasting. The real test will be whether these measures allow the country to anticipate changes rather than react to shortages.

In 2030 and onward, water security may depend not only on how much water Kazakhstan has, but on how accurately it can predict when that water will arrive and how efficiently it can use every drop.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Belgium Seek Deeper Trade and Investment Ties at Business Council
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Belgium are seeking to deepen cooperation in transport and logistics, critical minerals, energy, advanced technologies and manufacturing, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and King Philippe said at the Oct. 13 fourth meeting of the Kazakh-Belgian Business Council during the Belgian monarch’s state visit to Kazakhstan.

Belgium ranks among the 10 largest investors in Kazakhstan, with Belgian companies investing more than $15 billion in the country over the past two decades, Tokayev said, opening the council.

“More than 100 Belgian and joint ventures are successfully operating in our country in the fields of agriculture, healthcare and pharmaceuticals, advanced technologies and energy. At the regional level, Kazakhstan is Belgium’s largest trading partner in Central Asia,” Tokayev said.

He also highlighted King Philippe’s contribution to expanding bilateral trade and economic ties, identifying transport and logistics as one of the key areas for further cooperation.

Transport and logistics offer new opportunities

According to Tokayev, Kazakhstan is investing heavily in modernizing its railway and road infrastructure, seaports and terminals along the Middle Corridor. He proposed closer practical cooperation between the Port of Antwerp-Bruges and Kazakhstan’s Caspian ports of Aktau and Kuryk.

“In this context, Belgium’s extensive experience as one of Europe’s largest logistics hubs is particularly valuable to us. This will open up broader markets for Kazakhstan’s metal products, petrochemicals and agricultural products,” he said.

King Philippe also emphasized the complementary roles of the two countries in connecting Europe and Central Asia. According to him, Kazakhstan is a vital link across the Eurasian space.

“Thanks to its unique geographical location and significant natural resources, it has become a regional center for trade, investment and the development of the green economy, occupying a special place in the global economy. All this creates a natural foundation for mutually complementary cooperation,” he said.

AI and advanced technology on the agenda

Tokayev identified artificial intelligence and the technology industry as other priorities for strengthening the partnership. Kazakhstan is advancing initiatives such as Alem.ai and Alatau City, which are intended to develop next-generation centers for advanced industries and technological innovation.

“Belgium’s strong position in semiconductor research opens up new opportunities for joint projects and the development of our partnership,” Tokayev said.

The two countries could also expand cooperation in energy and petrochemicals. Tokayev described Kazakhstan as a reliable supplier of oil to European markets and highlighted opportunities in renewable energy, energy efficiency, industrial decarbonization and hydrogen production.

“I invite Belgian companies to implement joint projects in the deep processing of raw materials, the chemical industry and the production of high-value-added polymer products,” he said.

Critical minerals and industrial processing

Critical minerals were another central topic at the business council, alongside a Kazakh-Belgian roundtable on the sector held as part of King Philippe’s state visit. Tokayev said Kazakhstan already produces 21 of the 34 types of raw materials considered critical to European industry and supplies Belgium with titanium and molybdenum products.

“The partnership between John Cockerill and Qarmet to create new galvanizing and protective-coating capacity is a real example of our industrial cooperation. We also welcome the participation of Belgian partners in geological exploration and the deep processing of raw materials and metals,” Tokayev said.

Business ties and people-to-people cooperation

Tokayev also stressed Kazakhstan’s interest in attracting skilled and entrepreneurial people willing to work alongside local professionals.

“The more such people come to our country, the better it will be for all of us, as this contributes to strengthening both personal and professional contacts. Such interaction is highly valued in Kazakhstan. As President of Kazakhstan, I value first and foremost the intellectual abilities of people who come to our country, rather than their ethnic background,” he said.

King Philippe, addressing business representatives from both countries, called for stronger cooperation in promising sectors including energy, critical minerals, transport and logistics, finance and tourism.

“Belgium and Kazakhstan are separated by a considerable geographical distance, but in terms of ambition, pragmatic approach and determination, we are remarkably close,” he said.

World.title: Kazakhstan to Hold Early Maslikhat Elections This November
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan will hold early elections for local representative bodies, known as maslikhats, on Nov. 29, the Central Election Commission announced at an Oct. 13 meeting.

The elections will fill 3,447 seats across 228 maslikhats at the regional, city and district levels, Deputy Chair of the Central Election Commission Mukhtar Yerman said. Of the total seats, 668 will be in regional maslikhats, 626 in city maslikhats and 2,053 in district maslikhats.

The commission presented a draft resolution setting the election date for Nov. 29. Under Article 101, paragraph 3, of Kazakhstan’s Constitutional Law on Elections, early elections must be called by the Central Election Commission no later than two months after the early termination of a maslikhat’s powers.
