World.title: Iran’s production-sector financing rises nearly 12-fold
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. The value of financing instruments supporting Iran’s production sector increased nearly 12-fold during the period from March 21 through September 22, 2026, compared with the period from March 21 through September 22, 2025.

According to Trend’s analysis of statistics from the Central Bank of Iran, the total value of these financing instruments reached 3.03 quadrillion rials (about $1.68 billion) during the reporting period, compared with 254 trillion rials (about $141 million) during the corresponding period in 2025.

The value of credit-guarantee securities supporting production growth reached 596 trillion rials (about $331 million), compared with 124 trillion rials (about $69.1 million) during the corresponding period in 2025.

The value of electronic promissory notes used in the production chain totaled 2.25 quadrillion rials (about $1.25 billion), compared with 127 trillion rials (about $70.5 million) during the corresponding period in 2025.

The value of welfare cards linked to the credit-guarantee securities system for production growth amounted to about 149 trillion rials (about $82.6 million), compared with 2.5 trillion rials (about $1.4 million) during the corresponding period in 2025.

Factoring, or the financing of receivables, amounted to 35.4 trillion rials (about $19.6 million) during the reporting period.

World.title: Azerbaijan denies reports of hijab ban in medical institutions
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. The Azerbaijan Audiovisual Council and the Ministry of Health have issued a joint statement following the circulation of a fake document on social media and messaging platforms claiming that restrictions had been introduced on wearing the hijab in medical institutions.

The statement notes that the letter being circulated and attributed to the Ministry of Health is fake. The ministry has neither issued such a document nor given medical institutions any relevant instructions.

Presenting the fake letter as an official document misleads the public and constitutes disinformation.

The Azerbaijan Audiovisual Council called on media outlets and social media users to verify information through official sources, refrain from presenting the fake document as authentic, and avoid contributing to the spread of disinformation.

World.title: Iran’s East Azerbaijan customs exports rise 27% in value
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. Exports of goods through the customs offices of Iran’s East Azerbaijan Province rose by 27% in value and 4% in volume during the period from March 21 through September 22, 2026, compared with the same period in 2025.

Ali Asghar Abbaszadeh, head of East Azerbaijan Province customs, announced the figures, according to the Iranian Customs Administration.

"During the reporting period, 1.7 million tons of goods worth $1.08 billion were exported through the province’s customs offices," he said.

Abbaszadeh said the main exports included iron and steel products worth $211 million, copper and copper products worth $192 million, petrochemical and rubber products worth $107 million, mineral fuels and various types of bitumen worth $74 million, and grain and flour products worth $62 million.

According to the customs official, the goods were exported to 80 countries, primarily Türkiye, Iraq, Armenia, Afghanistan and Georgia.

During the same period, 278,000 tons of goods worth more than $688 million were imported into Iran through the province’s customs offices. Import value increased by 8%, while import volume rose by 25% compared with March 21–September 22, 2025, Abbaszadeh said.

He added that the main imports included machinery and equipment worth $113 million, tobacco products worth $91 million, vehicles and spare parts worth $53 million, petrochemical and rubber products worth $43 million, and red meat worth $29 million.

The goods were imported from 54 countries, including Türkiye, the United Arab Emirates, China, Germany and India, he said.

Abbaszadeh also reported that approximately 429,000 tons of transit cargo entered Iran through the province’s customs offices during the reporting period, an increase of 35% compared with the same period in 2025. Meanwhile, 878,000 tons of transit cargo left Iran through the province’s customs offices, up by 19% year-on-year.

According to Trend’s analysis of Iranian Customs Administration statistics, during the period from March 21, 2025, through January 20, 2026, East Azerbaijan Province’s customs offices handled exports totaling 2.8 million tons worth $1.47 billion and imports totaling 395,000 tons worth $1.29 billion.

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 15, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The 44-day second Karabakh war ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity.

Trend presents the chronicle of the 19th day of the Second Karabakh war:

- President Ilham Aliyev interviewed by the Turkish NTV channel.

- "Azerbaijan’s glorious Army has liberated Arish village of Fuzuli district, Doshulu village of Jabrayil district, and Edishe, Dudukchi, Edilli and Chiraguz of Khojavend district. Long live Azerbaijan’s Army! Karabakh is Azerbaijan!" President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev made a post on his official Twitter account.

- President Ilham Aliyev interviewed by Dmitry Kiselev, Director General of the Russia Today media group, for the Russian RIA Novosti news agency.

- First Vice President of Azerbaijan Mehriban Aliyeva made a post on her official Instagram account in connection with the shelling of the funeral procession in Tartar by the Armenian side.

- As a result of the actions taken by the Azerbaijani army, a large number of Armenian manpower and equipment were destroyed and disabled in different directions of the front.

- The Armenian armed forces, grossly violating the humanitarian ceasefire, fired at the territories of Goranboy, Tartar, Aghdam and Aghjabadi districts.

- The death toll as a result of the deliberate shelling of the funeral procession in Tartar by Armenia reached 4 people.

- The Prosecutor General's Office of Azerbaijan said that two civilians were injured as a result of shelling a residential building in Aghdam by the Armenian armed forces.

- The Armenian colonel, commander of the military unit of the Armed Forces of Armenia, was liquidated.

World.title: City man says he wants to help farmers deal with silent mental health crisis
World.content:
City slicker Dan Sutherland decided he wanted to show his appreciation for Western Australia's farmers by organising the West Coast Long Drive.

The convoy of iconic paddock-bashers roared their way through the Wheatbelt and Gascoyne in their 40 series LandCruisers.

It was a conversation starter, and exactly the attention the West Coast Long Drivers had been hoping for when they set out on an eight-day journey from Perth to Bullara Station, to raise awareness of the mental health challenges for farmers.

The West Coast Long Drive follows on from a similar event held in Queensland. (ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel)

"We've stopped in a lot of rural towns where there's just true Aussie battlers; the old fellas sitting around the bar, the old bar flies, farmers, pastoralists and truck drivers," Mr Sutherland said.

" You could have a really bad day and all it takes is for someone to say mate, 'I see you, I feel you, I care about you, I respect you and we're here for you'. "

Mr Sutherland said his love for his vintage car drew him to Queensland's Long Drive for Drought a few years ago.

He was struggling with his own mental health at the time, and said the stories from the farmers inspired him to bring the charity event back home.

"Just from the outside looking in, I've got a lot of compassion and respect for what they do," he said.

"The funding and help are available, but if farmers in Western Australia don't know about it they can't reach out."

The car enthusiasts spent eight days making the journey up the WA coast. (ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Along the way, the group raised nearly $40,000 for farmer support charity Farm Angels.

Going beyond statistics

Until a few years ago, Mr Sutherland said he had no idea of the silent mental health crisis impacting farming communities across the country.

Isolation and stigma around mental health are major barriers preventing farmers from accessing support.

More than half of farmers have felt depressed in the past two years, according to the 2026 National Farmer Wellbeing Report.

Loading...

And more than 90 per cent felt undervalued by the Australian public.

Behind these statistics are real people, like Long Drive participant and farmer Arran Teakle.

"The old black dog shows itself every now and then, I just grin and bear it most days," Mr Teakle said.

"We go through a fair bit; we feel a bit left out and it's something that needs addressing."

Farming pressures

Mr Teakle grows wheat, lupin and canola over 2,000 hectares on his family property in Northampton, about 450 kilometres north of Perth.

Five years ago, he lost 80 per cent of his sheds during Cyclone Seroja and has dealt with two mouse plagues and periods of low rain since.

The convoy travelling through the Mid West region. (ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Farming pressures are becoming increasingly widespread but Mr Teakle said it was ingrained in farmers to "take it as it comes".

"If it doesn't rain or if it rains too much, that's farming so we deal with that, we can keep going, it's the factors that can be controlled that really affect us such as the ban on live export and the cancellation of visas," he said.

"We do really need the support of the public when it comes to those sorts of issues; without the public support, you will see mental health issues increase."

The team stopped in at many towns along the route. (ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Mr Teakle said the West Coast Long Drive had helped him clear his head.

"After going on this long drive with Farm Angels I can see there are support networks out there," he said.

" It's just good to get out there and chat and ask how people are doing. "

The West Coast Long Drivers are hoping to get more people involved next year.

World.title: Automated feedlot proposal draws community ire in Victoria's south-east
World.content:
A proposal in Victoria's south-east to create one of the state's first undercover, automated cattle feedlots has drawn community opposition with residents saying it will create road safety and odour issues for neighbouring properties.

The proposal to build a 2,206-head feedlot at Llowalong, north of Maffra and Stratford, would see cattle housed in enclosed sheds and fed on a 90-day cycle before being transported for processing.

An artist's impression of the proposed 2,206-head feedlot at Llowalong. (Supplied: Wellington Shire Council)

At Wellington Shire Council's October meeting, local resident Nick Lee, speaking on behalf of his neighbours, called for the application to be rejected.

"The proximity to other farms and homes will have the following impacts: increased traffic movements and potential impacts on local road infrastructure, increased noise levels, odour and pollution of nearby residences, environmental and health concerns," he said.

"Llowalong Road is not suitable for that volume of heavy traffic.

"Adding more than 850 truck movements a year would materially increase the risk to residents, farmers, other road users and heavy vehicle drivers."

Nick Lee spoke at the Wellington Shire Council meeting earlier this month. (Supplied: Wellington Shire Council)

Opponents of the feedlot presented a petition against the proposal, with almost 700 signatures, to the Wellington Shire Council at its October 6 meeting.

The motion to reject the proposal was carried by the council, where it was referred to the general manager of development for it to be discussed at a future council meeting.

As a result, council chief executive David Morcom said a decision on the application would likely not be made until next year.

"These applications can be quite complex. There can be quite a lot of to-ing and fro-ing and we will certainly keep you abridged of that process," he said.

Proponent touts feedlot's benefits

The feedlot's proponent, farmer Angus Zilm, said the project presented an opportunity to introduce advanced cattle feeding technology in Gippsland, with a focus on animal welfare, efficient feeding and environmental management.

"A substantial amount of technical investigation, design and review has gone into preparing the application over the last two years," he said.

"We have worked with engineers and specialist agricultural and environmental consultants to assess the site, develop the proposal and prepare the supporting reports."

The proposed feedlot development would be built on vacant farmland in Llowalong. (ABC News: Jack Colantuono)

Mr Zilm said work was continuing as the team responded to the council's questions and community concerns.

"We know our neighbours have questions and we take that seriously," he said.

"We want to get this right, so we're working through the concerns with our specialist advisers and providing council with the information it needs."

Mr Zilm said the feedlot would offer contract feeding, allowing local cattle producers to have their animals fed at the site rather than managing the entire process themselves.

He said access to a facility closer to home could reduce transport costs, while the development could also provide educational opportunities for school and university students studying agriculture.

A map of the proposed feedlot and its proximity to surrounding homes in Llowalong. (Supplied: Wellington Shire Council)

Feedlots crucial for markets

According to a report by Deloitte Access Economics commissioned by Meat and Livestock Australia (MLA) the country's feedlot industry is expanding.

The report found feedlots spent $4.3 billion on cattle and feed in 2023 and 2024, while the number of cattle on feed more than doubled between 2000 and 2024.

Feedlots' share of cattle slaughter also tripled, rising from 12 per cent to 36 per cent.

The report estimated a hypothetical 5,000-head feedlot could generate $14.4 million in economic benefits, rising to $86.2 million for a 30,000-head facility.

Australia’s feedlot capacity and cattle numbers have climbed steadily in recent years. (Supplied: Meat and Livestock Australia)

Melbourne Veterinary School senior consultant John Webb-Ware said the feedlot industry played an important role in supplying Australian beef markets.

"To supply quality product year-round is a real challenge in Australia," Dr Webb-Ware said.

"There's obviously niche markets and very important markets for grass-fed cattle in Australia and overseas.

" But to supply the bulk of the quality products to our export markets … the most efficient way of supplying is through feedlots. "

The construction plan of the proposed feedlot on Llowalong Road and Nerina Lane in Llowalong. (Supplied: Wellington Shire Council)

Dr Webb-Ware also said feedlots were subject to criteria intended to address potential impacts on surrounding properties.

"There's pretty stringent requirements for feedlotting to counter the concerns for noise and smell and all that sort of stuff," he said.

"It's obviously got to tick off the specific requirements which are appropriate for the local area which [the Llowalong proposal] is going through that process."

World.title: Qld tourism businesses say fuel prices behind drop in visitor numbers
World.content:
Carly Clark is passionate about hosting visitors on her animal rescue property, but she says tourist numbers have declined by 30 per cent on her regional Queensland farm.

Splitters Farm is among the many tourism businesses in the Bundaberg region, a nearly 5-hour drive north of Brisbane, that rely on the drive tourism market.

"This September school holidays we saw that a lot of people were not travelling and that our numbers were down in both the accommodation and the day trips," Ms Clark said.

Splitters Farm, in Bundaberg, has many rescue animals. (ABC News: Johanna Marie)

Increased costs were "hurting everyone", the small business owner said.

"You've got [the] rising cost of insurances as well, and as a business we have to pass those insurance hikes onto our customers … so everyone's getting hit.

" I think grey nomads are naturally pretty frugal with travelling, but families definitely are being hit hard by [the] cost of fuel, cost of electricity. "

Animals roam around the farm stay in Bundaberg. (ABC News: Johanna Marie)

Megan Rippon, who travelled nearly 600 kilometres from Lismore in northern New South Wales with daughters Charli and Indi, said she was frugal in deciding where to spend money while holidaying in Bundaberg.

"I've got a hybrid [car] which helps but definitely thinking about the cost of fuel," Ms Rippon said.

"We're probably going to go to the beach and relax by the pool."

Megan Rippon with her daughters Charli and Indi at Splitters Farm. (ABC News: Johanna Marie)

Turtle tour bookings

The region's turtle season is fast approaching and despite weekend tickets normally being sold out beforehand, there are still thousands available.

"Mon Repos is a really special place. It's the main nesting place for the endangered loggerhead turtle," ranger-in-charge Cathy Gatley said.

Cathy Gatley and Stephen Bennett at Mon Repos Turtle Centre. (ABC News: Johanna Marie)

"You can drive to the park and up to the turtle centre and then walk along the beach with a guide to see turtles, hopefully, if turtles behave on the night."

The state member for Burnett, Stephen Bennett, said he wasn't concerned the Mon Repos tickets hadn't yet sold out as the season was only beginning.

Turtle hatchlings making their dash towards the ocean near Bundaberg. (ABC News: Jenae Jenkins)

"There's a lot of billboards going up now that will start to promote the turtles and the visitor experience, and Bundaberg and the Southern Great Barrier Reef are certainly a destination that we continue to promote," he said.

Caution on spending

According to Bundaberg Tourism, there were 750,000 overnight visitors to the region in the past financial year, injecting $430 million into the economy.

But the tourism body has observed a shift in booking trends in recent months.

Tourists are more conscious of how they spend their money, Bundaberg Tourism says. (ABC News: Johanna Marie)

"One of the things we have noticed is that booking window that people have when looking to make a trip has tightened, but that has been seen throughout the state and also throughout Australia," chief executive Duncan Littler said.

" People are being more considerate when they're looking for where they're going to travel, how they're going to travel and where they're going to spend their money. "

A nearly 2-hour drive south of Bundaberg, whale tour operators are wrapping up a less-than-bumper season in Hervey Bay.

Whalesong Cruises general manager Ben Duffy said bookings were also down 30 per cent this season compared to last year.

Ben Duffy says visitor numbers were down this whale season. (ABC News: James Taylor)

"People seem to be holding onto their disposable income rather than enjoy life," he said.

Mr Duffy would like to see a cut to the fuel excise to alleviate pressure on businesses and travellers.

"We do require fuel so our expenditure's up, and if the travel numbers are down … the overall income for people in the area is down."

Exploring closer to home

Ms Clark said it was a "period of uncertainty" for businesses and households.

She said while fuel prices were affecting long-distance travel, it could be an opportunity for locals to explore their own backyard.

"You've got the reef, the farm, you've got fantastic food and beverage options all within a really small space, 20 minutes from each other," she said.

World.title: Australia is the monster that turns World Cup dreams to nightmares
World.content:
Almost a decade ago, the women's Rugby League World Cup final was the last day before everything changed.

Australia's cracking 23-16 win over New Zealand in 2017 didn't just deliver the team its first-ever World Cup final victory on home soil; it was the last major match before the women's game was transformed forever.

The following season, the interstate series moved under the NRL banner, the first NRLW season kicked off, and women's rugby league began to take giant strides.

Australia's 2017 World Cup win was the last game before the women's game changed forever. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe )

A few players from that watershed moment are still around for this year's Rugby League World Cup, which begins tomorrow in Parramatta, when Australia plays Samoa.

Isabelle Kelly, Kezie Apps and Simaima Taufa are still wearing green and gold; Zahara Temara has switched to New Zealand and will play for the Kiwi Ferns in their tournament opener against Fiji on Sunday alongside Raecene McGregor and Apii Nicholls.

These six exist in a different world from the one they came from, one where the players are now faster, stronger, fitter and more skilful; where pathways have improved, and player numbers have exploded; and where the game has evolved to the point where this should be the last World Cup held simultaneously with the men's tournament because the product is strong enough to stand alone.

The women's World Cup will again be held alongside the men's tournament. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

But the issue heading into the tournament is at the top end of the product, because Australia's dominance has become one of the growing pains the game must endure as everyone else tries to catch up.

Since that win in 2017, the Jillaroos have won 15 of 16 matches. They have not conceded more than two tries in a game since 2018.

In the last World Cup, they won their five matches by a cumulative scoreline of 312-12, including a 54-4 massacre of New Zealand in the final.

Unconventional coach out to extend the Jillaroos reign Jessica Skinner once doubted her coaching style was elite. Now she believes it's exactly what the top level needs, and her journey from rural NSW has shaped why.

The last time they played England, they won 90-4, and those four points mark the only try they've conceded to a team other than New Zealand in their past 16 games.

They won the Pacific Championship last year, scoring 110 points and conceding just 12 across three matches, with the Kiwi Ferns copping a 40-8 belting in the final.

State of Origin regulars like Jesse Southwell and Abbi Church, both overlooked for the match against Samoa, can't make this team. A living legend like Ali Brigginshaw can't even make the squad.

The Jillaroos have nine players from this year's NRLW Dally M Team of the Year. In Tamika Upton, Olivia Kernick, Tarryn Aiken, Isabelle Kelly and Jess Sergis, they have the best player, forward, halfback and centres in the world.

Tamika Upton has won three of the last four Dally M medals. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

They are, without question, the best women's rugby league team ever, and they are so much better than everyone else that anything less than a dominant run to the final and a thumping victory at Lang Park will feel like a departure from a predestined fate.

Other teams have improved. New Zealand, which handed Australia its sole loss in recent years in 2023 and went down by just six points in one game last year, has risen highest with the tide.

As the Warriors settle back into the NRLW, they could rise higher still, and their squad for this year's tournament should put them in contention for the final.

Samoa is another side that has improved and could still get better. The Fetu have benefited from the injection of diaspora players like Taliah Fuimaono, Evania Isa'ako and Amber Hall, plus fresh faces like Queensland Origin flyer Destiny Mino-Sinapati and reigning NRLW rookie of the year Mercedez Taulelei-Siala.

Samoa will be making its World Cup debut. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters )

They are a vision of what is possible for the expansion of women's rugby league and beneficiaries of the improved pathways leading to the NRLW.

It will take time, because we are talking about change that can take a decade or more to become apparent, but the benefits are there for all to see in the men's game.

The women's game is on the same path; they're just not as far along. This is a brave, dangerous side with a real future, one which is easy to see unfolding before us.

One day a team like Samoa might be able to give the World Cup a real shake. But not these days.

The Samoans are currently 53.5-point underdogs against the Jillaroos in tomorrow night's match. They lost to them 60-0 in the corresponding clash last year.

Even that was nothing compared to the 90-4 belting England copped in Las Vegas last year, an eye-popping result that showed just how lopsided things had become.

England was humiliated in its last meeting with Australia. (Getty Images: Ethan Miller)

The English will get a chance at revenge in Perth next week, and they're a much better side than the one that travelled to Nevada.

Roosters backrower Jasmin Strange is a welcome addition, and they have a core of NRLW players, including North Queensland's Fran Goldthorp, Canberra forward Hollie-Mae Dodd and clever Newcastle playmaker Georgia Roche.

If they can keep things respectable against the Jillaroos, that will be progress.

That gap can close as more top-level talent filters through the ranks, for England and everybody else.

But it will take time to run the Jillaroos down. And because the women's game is semi-professional, it's unlikely to happen as rapidly as it has in the men's game, meaning progress could take a decade or more.

New Zealand shape up as the only side with a realistic chance of taking down Australia. (Getty Images: Ian Hitchcock)

Until then, there is no choice but to keep going.

Every nation will have a moment. Some will have more than one because there will be glories outside of absolute victory. Fiji will make its World Cup debut and Papua New Guinea will look to continue its steady progress of recent years.

A semi-final berth would be a major achievement for Samoa and a place in the final would be a shot in the arm for the game in England, so their group-stage clash is the pick of the early tournament matches.

The Kiwi Ferns will fancy their chances of an ambush should they meet Australia in the final, given the Jillaroos will have had a soft run in. They will point out that they are the one in 15-1, and perhaps they will be right.

But at the end lurks Australia, the monster at the end of the dream that turns it into a nightmare. And, just under a decade since the rest of history began, the truth of the pain it is about to inflict is simple.

This is the best collection of players ever assembled in women's rugby league, and if they are at any point over the next month beaten, it will be one of the biggest upsets the game has known.

World.title: Kimberley youth night spaces heralded as 'blueprint' for WA
World.content:
Isiah Brooking stands at a microphone on a characteristically warm evening in Western Australia's Kimberley.

"Night space come and play, it's a beautiful place you can come stay," he sings alongside a friend.

It is a performance that captures the hearts of those in the crowd in Fitzroy Crossing, about 2,600 kilometres north of Perth.

Children and community members gather for the Fitzroy Crossing Night Space two-year anniversary. (ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson)

More than 100 attendees gathered to celebrate the second anniversary of the town's Youth Night Space last month.

A similar milestone was marked 400km away in Broome, where an independent report has hailed its youth hub a success.

The Fitzroy Crossing hub was launched in 2024 by the Marra Warra Warra Aboriginal Corporation in response to calls from at-risk youth and their families in town.

Fitzroy Crossing's Night Space opened in September 2024. (ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson)

It has since grown to house a basketball court, multiple rooms and a lawn for play.

Isiah Brooking said some of his favourite things to do at the hub included getting something to eat and playing cards.

Isiah Brooking (left) said he liked playing cards and getting a feed at the night space. (ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson)

More than 950 children have engaged with the space since opening, and staff have served over 55,000 meals.

Fostering trust

Fitzroy Crossing Police officer in charge Mark Howes attended the event.

"When I first got here three years ago, that was a problem … young people committing lots of crimes," he said.

"Now they're nowhere near as much."

Senior Sergeant Mark Howes speaks at the Fitzroy Crossing youth space anniversary. (ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson)

Senior Sergeant Howes said the space helped build trust between young people and officers.

"Kids here wave to police," he said.

" Even when they're naughty and they come into the police station … we've got a good relationship and they tell the truth. "

Program manager Rochelle Dolby said witnessing the centre's progress had been special.

"To know what started from an idea, just supporting the kids coming each night, to then see everyone come and celebrate that," she said.

"It's a very nice feeling, and I feel very proud to be part of it."

Marra Worra Worra's Rochelle Dolby said the space had come a long way from the small house that first opened. (ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson)

Community blueprint

Broome's night space has won high praise for its facilities and the work of its staff in a recent independent evaluation.

Ngurra Buru opened its doors in 2024 as a pilot response to community and police concerns over the high number of young people wandering the town's streets at night.

Broome's Ngurra Buru Night Space has helped reduce youth crime in the town in its first two years. (ABC Kimberley: Mya Kordic)

Since opening, there have been about 9,900 interactions with children and teenagers during its 10pm to 5am hours.

"Often the young people will just come in, sit and socialise with other peers and share a meal together and then are happy to be returned back home to their primary residence," manager Fiona Hart said.

The evaluation report, led by the Kimberley Aboriginal Health Research Alliance and the University of Melbourne, included 20 responses from night space participants.

Fiona Hart says she commended the Ngurra Buru staff for making the night space such a culturally safe and supportive environment. (ABC Kimberley: Mya Kordic)

All surveyed children said they felt safe, had someone to talk to, and were provided with food and transport.

Ms Hart said she was proud of the facility, which has been dubbed a "blueprint" for other Western Australian services.

"There was a real effort made to create a space that felt like a home away from home," she said.

Crime rates down

In its first 13 months of operation, crime across three Broome suburbs significantly decreased, according to the report.

Property offences by year Broome Cable Beach Djugun 2024 1,699 701 176 2025 1,253 597 138 2026 (to June 30) 502 193 52 Source: WA Police Crime Statistics

Ms Hart said a combined effort from the community and authorities was the driving force behind the downward trend.

While the space is currently open five nights a week, she said continued funding would allow it to operate every night.

"The future vision is we could hit that seven-nights-a-week service delivery and have a great pool of staff," Ms Hart said.

Hopes for the East Kimberley

While Broome and Fitzroy Crossing are celebrating two-year milestones, Kununurra launched a temporary night space for the first time in August.

Hylton Quail hopes the youth night space will deliver similar outcomes for Kununurra. (ABC News: Phil Hemmingway)

WA Childrens Court president Hylton Quail in September said he hoped there would be a similar turnaround for the East Kimberley town.

"We're going to stop seeing burglaries and cars stolen at night because the kids are going to have somewhere to go," he said

"Some of them don't get fed otherwise."

A permanent facility in Kununurra is slated to open at the end of the year.

World.title: David Chau's mission to make finance news 'tolerable'
World.content:
It has been almost a decade since I started covering finance for the ABC.

That first year was particularly exciting, with Donald Trump waging a tariff war against Australia's largest trading partner and causing huge market shocks nearly every day with his stream-of-consciousness tweeting.

In that regard, the situation has not really changed.

But in other ways, things have become worse, particularly when it comes to our living standards.

Buying a home is more unaffordable than ever, despite the recent "downturn", while Australian households are now carrying the second-highest amount of debt in the world after Switzerland.

David Chau filming a TV news report for The Business. (Supplied)

Extremely high-risk and speculative investments have also exploded in popularity, particularly bitcoin, other cryptocurrencies, and now pretty much anything to do with artificial intelligence.

It is no wonder the cost of living has become the most popular discussion topic in our nation, for all the wrong reasons.

That is why I am excited to be spending more time with you in the years ahead, demystifying finance on the 7pm News, making it more relatable (and even fun) for a wider audience.

Looking back, one of my favourite pieces of audience feedback over the years was:

" I find business dreadfully dull, but I didn't mind your segment. It was actually quite tolerable! "

If more viewers who were not interested in business news before start paying attention, then it's mission accomplished.

A long and winding road

I must confess I am just as surprised as you that I have landed this gig, taking over from the legendary Alan Kohler.

It is definitely one of those "pinch me" moments in life.

One of David Chau's first roles at the ABC was presenting finance segments on Radio National. (Supplied: David Chau)

The other "pinch me" moment I had was more than 10 years ago, as I was poring through thousands of pages of evidence at a law firm, doing my best to stay awake.

Before starting at the ABC, I was a litigation lawyer, but I did not really enjoy suing people. As you can imagine, my career was off to a promising start.

After five years of sending threatening letters and trying to sound a like a legal tough guy, I decided it was time for a change.

I chose journalism because I wanted a career that was exciting, where I could meet all sorts of interesting people, and do work that served the public interest.

And, if we go even further back in time to the 1980s, I was the son of a Vietnam War refugee who did not grow up with much money.

My dad was a judo instructor and goldsmith before the Fall of Saigon.

David Chau's father, Hong, emigrated to Australia from Vietnam. (Supplied)

When he moved to Sydney, he did not speak English, nor did his qualifications transfer very easily. He was only able to find factory work.

That is why he regularly drilled into me the importance of education, finding a 'good job' and achieving financial security. He did not have most of those things.

So that is how I got into a regular news-viewing habit and started noticing Alan's finance reports.

That time I got GFC'd

My interest in finance and economics ramped up from 2009, when I found myself unemployed for several months.

I was sending hundreds of CVs and cover letters for any kind of work related to what I had just been studying at university for five years — and received a similar number of rejections.

From watching Alan's coverage, it did not take me long to realise that my job struggles were caused by some dreadful binge-borrowing overseas that led to this thing called the global financial crisis.

The global financial crisis unfolded when Kevin Rudd was prime minister. (AAP: Alan Porritt)

And I also learned firsthand that when Australia's unemployment rate quickly rises from about 4 per cent to 5.8 per cent, it is a particularly bad time for young job seekers with almost no experience whatsoever. Lucky me.

So I had to take radical steps to find decent work, such as move to Perth for a couple of years. Thankfully, there was still a mining boom happening there.

How did I get here?

A lot of people have asked me over the years: "How did you end up switching careers from law to journalism?"

Alan Kohler's last ABC sign-off Alan Kohler will walk out the door of the ABC's Melbourne studios tonight after presenting his final finance report, ending a 31-year career at the public broadcaster.

Well, fast forward to 2015. I reached the point where I was so jaded that I decided to quit the legal profession without a backup plan. (Older-and-wiser me would not recommend this unless you have your next job lined up.)

I did not know exactly what I wanted to do next. So trial and error was the only option for me, and I tried all manner of random jobs. Nothing was beneath me.

That is how I ended up as that guy who greeted and seated customers at Jamie Oliver's Italian restaurant, but that was for one night only as I was quite terrible at it.

I also operated a phone hotline, answering calls from people who wanted to lodge complaints about their lawyers (oh, the irony).

And I was briefly a costumed superhero at kids' birthday parties (I had to pay bills somehow).

One of the more sensible choices I made was to work at a small financial news publication and try my hand at business reporting.

David Chau on his first day at the ABC in May 2017. (Supplied)

It turned out I was quite good at it, surprisingly.

After trying financial journalism for a year, I decided it was time to advance my new career at a larger, more reputable organisation.

So I went on a relentless cold-calling campaign and somehow managed to get the ABC's business editor at the time, Ian Verrender, on the phone.

Sometimes landing an opportunity involves being somewhere at the right place, at the right time, which is exactly what happened to me.

Ian decided to hire me as the team's most junior producer and placed me on a three-month contract to see how I performed.

Lucky for me, I did not do too badly. So those temporary contracts kept getting extended and eventually I was made permanent.

Nine years later, I'm still here, and have since written hundreds of articles for the ABC and presented hundreds more finance reports across TV and radio.

The road ahead

Now back to Alan. I still find it hard to believe that he is retiring. He has been in the role for so long that I seriously thought he was going to do it forever.

I have always been impressed by how easily he can break down the most complex ideas in a way that anybody could understand.

I recognise that is an important responsibility, and some big shoes to fill.

Although having lived through some cost-of-living crises myself — including now, as the dad of a constantly hungry two-year-old boy — I can definitely relate to the pressures that many Australians are feeling.

David Chau with his partner Michelle and their son. (Supplied)

So you can rest assured that I will be delivering finance updates that are relevant to you, hopefully in a way that is more "tolerable" than you expected.

I hope you come along with me on this journey, perhaps even for the next couple of decades if I am lucky and able to match Alan's record.

David Chau is a finance presenter on ABC News, including on the 7PM News — Monday to Friday, from tonight.

World.title: Ancient ceramics retrieved from 'world's oldest known' shipwreck
World.content:
A Sydney ceramics expert has helped reveal the secrets of the "world's oldest known" shipwreck off Türkiye's coast.

The discovery was made in shallow waters off Kekova Island in the country's south and dates to the age of the Great Pyramid of Giza's construction, about 4,500 years ago.

The ship's wooden structure has long since disappeared, but a considerable amount of pottery vessels remained embedded in the rocky seabed below.

Sydney-based archaeologist from Macquarie University Karin Sowada was asked to study the artefacts of the wreck after being contacted by the director of the excavation.

Karin Sowada was invited by the director of the shipwreck's excavation to study the artefacts. (Supplied: Karin Sowoda)

Dr Sowada joined the research team, led by Hakan Öniz, an associate professor at Akdeniz University in Antalya, to examine the ancient ceramics known as amphorae.

"There were two types of objects discovered during the excavation; one was a series of ceramic anchors, the second type of material was the pottery and there was quite a bit of it left," she said.

Among the relics were jars up to 50 centimetres high.

Dr Sowada studied pottery found on the seabed to help date the wreckage. (Supplied: Karin Sowada)

Dr Sowada said they were used to transport materials and foods, such as grain and oil, as well as resins and wine.

"The material was actually heavily embedded in barnacles, around rocks," she said, noting the team used hammers and chisels to extricate them.

"The vessels and the anchors themselves were also placed in a water bath to help extract the salts from the material because even once one brings anything from this from the sea up to the surface, it needs to be treated carefully to ensure that the material doesn't actually start crumbling or disintegrating."

A 'three-dimensional jigsaw puzzle'

Dr Sowada used her expertise in Egypt and Bronze Age trade, combined with her specialist knowledge of ancient ceramics, to study more than 20 items and determine when and where they came from.

"[I was] trying to understand the clays, and sort of putting together this, this three-dimensional jigsaw puzzle, which was really quite exciting," she said.

Dr Sowada said the pottery was likely from a trade ship that had crashed against the rocks, abandoned by sailors who had jumped overboard in a bid for survival.

"I do think that we can say that this is the oldest shipwreck," she said.

"A lot of time and effort has gone into trying to understand the dating of the shipwreck, which we can do through the ceramics."

The discovery was made off Kekova Island, in southern Türkiye. (Supplied: Karin Sowada)

Dr Sowada said researchers were conducting further tests on a small amount of residue found in the jars, but the investigation into the wreck's origin story was in its infancy.

"At this stage, we can certainly say that this is at the very early edge or the very early side of what we know about ancient shipping," she said.

Lead researcher Dr Öniz told Reuters the colour of the clay and decorations also pointed to the age of the ceramic artefacts, crediting the project's use of multiple experts.

"When we recognised that this [shipwreck] was the earliest one, it was amazing," he said.

World.title: The data that shows who won and lost in this year's AFL trade period
World.content:
If footballing dreams are lived out in September, they are first shaped in October and November.

If you nail an off-season it can set you up for years to come. If you stumble it can hurt for even longer.

The 2026 off-season class was one of rare quality. Instead of list-cloggers and fringe players that sometimes monopolise trade chatter, this year's crop is full of proven stars.

Lachie Neale, Scott Pendlebury, Jesse Hogan, Toby Greene, Zak Butters, Rowan Marshall and Ben King all found new clubs, among a host of others. It would be hard to find a trade period with a better combined resume than the one we've just seen.

The 2026 trade period has seen 23 trades and seven free-agency moves take place, with 30 players finding new clubs for season 2027. The dealing isn't done yet, with more picks set to change hands before and during the draft.

While much of football — and football commentary — is about instant gratification, the trade period is often a slower burn. Most AFL grand finals are blowouts well before the final siren, and most trade periods have deals that hang in the balance until the final minutes.

This year the opposite was the case. Little suspense was left by the time the last day rolled around, while the ending to that grand final was one that will be remembered for years to come.

While winners or losers of the off-season often take years to fully work out, the direction each team is taking is usually much clearer after the final trade is called.

Dogs taking a big bite

Each trade period it seems like at least one side pushes firmly towards the present over the future. Last year the Saints were the most aggressive side, bringing in a host of players to hopefully kickstart their resurgence up the ladder.

This year it was the Bulldogs that were the busiest club in the league.

All up the Dogs brought in four new players, the most of any club this off-season. The centrepiece of the four was the move for free agent Zak Butters, but the acquisition of Jordon Butts should be equally important for an often under-siege defensive unit.

There are some slight queries about how Butters will fit alongside Marcus Bontempelli and Ed Richards, but with the Dogs captain turning 32 next year this potentially sets the midfield group up for contention over the next half decade. The Bulldogs' best over the past three seasons has rivalled practically any other side. The time is now for them to take the next step.

But the Dogs may not be the biggest winners of the trade period for next season in isolation. Geelong's acquisition of proven talent in Toby Greene, Jordan Ridley and Rowan Marshall looks like providing the most upside next year, while Hawthorn will also be quietly confident in Zach Merrett and Ben King.

At the other end of the "win now" scale, the preliminary finalist Swans will be forced to retool without Nick Blakey and Joel Amartey, and GWS have made the call to get younger with the loss of Toby Greene, Jesse Hogan, Kieren Briggs and Lachie Whitfield.

Blakey's big deal

Whispers about a Nick Blakey move became increasingly loud as the off-season progressed. The chatter about his discontent in Sydney didn't abate, and quickly the defender became the focal point of an otherwise quiet second week of the period.

There's a couple of good reasons for that too. It's uncommon that a 26-year-old who is arguably the best player in a valuable role becomes available on the trade market.

In all, no club this century has traded more pick value for a single player than North has just traded for Blakey. The trade takes them out of multiple drafts. If North Melbourne was to win the 2028 premiership, the value of the picks traded would still outweigh what Adelaide traded for Wayne Carey way back in 2002.

Beyond the stated cost above, it also has deprived them of another top draft pick — the likely early 20s they would have received in compensation for Essendon's upcoming bid on Dougie Cochrane.

North Melbourne had hoped to pair Blakey with Adelaide's Nick Murray to bolster its defence, but that fell through at the deadline. It could be a bigger loss than it appears. North's defensive stocks are some of the weakest in the league, and its ability to transition the strongest part of their back half game.

Future failing

As predicted here before the trade period began, most clubs were cautious of the value of next year's draft.

One of the clearest examples was offered by Melbourne early in the trade period in its public negotiations for newly minted Demon Zane Duursma.

"We offered (pick) 47, we also offered a 2027 future two, or 2028 future two," Melbourne list boss Tim Lamb told the media.

That pick 47 is notionally a third-round selection, indicating that the drop in value increases to about a round for the next two drafts, which are compromised by the new Tasmania team being handed high picks.

This was even clearer in the trade that took place between Richmond and Port Adelaide, with the Tigers sending pick 22 this year alongside their round one, two and three picks next year for Port Adelaide's fifth pick.

This reflected the general trend of how picks traded hands. Only clubs who have clear father-son or academy talents seemed to be on the hunt for picks next year, with other clubs pushing for lower selections this year or selections in 2028 instead.

Port Adelaide was the keenest to get 2027 draft picks through the door. That's no shock, given it has up to four tied talents. In fact, every club bar possibly Sydney to invest in next year's draft have prospective father-son or academy talents likely to be selected in the upper reaches of the draft.

Most other clubs were somewhat keen to escape the oncoming chaos, or try to move picks into the (slightly) less compromised 2028 draft. The compromised drafts might also be playing into another trend that has emerged recently.

The past two trade periods have seen a re-evaluation of how clubs see the value of players against picks. Instead of the promise of youngsters, the increasingly uncertain availability of young talent has turned the attention of clubs to proven talent instead.

World.title: ASX falls after Wall Street slumps as inflation gets worse; Netflix job cuts
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX falls after Wall Street slumps as inflation gets worse; Netflix job cuts Stan Choe Updated October 15, 2026 — 10:08am ,first published 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket has fallen in early trade after Wall Street dropped to its worst day since July following the latest signal that US inflation is getting worse. The S&P/ASX 200 was 53.9 points, or 0.6 per cent lower, to 8674 in early trade. The ASX lost 0.6 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar was weaker at US69.66¢. Markets now see a 39 per cent chance that the Fed will raise the federal funds rate at its next meeting in two weeks, up from the 22 per cent probability seen just a day earlier, according to data from CME Group. AP Photo/Seth Wenig The S&P 500 sank 1.1 per cent for a fifth loss in the six days since setting its all-time high. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 48 points, or 0.1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite slid 1.9 per cent as stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry led the way lower. Stocks felt pressure from rising yields in the bond market, where worries grew after a report said US consumers had to pay prices for fuel, food and other costs of living last month that were 3.7 per cent higher overall than a year earlier. That means inflation accelerated from its 3.4 per cent rate in August and was worse than the 3.6 per cent that economists expected.



Inflation has remained more painful than anyone would like since the economy catapulted out of the crevasse created by the COVID-19 pandemic. It’s accelerated recently in part because of jumps in fuel prices caused by the war with Iran, and the price for a barrel of Brent crude added 0.4 per cent Wednesday to $US106.06. Related Article Opinion

Bonds Trump’s America and Wall Street are in a dangerous spiral Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist That has added to the longstanding worries about fast-rising debt loads for governments, signals that the US economy is still growing and other factors that have sent bond yields to their highest levels in years. The centrepiece of the US bond market, the 10-year Treasury, saw its yield briefly jump above 5.32 per cent from less than 5.17 per cent just before the inflation report’s release. It eventually gave back much of the gain. Yields on shorter-term Treasurys had even bigger leaps as traders raised their expectations for coming hikes to interest rates by the Federal Reserve, though they also moderated as the day progressed.



The Fed recently raised the interest rate that it controls, which affects very short-term loans, for the first time in three years in hopes of reining in inflation. Higher rates do that by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money and slowing the overall economy. Traders now see a nearly 35 per cent chance the Fed will raise the federal funds rate at its next meeting in two weeks, up from the 22 per cent probability seen a day earlier, according to data from CME Group. Part of what’s keeping inflation high is that Americans overall are continuing to spend, which encourages businesses to keep raising prices for their products and services. As Americans become more “price-sensitive” and the economy also benefits from greater productivity by workers, Vanguard Senior Economist Adam Schickling said inflation should slow, but “patience will be required.” Netflix added 0.2 per cent. The streaming giant announced plans to lay off about 6 per cent of its workforce, amounting to nearly 1000 positions, as it makes wider “organisational changes.” Co-CEOs Greg Peters and Ted Sarandos announced the job cuts in a memo to employees Wednesday. They said the company’s product, tech, legal and human resources teams would be the most impacted.



Much of Wall Street’s pain on Wednesday was due to drops for companies riding the AI frenzy to huge profit growth and stellar stock gains. Higher bond yields making borrowing money more expensive could make it more difficult for companies to raise cash to build data centres and fill them with AI chips. World.title: ‘Betrayed’: Ukraine leader denounces Trump for siding with Russia amid row with Musk
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war ‘Betrayed’: Ukraine leader denounces Trump for siding with Russia amid row with Musk David Crowe Updated October 15, 2026 — 10:00am ,first published 5:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. London: Ukraine has suffered a severe disruption to Starlink networks run by tech titan Elon Musk after days of dispute with Donald Trump, sparking claims the US president has betrayed the country and sided with Russia. Ukrainian forces cancelled missions after losing access to high-speed services from Musk’s satellite company, days after the world’s richest man backed Trump in criticising Ukraine for attacking Russian targets. Victoria Deineko holds her daughter, Mia, in front of a multi-story residential building damaged in a Russian missile strike in Kyiv onTuesday. AP Photo/Evgeniy Maloletka The warnings led Musk to declare that any military use of the Starlink network was a matter for the US government, pointing to Trump as the ultimate authority on whether Ukraine could gain the satellite services it needed to fight Russia. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky went public with his concerns about Trump in an interview with media host Piers Morgan, declaring the American president was not on the “right side of history” and was siding with Russia.



Asked if he felt “betrayed” by what was happening, Zelensky replied: “Really, yes.” Then, when asked if he felt he was “losing America” as a supporter, Zelensky said: “Yeah.” A technician repairing a damaged Starlink satellite terminal board at an undisclosed location in Ukraine in July. Bloomberg “It is a pity that we are losing a strong partner,” he told Morgan in an interview aired late on Wednesday in London (about 3.30am on Thursday, AEDT). “We’re not selling our country. It’s not about business for us. It’s our life.



“That’s why it’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side. We are OK that he is in the middle, but if you are in the middle you have to stay in the middle. I think his advisers are wrong. “I don’t know who pushing him not to the right side – this is not to the right side of history.” President Donald Trump, right, presents the National Medal of Science to Elon Musk this month. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson The remarks represent a direct criticism of Trump for siding with Russia and its president, Vladimir Putin, at a time when European leaders are showing strong support for Zelensky amid the doubts about Trump’s judgement. So far, European leaders have avoided any public remarks that directly criticise the US president. Zelensky also confirmed the surprise slowdown in speeds and warned that more civilians would be killed if full Starlink services were not restored for Ukrainian forces.



“We understand what is going on – they switched off, it’s their decision,” Zelensky told Morgan. Related Article Analysis

Russia-Ukraine war The president of pretence: Why Trump’s latest ceasefire ‘trick’ failed its first test “People will die, of course, if attacks will continue and if Starlink will not work.” Former Ukrainian defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov entered the debate soon afterwards by claiming on X that the speed of the Starlink service was being restored and thanking Musk for his support. Musk reacted by drawing a distinction between the Starlink civilian service and the related Starshield system owned and controlled by the US government.



“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he said, referring to the American president. “Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.” View post on X The remarks from the world’s richest man appeared to leave responsibility for the issue with Trump. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment, Reuters reported. The satellite problems came hours after Zelensky revealed a separate halt to the usual supply of western intelligence about looming Russian missile and drone attacks, saying there was “no warning” of some of the latest strikes.



The two developments fuelled concerns about decisions in Washington that could restrict Ukraine’s military capacity at a time when Trump wants Zelensky to stop hitting Russian oil refineries. Ukraine depends on Starlink, which is part of the SpaceX group controlled by Musk, to guide missiles and drones that strike targets in parts of Ukraine occupied by Russian forces, and to support defensive drones to intercept Russian attacks. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, left, with Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky in London on Wednesday. Bloomberg “SpaceX implemented speed restrictions on Starlink terminals while in motion last night,” said presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov on social media on Wednesday morning (late that night, AEDT). “Currently, the restriction applies to the StarShield ‘military service package’ and limits speed to 100 miles per hour [160 kilometres per hour].



“Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is associated with the current political situation.” While Musk has clashed with Trump at times, he backed the US president in recent days in calling on Ukraine to replace Zelensky. View post on X “I agree, time for Ukraine to get a new leader,” Musk said on Sunday. When Trump said the attacks on oil refineries should stop, Musk posted: “Zelensky has gone too far.” The military-grade services on the Starlink satellite network are known as StarShield and are controlled by the Pentagon, leading to speculation that the “throttling” was the result of decisions by the US government rather than Musk.



Still, Polish Foreign Minister Radek Sikorski called on Musk to ensure Ukraine gained the services it needed. “Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?” Sikorski asked on X. “As your European customers, we are watching you.” A man hangs out the national flag at his damaged apartment balcony in Kyiv. AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky The disruptions increased concerns in Kyiv about more strikes on civilians when Ukrainian defenders lacked full capacity. Access to Starlink is a key factor in Ukraine’s ability to aim drones and missiles at Russian targets, but Musk has been accused in the past of using his personal power to intervene in the war.



Reuters reported last year that Musk gave an order to his staff in September 2022 that cut coverage to Ukrainian forces at a pivotal moment in their attempt to retake Kherson and other areas near the Black Sea. Russian forces lost access to Starlink this year, although the full impact of this change was unclear. The service can be so vital that the BBC reported that Russian soldiers would try to bribe Ukrainian collaborators to gain access to a Starlink terminal. Zelensky meets with King Charles at Buckingham Palace. Getty Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and 120 drones at Ukrainian targets on Tuesday night, Zelensky said on Wednesday. He said 600,000 people were without power as a result of the latest strikes, despite Trump’s claim that both sides had agreed to an energy ceasefire. Six people were killed and thirteen injured in Lutsk in western Ukraine on Wednesday, Zelensky said, when a drone hit a residential building and store.



Zelensky gained public support in the UK on Wednesday when he visited London and spoke with King Charles III at Buckingham Palace before holding talks with Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street. Burnham announced a faster delivery plan for British missiles that could help Ukraine intercept Russian jet-powered drones, but he avoided any move that might provoke Trump. When Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey asked Burnham in parliament if he agreed that the latest moves in the US were “another shameful Trump betrayal” of the Ukrainian people, the prime minister was cautious in response. Burnham said it was a “very dark and difficult moment” for Zelensky, but he made no criticism of Trump. London: Irish novelist Sally Rooney said on Wednesday that her books are being withdrawn from sale in the UK because of her support for Palestine Action, a protest group the British government has outlawed as a terrorist organisation. Her publisher, Faber, confirmed that the ban “has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work”. Author Sally Rooney. New York Times “To sell a writer’s work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher. As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format,” Faber said in a statement. Rooney said Faber’s decision to withdraw her books from sale in the UK was made “with my full agreement”.



“I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences,” she said in a statement. Loading Rooney, 35, is the critically praised author of four novels: Conversations with Friends, Normal People, Beautiful World, Where are You and Intermezzo. Her books have sold millions of copies, and both Conversations with Friends and Normal People were adapted for television by the BBC. A strong supporter of Palestinian causes, she wrote in The Irish Times in August 2025: “I too support Palestine Action. If this makes me a ‘supporter of terror’ under UK law, so be it.” She said she would use proceeds from her novels and TV fees to continue to support the group.



Britain’s centre-left Labour government outlawed Palestine Action after activists from the direct-action group broke into a Royal Air Force base in June 2025 to protest British military support for Israel’s military offensive in Gaza. The ban makes membership in or support for the group a crime punishable by up to 14 years in prison. More than 3000 people have been arrested since the group was outlawed, including for holding signs declaring “I support Palestine Action.” More than 1200 have been charged under the Terrorism Act, though none has yet been convicted. Civil liberties groups say the ban and subsequent arrests unjustifiably restrict the rights to protest and free speech. Lawyers for Palestine Action will ask the UK Supreme Court next month to overturn the ban. All cases involving people charged with breaching it have been put on hold pending the court’s ruling. AP

Steve Waugh is used to being the man behind the camera. But last Sunday, the former Australian Test captain was blown away by a volunteer’s eye for a shot when he captured his son’s catch “assist” in a local first-grade match, which is being compared to John Dyson’s “catch of the century” in 1982. After Randwick-Petersham smashed 2-210 from their 20 overs thanks to some more big hitting from Eknoor Singh (123 not out), Campbelltown Camden’s hopes of chasing down the big total suffered an early blow when Austin Waugh soared high and towards the boundary to secure the ball, before flicking it back inside the field of play to teammate Adam Lecky. Austin Waugh leaps high near the boundary to play his part in a classic catch in Sydney grade cricket. Peter Bannigan The catch left the visitors reeling at 1-7, with opener Bailey Abela the unfortunate man to have to walk off after thinking he had smashed Riley Ayre for six. Waugh, who was no stranger to taking a classic catch either, said he thought it was better than John Dyson’s famous catch in 1982, when West Indian Sylvester Clarke was forced to head back to the pavilion at the SCG.



John Dyson’s epic 1982 catch. Fairfax Media “I saw Dyson’s catch,” Waugh said. “This was, I think, a lot better because it was more dangerous with the fence behind you. And he actually jumped a lot higher as well. You’ll see how high he got off the ground, about six feet off the ground. “Yeah, it was better than Dyson, for sure.” While Austin Waugh wasn’t technically credited with the catch, he did all the hard work. Fearing the moment would be lost in time, Waugh snr, who had his camera buried away in his bag, was pleasantly surprised and relieved to know that the club’s local and trusty photographer was on hand to capture the incredible moment.



Related Article Australian cricket ‘Pick and stick’: Waugh urges Aussie selectors to stop ‘messing about’ “I was a bit lucky. I pointed in the right direction. Austin did all the hard work,” said Peter Bannigan. Bannigan was not even supposed to be at Coogee Oval for the T20 match. The 75-year-old had not missed a single Bathurst 1000 race since 1982, but some health issues, including a recent blood clot in his right eye, meant the Sydney local opted against driving out to the event. It’s a good thing he did. “I guess the photo I took at Coogee would have been a lot better than anything I took at Bathurst,” Bannigan quipped.



While Waugh said his son’s individual piece of magic had shocked him, he had been blown away by Bannigan’s quick finger and sharp eye. “This guy has been taking photos at Randwick Cricket Club for 25 years as a volunteer. He takes these amazing shots and the silhouette of the shadow on the fence is pretty incredible,” Waugh said. “People are saying it’s one of the best catches they’ve ever seen and he captured it.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

The Australian sharemarket has fallen in early trade after Wall Street dropped to its worst day since July following the latest signal that US inflation is getting worse. The S&P/ASX 200 was 53.9 points, or 0.6 per cent lower, to 8674 in early trade. The ASX lost 0.6 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar was weaker at US69.66¢. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 48 points, or 0.1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite slid 1.9 per cent as stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry led the way lower. Stocks felt pressure from rising yields in the bond market, where worries grew after a report said US consumers had to pay prices for fuel, food and other costs of living last month that were 3.7 per cent higher overall than a year earlier. That means inflation accelerated from its 3.4 per cent rate in August and was worse than the 3.6 per cent that economists expected.



Inflation has remained more painful than anyone would like since the economy catapulted out of the crevasse created by the COVID-19 pandemic. It’s accelerated recently in part because of jumps in fuel prices caused by the war with Iran, and the price for a barrel of Brent crude added 0.4 per cent Wednesday to $US106.06. It eventually gave back much of the gain. When Trump said the attacks on oil refineries should stop, Musk posted: “Zelensky has gone too far.” The military-grade services on the Starlink satellite network are known as StarShield and are controlled by the Pentagon, leading to speculation that the “throttling” was the result of decisions by the US government rather than Musk.



Still, Polish Foreign Minister Radek Sikorski called on Musk to ensure Ukraine gained the services it needed. “Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?” Sikorski asked on X. “As your European customers, we are watching you.” A man hangs out the national flag at his damaged apartment balcony in Kyiv. AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky The disruptions increased concerns in Kyiv about more strikes on civilians when Ukrainian defenders lacked full capacity. Access to Starlink is a key factor in Ukraine’s ability to aim drones and missiles at Russian targets, but Musk has been accused in the past of using his personal power to intervene in the war.



Reuters reported last year that Musk gave an order to his staff in September 2022 that cut coverage to Ukrainian forces at a pivotal moment in their attempt to retake Kherson and other areas near the Black Sea. Russian forces lost access to Starlink this year, although the full impact of this change was unclear. The service can be so vital that the BBC reported that Russian soldiers would try to bribe Ukrainian collaborators to gain access to a Starlink terminal. Zelensky meets with King Charles at Buckingham Palace. Getty Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and 120 drones at Ukrainian targets on Tuesday night, Zelensky said on Wednesday. He said 600,000 people were without power as a result of the latest strikes, despite Trump’s claim that both sides had agreed to an energy ceasefire. Six people were killed and thirteen injured in Lutsk in western Ukraine on Wednesday, Zelensky said, when a drone hit a residential building and store.



Zelensky gained public support in the UK on Wednesday when he visited London and spoke with King Charles III at Buckingham Palace before holding talks with Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street. Burnham announced a faster delivery plan for British missiles that could help Ukraine intercept Russian jet-powered drones, but he avoided any move that might provoke Trump. When Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey asked Burnham in parliament if he agreed that the latest moves in the US were “another shameful Trump betrayal” of the Ukrainian people, the prime minister was cautious in response. Burnham said it was a “very dark and difficult moment” for Zelensky, but he made no criticism of Trump. World.title: Sally Rooney’s books pulled from UK shelves over Palestine Action support
World.content:
CultureBooksLiterature Sally Rooney’s books pulled from UK shelves over Palestine Action support October 15, 2026 — 8:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. London: Irish novelist Sally Rooney said on Wednesday that her books are being withdrawn from sale in the UK because of her support for Palestine Action, a protest group the British government has outlawed as a terrorist organisation. Her publisher, Faber, confirmed that the ban “has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work”. Author Sally Rooney. New York Times “To sell a writer’s work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher. As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format,” Faber said in a statement. Rooney said Faber’s decision to withdraw her books from sale in the UK was made “with my full agreement”.



“I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences,” she said in a statement. Loading Rooney, 35, is the critically praised author of four novels: Conversations with Friends, Normal People, Beautiful World, Where are You and Intermezzo. Her books have sold millions of copies, and both Conversations with Friends and Normal People were adapted for television by the BBC. A strong supporter of Palestinian causes, she wrote in The Irish Times in August 2025: “I too support Palestine Action. If this makes me a ‘supporter of terror’ under UK law, so be it.” She said she would use proceeds from her novels and TV fees to continue to support the group.



Britain’s centre-left Labour government outlawed Palestine Action after activists from the direct-action group broke into a Royal Air Force base in June 2025 to protest British military support for Israel’s military offensive in Gaza. The ban makes membership in or support for the group a crime punishable by up to 14 years in prison. More than 3000 people have been arrested since the group was outlawed, including for holding signs declaring “I support Palestine Action.” More than 1200 have been charged under the Terrorism Act, though none has yet been convicted. Civil liberties groups say the ban and subsequent arrests unjustifiably restrict the rights to protest and free speech. Lawyers for Palestine Action will ask the UK Supreme Court next month to overturn the ban. All cases involving people charged with breaching it have been put on hold pending the court’s ruling. AP

World.title: ‘Better than Dyson’: Steve Waugh’s son takes flight in astonishing catch
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘Better than Dyson’: Steve Waugh’s son takes flight in astonishing catch Christy Doran October 15, 2026 — 8:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Steve Waugh is used to being the man behind the camera. But last Sunday, the former Australian Test captain was blown away by a volunteer’s eye for a shot when he captured his son’s catch “assist” in a local first-grade match, which is being compared to John Dyson’s “catch of the century” in 1982. After Randwick-Petersham smashed 2-210 from their 20 overs thanks to some more big hitting from Eknoor Singh (123 not out), Campbelltown Camden’s hopes of chasing down the big total suffered an early blow when Austin Waugh soared high and towards the boundary to secure the ball, before flicking it back inside the field of play to teammate Adam Lecky. Austin Waugh leaps high near the boundary to play his part in a classic catch in Sydney grade cricket. Peter Bannigan The catch left the visitors reeling at 1-7, with opener Bailey Abela the unfortunate man to have to walk off after thinking he had smashed Riley Ayre for six. Waugh, who was no stranger to taking a classic catch either, said he thought it was better than John Dyson’s famous catch in 1982, when West Indian Sylvester Clarke was forced to head back to the pavilion at the SCG.



John Dyson’s epic 1982 catch. Fairfax Media “I saw Dyson’s catch,” Waugh said. “This was, I think, a lot better because it was more dangerous with the fence behind you. And he actually jumped a lot higher as well. You’ll see how high he got off the ground, about six feet off the ground. “Yeah, it was better than Dyson, for sure.” While Austin Waugh wasn’t technically credited with the catch, he did all the hard work. Fearing the moment would be lost in time, Waugh snr, who had his camera buried away in his bag, was pleasantly surprised and relieved to know that the club’s local and trusty photographer was on hand to capture the incredible moment.



Related Article Australian cricket ‘Pick and stick’: Waugh urges Aussie selectors to stop ‘messing about’ “I was a bit lucky. I pointed in the right direction. Austin did all the hard work,” said Peter Bannigan. Bannigan was not even supposed to be at Coogee Oval for the T20 match. The 75-year-old had not missed a single Bathurst 1000 race since 1982, but some health issues, including a recent blood clot in his right eye, meant the Sydney local opted against driving out to the event. It’s a good thing he did. “I guess the photo I took at Coogee would have been a lot better than anything I took at Bathurst,” Bannigan quipped.



While Waugh said his son’s individual piece of magic had shocked him, he had been blown away by Bannigan’s quick finger and sharp eye. “This guy has been taking photos at Randwick Cricket Club for 25 years as a volunteer. He takes these amazing shots and the silhouette of the shadow on the fence is pretty incredible,” Waugh said. “People are saying it’s one of the best catches they’ve ever seen and he captured it.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.
