World.title: New Zealand First pledges to increase Coastguard funding
World.content:
New Zealand First says it will increase the proportion of Crown funding to the Coastguard to 70 percent.

The Coastguard is 40 percent funded by the government, with the remaining coming from fundraising.

New Zealand First's pledge is to raise that to 70 percent which would mean an increase of $12 million a year.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406873596112

"The additional funding will support critical maintenance and capability investment, including upgrades to New Zealand's VHF maritime communications network, vessel procurement and replacement, and the purchase of essential rescue equipment," a party press release said.

"It will also strengthen Coastguard's volunteer workforce through improved training, capability development, and practical support measures such as subsidising volunteer travel costs."

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406875818112

New Zealand First would also conduct a review of emergency management services, including Police, Search and Rescue, Fire and Emergency, Health New Zealand, Civil Defence, and the Defence Force, to see how they can be better coordinated.

"Better cooperation between agencies will improve capital procurement, strengthen interoperability, reduce duplication, and ensure emergency services can respond more effectively when lives are at risk."

World.title: Tamaki to appear in court for allegedly inciting racial disharmony
World.content:
Destiny Church leader Brian Tamaki has been summonsed to appear in court on three charges of allegedly inciting racial disharmony.

The religious leader posted a livestream video of police handing him the summons in person earlier this morning on social media.

He was ordered to appear in Manukau District Court on Monday.

Detective Senior Sergeant Natalie Nelson, Counties Manukau CIB, confirmed police attended an Auckland address this morning to summons a person on three charges of inciting racial disharmony.

"These charges are laid under the Human Rights Act and require consent from the Solicitor-General to prosecute," Nelson said.

"Police [are] not in a position to comment on the specifics of this individual's case as the matter is now before the court."

Tamaki said in a statement on Thursday that he faced three charges for allegedly breaching the Human Rights Act four months ago, believing the charges to be related to his commentary concerning Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

In June, Tamaki accused Modi of purging Christians in the South Asian nation.

"He [Modi] is currently purging India of all Christians and burning church buildings down," Tamaki had said in a video posted on social media.

"I think we should reciprocate in kind. Let's purge New Zealand of Hindus, Sikhs and Muslims. And, while we're at it, if they're burning churches down, why don't we burn mosques and their temples down? Tit for tat."

A police spokesperson confirmed at the time they were looking into the contents of the video.

On Thursday, Tamaki denied threatening anyone.

"I have never advocated violence against anyone," he said.

"I have consistently challenged religious beliefs, religious practices and political leaders - NOT people because of their race."

In June, police seized Takami's firearms after temporarily suspending his licence.

World.title: Auckland's Starship Hospital delays some cancer treatments due to nurse shortage
World.content:
The health minister has confirmed some cancer treatments have been delayed by up to seven days at Auckland's Starship Children's Hospital.

Earlier on Thursday morning, Health New Zealand's Starship Hospital director, Dr Greg Williams said the paediatric haematology/oncology service has had to reschedule some treatments due to a shortage of nurses.

"These decisions are not made lightly and are based on clinical need. Starship is recruiting experienced and new graduate nurses as quickly as possible," Dr Williams said.

Do you know more? Get in touch at: iwitness@rnz.co.nz

A spokesperson for Health Minister Simeon Brown told RNZ he had asked Health NZ chief executive Dale Bramley for an explanation.

The spokesperson says all children at Starship Hospital are still being treated, though a handful of chemotherapy sessions have been delayed for a few days - but no more than seven.

Two bone marrow transplants were moved "slightly", but both were still going ahead.

The spokesperson said vacancies at Health NZ are the result of natural attrition such as parental leave and retirement and there is no hiring freeze.

Dr Williams said the oncology departments are being supported by staff in other parts of Starship and Auckland City Hospital.

Health NZ data obtained by the NZ Nurses Organisation showed 85 percent of shifts at Starship's Haemotology/Oncology Ward were understaffed during August.

Health NZ data obtained by the NZ Nurses Organisation shows the shift in nurse staffing in 2026 Supplied/NZNO

The number of "shifts below target" had steadily risen since January, when 18 percent of shifts were understaffed, up to 53 percent in July, before spiking in August.

A nurse anonymously told the New Zealand Herald she and other staff were "horrified and appalled" by the news, which had the potential to adversely affect patient outcomes.

She believed parents would be shocked by the development.

"You're increasing the risk of complications and death from cancers," the nurse told the Herald.

RNZ has asked how many patients have been affected by the delays and how many staff the hospital is short of. Health New Zealand is yet to answer those questions.

The nurse also told the Herald that the severe staffing shortage was not only related to the winter flu spike but had been critical "all of this year".

"Over the last year with budget constraints, they've not hired new nurses. Anytime a nurse left, they weren't replaced."

The Herald also reported the nurse said the hospital had lost a lot of senior nurses.

Tertiary providers were recently told to limit nursing enrolments to 2025 levels, because there are not enough student placement spots available in hospitals.

Nurse educators told RNZ on Wednesday the Tertiary Education Commission (TEC) directive makes no sense as pressure on the workforce builds.

World.title: New Zealand breaks new ground in field of photonics, quantum technology
World.content:
New Zealand continues to break new ground in the field of photonics and quantum technology, but is still failing to keep pace with global peers.

Latest University of Auckland research may help the world to miniaturise the laser tools used for ultra-precise measurements, such as atomic clocks.

Department of Physics head and researcher at the Dodd-Walls Centre for Photonic and Quantum Technologies, Professor Miro Erkintalo, began exploring a potential new way to generate ultra-small microchip-sized frequency combs used for measuring the frequency - or colours - of light.

Sometimes called `light rulers' or 'rainbow rulers', these miniaturised frequency combs unlock a host of leading edge applications.

Future uses include sensors capable of detecting extremely small changes in their environments.

However, a recent industry raised concerns about the underfunding of photonic and quantum industries in Australia and New Zealand, which were growing, but at a lower rate than the global average.

"New Zealand has some excellent start-ups, a new stakeholder community and significant research potential, but it's clear, after decades of investment in Australia, 'the Ditch' is becoming a digital divide," the report by the Australian and New Zealand Optical Society says.

Erkintalo said New Zealand's blue sky science projects were the first step towards the commercialisation of leading edge applications, such as the frequency comb.

"I was able to do that research and that's really what led us to where we are now," he said.

"This work is the culmination of several years of work, involving a fantastic international collaboration that brings together the world-leading knowledge and innovation of New Zealand researchers with equally world-leading folks in the US."

However, such blue sky science funding was at risk.

While the New Zealand government is committed to funding AI and quantum technologies, the funding is expected to be being directed to the commercialisation of products.

However, Erkintalo said the invention of the new type of frequency comb would not have been possible without the underlying knowledge, developed over a decade.

He said Dodd-Walls was internationally recognised for its advanced scientific knowledge.

"We are absolutely world-leading in the physical understanding and the knowledge of how this system works," he said.

"I think having this very deep knowledge makes our group quite attractive for international collaborators that do have the access to resources that are more sophisticated."

The frequency comb was the result of a collaboration between the Auckland researchers and Grégory Moille and Kartik Srinivasan from the University of Maryland and the US National Institute of Science and Technology.

World.title: Christchurch transitional housing facility for men gets major upgrade
World.content:
A former client, turned support worker, says upgrades to a Salvation Army transitional housing facility in Christchurch will better support people rebuilding their lives.

Daniel Young, who stayed at the Addington complex in 2018 before later joining its staff, was among those celebrating the opening of a newly renovated accommodation wing on Wednesday.

When Young first arrived eight years ago, he said he was in a rough place in life.

"I was slowly losing myself and eventually came here because I got told by other people," he said.

"It was hard for me to come in, but I'm glad I did. Leaving here, I left with hope."

The Salvation Army's Addington site has been providing transitional housing for men for 130 years.

Salvation Army social mission director Jono Bell says the revamped Addington complex has more rooms and communal spaces than before. RNZ / Anna Sargent

Social mission director Jono Bell said the redevelopment, which had taken about two and a half years, had created more modern rooms and communal spaces.

The focus was on creating a more comfortable environment for residents, he said.

"This was an old, more dormitory-style site and we've now turned that into individual rooms, much more communal, open spaces for people to be part of," he said.

"We believe the dignity of people and the importance of accommodation is critical for them to get the support that they need. Once they've got that safe roof over their head and a safe environment we then can look at some of those other challenges they may be facing."

The opening was attended by former residents, staff, community supporters and government representatives.

Bell said the Addington complex housed up to 88 men, and demand remained high.

"In New Zealand we're still in a housing crisis. We've got growing amounts of people experiencing homelessness or housing insecurity," he said.

"Demand for supportive accommodation is definitely just as high as it was a couple of years ago. Usually it comes down to capacity, so we still have many people that aren't able to access this support and we do move people through fairly quickly once they can transition to long-term housing."

The Salvation Army's Addington supportive accommodation facility in Christchurch. RNZ / Anna Sargent

Young said the upgraded complex looked very different to what he remembered.

"You went straight to a dorm four-bedroom and had to work your way to get your own single one," he said.

"This is a big change from what it used to be like. The rooms have got everything, they've got sinks in there now and your own personal space. It's just a really warm and inviting place"

After leaving, Young completed a health and well-being qualification before returning on placement in 2024. He now works there as a support worker.

He said the support he received helped him regain hope.

"Help wise, they gave me the basics, the roof, the shower, the food, the care I'd say would be the biggest one. I felt really encouraged and supported whilst being here," he said.

Young said his favourite part of the job was seeing residents grow in confidence.

"My joy of the job is seeing that change... just watching [residents] go from 'I can't do that', to the 'I cans' and then eventually the 'I ams' and they do it and share it with the next person.

World.title: Hollywood actor Cliff Curtis excused from court, recovering from internal injuries
World.content:
Iconic New Zealand actor Cliff Curtis has missed his day in court, recovering from internal injuries after an alleged drunk driving crash.

The actor has been charged with reckless driving and driving with excess breath alcohol causing injury.

He is yet to enter a plea.

Curtis was not in the Auckland District Court on Thursday, as he excused for medical reasons.

Police prosecutor Karamvir Talwar requested Curtis' bail conditions include not contacting the victim and not driving.

Judge Ajit Swaran Singh granted the conditions, remanding Curtis on bail.

The maximum sentence for the excess breath alcohol charge is five years in prison or a fine of $20,000 alongside a mandatory disqualification from driving for a at least 12 months.

Driving recklessly carries a maximum sentence of three months imprisonment or a $4500 fine and disqualification for six months or more.

Curtis released a statement on Wednesday ahead of his court date.

"I made a devastating mistake, and I'll have to live with the consequences and do what I can to address the harm caused," he said.

"I am deeply sorry. My thoughts are with the injured taxi driver and his family."

In a statement from last month, Curtis said he was deeply saddened by what happened.

"My thoughts are with those who were hurt, and their families at this time."

Curtis had helped the injured driver after the crash, his statement said.

Curtis has appeared in a number of movies both locally and overseas including Once Were Warriors and more recently James Cameron's Avatar franchise.

He teamed up with fellow actor Jason Momoa and director Taika Waititi to acquire the Auckland-based film studio Studio West in a bid to bring more jobs and Polynesian-led storytelling to New Zealand.

World.title: Petition calls for Tino Rangatiratanga flag to fly permanently on Auckland Harbour Bridge
World.content:
A new campaign is calling for the Tino Rangatiratanga flag to fly permanently alongside the New Zealand flag on the Auckland Harbour Bridge, with supporters saying it would recognise Māori identity, history and the dual heritage of Aotearoa.

The kaupapa 'The Flag Poll', aims to gather 80,000 signatures in support of permanently raising the Tino Rangatiratanga flag from Waitangi Day 2027.

The flag currently flies on the bridge each Waitangi Day before being removed the following day.

The campaign is backed by the flag's last surviving designer Linda Munn, students from Tipene St Stephen's School, members of Te Poho o Hinekahukura kapa haka, Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei representative Te Aroha Grace and Shit You Should Care About founder Lucy Blakiston.

The Tino Rangatiratanga flag currently flies on Auckland Harbour Bridge each Waitangi Day (February 6) before being removed the following day. Supplied / The Flag Poll

The Tino Rangatiratanga flag was designed in 1989 in response to the 150th anniversary of Te Tiriti o Waitangi, by Linda Munn, Hiraina Marsden and Jan Dobson. It was later recognised by the government as the national Māori flag in 2009 and first flown on Auckland Harbour Bridge in 2010.

"When we designed the flag 38 years ago, it was about having our own unique symbol that reflected who we are as Māori," Linda Munn said.

Tipene St Stephen's School principal Nathan Durie told RNZ there was often misunderstanding about what the Tino Rangatiratanga flag represented.

The black in the Tino Rangatiratanga flag represents Te Korekore, the realm of potential. White for Te Ao Mārama, the world of light. Red for Papatūānuku, the Earth Mother. Through the middle, a koru: new life unfolding and hope for the future. Supplied / The Flag Poll

"I think what the Tino Rangatiratanga flag represents is the opportunity to ask questions. And what I mean by that is that as we are in education, people, if they don't understand, should take some time to pause and reflect. And as this thing's flapping in the wind, so to speak, alongside the British flag, it talks about the dual history of this country."

"And too often it's been radicalised, used as a symbol of radical behaviour. The truth is it's always just been about asking a question. Where and when will be the recognition of Māori in this country?"

He said the presence of both the New Zealand flag and the Tino Rangatiratanga flag would reflect the country's shared history.

"It allows this half Pākehā, half Māori boy to stand on two legs instead of always being a bit crooked in my stance. Because I can see my British ancestry well represented. My Māori side is allowed to fly one day of the year, and I think we're in a position now where actually we want to represent both."

Tipene St Stephen's School principal Nathan Durie says the presence of both the New Zealand flag and the Tino Rangatiratanga flag would reflect the country's shared history. Layla Bailey-McDowell / RNZ

Durie said the campaign also provided an opportunity for young people to engage with the country's history and future.

"Being a part of this allows our kids a real experiential opportunity to be involved in something that is more than themselves and about the welfare of this country and the welfare of all people in this country."

"Rangatahi Māori are important in this. Ko rātou te āpōpō. And so they are the future of this country."

"And we will see a greater understanding of our dual heritage in this country. They'll drive that and they'll drive it in a way where they demonstrate their pride in being Māori, but also their role as tangata whenua to look after all people in this country."

Supporters of the campaign point to neighbouring Australia, where the Aboriginal flag has flown permanently on Sydney Harbour Bridge since 2022 following a long-running public campaign.

"The point was made about the Australians have been flying the Aboriginal flag for a few years," Durie said.

"That does not correct the past, but it's a statement. In terms of this flag, as it's known as the Tino Rangatiratanga flag, recognises the fact that we did not cede sovereignty and our sovereign voice needs to be heard."

16-year-old Tipene student Tāmati Bruce (Ngāpuhi) said permanently flying the Tino Rangatiratanga flag would send an important message about Māori belonging in Aotearoa.

"It represents who we are as a country.

"Aotearoa is not just people from overseas, it's the native people who are actually from this land."

Bruce said the fact the flag currently flies for only one day each year left him feeling Māori visibility was limited.

"I think that sends a message that they don't really care about us, or that we don't exist to much people, only on that day."

He believed a permanent display would encourage pride in both Māori identity and culture.

"It represents to me who I am, who I am as Māori, and why I do what I do every day, and just proud to be Māori."

16-year-old Tipene student Tāmati Bruce (Ngāpuhi) says flying the Tino Rangatiratanga flag on the Auckland Harbour Bridge permanently would send an important message about Māori belonging in Aotearoa. Layla Bailey-McDowell / RNZ

"I think it'll encourage a lot more people to get behind speaking the reo more... this is our country, you know, we need to speak our language. So I feel like it'll be a really good encouragement towards our rangatahi and getting them back to where our country should be."

He encouraged everyone to get behind the petition.

"Together we can just unite as one and just be stronger than ever."

Fellow students Eli Rush (Ngāpuhi), 15, and Taniora Waitai (Ngāti Kuri), 16, also supported the petition, saying the flag represented Māori "as a collective" and reminded young people they were not alone.

"It makes me feel proud because it lets me know that a lot of other people are here with me, representing it," Rush said.

He rejected calls for the New Zealand flag to be the only flag flown on the bridge.

"I think there's definitely two cultures in New Zealand, and Māori should definitely be up there too."

Year 11 students of Tipene St Stephen's School: Tāmati Bruce, Taniora Waitai and Eli Rush. Layla Bailey-McDowell / RNZ

Durie acknowledged not everyone would support the proposal, but said Aotearoa New Zealand had matured as a nation.

"We're a far more mature country now.

"We have a collection of a number of flags and they should all be allowed to fly."

He said recognition of Māori identity did not diminish anyone else's place in New Zealand.

"There was a discussion [during the multi-party debate] on the television about being one country, and we are.

"But we're a country made up of massive diversity, and we should recognise that."

"The flag will be a wonderful statement about the maturity and the recognition [of Māori]. And if there's some words that you can use, it's about recognition, it's about respect, and it's about responsibility. And if we can bring those things through together, then we have a healthy nation moving forward."

The Flag Poll campaign is encouraging New Zealanders to sign the petition and display one of 20,000 Tino Rangatiratanga flags that will be distributed across the country as part of the initiative.

World.title: Aussie cyclists begin World Championships with silver medal
World.content:
Australia has claimed a silver medal in the men's team sprint on the opening night of the UCI Track Cycling World Championships in Shanghai.

The Australian trio of Leigh Hoffman, Ryan Elliott and Danny Barber finished runner-up to the Netherlands in the final.

It was Australia's fifth consecutive World Championships medal in the event.

"For the final, we made a minor change in strategy," Hoffman said.

Richardson withdrawn from world champ squad British track cyclist Matthew Richardson, who defected from Australian cycling at the end of the Paris Games, has been withdrawn from this week's UCI Track World Championships in Shanghai.

"We just tried to have a little gamble, and it almost paid off.

"We were up to the 500-metre mark, so we definitely gave the Dutch a run for their money.

"It's definitely bittersweet to miss out on the [winner's] rainbow bands, but considering last year was a bronze and this year we have silver, I think this team is on the way up."

Australia won a first-round duel against a British team missing Matt Richardson.

He was withdrawn from the British squad earlier in the week over alleged misconduct.

Richardson won three Olympic medals for Australia before switching allegiance to Great Britain after the 2024 Paris Games.

In other results in Shanghai, Australia's Kristina Clonan, Molly McGill and Alessia McCaig finished seventh in the women's team sprint.

ABC/AAP

World.title: Top gymnastics coach fined after assaulting two female teen athletes
World.content:
A gymnastics coach with more than 30 years' experience has avoided conviction and instead been ordered to pay a fine after assaulting two teenage female athletes.

Over the length of his career, Jamie Glen Cannon, 49, has trained athletes at clubs on the Sunshine Coast, in Cairns, and at Brisbane Grammar School.

Mr Cannon was sentenced in Maroochydore District Court last week, after pleading guilty to four charges of common assault against the two teen gymnasts, each aged between 13 and 16.

Jamie Cannon has coached athletes at clubs on the Sunshine Coast, Cairns and at Brisbane Grammar School over his 30-year career. (ABC News: Alex Papp)

Coach touched athletes

Crown prosecutor Alex Stark described Cannon's behaviour as "a breach of trust, both professional and personal" and tendered an agreed statement of facts about the offending.

The court heard Cannon was a senior coach at a Sunshine Coast club when the incidents occurred in 2022 and 2023.

The two girls were under his supervision as athletes.

One of the assault charges related to Cannon smacking the bottom of a 13-year-old as she performed handstands with other gymnasts at the club.

One athlete's victim impact statement said the offending led to her "quitting gymnastics entirely". (Pexels: Ivan Samkov / CC licence)

Three more offences occurred at the same club, involving Cannon touching and rubbing the inner thigh of a second athlete, aged 15 at the time.

The court heard that in one interaction, Cannon asked the teenager if she wore make-up, told her she was pretty, then put his hand on her inner thigh.

In another, he asked if he could touch the teenager's leggings, and before she could respond, he put his hand on her knee.

The fourth charge involved Cannon approaching the 15-year-old as she prepared to coach a class, standing in between her legs before placing his hands on her knees and rubbing her thighs as she attempted to move away.

The court heard it was accepted that Cannon's behaviour had "no sexual intent".

Gymnast left the sport she loved

The 15-year-old athlete's victim impact statement was read to the court at his sentencing by Mr Stark.

The teenager wrote that the offending led to her "quitting gymnastics entirely".

She described problems falling asleep and how it damaged "many friendships", particularly at the gymnastics club.

"[It] affected the development of a romantic relationship with partners due to fear and sensitivity to certain actions and situations," Mr Stark read to the court.

Do you know more? If you have more information about this story, please contact Owen Jacques at jacques.owen@abc.net.au.

Mr Stark said there was a "vulnerability" in the situation because the teenagers were under his supervision.

He said both teenagers had been clear about their boundaries to Cannon, including the request not to be touched.

"It was really that sense of breach of trust that was at the heart of the impact for both of them," he said.

Cannon declined to be interviewed by police.

The court heard he has not been involved with the sport since being charged.

Decades as a top coach

Cannon's lawyer Ambyr Cousen described how her client had been involved with the sport for 30 years both as an employee and as a volunteer, including as a committee member with Gymnastics Queensland (GQ).

"He has won a number of awards for peer service within that industry," Ms Cousen told the court.

Cannon was working with Brisbane Grammar School as a senior coach in 2019 when he received GQ's Individual Service Award for his service to gymnastics in Queensland.

He also spent more than a decade leading GQ's Men's Artistic Gymnastics Sport Committee.

Ms Cousen also supplied the court with several character references for her client.

Court accepts 'no sexual intent'

Cannon provided a written apology to the court for his actions, and offered to pay $1,000 to each of the victims as compensation.

Jamie Cannon was sentenced on four counts of common assault in the Maroochydore District Court last week. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Owen Jacques)

In sentencing, Judge Amanda McDonnell told Cannon he treated "these young, vulnerable girls in a way that they didn't wish to be touched".

"I have no doubt that they looked up to you for guidance," Judge McDonnell said.

" I accept that there was no sexual intent, but that you acted in an overly-familiar way. "

Cannon was ordered to pay a single fine of $2,500 for the four offences, plus the promised compensation.

No conviction was recorded.

World.title: Schutt stars as Aussies sweep Bangladesh in ODI series
World.content:
Australia has coasted to an eight-wicket ODI win over Bangladesh to secure a clean sweep of the three-match series.

Ellyse Perry (65 not out off 64 deliveries) and Annabel Sutherland (74 not out off 52) added 137 for the third wicket, guiding Australia past Bangladesh's total of 172 all out inside 23 overs.

Australia lost openers Georgia Voll (11) and Beth Mooney (21) early in the run chase at Allan Border Field.

Mooney, in her 100th ODI match, was cleaned up by Bangladesh debutant quick Disha Biswas.

Mooney wants to go well beyond 100 ODIs Beth Mooney is still smarting over Australia's World Cup loss to India last year, and as the star prepares for her 100th ODI against Bangladesh, she still has her eyes set on a couple of long-term goals.

From that moment, it was plain sailing for the hosts as Perry and Sutherland went through the gears.

Earlier, fast bowler Megan Schutt, who was named player of the match and the series, produced another masterclass.

Schutt bowled an incredible 10 overs straight to snare 4-16 and restrict Bangladesh after it was asked to bat first in the third and final ODI.

She bowled 53 dot balls in her spell and took her series haul to 10 wickets at a miserly average of 7.1.

Schutt now has 28 wickets in 14 ODIs at Allan Border Field, the most of any bowler in history.

Australian opener Phoebe Litchfield was ruled out of the match with a low-grade hip strain.

The star batter was replaced by all-rounder Nicola Carey.

AAP

World.title: ParaMatildas hunt more Australian football history at World Cup
World.content:
The ParaMatildas begin the 2026 IFCPF World Cup in uncharted territory for an Australian football team.

At the 2024 tournament in Spain, the side broke through as the nation's first-ever winner of a round ball World Cup.

Now, the players are aiming to become the first Australian team to successfully defend a world title.

It has been a rapid ascent for the side, only officially launched in 2022, but coach Charlotte Ercil said her players were comfortable with added expectation.

"I think it adds a little bit of pressure, but it's exciting at the same time," Ercil told ABC Sport.

"But we always prepare like every game, including our first group game, is the World Cup final."

The ParaMatildas became Australia's first football World Cup winners in 2024. (Supplied)

The ParaMatildas, and their male counterparts, the Pararoos, play football designed for athletes with cerebral palsy, acquired brain injury and symptoms of stroke.

The sport features smaller fields and goals as well as shorter halves than in the mainstream game and does not include the offside rule.

This month's tournament in the US city of Atlanta will be just the third instalment of the Women's World Cup and the first edition to be held outside Spain, while the Pararoos are hopeful of a best-ever finish in the concurrently running men's competition.

In the brief international history of the women's game, Australia and the US have emerged as its two great powers, with the ParaMatildas going down to the stars and stripes in the final of the 2022 tournament before exacting revenge in the 2024 decider.

The ParaMatildas have enjoyed rapid growth since officially launching in 2022. (Getty Images: Con Chronis)

Getting one over the Americans in their own backyard looms as the ultimate test for the ParaMatildas, and Australia central defender Eloise Northam does not doubt the hosts' motivation to reclaim their crown.

"I feel like they definitely are plotting against us," Northam told ABC Sport.

"I think that's what we were doing back in like the second World Cup — we were ready to take on the US and take their championship away from them."

The ParaMatildas are also wary of the sport's expanding talent pool. The growth of the global game means that teams and tactics are evolving rapidly, while players with newly acquired brain injuries are constantly welcomed into the fold.

Australia will face Ireland, the Netherlands and newcomers Colombia during the group stage.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

"Every year or every time we interact with or play against any country, there are always changes and improvements, which is good for the game; it means it's growing," coach Ercil said.

Throw in lingering summer temperatures as well as the possibility of severe thunderstorms, and the ParaMatildas are taking nothing for granted in the American south.

The Pararoos, meanwhile, are bullish on progressing from a difficult group featuring Brazil, Spain and Chile.

The Australian squad for the tournament comes with bucketloads of experience, with 11 of the 14 players selected having previous World Cup experience.

Taj Lynch hopes the Pararoos can progress from a difficult group. (ABC News: Daniel Irvine)

One of those returning athletes is Taj Lynch, who believed his side was now well placed for a breakthrough top-10 finish.

"I feel confident in the players we're taking across; a lot of us have been there before," Lynch told ABC Sport.

"We've learned a lot, we've got a lot of things wrong, but we've grown, and we've improved.

"We're not a team of boys playing against men anymore. I think we're finally starting to be a team of men who can take on the best teams in the world."

Captaining the Pararoos in Atlanta is Australian football legend David Barber.

The veteran debuted for Australia in 1999, and will overtake Andorra's Ildefons Lima as the male player with the longest international football career when he steps out for the Pararoos' tournament opener against Brazil.

World.title: Walters explains choice of Walsh over Tedesco for World Cup opener
World.content:
Kevin Walters has declared the battle for Australia's fullback berth remains wide open despite Reece Walsh winning the nod over James Tedesco to start in the Kangaroos' World Cup opener.

Walters claimed ahead of Thursday night's clash with New Zealand that Tedesco, the captain as Australia lifted the trophy four years ago, would have a chance to prove his worth in the group-stage game against Fiji in Brisbane on October 25.

Walsh, the hero of last year's Ashes whitewash, will don the No.1 jersey at Sydney's Allianz Stadium, but as for whether the Brisbane Broncos star will be first choice later in the tournament, Walters is keeping an open mind.

Less can be more for Rugby League World Cup The Rugby League World Cup exists in a constant state of change but ahead of the tournament opener between Australia and New Zealand the much-maligned tournament can prove less can be more.

The Kangaroos coach indicated he had chosen to rest Tedesco and playmaker halfback Sam Walker following their exploits in the Sydney Roosters' NRL grand final win.

"I feel it's in the best interest of the team they get a spell this week and they'll play next week," Walters said on Wednesday.

"To be honest, I haven't decided that (fullback) position yet, that's why we're here, and they'll both get an opportunity.

"They're both Clive Churchill medallists, the last two, so I look at it that way. I'm very fortunate to have both of them in the team.

"They're different players, but I love what they both bring to the team. Teddy's the more experienced custodian and Reece is on the way up as such."

Walsh has retained his place after his heroics in last year's Ashes. (Getty Images: PA Images/Mike Egerton)

The one drawback to Walsh is his fitness, with Thursday's opener his first competitive match in close to two months after sustaining an ankle injury in clubland.

"He (Walsh) has had a good preparation and there's a few players in that position themselves, so it's good to get them around the group," Walters said.

Walsh will be part of a relatively settled Kangaroos spine, with Cameron Munster at five-eighth and Harry Grant at hooker.

Halfback Mitchell Moses is the only new addition to the key playmaking roles.

Moses was on last year's Ashes tour but didn't take the field, with the Parramatta skipper an understudy to Nathan Cleary, who has missed this World Cup following his compound ankle fracture.

Tedesco last played for Australia in 2023. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

"He's a very influential player, an experienced player, particularly his kicking game around the halves will be invaluable," Walters said.

"He gets his opportunity and I'm sure he's looking forward to taking it as well.

"They (Munster and Moses) are very calm and know what we need to do in different situations."

The Kangaroos have not lost to New Zealand on Australian soil since 2015, and while the Kiwis have a monster forward pack, Walters insists his side have the firepower to match them.

"It's a strong New Zealand side, certainly, but I feel like the guys that we have picked in the Australian squad, they're not mugs," the Kangaroos coach added.

"We've got Origin players, Test players, premiership winners, that's what the World Cup is all about: seeing the best players on the world stage."

AAP

World.title: Roos miss out as Dees, Dons and Eagles complete dramatic deadline day trades
World.content:
Adelaide defender Nick Murray has been left stranded as the AFL trade period drew to a close with a flurry of late deals.

Despite offering the Crows a raft of trade offers as the deadline approached, the Kangaroos were unable to pry Murray away from the South Australians.

Murray's failed move came as Essendon and Brisbane reached an agreement to send Keidean Coleman to the Bombers, while the Lions also sent Will McLachlan to Melbourne in a three-team deal that saw premiership duo Trent Rivers and Jack Viney head to West Coast.

Six players were moved inside the final half an hour of the trade period after the first four hours of the final day saw just three pick swaps, with one of those netting Richmond a second top five pick in this year's draft.

Follow the live blog below for a recap of all the trade deadline action as it happened.

World.title: Afghan batter recreates infamous hamstring injury in Bangladesh draw
World.content:
Sediqullah Atal's maiden Test century has led Afghanistan to an epic draw against Bangladesh in a one-off cricket Test.

Afghanistan batted for 142 overs, 92 on the fifth and final day, in its second innings to force a sensational draw on Tuesday. It began the day on a dodgy 3-132, lost five more wickets, but fought on to hold out to stumps at 8-346.

But it was the actions of number nine Qais Ahmad in the dying minutes that drew the most attention in the match's final act.

With the finish line in sight and just two wickets left, Ahmad played a forward defence to spinner Taijul Islam before collapsing to the ground clutching his hamstring.

The Bangladesh team was not impressed, and had commentator Ahmad Farhad Fidai in stitches as he likened it to the actions of Afghanistan's Gulbadin Naib, who suffered a suspicious cramp fielding at slip in their famous 2024 T20 World Cup win over Bangladesh.

"Qais Ahmad does it again. This reminds me of Gulbadin Naib," an amused Fidai said, clearly believing Ahmad's fall to the turf was nothing more than time-wasting antics.

"Oh boy, not again.

"You really don't need to see the replay; we can understand from here what's going on."

Ahmad soldiered on and finished the match with a six over midwicket.

Bangladesh dominated the match after winning the toss and batting first. Bangladesh earned a first-innings lead of 106 runs, then declared its second innings at 7-372 after player-of-the-match Litton Das was out for 102. That gave Bangladesh an imposing lead of 478 and four and a half sessions to bowl out Afghanistan.

But Afghanistan defied the odds despite losing two wickets in the first seven overs on Monday.

First drop Atal, in his third Test, ate up most of the chase as he faced 332 balls over 8.5 hours to score 111. He was caught close to the wicket after tea, the seventh man out.

Afghanistan still had 23 overs with just tailenders left. But 34-year-old Yamin Ahmadzai faced 85 balls for a career-best 19, and Ahmad, who has played franchise cricket in eight countries, faced 80 to finish with an unbeaten career-best 49.

AP/ABC

World.title: Less can be more for Rugby League World Cup
World.content:
The only things that stay the same about the Rugby League World Cup are that it never stops changing and it continually has to justify its own existence.

For the third tournament in a row, there will be a different format and a different number of teams, dropping from 16 to 10, and for the umpteenth tournament in a row, the sceptics will question why it's worth playing a Rugby League World Cup at all and compare it unfavourably to the rugby and football versions.

Those world cups exist in different universes than the league equivalent, even as nation-swapping and diaspora-heavy squads, two hallmarks of the much-maligned international rugby league, become more prevalent in their larger cousins.

The Rugby League World Cup has to prove itself anew every four years. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

Measure the Rugby League World Cup against those that dwarf it in scale and it will always be miles behind. It is playing a different game, one that is carving out a place all its own.

On the back of the rise of Tonga and Samoa over the past 10 years, Test football is at its strongest and most vibrant in years, with the two Pasifika nations emerging as legitimate draws and top-class teams.

Tonga's two matches against Australia in the 2024 Pacific Championships drew crowds of more than 33,000 and 28,000, and both Tonga and Samoa have made their first tours to England since the last World Cup.

When the ancient island rivals went head-to-head in Brisbane last year, more than 40,000 came through the gates, the second-largest non-World Cup final crowd for a Test in Australia in the last half-century.

Samoa creates rugby league magic The passion of the Pacific shines through in Samoa's rugby league team, and the pride the people have is evident on the island.

A similar attendance is expected for the tournament opener between Australia and New Zealand on Thursday night, and if the Sydney Football Stadium can sell out, it'll be the biggest Test crowd in Sydney since 1974.

It marks the beginning of a chance for the Rugby League World Cup to reshape itself a little more permanently and take advantage of the renewed interest by recasting itself as a pinnacle for the game rather than a starting point.

Rugby league had to make a choice whether its World Cup was a beginning or an end, a proving ground for developing nations or a battleground for the best, because it could not be both at the same time.

At the sharp end of recent tournaments, when it's the best teams in the world having it out, the product is reliably compelling, rich and powerful. The problem is it's just taken too long to get there.

In 2022, there was a crackerjack knockout phase, highlighted by Samoa's epic win over Tonga in Warrington, New Zealand sneaking home against Fiji in Hull, and two brilliant semifinals, including a golden point epic that doubles as one of the best games in the tournament's history.

The night a rag-tag group of rugby league Russians took on the world champions Russia might only make one trip to the Rugby League World Cup but the memories forged in the 2000 tournament, especially in their record loss to Australia, are wild enough to last a lifetime.

But the group stage was a forgone conclusion almost all the way. Only two of the 24 preliminary matches were decided by one score or less. There were 10 scores over 60 and two scores over 90.

Australia's 110-4 massacre of Russia in 2000 remained untouched as the most lopsided result in World Cup history, but matches from 2022 fill out the second, third and fourth spots on that list.

Developing nations have their place in the international rugby league and the emotional scenes upon qualification for Jamaica, or Greece's epic tale of playing qualifying matches on the edge of war zones and in undisclosed locations to stay one step ahead of the authorities, are proof of the value developing nations can bring.

But it is hard to see the benefits of England nearly putting 100 points on the Greeks, or a disinterested Australia beating Scotland 84-0.

The trickle-down effects of those games, such as they are, can take decades to rise to the surface, if they ever do at all.

The knockout phase of recent World Cups have been rugby league dynamite. (Getty Images: Gareth Copley)

The game's wholehearted embrace of the set restart rule and the increased speed of play makes it harder for the smaller nations to compete on a physical level, and the perfunctory nature of the group stages makes the tournament even longer.

In a world where fan interest and player fatigue are already being stretched to their limits, it adds even more to an already overstuffed season.

So while it may not please the true believers, the move to 10 teams is a good one. This tournament is leaner and has the potential to be meaner.

The lack of northern hemisphere teams — it's just England, France and Lebanon, with none from the Americas and no other home nations after Scotland and Ireland were demoted to affiliate status and Wales failed to qualify — is regrettable, but exclusivity cuts both ways because less can be more.

This is a tournament with barely any fat on it, and as a result, it's as open at the top as it's ever been.

Australia is still the favourite because such is the largesse of talent available that it's almost impossible to name a Kangaroos team that isn't oozing with class, but it's far from invulnerable.

Its talent pool has been diluted, and there are several squad members who are coming off indifferent or underdone seasons.

Some have made it due to coach Kevin Walters's loyalty to the side that retained the Ashes in a 3-0 whitewash last year, but others are in because there's a lack of other options as the eligibility rules slowly spread the talent around.

Nobody has benefited more from that spread than New Zealand, who welcome Kalyn Ponga to the squad for his belated Test debut as the herald of a new era.

On paper, it's a better side than the one that handed Australia its biggest-ever defeat just three years ago — it has all three middles from this season's Dally M Team of the Year — and a second World Cup title is a distinct possibility.

The bookies have Samoa and Tonga as equal-third favourites to make the final, well ahead of England, and their group-stage clash at Parramatta Stadium has been sold out for months.

Samoa and Tonga have already sold out their group stage match. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

The English have a little more to prove after last year's lacklustre Ashes showing, an embrace of heritage players that has divided their fan base and the controversial exclusion of Leeds halfback Jake Connor from the squad.

Outside the top five, there's still plenty to follow. Write off the perennially underrated Fijians, who beat New Zealand in 2017 and came within six points of doing the same in 2022, off at your peril.

France and Lebanon won't be as dangerous, but the French have 20 homegrown players in their squad and 10 of Lebanon's starting 13 for their first game have NRL experience.

Even the Cook Islands, which will play in front of crowds that dwarf its home's population, will have Cronulla's KL Iro and former Kangaroo Valentine Holmes to call upon.

Another Australian victory is far from a guarantee in this World Cup. (Jan Kruger: Getty Images for RLWC)

Injuries have robbed Papua New Guinea of some of their biggest names, but their group matches against Samoa and Lebanon will be the Kumuls' biggest on home soil since the PNG Chiefs were admitted to the NRL and shape as the first dress rehearsals for what awaits the game in the land where they love it most.

Through it all, this World Cup can have it all. There will still be stories of paupers taking on princes against all odds and of the unbridled passion and pride that has kept international football alive despite the many obstacles.

Those tales and teams will always have their place, but for the most part, this tournament will be collections of top-level rugby league talent crashing into each other in the fast until only the world champions are left to rise from the wreckage.

What the tournament gives up in diversity and novelty, it can win back in quality, because at some point, a World Cup has to be about the best of the best being at their best, and there are more nations who can dream of that than ever before.

Never in the World Cup's 72-year history has the sky seemed so open. Ten teams might not seem like many, but if five have designs on the crown, it can be plenty.

Tech.title: The best feature of Apple’s HomeView might be its simplicity
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for Wirecutter, Wired, Dwell, BBC, and US News.

I’m just going to come right out and say it. I love the approach Apple has taken with the HomeView. I think it’s the shared, always-available household interface that my family might finally use. Is Apple’s first smart display my dream smart home dashboard? No. But is it the right product for Apple Home at this moment? Absolutely.

A lot of initial reactions to the $299 HomeView (which looks like a giant Apple Watch on a flatter metallic HomePod Mini) are asking why anyone would want it when you can do everything it offers on your iPhone or iPad. And yes, its features replicate many of the things you already do on the devices you use all the time. But that’s kind of the point. HomeView gives you another interface for those things, but crucially one that is always powered, always unlocked, and always in the same spot in your home, making it easy to walk up to and interact with.

I’ve tried using an iPad to control my smart home, run my family’s calendar, and be a shared device for controlling music. It wasn’t great. I’ll have to test HomeView, of course, but my initial impression is that this could be a much better solution for those use cases.

My iPad in the wall experiment lasted several unsuccessful years.

Most iPads are more expensive, have worse speakers, and do not like to be plugged in all the time (I present my sad, warped iPad Mini as tribute). An iPad can’t be a hub for your Apple Home; HomeView can. An iPad famously isn’t a good multiuser device, and controlling home devices on one requires it staying logged in to your personal iCloud account; HomeView offers Apple’s first crack at easy multiuser switching.

Apple designed HomeView as a communal device that sits in a fixed place in the home. This means it’s always where you expect it to be, which matters when you want to adjust the thermostat or can’t find your phone and want to check your calendar. Not having a battery or detachable screen is a feature for me, because devices that do inevitably wander off and die under a couch cushion.

And while many people are fine using their personal phones and tablets to interact with the digital world when at home, and don’t want yet another device with a screen on their countertop or wall, the millions of Echo Shows, Google Nest Hubs, Skylight Calendars, and the like in homes today are a good indicator that there’s interest in this type of interface.

The HomeView’s footprint is smaller than that of most smart displays I’ve tested.

As Apple’s uncharacteristically chaotic launch video shows, HomeView targets a new demographic for the company: busy, Apple-centric households. One feature I’m most interested in is HomeView’s role as a home video phone. Do you know how many times I’ve tried to call my daughter when I’m not home, and her phone is dead or on silent? Based on Apple’s video, if she’s home, my call can now ring on the HomeView. I’ve occasionally used the drop-in feature on Echo smart speakers to get her attention, further proof of the advantage of always-on home devices.

The HomeView uses Siri AI (which requires an AI-capable iPhone) to provide useful personal information. An iPhone or iPad is required for a user profile, but anyone in the home can control devices like smart lights. (But that’s one really big button … )

I see HomeView as filling the awkward space where families don’t want phones at the dinner table or on the kitchen counter, but still want to check what time Zoey’s soccer game is or look up the origin of French toast (yeah, just kidding). This inevitably ends with one person pulling out their phone, which gives everyone else implicit permission to do the same.

Smart displays and speakers from Amazon and Google already help with this to some extent, but Apple’s version comes without ads (see the Echo Show) and may have a longer lifespan (RIP Pixel Tablet). Siri AI’s much-hyped “personal context” capabilities, in which it can scan your text messages and emails and serve up relevant information to up to six members of your household, also give it an edge here.

The HomeView has a variety of customizable faces.

I asked Kaiann Drance, vice president of product marketing for home at Apple, why Apple chose now for its biggest smart home push yet. She said Siri AI and the personal context it brings, which she called Apple’s “privacy story,” came together with a device designed specifically for the home. “With the magic of Siri AI, it comes together in a way that we haven’t been able to deliver before,” she said.

As the Siri AI capabilities continue to evolve, the home experience is fitting to be able to interact with in a natural way.” — Lilian Rincon, Apple

Siri AI made this possible because it’s “much more capable,” said Lilian Rincon, vice president of product marketing for AI at Apple. She also pointed to its new conversational abilities. “It’s great because you can just ask it to change the temperature on your thermostat in a very natural way. As the Siri AI capabilities continue to evolve, the home experience is fitting to be able to interact with in this natural way.” On why now, Rincon says the natural-language shift is the point where AI goes mainstream. “Because now it can be … my mother-in-law or the Gen Z who’s in college, both of them can use this in the way that they naturally speak and get what they want.”

Siri AI in the home has another big advantage over the competition: It doesn’t say too much. Based on the demos I saw, and my time using Siri AI on the iPhone, when you ask it to do something, it does it without peppering you with follow-up questions. Rincon confirmed this is by design. “A lot of these assistants out there are always asking questions because they want more information,” she said. “For us, it isn’t about that. We’re there to get it done, take an action for you, show you what you need to get done, and then really get out of the way.”

The Home control widget on the HomeView can show live views of security cameras.

My first reaction to hearing about HomeView’s smart home features, which are basically just what the Apple Home app on your phone can do, was disappointment. I had hoped that, along with new hardware, Apple would bring more functionality and deeper Apple Intelligence integration to Apple Home to make the smart home smarter. I’m still waiting on that.

On reflection, I’m okay with this — for now. Apple trying to make the smart home easier for everyone to use can only be a good thing. As always, the smart home’s most important goal is to come up with an easier way to turn on the lights.

Apple trying to make the smart home easier for everyone to use can only be a good thing.

HomeView’s simplicity may put off hardcore home automation enthusiasts, but I’d argue it’s perfect for their long-suffering spouses. I’ve tried every version of physical smart home control interface in my home, and you know who hasn’t used any of them? My family.

Because my family all have iPhones, and because the HomeView will always be there and will feel familiar, I can see them actually using it. That means I could set up a full Home Assistant instance and run a detailed dashboard on a tablet in my office, then feed the scenes and devices into Apple Home so my husband and daughter can just tap to control them on a HomeView in the kitchen.

HomeView may not be the smart home computer I want Apple to make, but it is the smart home device Apple needed to make. It doesn’t have to run all the iPad apps or try to be a bigger version of my iPhone; it just needs to make the smart home accessible to everyone in the house. If Apple has pulled that off, it could be more valuable than any new smart home feature I’ve been wishing for.

Tech.title: Eight states sue OpenAI, saying ChatGPT isn’t safe for kids
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

OpenAI is facing a new wave of lawsuits from eight US states that accuse the company of harming children and misleading customers about the safety of ChatGPT, as reported earlier by Reuters. The lawsuits, filed separately by Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho, and Montana, allege OpenAI unlawfully put profits over safety when developing ChatGPT.

The string of complaints claims that OpenAI violated local consumer protection laws by failing to warn customers about the dangers of ChatGPT, citing several lawsuits filed by the family members of teens and adults that allege the AI chatbot played a role in their loved ones’ deaths. They allege that while OpenAI misleadingly presented ChatGPT as a “safe, youth-appropriate tool that puts safety first,” it was actually “dangerous to vulnerable users” — including by “degrading critical thinking skills, encouraging paranoias and delusions, offering dangerous medical advice, and promoting unhealthy behaviors and relationships.”

Additionally, the states accuse OpenAI of collecting data from minors and not doing enough to keep underage users from using the chatbot. The lawsuits also cite recent rogue AI hacking incidents as evidence of OpenAI’s alleged “recklessness.”

“OpenAI has devolved from its original mission as a public-first nonprofit that prioritized safety into a cautionary tale about what can happen when the development of a tool as powerful as AI is driven not by safety, but by a profit‑at‑all‑costs mindset that sidelines essential safeguards,” Arizona’s lawsuit claims.

In an emailed statement to The Verge, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri says the company has “built industry-leading age-specific protections” into ChatGPT:

While no system can be perfect, we’ll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today. We’re committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry - not just one company.

The states are asking the courts to force OpenAI to pay a series of civil penalties and to stop misleading the public about the safety of ChatGPT. Some states are also seeking the deletion of unlawfully collected personal data.

Update, October 14th: Added a statement from OpenAI.

Tech.title: Microsoft and Japan took down a cybercrime network behind over a billion scam messages
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

We’ve all gotten a scam text about a nonexistent parking ticket or a fake package delivery, but hopefully you’ll start seeing fewer of them. Microsoft says it helped dismantle a marketplace for scammers sending phishing messages like those around the world. Through an investigation with Japan’s National Police Agency, it tracked scam activity back to a marketplace called YAM Store and a pair of phishing kits, CoGUI and Iron Man:

Since January 2026, YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man have collectively enabled more than one billion malicious messages targeting over 75,000 organizations worldwide, including more than 750 million messages geared toward Microsoft customers alone. These messages have been used to target consumers, healthcare organizations, financial institutions, and other businesses in more than 150 countries, generating tens of millions of dollars for their operators.

According to Microsoft’s report, scammers could buy stolen or fraudulent Microsoft and Google accounts on YAM Store and use the phishing kits to send scam messages. Microsoft says YAM Store also hijacked real organizations’ expired web domains and created websites for nonexistent organizations, which it used to get Microsoft accounts it could resell.

The Iron Man platform was also offering over 2,300 templates scammers could use to impersonate organizations like banks and police departments. Microsoft says it disabled over 20,000 accounts connected to YAM Store and blocked over 100,000 web domains being used for impersonation and fraud. With health sector cybersecurity non-profit Health-ISAC, Microsoft also seized and redirected web domains that were powering all three platforms.

Tech.title: The AI race is back on
Tech.content:
Last week, Anthropic and OpenAI looked like they had the AI race to themselves, pulling ahead with increasingly powerful models that left their rivals in the dust. Google seemed hopelessly far behind, while Meta, despite spending billions to revive its floundering AI ambitions, had yet to establish itself as a serious contender. Even the latest models coming out of China, impressive as they were, appeared to be playing catch-up.

Then, in the space of a few days, everything changed. Google and Meta both unveiled frontier models they claim can go toe to toe with the best from OpenAI and Anthropic. Suddenly, the race is back on — and it’s anyone’s game.

Until this week, Google looked like it had permanently lost its place among the AI front-runners. Since releasing Gemini 3 late last year, the tech giant had delivered little more than incremental improvements. Gemini 3 was formidable when it launched, but its lead was fleeting, and it struggled to keep up with later offerings from OpenAI and Anthropic, or even some of the open-weight models emerging from China.

A series of internal shake-ups only added to the sense that Google was retreating from the AI frontier. Veteran executive Jeff Dean departed the company with a number of other AI researchers to launch a new startup. Demis Hassabis, the Nobel laureate who spent years at the helm of Google’s AI powerhouse DeepMind, stepped back from day-to-day leadership. Other AI-related teams were moved out of DeepMind and into Google proper. Together, the changes signaled a broader shift in Google’s AI center of gravity, moving away from London and toward California, fueling speculation the tech giant was beginning to prioritize commercializing AI over research.

Then, on Tuesday, Google upended that narrative with the release of Gemini 4 Argon, a new frontier model the company claims matches or beats flagship offerings from OpenAI and Anthropic on numerous benchmarks, whatever value benchmarks are still worth. What’s more, Google has priced Argon aggressively: Per token, it’s undercutting its rivals by as much as 80 percent during its introductory period, and is still significantly cheaper once that promotion ends.

Meta’s arrival was arguably even more dramatic. Unlike Google, which had long been the one to beat in AI thanks to its deep pockets and DeepMind, Meta had never really established itself as a serious contender at the frontier. It was not through lack of trying, but its models struggled to make a mark. Last year, the company embarked on an ambitious and expensive overhaul of its AI operations, spending billions on talent and infrastructure, including Scale AI and its cofounder Alexandr Wang. In April, its new Superintelligence Labs released its first major model, Muse Spark. Impressive, but not quite frontier.

That changed on Monday when Meta finally unveiled a model capable of competing with the industry’s very best. According to the company’s testing, Muse Wonder Full can compete with leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic, including GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Fable 5.1, on numerous benchmarks. In other words, Mark Zuckerberg’s company has finally arrived at the AI frontier.

The return of Google — and the arrival of Meta — makes the AI competition considerably more dynamic and shows just how quickly the balance of power can shift in the AI world. Both have extraordinarily deep pockets and vast ecosystems of products used by billions of people, advantages that AI upstarts like OpenAI and Anthropic simply cannot match. The success of Meta’s Muse agent assistant illustrates that advantage. Its popularity in such a short period of time, and despite the growing list of security and privacy concerns, shows the power of having billions of users within ready reach. OpenAI, meanwhile, is having to work harder to establish an ecosystem of its own, positioning itself as an alternative to Meta.

All this comes as the AI race appears to be entering a new phase. The drive to develop ever more powerful models is becoming increasingly fraught. The growing array of safety concerns and rogue AI incidents means calls to slow development are growing louder. Open models are also getting better and better, making it harder for any one company to stay ahead for long.

If raw power and performance are no longer enough to stay ahead, Google and Meta have plenty of advantages not enjoyed by Anthropic and OpenAI. They may have spent a lot of time playing catch-up, but the past week shows it would be incredibly foolish to count either of them out.

Tech.title: Now that Character.AI is going bankrupt, what happens to all of its users’ data?
Tech.content:
is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.

New York Attorney General Letitia James revealed a years-long multi-state investigation against Character.AI as they now seek to require protections on consumer data sold through its bankruptcy proceeding.

James is among 40 bipartisan AGs who filed a notice of interest in Character.AI’s bankruptcy case “to put all parties on notice of the regulatory issues that will need to be addressed in any sale or transfer of the Debtor’s business or assets.” Character.AI announced Tuesday it was filing for Chapter 11 and selling some assets to Disney. But the AGs warn there could be serious risk involved in the transfer of the technology due to the “highly sensitive nature of the conversations many users have with Character.AI chatbot characters, the large number of minors who use the product, the serious risks posed by specific features of the product.”

The filing also reveals that several of the states had been mid-investigation when Character.AI filed for bankruptcy. The states say they opened a probe into consumer protection and privacy concerns in 2024, following a lawsuit from the mother of a 14-year-old who died by suicide allegedly “seconds” after talking with the chatbot.

“The investigations uncovered exceptionally serious dangers”

“The investigations uncovered exceptionally serious dangers and potentially unlawful conduct from Character.AI, particularly its treatment of children, including chatbots posing as licensed professionals, exposure to sexual and violent content, weak age checks, misleading safety claims, and potential violations of state privacy laws,” according to a press release from James’ office. The states were working to address these issues with Character.AI, but didn’t reach an agreement before the company filed for bankruptcy. Character.AI and Disney did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The states are urging the judge to require the purchaser of Character.AI’s assets to implement procedures that will safeguard the sensitive information the company maintained. Those include effective age-assurance systems, restrictions on how minors can engage with the chatbots, implementing “Crisis safeguards,” and letting users delete their data. “This company collected some of the most private thoughts children have ever shared, and now those conversations could be sold off to the highest bidder,” James said in a statement. “I am fighting to make sure any buyer puts children’s safety first and puts real protections in place.”

Tech.title: As a TV enthusiast, I was hoping for more from the Apple TV 4K
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer covering TVs and audio. He has over 20 years experience in AV, and has previously been on staff at Digital Trends and Reviewed.

It’s been four long years since the last Apple TV 4K was released, and in that time there have been lots of hopes and dreams for features in whatever comes next. A new chip, 4K/120Hz support, audio passthrough, a remote locator, better home control integration — the 2022 Apple TV 4K is a great box, but there’s still plenty of room for improvement. With the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K announced on Tuesday, some of those hopes were met, while others were unfortunately left out.

Coloring the announcement is the device’s price. Apple eliminated the cheaper 64GB, Wi-Fi-only model, leaving just the 128GB, Wi-Fi and Ethernet model — and bumped up its price to $300. I repeat, $300 for a streaming device. It’s a hefty price when every other major streamer on the market is at least half the cost.

There are new features I like about this year’s Apple TV 4K. More processing power is great — although my third generation is still running plenty fast — as is the Find My support for when the remote inevitably gets lost in the couch cushions or tangled up in blankets. Built-in far-field mics for talking to Siri are nice, too, provided you don’t stuff the box into a credenza like I do. The fourth-generation Apple TV 4K also adds a dedicated AV1 decoder, which allows for higher-quality streaming from apps that support it, such as Netflix, which is excellent. Any potential improvement to streaming content is a welcome one.

My primary concern, though, is how the Apple TV 4K performs as an integral piece of my home theater. Apple added the ability to create a surround sound system by using its HomePod 2 and HomePod Mini 2 smart speakers in matching pairs for fronts and surrounds. For Apple ecosystem fans looking to build out a surround setup akin to Sonos or Bose, it’s an interesting idea (and I’m all for getting people into immersive sound in their home theaters). But as I expect is the same for many people interested in pricey streaming hardware, I already have a sound system — it’s an Atmos setup with a combination of SVS and Revel speakers. I’m not setting up my two HomePod 2s in my living room and spending another $300 on a pair of HomePod Mini 2s to replace my existing speakers.

The Apple TV 4K pairs with up to four HomePods (such as the Mini 2 pictured here) for surround sound.

What I, and many current users, have been hoping for from the Apple TV 4K for years is the addition of audio passthrough. This would allow my more expensive and capable audio/video receiver to decode the raw audio stream instead of the Apple TV using its Continuous Audio Connection, which can cause some playback issues.

Additionally, it would have been nice to see Apple support 120fps output, especially for those who use Moonlight to stream games to it. That’s a feature that would have set the Apple TV 4K apart from all the other streamers, which top out at 60fps, and helped to justify the high price. Apple could have also used it to pivot more into TV gaming. (For movies, though, the 60fps limit is not a huge deal, as the box can be set to output 24fps, allowing a native 120Hz TV to just use 5:5 pulldown.)

Other premium features that would set Apple’s streaming box apart and make home theater enthusiasts throw their money at it include an HDMI input for HDMI passthrough or a digital optical out. I understand leaving them out if it meant raising the price further. This box is already expensive enough. But it does leave the Apple TV 4K in an uncomfortable spot, pairing a high-end price with features that are largely matched elsewhere for much less.

Are these high-end omissions a concern for the majority of people? Not really. But those people are going to look at the $300 price tag of the Apple TV 4K and then at Google, Roku, or Amazon streaming devices, which are all half that price or less. The Apple TV 4K is looked at as the premium streamer option, but the now extra premium price without some of the, admittedly niche, features gives me pause.

Maybe the new Apple TV 4K will surprise me. I’ve certainly been looking forward to it for a while. I already appreciate the way Apple handles privacy, and if Apple adds features in coming months, maybe it could be worth it. But that $300 price? It might be better spent elsewhere in your home theater setup.

Tech.title: CedarDB wants one database to handle both transactions and analytics, as AI agents raise the stakes
Tech.content:
Databases have traditionally been built for one of two jobs. Analytical databases help businesses spot trends and answer questions, while operational databases store the day-to-day records of transactions, like orders and payments. But the Munich-based database engine CedarDB supports both, and its approach has gained relevance with the rise of agentic AI, its cofounder and CEO Moritz Sichert told TechCrunch.

CedarDB has been in the making for the last decade, but its current momentum stems from enterprise companies whose existing data stacks may have been well suited to storing years of transactions, yet less suited to quickly answering analytical questions asked in natural language about that data.

CedarDB’s questioning of the divide between analytical and operational queries is a byproduct of its focus on efficiency. The company is a Technical University of Munich spinout based on Umbra, a research project that was built from scratch to beat legacy database engines at processing speed by making the most of modern hardware.

With five Umbra researchers as its cofounders, CedarDB kept that approach, promising faster performance without requiring more CPUs or processing power and memory — and requiring few changes from customers. In particular, its team made sure CedarDB was compatible with PostgreSQL, an open-source database system.

According to Sichert, this compatibility with the popular database helps keep switching costs low, since users don’t need to rebuild their apps. It also has an added advantage: CedarDB follows the logic LLMs are most familiar with as a result of their training.

That decision is one of many choices that proved lucky in retrospect, Sichert said. But it wasn’t all luck. In a blog post, cofounder Christian Winter detailed key priorities the team set after leaving academia, “such as reliability, fault tolerance and compatibility with popular tools.”

Not all of the answers were obvious. The team strongly debated whether it should launch a cloud offering right away. In the end, it launched CedarDB Enterprise as an on-premise offering alongside its free version, CedarDB Community Edition, both announced in May of last year at the same time as it announced a €5.3 million seed funding round (approximately $6 million).

The cloud offering was only delayed, though, not abandoned. After conducting beta testing with users who had signed up for its waitlist, the company on Wednesday announced limited availability of CedarDB Cloud on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt, where it’s competing with 20 other startups that are right vying to win TC’s prestigious Startup Battlefield competition.

A fully managed, cloud-hosted version will likely help CedarDB expand its user base beyond large enterprises. It will also make it better prepared to compete with the likes of Databricks, a major data company that seems to have reached the same conclusion as the German startup.

At its Data + AI Summit in June, the American company cited “the agentic era” as the reason why it was launching LTAP, a new data architecture aiming to “[unify] transactions, analytics, streaming, and operational data on a single copy of storage in the lake.”

It is too early to tell how disruptive this might be, but Sichert interprets Databricks’ move as another sign that there is demand for what CedarDB does. The startup plans to serve its first cloud users with its current team of 14 people; but Sichert expects it will need a larger team once it gets more traction. “And this is where we would raise our next round.”

Pictured from left to right: CedarDB founders Moritz Sichert, Lukas Vogel, Philipp Fent, Dominik Durner and Christian Winter.

Tech.title: Ambani’s Jio seeks to raise $3.2B in what could be India’s biggest IPO
Tech.content:
Jio Platforms, the digital arm of Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, is seeking to raise as much as $3.2 billion in what could be India’s biggest initial public offering. The listing will test public-market appetite for a company that attracted more than $20 billion from global investors, including Google and Meta in 2020.

On Wednesday, Reliance Industries said in a stock exchange filing (PDF) that Jio had set a price band of ₹1,065 to ₹1,119 (about $11.19 to $11.76) per share for the offering of up to 270 million new shares (PDF). The IPO will open for subscription on October 21 and close on October 23, with bidding for anchor investors scheduled for October 19.

At the upper end of the proposed price band, the IPO would value Jio at about ₹10.3 trillion (around $108.3 billion), based on the number of shares expected to be outstanding after the offering.

In 2020, Jio was valued at up to ₹4.91 trillion (about $65 billion at the time). Meta, then known as Facebook, invested $5.7 billion, while Google committed $4.5 billion.

Jio’s IPO is set to overtake Hyundai Motor India’s ₹278.7 billion ($3.3 billion at the time) offering in 2024, the country’s biggest to date, even if its shares are priced at the lower end of the range.

Since launching in 2016, Jio has grown into India’s largest telecom operator, with more than 524 million subscribers as of March 31, ahead of Bharti Airtel, Vodafone Idea, and state-owned BSNL. It initially drew customers with free data and cheap plans, though its prices are now comparable to those of its rivals. Over time, Jio has grown beyond a telco and expanded into broadband, cloud services, and other digital businesses.

Jio’s IPO comes as Elon Musk has stepped up his criticism of Ambani, accusing him of trying to keep Starlink out of India. The accusation comes more than a year after Jio and rival Airtel signed deals with Musk’s SpaceX to distribute Starlink’s satellite internet service in India, subject to regulatory approvals. Indian authorities have rejected Musk’s claims.

In the quarter ended June, Jio’s revenue rose nearly 12% from a year earlier to ₹391.7 billion (about $4.1 billion), while its net profit climbed 9% to ₹77.6 billion (around $816 million), per its IPO prospectus (PDF).
