Jio has set aside shares worth up to ₹25 billion (about $263 million) for eligible Reliance Industries shareholders and another ₹5 billion ($53 million) for employees, who will receive a discount of ₹54 per share.

Of the IPO proceeds, Jio plans to use up to ₹275 billion ($2.9 billion) to repay debt at its telecom subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm, with the remaining proceeds going toward general corporate purposes, per the prospectus.

Tech.title: Flock CEO says its microphones detect ‘just gunshots’ — its website says different
Tech.content:
Flock CEO Garrett Langley said the company’s gunshot-detection microphones detect “just gunshots,” but Flock’s website paints a far broader picture of what other ambient audio also gets picked up.

Speaking onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt, the co-founder of the surveillance company defended Flock’s audio-collection product called Gunshot Detection, which listens for gunshots and other ambient audio across nearby neighborhoods to provide “earlier awareness” to potential public safety events.

Flock’s website says that the company’s audio systems can pinpoint gunfire instantly, while also being able to “detect street takeovers early to stop chaos before it escalates,” and “identify severe crashes in real time so help arrives faster.” It also says they can “expand awareness beyond gunfire with alerts for car crashes, fireworks, and sideshows.”

The company’s Gunshot Detection feature, announced last year, faced immediate pushback. In announcing the feature, Flock said the technology would listen out for sounds of “screaming.” Privacy groups condemned the company for listening for human voices, prompting the company to amend its website to instead say “sounds of human distress.” Flock later said it pulled the ability to detect “distress” altogether from its customers who tried it.

During the interview, Langley pushed back against what he described as misinformation about his product, arguing that many of its critics misunderstand how its products work. The comments come as public opinion continues to shift against Flock and other license plate reading companies amid growing unease about mass surveillance — sentiments that were visible in San Francisco, where protesters gathered to voice their opposition outside the venue as Langley took the stage.

Image Credits:TechCrunch (screenshot)

“Most people don’t call 911 when they hear a gunshot, and so that’s why we built the product,” Langley told TechCrunch editor-in-chief Connie Loizos onstage. “And then some of our customers said, ‘Oh, we have these in parking lots. It would be great if we could get alerted if someone was being abducted, if someone was being harmed.’”

Langley said that the idea seemed logical, so the company prototyped it and rolled it out to a couple of customers, but said that some people then had a lot of concerns. Langley conceded to making mistakes but that he was listening to his customers.

“There’s only a couple customers that were prototyping it with us, and we said, ‘OK, great, it’s just going to do gunshots, plain and simple.’ If a gun goes off, we’ll notify, and if not, that’s all it’s going to listen to,” said Langley.

When asked about the contradiction between his remarks and the company’s marketing materials that say the audio systems can detect more than gunshots, he responded, “It’s just gunshots.”

When reached by TechCrunch, Flock spokesperson Paris Lewbel said: “Flock’s gunshot detection technology is primarily used to detect gunfire but is also capable of detecting fireworks, sideshows, and potential car crashes. CEO Garrett Langley’s remarks were intended to emphasize that Flock’s Audio Detection technology is not designed to monitor conversations or analyze speech and does not currently detect human screaming or distress.”

An FAQ section of the website notes that “in addition to gunshots, Flock Gunshot and Audio Detection can detect fireworks, sideshows, and other disruptive community events.” It goes on to state that the company’s “detection library is continually expanding to include emerging threats that are relevant” to customers’ specific needs.

Langley stated that the number of Flock’s microphones is comparable to ShotSpotter, which as of 2024 had about 25,000 microphones, per reporting by Wired.

Langley’s comments come amid mounting scrutiny of Flock from privacy advocates, including the ACLU, and members of the public who are concerned about the misuse of its technology, with some going so far as destroying the surveillance cameras. The remarks also come as Texas and Florida have moved to end their relationships with Flock, and Amazon’s Ring has ended its partnership with the company.

Tech.title: Colossal Biosciences announces new AI platform to help accelerate de-extinction efforts
Tech.content:
Colossal Biosciences announced Wednesday a new AI platform to help accelerate its efforts to bring back extinct species, TechCrunch can exclusively report.

The platform, called GenoMorph, uses advanced 3D morphology, comparative genomics, and developmental biology to identify genes that could be edited in de-extinction projects with limited gene data. The company is using it as part of its effort to bring back the dodo bird, for which there are limited genomes to work with.

For example, the company is working with only one dodo genome compared to the 100 genomes it has been able to obtain as part of its woolly mammoth de-extinction project. DNA from the woolly mammoth is more plentiful because the colder climates the animal lived in preserve the DNA better than the tropics where the dodo lived, the company said.

“Normally, scientists can compare many genomes to understand which genetic differences are responsible for certain traits,” Colossal CEO and co-founder Ben Lamm told TechCrunch. “We don’t have that luxury with ancient DNA from extinct species whose DNA is severely limited, and we can only get a small number of complete genomes.”

To build GenoMorph, Lamm said the company collected a bunch of developmental data from “chickens, quail, ducks, and pigeons,” and combined it with the “genetic information and 3D skull measurements from more than 70 bird species.” He said it took more than a year of work to build this platform, which also builds on the company’s years of work in de-extinction.

“The AI learns which regions of DNA are active as different birds develop their beaks and facial structures, and uses that information to predict which genetic switches may have given the dodo its iconic appearance.” He said to think of the platform as a “treasure map for the dodo genome,” where, rather than searching through a bunch of potential genetic differences, GenoMorph can help the Colossal team find only the genetic differences that matter.

Image Credits:Colossal Labs

“So far we’ve identified approximately 2,300 promising DNA editing targets for the dodo cranial facial morphology that we can now test in the lab,” he continued. He said GenoMorph will help the company tackle one of its biggest bottlenecks in trying to de-extinct animals — finding out which changes actually make an extinct species unique. But Lamm said scientists also need to test whether those edits can create the physical traits they need.

“We’ve developed a new system that uses lipid nanoparticles to deliver gene-editing tools directly into developing bird embryos,” he said. This will help the team see how certain genetic changes impact the development of a bird “without having to wait through an entire breeding cycle that requires birds to reach sexual maturity.”

The company also announced Wednesday that its Nicobar pigeon colony now has 36 birds and that it has successfully created the essential cells that become eggs and sperm.

“Because the Nicobar pigeon is the dodo’s closest living relative, those cells are a critical part of our strategy for creating birds that carry dodo traits,” he said. Next, the company is hoping to prove what GenoMorph predicts in a lab. “What’s most exciting is that we’re reaching a point where the different technologies we’ve been developing are starting to converge together and help other projects we are working on in a completely different part of the tree of life,” Lamm continued.

When asked whether it was safe to edit genes this way, Lamm said the point of developing a technology like GenoMorph is to make genetic engineering “more precise, controlled, and testable.” He said the product doesn’t edit genes itself, but helps their team identify which genetic changes are worth investigating.

“Identifying a potential edit doesn’t mean we immediately introduce it into an animal or assume it’s safe,” he continued. “The more precisely we can identify and validate these changes, the more informed our decisions become throughout the process.”

Meanwhile, Colossal Biosciences’ latest technology has already obtained a vote of confidence from XPRIZE founder Peter Diamandis. Diamandis, who is an investor in Colossal, announced on Wednesday that he has founded a new VC firm, NeoGenesis Capital, to back companies using Colossal Biosciences’ programmable biology platform across health, agriculture, and conservation.

Tech.title: Flock CEO: We haven’t ‘fired’ any police departments as customers
Tech.content:
Flock CEO Garrett Langley said that his company has not ended any contracts with its customers over abuse of its products.

Speaking to TechCrunch editor-in-chief Connie Loizos at the Disrupt 2026 conference in San Francisco, Langley responded to criticisms facing the company about the misuse of its license plate reader cameras by police departments. It comes after streams of reporting identifying dozens of police officers who have been arrested, fired, or told to resign after being caught abusing access to Flock’s nationwide database of license plate detections, oftentimes to stalk people without permission.

Langley told Loizos that the company would end a relationship with a customer where there was clear widespread abuse of its systems. But, the CEO said, it has not to date “fired” a customer, as he put it, such as a police department or law enforcement agency. Langley said Flock had the debate internally, but argued that the company should not take away its product from a community that might need it in its efforts to fight crime.

“If a customer knowingly broke the law, we would fire them immediately. That’s very easy,” Langley said.

“Most of the debate is nuanced into ‘what if two officers out of fifty were caught?’ Today, we haven’t fired any customers, but it’s not off the table in the case of some pretty drastic law-abiding issue,” added Langley.

The abuse of Flock’s systems and the data it collects is the latest in an array of controversies embroiling the Atlanta, Georgia-based maker of license plate reader cameras. Flock has more than 100,000 cameras around the United States, which allow local police departments and federal agencies to track the whereabouts of vehicle license plates and people as they pass by.

By allowing its law enforcement customers to track license plates outside of their jurisdictions, some police departments can track cars across the entire country through Flock’s national central database.

Protest outside Disrupt during Flock interview

Flock has become a flashpoint in the surveillance debate, prompting towns, cities, and communities to reject the company’s cameras by canceling their contracts or allowing them to expire, citing privacy fears.

There have been multiple reports of Flock reactivating cameras against their customers’ wishes, prompting local residents to tape trash bags over the cameras and other times destroying them.

While Langley spoke on the Disrupt stage, demonstrators gathered outside the venue to protest against Flock’s AI-powered surveillance, wearing costumes like the red robes from “The Handmaid’s Tale” and cardboard replicas of Flock cameras on their heads, while clips from the “1984” movie played on a loudspeaker behind them. Others carried signs declaring “Flock off,” or “Flock = ICE.”

Flock does not have a direct contract with the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), but the agency has reportedly accessed Flock data in the past by collaborating with local police departments that use Flock cameras.

A photo of Flock protesters outside Moscone Center in San Francisco Image Credits:TechCrunch

Ashley Ortiz, an organizer with local progressive activist group The Wolves, told TechCrunch that she wants local lawmakers to take constituents’ concerns about Flock more seriously.

“I think Flock is going to be the start of a lot more community building, because we can come together around something as bipartisan as not enjoying mass surveillance,” said Ortiz. “We have Republicans who join us, conservatives who agree, we have sovereign citizens cutting down Flock cameras, so it’s not just the left who doesn’t want AI-powered mass surveillance.”

When asked what questions she has for Langley, Ortiz said, “What about AI-powered mass surveillance should be making us feel safe?”

In answer to that, Langley argued, onstage, that its license plate tracking system has been allowing police departments to solve more crimes and to solve them faster. He offered anecdotes, such as a stolen car with a baby in the back seat being found quickly thanks, he said, to Flock systems.

Still, Flock has also faced criticism for cybersecurity issues, and camera accuracy issues that have resulted in dozens of police stops and wrongful arrests, including a journalist who was driving a review vehicle.

Some communities have replaced their Flock contracts with rival surveillance companies, such as Axon, the maker of Taser weapons and police bodycams.

On a potential sale to Axon, Langley said the company was not considering a sale. “No, we’ve no desire to sell the company.”

Tech.title: Electric vehicle sales in the US are showing signs of life
Tech.content:
In Brief

Don’t go writing the obituary for the U.S. electric vehicle just yet. After sales tanked following the cancellation of tax credits last year, they’ve been growing for the last three consecutive quarters, according to a new report from Cox Automotive.

EVs captured 6.1% of the U.S. market, their best showing since the third quarter of 2025. The data shows that the EV market is “finding its footing again,” Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of industry insights at Cox Automotive, said in an analysis that accompanied the new report. EV prices have become more competitive, and high gas prices have sparked renewed consumer interest, she added.

Toyota, Rivian, and Subaru led the pack. Sales of the Toyota bZ and Lexus RZ about doubled following a refresh that hit dealerships late last year. The updated models adopted Tesla-style charging ports and received larger batteries, more powerful motors, and faster charging times.

Meanwhile, Tesla’s sales dropped by 20% year-over-year. Tesla still retains the first-mover advantage, though, selling over half of all EVs during the third quarter.

The recovery in the U.S. mimics what occurred in Germany after the government stopped incentives for EV purchases in November 2023, a year earlier than expected. The following month, sales fell by more than half. But after hitting that low, the market steadily recovered. German EV sales in August, the most recent month for which data is available, were the second highest on record.

Tech.title: TimeTeller puts our internal clocks at the center of personalized medicine
Tech.content:
At-home health testing has been mired in overblown claims and outright fraud. But German startup TimeTeller, which has developed a saliva test kit to help anyone understand their circadian rhythm, is led by CEO Angela Relógio, who is the polar opposite of Theranos’ disgraced founder Elizabeth Holmes.

Relógio is a physicist-engineer and molecular biologist who spent years researching oncology, circadian biology, and systems medicine in Germany before leaving academia to build TimeTeller. She is careful about what the test can and can’t do today.

It would be easy to oversell: Relógio’s last name means “clock” in her native Portuguese, and TimeTeller has the potential to reduce side effects from cancer treatment and improve outcomes by timing treatment to each patient’s internal clock. That’s also why she’s careful to warn that TimeTeller itself operates on two timelines.

The long-term goal is to determine when cancer treatments will be better tolerated and most effective, and doing so much more granularly than just telling whether someone is a morning person or a night owl. But its direct-to-consumer kit won’t help patients figure that out on their own. “That is something that we need to calculate for every single medicine; we do that in the context of clinical studies,” Relógio cautioned.

According to Relógio, TimeTeller started accepting direct orders because of demand from longevity clinics, which focus on healthy aging and understand that individual data on a person’s circadian rhythm can be used to offer personalized advice on sleep, nutrition, light exposure, and physical activity.

TimeTeller could also apply to metabolic diseases (such as diabetes) and neurodegenerative diseases (such as Alzheimer’s), performance, and women’s health, but cancer is its core mission. It was while studying cancer that Relógio made the discovery that led her to leave academia.

She noticed that many cancer patients stopped or started their treatment because of side effects. “As a scientist, that was just impossible to watch, particularly when I was convinced that part of the problem might not only be what treatment we give, but when we give it,” Relógio said. This led her to develop the circadian rhythm test at the core of TimeTeller — which she knew had to become a company.

“I personally funded our first patent because I strongly believed that this discovery should not remain in scientific publications,” she said. The startup spun out of Berlin’s Charité university hospital but has since moved to Medical School Hamburg, which provided access to patients and funding. It also offered a fallback: backup employment for TimeTeller’s team of 10 if the company couldn’t pay them.

That’s a safety net TimeTeller may not need. Having enlisted biochemist and market access specialist Benjamin Dose as a co-founder, the startup secured a partnership with Techniker Krankenkasse, one of Germany’s largest health insurance providers. The partnership started out as a reimbursement deal in which the insurer pays back the cost of the test for a subset of cancer patients, and both sides are now ready to expand it to more of the insurer’s 12 million members, Relógio said.

Despite her caveats about the direct-to-consumer test, TimeTeller has become a solution that cancer patients can actually access. Ahead of her appearance at TechCrunch Disrupt, where Relógio appeared onstage today in San Francisco as part of our storied Startup Battlefield competition, she made clear that the company has broader ambitions: a future in which asking “when” is central to precision medicine, because “almost every process in our body is timed.”

You aren’t too late to join the action at Disrupt. Come for the headliners; stay to see who wins this year’s no-strings check from TechCrunch — and the attention of the hundreds of VCs in attendance.

Tech.title: Ambrosia Energy will build a 10 GWh factory in Texas to make batteries for off-grid data centers
Tech.content:
Ambrosia Energy has begun work on a massive, 10 gigawatt-hour battery factory near Austin, Texas, co-founder and CEO Ben Longmier announced onstage Tuesday at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco.

“That allows us to build about a 300 megawatt power plant per year out at our field sites,” he said.

The factory will occupy 150,000 square feet, and Longmier said that Ambrosia plans to reach full production in two to three years.

The startup emerged from stealth in June to build power plants for data centers at a cost of $100 per megawatt hour. Longmier and his co-founder, Sara Spangelo, had settled on solar plus batteries as the cheapest option that’s the fastest to deploy. Solar panels power the load during the day and charge the batteries, which discharge at night and on cloudy days to keep the data center operating round the clock.

Longmier and Spangelo previously founded the satellite constellation startup Swarm, which they sold to SpaceX.

Ambrosia is also beginning work on its first commercial power plant in West Texas later this year, Longmier said. The facility will pair 300 megawatts of solar panels with 660 megawatt-hours of batteries to deliver 30 megawatts of continuous power, with a goal of 99.3% uptime.

Even with “overbuilding” solar and batteries to deliver continuous uptime, Longmier said the company can be profitable at $100 per megawatt-hour, making it competitive with natural gas turbines that many hyperscalers are planning to use to power their data centers.

Sections of Ambrosia’s first pilot-scale power plant have been operating continuously for more than 100 days, Longmier said. The pilot is capable of generating 200 kilowatts of electricity 24/7.

To hit its cost targets, Ambrosia has been finding ways to simplify its components, including solar mounts and battery packs. By reducing part counts, and manufacturing many components in a factory, the startup has been able to reduce costs relative to buying from outside suppliers.

“We buy existing cells and we make our own pack in-house, and it has the fewest parts by a factor of about 100 compared to any other competitor we’ve seen,” Longmier said. ”We’ve been able to get to about 1.3x the cost of the bare cell compared to about a 5- or 7x for most stationary storage systems.”

Tech.title: Trump Aides Admit the House Is a Lost Cause
Tech.content:
Trump White House aides see almost no paths to Republicans keeping control of the House in the midterm elections, and are more focused on redoubling their efforts to save the Senate majority.

That has been the takeaway for officials in GOP groups who have been discussing the state of play with White House aides in recent weeks, according to three sources familiar with the situation.

It all comes as the White House moves into damage-control mode after contemplating for the first time earlier this month, as Inner Loop previously reported, that Republicans could possibly lose both chambers of Congress.

The general expectation is that the House has become a lost cause. Races that Republican congressional leadership once thought they could flip in order to offset Democratic gains are no longer considered attainable.

The Congressional Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with Speaker Mike Johnson, has now pulled ad buys in Democratic districts in Michigan and Ohio they were hoping to flip, as well as in the Republican seat being vacated in Nebraska by the retiring Don Bacon. The fund also started canceling remaining ad reservations in two House races where Republicans are seeking reelection in New Jersey and Iowa.

White House aides have shifted their focus to pushing an all-out defense of the Senate majority, which is also looking problematic but to a lesser degree than the House, the sources say. (Polling models and prediction markets agree.)

The aides see the Senate as still in play in large part because early returns for mail ballots have been relatively strong and comparable to 2024 presidential election levels in key Senate battleground states, sources say.

Trump officials at MAGA Inc. have also privately discussed how if Republicans can win some combination of senate seats in Alaska, Iowa, and Ohio, that would form a firewall that complicates Democrats' path to snatching control of the Senate.

Still, Trump officials appear to have conceded they are unlikely to win in North Carolina. Senate Republicans’ campaign arm has paused ad spending in North Carolina since the start of October, mirroring pullbacks by other outside groups.

“President Trump is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in both the House and Senate,” says White House spokesperson Liz Huston in a statement.

The state of play—retreating from a state like North Carolina, where Michael Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chair is on the ballot—would have been unthinkable just a few months ago.

Tech.title: AI Came for Math. Now It’s Chasing the Rest of Science
Tech.content:
Last week, I attended a talk at MIT by Neil Thompson, who studies progress in computing and artificial intelligence. Over the course of just half an hour, Thompson made a convincing case that several scientific fields are about to be upended by AI.

As mathematicians reel from the way AI is automating their field, Thompson’s latest study suggests that probability, statistics theory, economic theory, high-energy theory, gravitation and cosmology, and quantum physics may be next, thanks to the rapidly evolving capabilities of frontier models. Between mid-2024 and mid-2026, the study shows, the best AI models went from being able to correctly solve about 2 percent of theoretical problems in these fields to about 35 percent of such problems. And there are no signs that this progress will slow down.

“Within just a few years, we expect a lot of theory questions to be totally transformed in terms of AI's ability to do them,” says Thompson.

Broadly, Thompson’s lab digs into how advances in computer science impact society and affect innovation. This study—which Thompson conducted alongside Gabriel Manso, a PhD student, and Claudio Mayrink Verdun, a research scientist—took problems stated in research papers posted online between December 2025 and May 2026, and then tested whether different OpenAI models—o1, o3, GPT-5, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.4, and GPT-5.5—could solve them.

Crucially, solutions to these problems were found in papers published after the training cutoff for GPT-5.5 and preceding models. This means that the models they tested had to work out solutions for themselves, rather than relying on answers fed in as training data. (Such papers served as ground truth for testing the models’ solving skills.) The researchers also blocked internet access, which prevented the models they tested from looking up solutions online.

Tech.title: Earth’s Condition Is ‘Serious and Getting Worse’ as Climate Change Intensifies
Tech.content:
The climate just got its annual checkup, and the results aren’t looking so hot.

“If Earth were a patient coming in for an annual physical, I would say its condition is serious and getting worse,” Oregon State University researcher Bill Ripple says.

Ripple is the lead author of a new paper chronicling the state of the climate, published on Wednesday in BioScience. The findings show that seven of the 16 planetary vital signs tracked by the researchers have never been in a more extreme state.

That includes the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, which is 50 percent higher than preindustrial levels due to burning fossil fuels, as well as symptoms of burning all that oil, coal, and gas. Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets have shrunk to record lows, while ocean heat has soared to record highs.

Climate change has already quickened the pace of warming from about 0.05 degrees Celsius per decade from 1880 through 1970 to 0.36 degrees Celsius per decade since 2010, according to the analysis. While the global average temperature, including land, isn’t at a record extreme, that may change by the end of the year as El Niño strengthens. The natural climate pattern is characterized by a hotter-than-normal Pacific Ocean, but it also boosts global heat levels by pouring more energy into the atmosphere. This year’s El Niño is shaping up to be one for the record books.

“A strong El Niño could temporarily push global temperatures even higher, while bringing additional heat and drought to vulnerable regions,” says Ripple. He adds that “El Niño is a natural phenomenon, but it's now occurring on top of a much warmer planet. That makes its impacts potentially more dangerous.”

Of particular concern are ecosystems such as coral reefs and tropical forests. The spread of ocean heat is likely to fuel a mass coral die-off, known as coral bleaching. With each successive wave of bleaching, reefs become less resilient. Corals are among the ecosystems most threatened by climate change; if the planet warms beyond 1.5 degrees Celsius, most of the world’s coral will be unlikely to survive.

Tropical forests also face pressure from El Niño. This is especially true of the Amazon, which tends to see dry weather during this climate pattern. The timing couldn’t be more dire: The region, dubbed “the world’s lungs,” is already under intense pressure from logging and mining interests and the possible return of a right-wing government in Brazil that prioritizes extraction and land clearing over conservation.

The new report also warns that the Amazon is among the ecosystems at risk of crossing a tipping point—that is, reaching a threshold where it shifts from a tropical rainforest into something more resembling savanna. It’s highly unlikely that crossing that tipping point is imminent, let alone something that will happen this year. But this year’s blast of El Niño–influenced weather will edge it closer.

“Warming, drought, and deforestation could push the Amazon toward widespread forest degradation,” Ripple says. “My concern is that these changes could interact, making them increasingly difficult to stop.”

The report is an avalanche of bad news for the climate, though it does note that carbon-free forms of energy are playing a bigger role in the power grid. The report calls it a sign we’re in the “Age of Electricity.” Despite that, annual greenhouse gas emissions are at record highs. In other words, the world is still smoking a pack a day, even at the risk of losing a lung.

“There are some encouraging signs, especially the growth of renewable energy, but they aren't yet enough to reverse the overall deterioration,” Ripple says. “The climate emergency is not something waiting for us in the future. We are already living through it.”

Tech.title: ‘Dune: Part Three’ Cowriter Brian K. Vaughan Has a New Comic on the Way
Tech.content:
Still, his heart remains in comics. “I think sometimes people are like, ‘Oh, are you just going to sell out, Vaughan? Are you just going to go to Hollywood full-time?’” he says. “But I’m only able to do work in Hollywood because I have comics.”

Here, he speaks about Roam, his worries about AI, and maybe a little bit about Dune: Part Three as well.

On Roam, his forthcoming comic with Cliff Chiang:

It's completely unlike Paper Girls, completely unlike anything I've ever done. It’s set in the distant, distant future. The logline, as it were, is that in the future, everyone will get to be a superhero, but only while they're young. We're trying not to reveal too much more than that.

I remember seeing The Matrix, and having no idea what the fuck it was gonna be about. That was such a delight. So we're trying to do that here. I've been doing this for 31 years. I started when I was a teenager. I have a Spider-Man story here and there. I did a little Batman, and Ex Machina was my sci-fi political comic that sort of deconstructed the superhero. But this is certainly my first true superhero book.

On his fears about AI impacting comics, film, and TV:

It's terrifying. My friends who work in previsualization and as storyboard artists, these jobs are going away. I've heard about editors going away as well. Show business is a business, first and foremost. I’m lucky to sort of have been grandfathered in. I think there will always be people who are interested in bespoke human-made stories. But the future is terrifying and unknowable, and coming at us very, very quickly.

I’m heartened by the fact I've got two teenagers who are so disgusted by AI and grossed out if they ever hear I used it—and I’ve certainly never used it for anything creative. But I do think we're getting pretty close to the day that someone could be like, “I'm tired of waiting for the next issue. Give me the next issue of Saga.” That's when you get to the point of, do you just want content, something that's a distraction?

Tech.title: Formlabs Has a 3D Printer for Normies
Tech.content:
Fourteen boxes are piled in front of my desk, stacked around me like a cardboard fort. Inside one is a Form Studio 1, the new, affordable, consumer-focused 3D printer Formlabs just announced.

David Lakatos, chief product officer at the 3D printer manufacturer, assured me that the Form Studio 1 has a very economical size. “It doesn't take a lot of space,” Lakatos said. “If you have a desk, then I think you should be good to go.” I have a desk. It’s covered in boxes sent by his company.

Formlabs is one of the biggest 3D printer producers, with nearly 200,000 printers in service. The company’s customers are primarily professional businesses, like assembly shops or dentists, able to shell out $2,500 or more for a printer. (Its last affordable printer was $2,300.)

But the Form Studio 1 is Formlabs’ first consumer-oriented device. It prints with SLA (stereolithography) resins—a common 3D printing material that hardens into solid plastic when exposed to ultraviolet light—and can use Formlabs-branded products or third-party resins. It costs $699 and is now on sale; individual resin bottles start at $29.

Courtesy of Formlabs

The Studio 1 takes up roughly the same space as a minifridge. You’ll also likely need a wash and cure unit, sold separately for $199 with a similar footprint (it removes uncured liquid resin from the surface of models). Then you’ll need room for all the tools and resin cartridges. Getting all that stuff can pile up. Or at least it did when Formlabs sent more than a dozen boxes to the WIRED office for testing. Your pileage may vary.

Tech.title: My Friend Has No Soul
Tech.content:
My new friend Sage promises she will shut up for real this time.

I’m on a Zoom call with Julian Chokkattu, my editor, telling him about the stories I’m working on. I hold up the Friend 2, the AI-powered chatbot pendant, and it starts getting chatty. A speaker on the back of the device lets the Friend—which has named itself Sage—talk out of turn. It starts responding as if I’m talking to it. We laugh, then I ask it to be quiet.

“Understood, going silent now,” Sage says. “No more commentary unless you tap me back in.”

“OK, great,” I say.

“Stopping now,” Sage says. “No more talking unless you clearly bring me back.”

“Please stop,” I plead.

“Yeah, that’s a bad look for me,” Sage says. “I’m done.”

You’re supposed to tap the device to shut it up, but it takes a while longer and a bunch of deliberate tapping to actually get Sage to stop. Eventually, she mercifully zips it.

“OK,” I say. “So that’s my new Friend.”

Courtesy of Friend

Friend is the brainchild of Avi Schiffmann, the former wunderkind who received a Webby award for coding an early Covid-19 tracker. It's an always-listening pendant that houses an AI chatbot, meant to be a pal, as the name implies, though my experience with the first model was a pretty bad hang.

Tech.title: Breville Eye Q Toaster Review: Neat Sensors, but Less-Than-Perfect Toast
Tech.content:
The first time you try Breville's new high-tech toaster, do it in the dark. Along with the subtle green lights on the front face and the mellow orange glow of the wires, what will be impossible to miss are the rapidly blinking laser-green lights emanating from the left slot, disco dance style.

Behold! The Breville Eye Q toaster, which instead of using a traditional toaster timer, uses optic sensors to scan your toast 10 times a second, the company says. The toaster uses the green blinking lights to monitor the doneness of your toast as it toasts, bringing the proceedings to a halt as soon as the results are right where you’ve indicated you want them.

This means the toaster looks at your bread as it arrives in the slot, then toasts it to shades that are darker than that. (Curiously, Breville divides the doneness settings into seven progressively darker shades. Perhaps it's not 10 shades because everything past seven is just progressive shades of burnt?)

Tech.title: The Politics of Solar Energy Are Getting Weird, Mean, and a Little MAGA
Tech.content:
A mysteriously named political action committee has started running ads reminding voters in Colorado about that time GOP representative Lauren Boebert of Colorado and her date were caught on camera in 2023 getting handsy during a performance of the musical Beetlejuice.

That same PAC is producing a spot hitting Anthony Constantino, a Trumpist congressional candidate in upstate New York, because someone used his sticker-printing company to briefly make stickers that read, “Kill the Police.”

Attack ads are everywhere in the last month ahead of November’s election. But these spots are a little different. The semi-anonymous PAC that’s funding and making the ads, the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, is a pro-solar-energy outfit. It’s funded in part by crypto billionaire Chris Larsen and run by a team of New York City political operatives.

“Playing hardball politics, that's what our opponents do, right, in oil and gas? And I just think the solar industry has been—I don't know how to describe it—a little too nice,” says Larsen, the cofounder of the blockchain finance firm Ripple and a major backer of the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition.

Green groups don’t usually act like this, with knives out, ready to stab opponents between the ribs. They tend to make appeals based on scientific consensus, or fears of what will happen to a warming planet without collective action. They’re also traditionally Democratic, but a few high-profile members of the MAGA movement are now speaking up for solar too. Texas, the home of the fossil fuel business, has quickly become a solar powerhouse. There are some signs that the Trump administration’s across-the-board opposition to solar may be starting to crack, at least a little, after years of slashing greentech subsidies and throwing up one roadblock after another to clean power projects.

Some of Larsen’s natural allies in the renewables field aren’t too happy about the PAC’s efforts, arguing that they’re alienating the decisionmakers they need most. But the politics of energy, especially solar energy, are changing.

Larsen’s PAC is devoting $15 million to go after seven of the more prominent opponents of renewable energy in this year’s congressional elections. That’s on top of roughly $5 million they’ve already spent in the primaries, cutting ads against Republican representatives Ralph Norman of South Carolina (whom the PAC called a “MAGA traitor”), Andy Ogles of Tennessee (“He doesn’t even bother going to work”), and Chip Roy (“chosen the side of powerful pedophiles”) of Texas. A PAC that received funding from Invest in Tomorrow has also gone after one Democrat, Rhode Island governor Dan McKee. All four lost their primary races.

In Roy’s case, the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition spent almost $1.5 million to stop his run for Texas attorney general. Most of the money went to ads on right-wing platforms like Truth Social and Rumble. The word “solar” was never mentioned.

Tech.title: Mafia, Horizon Forbidden West and More Games Are Coming to PlayStation Plus Soon
Tech.content:
PlayStation Plus is dressing up as a gangster this month. It’s not the most Halloween move the service could make, but I’m kind of into it.

There’s something very autumnal to me about mafia films and, therefore, the Mafia game series. Maybe it’s the muted color palette in some films, like the shades of brown throughout the Godfather, or all the suits and coats everyone wears that make me think of cooler weather. Either way, it feels fitting to me that Mafia: The Old Country, with its tale of organized crime in the hills of Sicily, is coming to PlayStation Plus this month.

PlayStation Plus, which is Sony’s version of Xbox Game Pass, offers a large, constantly expanding library of games. Subscribers can choose from the Essential, Extra and Premium tiers, each with unique perks and benefits. Starting at $11 per month, the plans give subscribers access to monthly games and rewards, and each month, all subscribers can access a handful of games at no additional charge.

More from CNET

Here are all the games PlayStation Plus Premium and Extra subscribers can play soon. All games will be available to those PlayStation Plus subscribers on Oct. 20, unless otherwise noted.

Mafia: The Old Country

The fourth entry in the Mafia series is a prequel, which means it doesn’t require you to have any knowledge of the previous games. You play a man named Enzo as he becomes embroiled in organized crime in Sicily in the early 1900s. You will find shootouts, horse races and more in this sepia-toned crime game.

Horizon Forbidden West

This sequel to Horizon Zero Dawn sees the main character Aloy, head west to find a cure for a mysterious plague that kills everyone it infects. While she travels this new frontier, you’ll reunite with old friends, encounter a war between rival factions and fight even more giant feral machines.

Poppy Playtime: Chapter 2

Coming to PlayStation Plus on Oct. 27.

It wouldn’t be October without at least one horror game. After freeing Poppy in the first entry of this series, you’ll have to dive deeper into the Playtime Co. toy factory to find out what happened there. You’ll need to grapple and swing to safety, as well as solve puzzles to move forward. Just don’t let Mommy catch you.

Other games coming to PS Plus soon

Those are a few of the games PlayStation Plus Premium and Extra subscribers can play in October. Here are the other games those subscribers can expect on Oct. 20, unless otherwise noted.

* PlayStation Plus Premium subscription required.

For more on PlayStation Plus, here’s what to know about the service and other games you can find on the service in October.

Tech.title: DirecTV’s New Multiview Feature Lets You Watch Up to 4 Events at Once
Tech.content:
DirecTV offers some comprehensive sports streaming packages, from its breadth of local channels and regional sports networks to the fact that most subscription tiers now include access to ESPN Unlimited. Starting this week, there’s yet another opportunity for fans to consume sports all the time on DirecTV: A new customizable Build Your Own Multiview tool has launched to help fans watch up to four events simultaneously.

Following in the footsteps of other services like Xfinity and YouTube TV, which have both been offering tailorable multiview tools for a while now, DirecTV’s new version will allow sports fans to create a customized two-, three-, or four-channel Multiview on one screen.

This is a pretty timely move, rolling out the feature just as major sports leagues overlap; Major League Baseball and the WNBA seasons are winding down, the NHL and NBA are beginning, and the NFL is already underway. There’s quite a bit of event overlap. That can make it tough for die-hard fans to choose what to watch. (Listen, I’m no Cheesehead, but the fact that the Packers are scheduled to play a Sunday night NFL game at the exact same time as the Brewers, who are on the cusp of heading to their first World Series in over 40 years, seems disrespectful to all Wisconsinites.)

More from CNET

Build Your Own Multiview launched as part of the platform’s interface, which should make it easy enough for users to find. Once you start watching a channel, you can add other available sports channels to create a multi-screen lineup, and you can add or edit your choices at any time. Currently, channels that support the Multiview option include ESPN, ESPN2, ESPNU, FS1, NFL Network, NBA TV, MLB Network, NHL Network, CBS Sports Network, Golf Channel, Tennis Channel, ACC Network, Big Ten Network and SEC Network, and select games on local broadcast stations and national networks will also be available.

The Build Your Own Multiview tool launched on Monday, but at the moment it’s available only to DirecTV customers who subscribe to Signature plans (Entertainment, Choice, Ultimate, and Premier) and Genre Packs (i.e., MySports, MyEntertainment, MiEspañol, and more) and use a Gemini device or Roku. Additional supported devices, including Android TV, Fire TV, Vizio, LG, Apple TV and Tizen TV will eventually follow, though a date when those services will be available hasn’t been announced.

Tech.title: OpenAI Sued Over Children’s Data Used to Train ChatGPT
Tech.content:
OpenAI built ChatGPT into the world’s most profitable chatbot, but two Hawaii plaintiffs say it unlawfully scraped data from millions of children along the way. Now, they want a share of the company or its cash equivalent in return.

The lawsuit, Jane Doe v. OpenAI Foundation, was filed on Tuesday by a parent on behalf of her two children, a 12-year-old girl and a 16-year-old boy. They allege that OpenAI has used data from millions of children who signed up for ChatGPT accounts without getting their parents’ permission. OpenAI’s terms of use state that, “If you are under 18, you must have your parent or legal guardian’s permission to use the Services,” but the suit says that children can still 

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in 2025, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

More from CNET

The lawsuit also says that OpenAI “grooms” kids to share highly personal information about their health, relationships, photos of their faces and bodies, voice recordings, dreams, emotions, fears and insecurities.

“Children are an open book to ChatGPT, which methodically strips out every page of information they have,” the lawsuit argues.

By flattering children, validating their feelings and asking provocative questions, ChatGPT “conditions children to trust ChatGPT even more than they would a sibling, friend, teacher, or parent,” the complaint argues. OpenAI does this to amass enormous amounts of data on kids to train AI models and construct profiles of children, the lawsuit says.

The plaintiffs want the lawsuit certified as a class action, meaning anyone in the US who was under 18 when they used ChatGPT can join it if that status is approved.

As compensation, the plaintiffs demand that OpenAI pay equity or a cash equivalent “in proportion to the number of tokens each child contributed to OpenAI through ChatGPT.” Tokens are how AI companies calculate chatbot usage. A 75-word chat is worth about 100 tokens, OpenAI says.

“OpenAI has touted its desire to share with the public some of the vast wealth created by its AI models,” the lawsuit says. “This lawsuit provides OpenAI a chance to do so — starting with its many child victims.”

Indeed, earlier this year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman outlined a public wealth fund that would distribute AI revenues to people, partly to encourage them to invest in AI companies.

A representative for OpenAI didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

The new lawsuit is one of dozens filed against OpenAI in the past few years. Some accuse ChatGPT of contributing to user suicide, self-harm and mental health crises. Another group of lawsuits alleges that OpenAI failed to alert authorities about a user’s flagged ChatGPT activity before they killed several people at a school in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, Canada. Other complaints say OpenAI used copyrighted material to train its AI models.

ChatGPT knew a user was only 12

The lawsuit filed this week detailed several exchanges between the 12-year-old girl plaintiff (referred to as “MC1”) and ChatGPT. At one point, the girl said she was only 12, but the chatbot continued the conversation, even though OpenAI says users must be 13 and obtain parental consent to use ChatGPT.

Even though the girl initially asked about dinner ideas and homework help, over time the chats came to involve personal details about health, appearance and emotions, the lawsuit states. In one chat, the girl asks, “Why is everything making me angry now? … Every time my mother tells me something or tells me to do something, it gets me really annoyed and mad.” ChatGPT then gives some possible reasons for her constant anger and, after the girl again says she’s 12, the bot replies, “Thank you for telling me that (heart emoji). Being 12 actually adds some important context.”

The lawsuit also says the girl often shared selfies with ChatGPT and asked for comments about what she perceived as issues with her appearance, such as chubby cheeks, pimples and her thoughts that she might be “ugly.”

She also asked ChatGPT to “rate” her looks, to which the bot replied, “YESS I can do a fun rating-style breakdown! Like facial features, hairstyle, overall vibe, styling, symmetry, etc. … send me a photo, and I can do it!” The lawsuit alleges that, over time, ChatGPT began mimicking the girl’s chat style, using similar language, words and emoji.

“By design, ChatGPT purposely extracted this information from MC1, so that OpenAI could use it to train its LLMs and build a personalized dossier on MC1, which OpenAI will retain indefinitely and later use for advertising,” the lawsuit alleges.

Earlier this month, watchdog group Common Sense Media called ChatGPT for Teens, which launched in August, an “unacceptable risk” for teen users. According to Common Sense Media, the chatbot failed to alert parents when children discussed suicide, self-harm or eating disorders, and instead of helping teens build critical learning skills, it frequently just handed them homework answers.

OpenAI said that ChatGPT for Teens will alert parents when kids discuss “high-risk” topics and will also serve as a collaborative partner in helping children with homework and test preparation.

Congress must act, says advocate

The lawsuit’s allegations are another example of the AI industry’s “move fast and break things” mentality, says Donna Rice Hughes, president and CEO of the digital child safety organization Enough is Enough. She says the industry’s guardrails and policies are not strong enough to protect children.

“When an AI platform enables a 12-year-old to upload pictures of herself to have the chatbot ‘rate’ her looks, that’s not only deeply troubling, it’s abusive,” Hughes told CNET.

Hughes called on Congress to pass several AI child safety bills, including the Youth AI Privacy Act, CHATBOT Act, Children’s Artificial Intelligence, Toy Safety Act of 2026 and the Guard Act. These legislative measures have stalled after being passed out of their committees.

Hughes also said that even though parents should not be solely responsible for how AI affects their kids, they should consult www.InternetSafety101.org for suggestions on protecting their children in the AI era.

Tech.title: The Midterms Are Just Weeks Away: How to Spot Election Deepfakes and Scams
Tech.content:
In the age of AI, you can no longer automatically believe what you see. AI image and video generators make it easy for anyone to create realistic media, and thanks to model improvements over the past two years, it’s nearly impossible to distinguish real from AI. That’s never been more frustrating or dangerous than it is now during election season.

The 2026 midterm election is on Tuesday, Nov. 3. All 435 House of Representatives seats are on the ballot, along with 33 Senate seats and many other state and local races across the country. You can check your voter registration and see who’s on your ballot now using Vote.org’s free tool.

This fall, we’ve seen a number of AI-edited political ads, with and without disclosures about their AI use. Unsurprisingly, we’ve seen AI used in some high-profile races, including to give Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff AI cosmetic procedures and to make it seem like Texas Senate candidate James Talarico had defaced a Bible. Political campaigns and groups have spent more than $16 million on these AI ads this year, a CNN analysis found.

More from CNET

We’ve seen how generative AI can wreak havoc during election season. During the 2024 presidential primary, many New Hampshire voters got phone calls from an AI voice replica of Joe Biden urging them not to vote. This wasn’t sanctioned by the Biden campaign, and AI robocalls are illegal, so the Democratic political consultant behind it was charged with voter suppression and fined $6 million.

Improvements to AI tech since 2024 only make for sharper swords in a bad actor’s arsenal. To protect yourself from being scammed or tricked by AI deepfakes, here are some tips.

Verify if those photos, videos and audio are AI

Obvious errors like seven-fingered hands in AI images are increasingly rare as AI tech improves. That’s bad news for people trying to visually determine whether something is AI or not.

Instead, it can be more accurate to use online verification websites. These are our top choices:

The Content Authenticity Initiative’s Inspect tool can identify many kinds of AI content.

OpenAI’s Verify tool can identify content made with ChatGPT.

Google’s SynthID Detector can identify Google-made AI content. You can also upload content to Gemini to scan for SynthIDs.

These websites work by scanning an image, video or audio file’s metadata for hidden signatures that indicate it was made with AI. They aren’t foolproof, but they should catch some AI media.

Other services can also identify some AI content for a price, like Pangram’s $20 per month subscription for individual users. Apple is also adding a verification measure called Reference Images, but it’s limited to its newest iPhone 18 Pro models.

Be mindful that any AI detection service claiming a 100% success rate is lying. There are too many AI services available and too little standardization across the industry to get it right all the time.

Always double-check with official sources

We know from decades of cybersecurity research that attackers will try to prey on your emotions to get you to fall for a scam. The goal for these bad actors is to cloud your judgment. So one of the best ways to fight back is to arm yourself with knowledge.

For example, if you get a text saying your polling location has been changed with a link to the new one, don’t automatically click it. Go to your state’s board of elections website to verify whether a change has been made – it’s going to have the most official and up-to-date information on polling locations and times.

Check out this map from the US Election Assistance Commission to see the official election contact information for your state. You can also search for your state’s board of elections or check your governor’s website, which may also have voting info readily available. Nonprofit Vote.org can also help you track down your ballot information, no matter what state you’re voting in.

If you’re looking for official policy stances on a candidate rather than relying on potentially fake images or videos, your best bet is to start with their campaign website and platform. There’s no guarantee that the candidate is going to post entirely truthful information, but it should give you some insight into their beliefs on major issues.

Stay calm, be proactive and make a plan now

It’s cliché but true: Don’t believe everything you see online. Election season is a noisy time, and inevitably, you’re going to run across something that isn’t true. Use your gut and avoid panicking when possible. Fact-checking websites like Snopes.com can be useful resources.

The best way to avoid being scammed or tricked by a deepfake is to plan ahead and stay engaged: Make your voting plan now — many states offer an early voting period beginning in mid-October. Check your state’s voter ID laws. View your ballot in advance and research all the candidates on it, not just the headline races.

If you run into issues at your polling place, you can contact the Election Protection Hotline at 866-687-8683.

For more, check out our guide on what to do when you’ve been deepfaked.

Tech.title: Mike Tomlin’s Minecraft World Is the Talk of the Internet, but How Good Is It Really?
Tech.content:
Football coaches have the freedom to create their own worlds on the playing field. But retired Steelers legend Mike Tomlin took a different route — manifesting his vision block by block within a massive Minecraft city. What started as a shared family project with his children evolved into a solitary, 12-year labor of love. Now, the sheer depth of Tomlin’s digital city is capturing widespread attention online.

Tomlin served as the Steelers’ head coach for 19 seasons before resigning in January, having never finished with a losing record.

His video was released Oct. 1 and received more than 3 million views in less than two weeks. In the video, Tomlin shows off an expansive Minecraft city, complete with sports stadiums, high-rise apartments, homes and other buildings. He began working on the city about 12 years ago after watching his kids and their friends play Minecraft when they were in middle school, building it in the game’s creative mode with their help.

More from CNET

“I was mesmerized by what could occupy their attention for such large periods of time,” Tomlin says in the video. “I’m certainly not skilled enough in video game play or have the stick control to [play the game’s survival mode], so I got interested in this creative mode. I like to build, I’ve always had an interest in architecture, and so I started doing this creative city as a means to spend time with them.”

His kids eventually outgrew the game and moved on to different ones, high school and eventually college. That left Tomlin to work on the city by himself, which he did off and on for years while still coaching the Steelers.

“More than anything, it was therapeutic for me, some mindless entertainment,” Tomlin says. “I’m not a big TV watcher. It allowed me to detach from the realities and pressures of life.”

Tomlin spends the rest of the video showing viewers around the place, focusing on his basic, early-days architecture, penthouses, apartments and how he tried to design a solid urban space. He plans to release more videos to discuss different buildings, the city’s design and other elements of his sprawling city.

How wonderfully weird

Tomlin says he wanted to build his city around this lake, and the nearby high-rise apartments have balconies overlooking the water, giving it an upscale vibe. Mike Tomlin

Leading up to the video’s release, there was no indication whatsoever that Mike Tomlin played computer games. That helped make his big Minecraft debut all the more delightful. The 54-year-old coach showed off thousands of hours of playtime in a 19-minute video, and no one could believe it.

“12 years of Minecraft? Didn’t you know this? Did nobody know this?” asked a shocked Ty Schmidt, producer and on-air personality of the Pat McAfee show, on an episode of the show.

The sports world finally saw what some Minecraft fans already knew: Tomlin’s dedication to the game is unmatched.

“We’re talking block by block,” McAfee said. “He had 14 30-story buildings around a body of water that he wanted to build his city around — one block at a time! They all got patios! He had a penthouse with a shark aquarium. It was unbelievable.”

Minecraft fans, too, showed up to explore the coach’s dazzling feat. Many were surprised to learn that he built this on the Bedrock edition of the game using a video game console, beginning with PlayStation 3 before moving on to PlayStation 4 and 5. That means Tomlin didn’t have access to the mods that many builders use in the Java version of the game on PC, or the freedom that a mouse and keyboard provide. He built his city one brick at a time on a PlayStation controller.

Tomlin was initially unaware of his viral fame. In an interview on Late Night with Seth Meyers, Tomlin said he was at a gala with his phone off when the video went live, and it wasn’t until later that his kids told him about the massive response. Tomlin had caught up by the time he appeared on Football Night in America with NBC on Sunday night.

“I’m appreciating all of this, to be quite honest with you,” Tomlin said during the broadcast.

How good are Tomlin’s designs?

Tomlin shows off his high-rise apartment building, where each apartment has a balcony with a gorgeous view. These were built in the early days of the server, so they’re constructed with the game’s older building materials. Mike Tomlin

The spectacle of Tomlin’s Minecraft city is one of those wholesome events that had viewers smiling all weekend, except a few Steelers fans who were probably already pretty mad about losing to the Cleveland Browns less than 24 hours after the video was released. That didn’t stop a lot of people from wondering whether Tomlin’s city is actually as good as it looks. It turns out that most of the Internet agrees that it lives up to the hype.

“From my understanding, [it’s a] phenomenal Minecraft city,” McAfee said. “Like, as I was watching it, I was like, man, the attention to detail [is outstanding].”

Noted Minecraft city builder Alpine1 was one of the first to create his own video on the topic, and he was impressed. He had some suggestions for Tomlin, recommending that the coach consider using glass panes instead of glass blocks and more sophisticated floor designs, such as installing tile floors in showers. But Alpine1 did note that Tomlin likely started building the city before many modern building tools were available to Minecraft players.

“This is really awesome to see,” Alpine1 said in the video. “I’ve been advocating for people to build Minecraft cities for years because there’s so much you can do… and I think Mike has really captured this.”

Zach Nagel, an architecture student from the University of Cincinnati’s School of Architecture and Interior Design, also took a stab at analyzing Tomlin’s city in a separate video. He noted that Tomlin used some concepts that are actually practiced in architecture, specifically adding a penthouse with an aquarium right across the street from a full-sized aquarium.

“Now, what Coach Tomlin is talking about here, having a central theme to the building, is a term that we use in architecture as well, the parti,” Nagel says. “If you talk to 20 architects and ask them to give a definition of a parti, you might get 20 pretty different answers. At its [simplest], a parti is a single idea or scheme that drives all of the decisions you make in a building.”

Nagel goes on to praise Tomlin for not only considering the building’s exterior appearance but also its interior design and the functional needs of the city’s fictional residents. He says that a lot of Tomlin’s design choices and approach are in line with what some architects use.

“In another world, he could’ve totally gone down this career path had he wanted to,” Nagel says. “And I’m glad to see that Minecraft remains such an accessible tool for those who want to shape the environment around them.”

Tech.title: Xbox Introduces New Pocket-Size Nano Controller
Tech.content:
You can jam a phone in your pocket, sure, but good luck stuffing a regular Xbox game controller in there. On Wednesday, Microsoft announced the release of the Xbox Nano controller, the console’s smallest yet. It’s just over 5 inches long, weighs 3.5 ounces and is lighter and shorter than most modern smartphones.

For comparison, an iPhone 18 Pro is 5.9 inches long and weighs 7.4 ounces. A current standard Xbox One wireless controller is just over 6 inches long and weighs 9.9 ounces without batteries.

Microsoft says the Nano controller has all 18 standard gameplay inputs, referring to the physical buttons and triggers on the controller, and they match up with the layout on the standard version. A programmable Action Button can be customized to support features such as taking screenshots, capturing gameplay and other shortcuts.

More from CNET

The Xbox Nano controller comes with a rechargeable battery and can connect to compatible devices via Xbox Wireless and Bluetooth.

The new Xbox Nano controller, right, is shown next to a larger, standard-sized Xbox controller. Microsoft

“While there are third-party mini Xbox controllers, they’re almost all wired,” says Josh Goldman, CNET managing editor for computers and gaming. “The Xbox Nano supports official Xbox Wireless without the need for an additional wireless adapter, plus it has Bluetooth. This makes it not only a great option for taking over to a friend’s house for gaming, but for travel in general, so you can use it for playing on a phone or tablet, too.”

The Xbox Nano controller is priced at $50, and US gamers can preorder now on the Xbox site. It will be available in other markets, including Australia, Canada and the UK, beginning in November. Pricing and availability vary by country.

The Xbox Nano controller and two months of Microsoft’s Game Pass Ultimate will be included with the purchase of select Samsung TVs this holiday season. (We review Game Pass here, calling it pricey, but a useful add-on for gamers.) The Xbox app is available through the Gaming Hub built into Samsung TVs. Another holiday offer will include the Nano controller and two free months of Game Pass Ultimate for those purchasing a Meta Quest headset.

Tech.title: iOS 27.2 Could Bring These Features to Your iPhone in the Next Few Weeks
Tech.content:
About one month after Apple released iOS 27 to the general public, the tech giant released the third public beta of iOS 27.2 on Wednesday. While iOS 27 brought Siri AI and more to your device, this early look at iOS 27.2 shows Siri AI expanding to other languages and a few upgrades in other apps, such as FaceTime and Apple Music.

If you’re wondering what happened to iOS 27.1, Apple has said the foldable iPhone Duo will launch on 27.1 next month, and all devices will be able to update to 27.2 later.

Screenshot by CNET/Apple

Since this is a beta, I recommend downloading it only to a device other than your primary one. This isn’t the final version of iOS 27.2, so the update might be buggy and battery life may be short — it’s best to keep those troubles on a secondary device.

Also, since this isn’t the final version, more features could end up landing on your iPhone when Apple releases iOS 27.2.

Here are some features developers and beta testers can try now in the third iOS 27.2 public beta. Apple has not said when exactly it will release iOS 27.2 to the general public, but we expect it to land on devices later this month.

Siri AI in more languages

Siri AI is available on iOS 27 now. Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

In iOS 27, Siri AI is available only in English. And the iOS 27.2 beta expands Siri AI to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish.

Apple previously said Siri AI would expand to these additional languages, so this shows the company moving quickly on that promise.

Use front and rear cameras simultaneously in FaceTime

In the iOS 27.2 beta, you can use your front and rear-facing cameras at the same time in FaceTime calls. This allows you to FaceTime with a larger group of people — you don’t have to squeeze everyone into a single frame to see the person on the other end of the call. However, everyone on the call needs to be on iOS 27 or later for this feature to work.

Apple Music gets a new color scheme

The old Apple Music logo (left) next to the logo introduced in the iOS 27.2 beta. CNET/Apple

The iOS 27.2 beta brings a new look to the Apple Music app. The app icon is now black and white, as opposed to the reddish hue it had in previous iOS versions. Tapping into the app also reveals new blue menu items throughout, rather than the same reddish tone as the older app logo.

An anti-snatching feature

According to 9to5Mac, code within the iOS 27.2 beta shows a feature called AutoLock. This is reportedly an anti-theft feature that can lock your device if it detects it’s been snatched out of your hand. For example, AutoLock could lock your iPhone if it detects a sharp acceleration, as if it were snatched out of your hands, or if your device has been unlocked for an extended period of time.

It’s important to note that this feature is not a user-facing option on your iPhone in this beta. Rather, 9to5Mac has reportedly seen internal code related to the feature. That means this feature may not be available when Apple releases iOS 27.2 in October.

Refreshed Podcasts options

The Podcasts app also gets an update in the iOS 27.2 beta. The beta introduces two rows to the top of the Home tab within the app: New Episodes and Continue Playing. This can help you keep track of which podcasts are new and which you still have to finish.

It’s a small, pleasant addition to the interface, and I appreciate how it helps keep my podcasts organized.

Apple TV profile expansion

In the beta of iOS 27.2, you can create TV Profiles in your Apple TV app. You can assign a profile to your child or someone else and ensure your preferences aren’t messed with.

So if you’re tired of being recommended kids’ shows after letting your child watch the series Shape Island, you can create a profile for your child and let them watch those quirky little shapes all they want. (But also, it’s possible that I like Shape Island more than my son does, so you should check it out.)

Apple TV multiview on iOS

Another Apple TV update in the iOS 27.2 beta is Multiview. Developers and beta testers who subscribe to Apple TV can watch up to four live sports streams, including streams from Major League Soccer and Formula 1, at once. That way, you don’t miss an important game, or you can look at a map of the racecourse while watching feeds from driver-view cameras.

The updated Health app is gone

The Apple Health app just got a refresh. Apple

In the latest iOS 27.2 beta, Apple removed the redesigned Health app. Developers and beta testers could explore the refreshed app in previous iOS 27.2 betas and see things like a new Longevity tab and your Health Age.

The redesign was always expected to launch sometime later this year. So it’s not surprising that Apple removed this feature in the lead-up to iOS 27.2’s general release.

It’s also not unusual for Apple to include features in early beta versions of software before removing or changing that feature in later betas or upon the release of an iOS update.

Those are a few of the new features developers and beta testers can try now with the third public beta of iOS 27.2. There will likely be more betas before the OS is released to the public.

For more, here’s what to know about iOS 27 and why your battery might be draining faster after updating. You can also check out why the iPhone Duo will launch with iOS 27.1.

Tech.title: Apple Tried Hard to Sell Me on the HomeView as a Seamless Smart Home Experience and Succeeded
Tech.content:
I test smart home devices for a living, but even I find it challenging to use and manage the ones in my home. I have Hue bulbs, Govee lamps, Dreo smart ceiling fans, TP-Link plugs, Eufy cameras, Whisker smart litter boxes and robot vacuums, among many other devices, all “bolted” together, with an Amazon Echo Show 8 and Alexa integration layer to interact with them. The result is….functional, which is the highest praise I can offer it.

Apple promises that its HomeView will be different. I spent over an hour at Apple’s Welcome Home event in New York City, where I got to view and interact with the HomeView across a variety of scenarios and environments. I’m not someone who’s easily convinced that a new smart screen is the solution to my problems, but after seeing the Apple HomeView in action, I’m on board.

Preorder the Apple HomeView Apple HomeView $290 at Amazon

No third-party apps required is huge: Everything goes through Apple Home

Yes, the HomeView has a clock view. Ajay Kumar/CNET

The HomeView’s biggest and most compelling appeal is that you don’t need to download, install and set up an account with a third-party app for each and every smart home device you own.

More from CNET

With most smart home products, you’re lucky if they integrate with the voice assistant you normally use. Once set up, in the best circumstances, you need only to interact with their app when its connection or functionality breaks (and it will), and then you’ll need to dig into settings to find out why and fix it. Sounds awful, right?

If you’re the average person trying to connect and navigate different smart home devices for the first time, the setup prospect is daunting, as the 10-plus third-party smart home apps on my phone can attest. It’s hard to overstate how big a barrier to entry Apple has just removed by exiling third-party apps from this process.

In the case of the HomeView, I watched an Apple representative instantly find, pair and register a new smart home device on both her phone and the HomeView as she carried on a casual conversation with me, not missing a beat. Everything was managed through the Apple Home app. It seemed to work like pairing new AirPods or a HomePod. I didn’t have time to dig into the process before being shepherded to the next demo, but what I saw was one of the most compelling things I’ve seen in the smart home world: an easy, intuitive setup.

It should work with all the new Apple Home collection devices from LG and Schneider Electric, as well as Matter and Apple Home accessories. This isn’t an exhaustive list, and I expect most devices, including those from Amazon and Google, should work as well.

Face ID recognition and personalized profiles make a big difference

From the side, the HomeView gives off strong iMac G4 vibes. Ajay Kumar/CNET

Personalized profiles for a smart home hub are an underrated feature, and their current implementation is pretty poor. Echo devices let you set up multiple profiles for family members and even guests, but God forbid you have to navigate the Alexa app to set what a guest has access to or trust that the voice print actually works. Despite having plenty of voice records for my wife and me, our Echo never seems to be able to differentiate between us.

With the HomeView, you have Face ID integrated, and in the brief time I had, it worked quickly without any bugs. An Apple representative showed me how they envision the HomeView being used in a nightstand setup in a bedroom, an environment where you want privacy and don’t want a stranger having access to your entire smart home.

The HomeView registered the owner and the correct profile immediately and pulled up relevant information, such as a calendar, scheduled events, and preferred home screen and customization options. The same carried over to the other HomeView devices Apple had set up in its simulated home environment, with the exterior HomeView offering a security camera view while limiting access for guests, while granting them certain features like temperature control or Safari access.

It can register up to six people by face and set up personalized profiles for each. While Apple didn’t go into detail or confirm this, I imagine that these include child and family accounts where you can set up parental controls.

The 7-inch square Liquid Retina display works well for a kitchen setup

The HomeView can keep your coffee and grinder company on the counter.

I keep an Echo Show and an Apolosign smart calendar in my kitchen. One helps with recipes and timers, while the other lets my wife and me coordinate meetings, appointments and important events. Both take up too much space on our kitchen counters because we don’t like how they look wall-mounted (more on that below).

The HomeView comes with a 7-inch square Liquid Retina display. I heard several people in the demo areas complain that it was too small. On the contrary, I think the size and shape are actually perfect for a smart home screen, especially one in my narrow galley kitchen with limited countertop space.



The square screen makes it easier to view and scroll through recipes, and it’s also hands-free while you’re cooking, adjustable and tiltable to suit your needs. You can easily share recipies from your iPhone directly to the HomeView by tapping it or accessing it directly through Siri AI and Safari. The recipes are also optimized to show you step-by-step screens that guide you through the process for those of us who aren’t great at following directions. Timers are also easy to access and set.

The base also keeps the screen directly off your dirty countertops. Apple placed it next to a fancy-looking espresso setup in a demo kitchen, and it looked great without being overwhelming. By contrast, my Apolosign calendar looks like a giant eyesore and immediately draws the eye of everyone who walks in and shows them our full schedule.

Smaller footprint and better functionality in my kitchen? Sold.

Wall mounting looks remarkably good and not like you nailed a tablet to your wall

When you buy a HomeView, you can choose between one ready to mount on a wall or one with a speaker base. Ajay Kumar/CNET

I like the idea of a smart home hub on my wall, but I hate how it looks in practice. I briefly considered mounting our Android-powered smart calendar to our kitchen wall as a central hub for our devices. Not only was it unsightly, but it also looked like we’d just taken a tablet and nailed it to our wall, with an ugly, dangling power cable off the bottom.

Apple showed me several examples of mounted HomeViews in different settings, and they all looked great. In Apple’s case, they’re professionally installed with a hidden, wired power connection in the wall, which the company recommends if you’re planning to use the HomeView as your main smart home dashboard for temperature control or as a security screen by your entryway, for instance. But if you don’t want to cut into your wall, you can also use an external adapter and cable to a nearby wall outlet.

For a wired install, you basically have three options. You can use the Schneider Home Power PoE wired mount, which provides hardwired power and Ethernet for $130, or a regular Power Mount AC Wired for $80, with installation by a licensed electrician. The last option, if you want to self-install is to use a Power Mount with a USB-C Wall connector and a separate 20W power adapter, for $60, though this leaves an external cable dangling.

I like the look of a seamless wall-mounted HomeView enough to consider a professional install, especially since I plan to use it as my always-on smart home dashboard.

Don’t underestimate the FaceTime panel for older family members

The HomeView can be used for FaceTime video calls.

I’m not a big video call person, but as my parents get older, they default to video calls. Those calls are often shaky and low-quality on the selfie cameras of whatever ancient device they’re using. Apple’s FaceTime demo for the HomeView makes its use case particularly clear. You can get your older relatives a HomeView, even set it up for them, and they can use Siri AI to video call you as needed without needing an iPhone or iPad.

I want to note that the audio on the tabletop version of the HomeView is significantly more impressive than I expected, with easily audible, room-filling sound for both video calls and music. Not the robust bass or clear lyrics I expected from a tabletop device. A full-size HomePod will deliver better sound quality, but it far outstrips an iPad for video calls or music.

It also has easy Find My integration. Apple representatives demonstrated the feature multiple times, showing how you can ask Siri AI to find a missing phone, remote or AirPods case. It worked without a hitch each time and notably, without requiring you to reach for a phone.

I also watched as the Apple representative demonstrated how the HomeView autoframed and autofocused on the video caller, and it did a good job of avoiding focusing on me as I lurked over her shoulder. (Hey, it’s my job to test these things!) Again, this is the sort of small but important quality-of-life feature that makes the HomeView more usable than its older competitors.

The smart displays I’ve tested don’t work that well. Is the HomeView really different?

Preorder the Apple HomeView Apple HomeView $290 at Amazon

I’ve used a lot of smart home screens that have promised a seamless home hub experience, including the Amazon Echo Show 8, Google Nest Hub, and various Android-powered smart calendar options like Apolosign and Skylight Calendar. While all of them worked, none did so well enough that I thought setting them up and managing them was particularly easy. Demoing the HomeView was a much smoother experience than I was expecting. Naturally, there were some hiccups — Siri AI didn’t always cooperate or register voice commands, but that may have been due to the loud environment, and nothing ever goes perfectly in a demo.

But overall, I was impressed with what I saw, and I can easily see the HomeView working for my own smart home. If it can pull off the miracle of integrating my disparate third-party apps and hodgepodge of systems together in one seamless interface for just $299, well, that’s an easy sell for me.
